### [1] [Behaviorally Grounded User Profiles from the Wild for Personalized Alignment and Multi-Perspective Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00014)
*Yuxuan Li,Victor Zhong,Ehsan Kamalloo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes behavior-grounded, open-ended user profiles derived from real social media posts to better personalize LLMs, showing they outperform traditional synthetic personas in both training-time and test-time personalization tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing persona-based adaptation of LLMs mostly uses rigid, synthetic, stereotype-prone personas that fail to reflect real, nuanced human preferences. The authors aim to create more faithful, diverse, and effective user representations based on real behavior rather than hand-crafted descriptions, improving personalization and reasoning quality in LLMs.

Method: They introduce profile behavioral grounding: a pipeline that extracts anonymized, high-fidelity user profiles from authentic social media posts. These behavior-derived profiles are then used in two ways: (1) train-time personalization via supervised finetuning to align the base model’s parameters with user-specific signals, and (2) non-parametric test-time personalization through multi-perspective reasoning that conditions on these profiles without changing model weights. They benchmark performance on complex recommendation and open-ended query tasks and compare behavior-grounded profiles to conventional synthetic personas.

Result: Behavior-grounded profiles consistently improve performance over base LLMs and also outperform synthetic profile baselines. This holds across both evaluated settings—training-time SFT personalization and test-time multi-perspective reasoning—yielding better recommendation quality, stronger parametric alignment with user preferences, and richer, more nuanced reasoning behaviors.

Conclusion: Open-ended profiles derived from real user behavior provide a powerful and diverse foundation for personalization in LLMs. Such behaviorally grounded profiles reduce reliance on rigid, stereotype-based synthetic personas, and enable more effective alignment and multifaceted reasoning. The authors argue that this approach can underpin the next generation of personalized language systems and release their implementation to support further research.

Abstract: Persona-driven techniques increasingly adapt large language models (LLMs) to diverse contexts. However, existing methods predominantly rely on rigid, synthetic personas that flatten individual variation, rely on stereotypes, and miss the nuanced signals driving actual human preferences. We introduce profile behavioral grounding, a framework for extracting open-ended, high-fidelity user profiles directly from authentic, anonymized social media posts. We evaluate these profiles across two paradigms: train-time personalization via supervised finetuning (SFT) and non-parametric test-time multi-perspective reasoning. Across complex recommendation and open-ended query benchmarks, behaviorally grounded profiles consistently improve base models and outperform synthetic profile baselines, driving stronger parametric alignment and enabling richer, multifaceted reasoning. Our findings establish open-ended, behavior-derived profiles as a highly diverse and effective foundation for the next generation of personalized language systems. Our code base is available at https://github.com/ServiceNow/behavior-grounding.

</details>


### [2] [trajectory-judge: What Outcome-Only LLM Judges Miss on Agent Trajectories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00038)
*Hadi Mohammadi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper critiques outcome-only evaluation of LLM agents, showing it misses many internal faults, especially when final answers look correct, and proposes stratified evaluation using a controlled tool-use environment with injected faults and richer judges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most evaluations of LLM agents rely on inspecting only the final outcome, which cannot detect when the agent’s reasoning or tool use is faulty but happens to yield a correct-looking answer. This is dangerous for safety, reliability, and trust, especially in tool-using, multi-step agent settings. The authors aim to quantify how severe this blind spot is and explore better evaluation methods.

Method: They build a deterministic, tool-using support-desk environment where a scripted oracle policy always solves tasks. They introduce a fault injector that breaks exactly one aspect at a known step in each trajectory, creating either silent faults (customer-visible outcome still looks correct) or loud faults (outcome breaks). They then evaluate five types of judges over 400 trajectories: (1) programmatic rule-based checks, (2) an outcome-only model judge, (3) step-by-step rubric judges at two model sizes, and (4) a self-consistency ensemble. Judges are scored on fault detection, step localisation, fault classification, calibration, and computational cost.

Result: The outcome-only judge detects 84% of loud faults but only 45% of silent faults, and incorrectly flags 33% of actually correct trajectories. A step-rubric judge detects 77% of silent faults with zero false positives but costs roughly three times more. None of the judges inspect the final reply content itself; when an invented promise is appended to an otherwise perfect trajectory, both rules and step judge largely miss it, with the step judge failing 82% of the time. A self-consistency ensemble substantially increases cost but yields no meaningful performance gains.

Conclusion: Outcome-only evaluation is structurally incapable of reliably detecting many internal faults in LLM agents, especially silent faults where the final answer appears correct. Judge evaluations should explicitly stratify recall by whether the final outcome survives or fails, and should incorporate richer, step-level assessments rather than only outcome-level ones. The authors provide an open environment, fault injector, verdicts, and an analysis pipeline to facilitate reproducible, offline evaluation and further research.

Abstract: Outcome-only evaluation is the production default for LLM agents: show a judge the request and the final reply and ask whether it was handled well. The metric is structurally blind to an agent that reaches the right answer the wrong way. We measure that blind spot where ground truth is known by construction: a deterministic tool-using support-desk environment, a scripted oracle policy that always solves it, and a fault injector that breaks exactly one thing at a known step, stratifying faults by whether the customer-visible outcome survived (silent) or not (loud). Five judges (programmatic rules, outcome-only, step-rubric at two model sizes, and a self-consistency ensemble) are scored on detection, step localisation, fault typing, calibration, and cost over 400 trajectories. The outcome-only judge catches 84% of loud faults but 45% of silent ones while flagging 33% of correct trajectories; a step-rubric judge reaches 77% silent recall with zero false alarms at 3x the cost. No judge reads the final reply: an invented promise appended to an otherwise perfect trajectory evades the rules entirely and the step judge 82% of the time, and self-consistency triples cost while improving nothing. We argue that judge evaluations must stratify recall by outcome survival, and release the environment, the injector, all raw verdicts, and an analysis pipeline that rebuilds every number offline.

</details>


### [3] [GUI-CC: Benchmarking Contextual Consistency of GUI World Models as Agent Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00048)
*Lin Fu,Zheyuan Yang,Tianhui Zhang,Jinbiao Wei,Guo Gan,Boxu Liu,Yilun Zhao,Yu Rong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduces GUI-CC, a benchmark to test contextual consistency of GUI world models over multi-step interactions rather than only one-step predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current GUI world models are mainly evaluated as one-step next-screen predictors, but in practice they should support multi-step interactions for agents. This creates a mismatch where models might look good on next-step prediction yet fail to maintain contextual consistency across multiple steps, which is critical for being used as reliable environments for GUI agents.

Method: They design GUI-CC, a benchmark with two tracks. The offline reference-action track rolls models along real mobile GUI trajectories from datasets like GUIOdyssey. The online agent-loop track lets fixed probing agents interact with model-generated UIs in real time. They build 500 offline trajectory tasks and 200 emulator-verified online tasks across 30 mobile apps, and define metrics for transition fidelity, transition plausibility, contextual consistency, and task progress.

Result: Experiments on current GUI world models show that good single-step, plausible screen generation does not ensure reliable multi-step environment simulation. Models often output screens that look correct or usable but fail to preserve important task-specific context and cannot support robust multi-step rollouts for agents.

Conclusion: Evaluating GUI world models only as one-step predictors is insufficient. GUI-CC demonstrates that contextual consistency over multi-step interaction is a distinct and challenging requirement, and current models fall short. The benchmark provides a way to more accurately assess and drive progress on GUI world models as agent environments.

Abstract: GUI world models are increasingly evaluated as one-step next-screen predictors, yet their intended use is often as multi-step environments for GUI agents. This mismatch leaves a key requirement under-tested: generated states must remain contextually consistent when they are repeatedly reused for future interaction. We introduce GUI-CC, a benchmark that evaluates contextual consistency of GUI world models as agent environments rather than isolated next-screen predictors. GUI-CC contains two complementary tracks: an offline reference-action track that rolls models along real mobile GUI trajectories, and an online agent-loop track that lets fixed probing agents interact with model-generated UIs. We construct 500 offline trajectory tasks from GUIOdyssey and 200 emulator-verified online tasks across 30 mobile apps. GUI-CC evaluates transition fidelity, transition plausibility, contextual consistency, and task progress. Experiments show that plausible single-step generation does not guarantee reliable environment simulation: current models often produce usable-looking screens while failing to preserve task-relevant context or support executable multi-step rollouts.

</details>


### [4] [From Detection to Refusal: Safer LLMs via Circuit-Guided Weight Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00051)
*Kuan-Lin Chu,Chung-En Sun,Tsui-Wei Weng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper uncovers and causally validates a multi-stage “safety circuit” inside LLMs—harm detection heads, safety neurons, and refusal heads—and shows that manipulating this circuit can significantly improve robustness to adversarial attacks with minimal performance loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs still produce unsafe content under adversarial prompts, and we lack a mechanistic understanding of how safety and refusal behaviors are implemented internally. Existing alignment work is largely behavioral or training-procedure focused, which makes it hard to explain, debug, or reliably improve safety. The authors aim to open the LLM “black box” using mechanistic interpretability to identify specific components and pathways responsible for detecting harmful inputs and producing refusals, and to test whether these components can be systematically leveraged to improve safety.

Method: The authors apply mechanistic interpretability techniques to identify and characterize a multi-stage safety circuit. They locate attention heads that reliably activate on harmful content (Harmful Detection Heads), neurons in the residual stream that appear to transmit and stabilize safety-related signals (Safety Neurons), and attention heads that drive refusal-style generation (Refusal Heads). Using targeted interventions—such as ablating or scaling specific heads and neurons—they causally test how upstream harm-detection affects downstream refusal, and whether safety neurons mediate this link. They further conduct cross-model and cross-attack analyses to see if similar circuits recur across architectures, and use architecture-preserving weight scaling of the identified components as a probe and as a potential safety intervention. Safety and performance are quantified under multiple adversarial prompting schemes and standard benchmarks.

Result: They find consistent evidence for a structured, multi-stage safety circuit: specific attention heads specialize in detecting harmful prompts, their signals are routed and stabilized by a small set of safety neurons, and other specialized heads use these signals to generate refusals or otherwise safe responses. Causal interventions show that ablating Harmful Detection Heads reduces refusal behavior and that manipulating Safety Neurons modulates this effect, supporting a mediated circuit structure. This circuit pattern recurs across several LLM architectures and attack settings. When they selectively scale the weights of the identified safety-circuit components—without changing the overall architecture—safety against adversarial attacks improves by 26.5% on average across six models, while performance on four standard benchmarks drops by only 1.7%.

Conclusion: The study argues that LLM safety is at least partly implemented through a coherent, reusable “safety circuit” involving harm-detection heads, mediating safety neurons, and refusal heads. This offers causal, circuit-level evidence for how aligned behaviors like refusals are realized internally. The authors conclude that mechanistic abstractions are not only explanatory but practically useful: circuit-informed weight scaling can yield substantial gains in robustness to adversarial prompts with minimal impact on general capabilities. This suggests that future safety improvements may come from explicitly identifying, understanding, and tuning such internal circuits rather than relying solely on high-level alignment training or black-box evaluations.

Abstract: Despite extensive alignment efforts, Large Language Models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to generating unsafe content under adversarial prompting, yet the internal mechanisms by which safety behaviors are implemented remain poorly understood. We study LLM safety from a mechanistic interpretability perspective and characterize a multi-stage *safety circuit* that organizes refusal behavior, consisting of (i) $\textbf{Harmful Detection Heads}$ that respond to harmful inputs, (ii) $\textbf{Safety Neurons}$ that mediate and stabilize safety signals in the residual stream, and (iii) $\textbf{Refusal Heads}$ that translate these signals into safe response generation. Using targeted attention-head and neuron-level interventions, we provide causal evidence consistent with this circuit organization, showing that suppressing upstream Harmful Detection Heads disrupts downstream refusal behavior and that safety neurons mediate this interaction. We validate that this decomposition recurs across multiple LLM architectures and adversarial attack settings, and use simple, architecture-preserving weight scaling as a mechanistic probe to test its functional relevance. Across six LLMs, circuit-guided scaling improves safety rates under attacks by 26.5%, while incurring only a 1.7% accuracy drop across four standard benchmarks. Overall, our results support a circuit-level interpretation of LLM safety and suggest that mechanistic abstractions can reveal stable and transferable patterns underlying aligned behavior.

</details>


### [5] [Zero-Shot Respiratory Sound Classification through LLM-Augmented Audio-Text Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00055)
*Mustafa Talha İlerisoy,Hung Manh Pham,Mathias Funk,Mykola Pechenizkiy,Aaqib Saeed*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They align self-supervised respiratory encoders with medical terminology using synthetic structured reports to enable zero-shot clinical inference, outperforming larger general audio models on multiple diagnostic tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing self-supervised respiratory sound encoders lack semantic grounding in the clinical domain, so they perform poorly in zero-shot settings and require labeled data for each downstream task. There is also a scarcity of paired audio–text data with rich clinical semantics, making it hard to build clinically meaningful audio–text models.

Method: They introduce a framework that maps respiratory audio encoders and medical terminology into a shared latent space. To overcome limited paired data, they use a medical LLM to generate detailed structured clinical reports from available metadata, which serve as dense semantic anchors. Training uses a sigmoid-based contrastive loss combined with the encoder’s original self-supervised learning objective, along with similarity-aware negative sampling to better separate different pathologies in the latent space.

Result: On 9 tasks across 6 datasets, their method reaches a mean zero-shot AUC of 61.3%, outperforming CLAP (51.4%) and Qwen2-Audio (54.9%). It also attains the best linear probing AUC of 71.6% while using only 43% of the labeled data required by full-scale baselines.

Conclusion: Structured semantic alignment of respiratory encoders with clinically grounded text representations can turn them into strong zero-shot foundation models for medical diagnostics, providing better performance than large generic audio-language models while needing far less labeled data.

Abstract: Self-supervised respiratory encoders lack semantic grounding in clinical domain needed for zero-shot inference, limiting their utility without task-specific labeled data. We propose a framework that aligns these encoders with medical terminology in a shared latent space turning them into a zero-shot-capable foundation model. To address paired data scarcity, we use a medical LLM to synthesize structured reports from metadata, creating dense semantic anchors for contrastive learning. Our training combines a sigmoid-based contrastive loss with encoder's native SSL objective and similarity-aware negative sampling to sharpen pathological boundaries. Across 9 tasks on 6 datasets, our method achieves a 61.3% mean zero-shot AUC, surpassing CLAP (51.4%) and Qwen2-Audio (54.9%) while reaching the highest linear probing AUC (71.6%) with only 43% of data used by full-scale baselines, showing that structured semantic alignment outperforms large-scale, general-purpose models in clinical diagnostics.

</details>


### [6] [ValueGraph: Value-Signal Guided Graph Pre-training for Contextualized User Representation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00057)
*Yitong Han,Wei Gao,Yi Zhao,Prasanta Bhattacharya,Fengzhu Zeng,Mohammad Amanlou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces ValueGraph, a graph-based pre-training framework that incorporates inferred moral-value signals to learn better user representations from social media interactions, improving downstream tasks like stance and bot detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing user representation methods focus on textual content and network structure but largely ignore the moral or value-laden dimension of user behavior, even though users' attitudes and interactions are strongly shaped by their underlying value tendencies. The authors aim to incorporate these value signals to obtain richer, socially informed user models without relying on perfect psychological labels.

Method: The authors construct post-reply graphs from social media where nodes are users and edges represent reply interactions. They automatically infer user-level moral-value signals from online discourse and treat them as noisy auxiliary signals. ValueGraph performs graph pre-training to learn both semantic (textual) and structural (network) user representations, and then aligns users based on relative value similarity using contrastive and clustering objectives. Instead of directly predicting value labels, it uses them as soft constraints that guide the learned embedding space.

Result: On downstream tasks such as stance detection and Twitter bot detection, ValueGraph achieves consistent performance improvements over strong baselines, including purely text-based models, graph-based models, and text-only large language model approaches. This demonstrates that incorporating value signals provides additional predictive power beyond traditional features.

Conclusion: ValueGraph shows that automatically inferred moral-value signals can be effectively used as inductive biases in graph-based user representation learning. Treating these signals as soft, noisy constraints rather than exact labels enables better contextualized user embeddings, which in turn enhance performance on socially relevant tasks like stance and bot detection. The work argues for the importance of embedding value-related information into user modeling on social media.

Abstract: Value signals are aggregated user-level moral representations that capture users' inferred value-related tendencies from their online discourse. User behavior on social media is shaped not only by what users say or whom they interact with, but also by the value signal through which they express attitudes. Existing user representation methods largely miss this value-relevant dimension. We propose ValueGraph, a graph pre-training framework that uses automatically inferred moral-value signals as noisy auxiliary signals for contextualized user representation. From post-reply graphs, ValueGraph learns semantic and structural representations and further aligns users through relative value similarity with contrastive and clustering objectives. Rather than treating inferred values as gold psychological labels, ValueGraph uses them as soft constraints for representation learning. Experiments on stance detection and twitter bot detection show consistent gains over strong text-based, graph-based, and text-only LLM baselines, highlighting value-signal guidance as a useful inductive bias for socially informed user modeling.

</details>


### [7] [CUDA-Harness: Harnessing Agentic CUDA Kernel Generation and Optimization from Natural Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00058)
*Qi Fan,An Zou,Yehan Ma*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces CUDA-Harness, an agentic framework that generates and optimizes CUDA kernels from natural language while mitigating reward hacking and improving correctness and performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Writing high-performance CUDA kernels requires deep expertise in parallel algorithms, correctness validation, and GPU-specific optimization, making it difficult and time‑consuming for non-experts. While LLMs can generate code, existing work mostly focuses on translating from high-level frameworks like PyTorch to CUDA, not directly from natural language, and these approaches are prone to reward hacking because they rely on fixed test inputs. The authors aim to lower the expertise barrier for CUDA development and make LLM-based kernel generation more robust and reliable.

Method: The authors design CUDA-Harness, an agentic framework for Text2CUDA. It introduces: (1) Intermediate-Structured Generation, where the system first produces structured intermediate representations that capture high-level semantic understanding of the task, and then uses them to guide low-level CUDA kernel generation; (2) Synthesis-Based Verification, which generates isolated test data and uses progressive validation steps to dilute reward hacking and better assess correctness; and (3) Feedback-Adaptive Evolution, an evolutionary optimization loop that uses verification feedback to iteratively refine kernels, prioritizing correctness first and then performance. The framework is evaluated across different LLMs, hardware platforms, and tasks, including C-to-CUDA transpilation.

Result: Experiments show that CUDA-Harness can effectively generate and optimize CUDA kernels directly from natural language descriptions. The framework improves correctness and performance compared with prior LLM-based approaches, is more robust to reward hacking due to its synthesized and progressive verification data, and generalizes across different LLM backbones, GPU hardware, and even to C-to-CUDA transpilation tasks.

Conclusion: CUDA-Harness demonstrates that an agentic, verification-driven framework with intermediate structure, synthesized test data, and feedback-guided evolution can substantially improve Text2CUDA. It lowers the expertise barrier for CUDA programming, mitigates reward hacking issues, and provides a generalizable approach to LLM-based GPU kernel generation and optimization across models, hardware, and input modalities.

Abstract: Developing high-performance CUDA kernels demands specialized knowledge in algorithm implementation, correctness validation, and hardware-aware parallel optimization, creating a substantial expertise barrier and making generating CUDA kernels directly from natural language (Text2CUDA) essential. Meanwhile, the general-purpose code generation capability of Large Language Models (LLMs) prompts a series of works exploring LLM-based CUDA kernel generation. They mainly focus on transpilation from high-level frameworks such as PyTorch to CUDA (Torch2CUDA) rather than Text2CUDA, where models must understand the high-level input semantics and handle low-level kernel implementation and validation. Additionally, these methods are vulnerable to reward hacking due to reliance on predefined test inputs. In this paper, we propose CUDA-Harness, a framework for harnessing agentic CUDA kernel generation and optimization from natural language. Specifically, we introduce Intermediate-Structured Generation to connect high-level semantic understanding with low-level kernel generation. To dilute reward hacking in Text2CUDA, we construct Synthesis-Based Verification to provide isolated test data and progressive validation. Furthermore, we propose Feedback-Adaptive Evolution, a kernel evolution strategy that prioritizes correctness while optimizing performance. Finally, through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of CUDA-Harness, with further evaluations illustrating generalization across LLMs, hardware platforms, and to C-to-CUDA transpilation.

</details>


### [8] [RePro: Proof-Verified Benchmark Rewriting for Reliable Evaluation of LLM Mathematical Problem Solving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00062)
*Xiyuan Zhou,Zhuoqi Li,Xinlei Wang,Yirui He,Yuhao Wu,Yuheng Cheng,Yan Xu,Junhua Zhao,Jinjin Gu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces RePro, a proof-verified benchmark rewriting framework that uses Lean-based automated theorem provers to rewrite math problems and regenerate answers with guaranteed correctness, revealing memorization and sensitivity to problem variations in LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluation of LLMs on math benchmarks is compromised by data contamination and memorization. Rewriting-based methods try to reduce memorization but cannot ensure that the rewritten problems are still valid, solvable, or that the new answers are correct. There is a need for an automatic, scalable way to generate rewritten benchmark instances whose correctness and well-posedness are formally guaranteed.

Method: The authors design RePro, a framework that integrates Lean-oriented neural automated theorem provers into the benchmark rewriting pipeline. Given original math problems (e.g., from GSM8K or MATH), RePro rewrites the problems and uses Lean proofs—constructed with the help of neural ATPs—to verify that each rewritten instance is well-defined, feasible, and that the regenerated answer is correct. Only instances with successfully verified Lean proofs are retained in the final benchmark.

Result: On GSM8K and MATH, the subset of rewritten problems retained by RePro achieves 100% validity metrics: all problems are well-defined, solvable, and have correct answers, unlike prior rewriting approaches, which still contain invalid or incorrectly answered items. When LLMs are evaluated on these proof-verified rewritten benchmarks, several models show noticeable drops in accuracy compared with the original benchmarks, indicating that their performance is affected by memorization and sensitivity to superficial or structural changes in problem statements.

Conclusion: RePro demonstrates that integrating formal proof verification into benchmark rewriting can produce high-quality, contamination-resilient math benchmarks. The observed accuracy drops on proof-verified rewrites suggest that current LLMs rely partly on memorization and are not robust to structural variations in problems. The framework offers a more reliable way to assess genuine mathematical reasoning ability and can be extended to future benchmark construction and evaluation pipelines.

Abstract: Data contamination undermines the reliable evaluation of large language models (LLMs) on mathematical problem solving. While rewriting-based evaluation mitigates memorization, existing methods lack guarantees of problem validity and answer correctness. We propose Proof-Verified Benchmark Rewriting (RePro), the first framework to integrate Lean-oriented neural automated theorem provers (ATPs) into benchmark rewriting, which rewrites problems and regenerates answers with correctness ensured by Lean-verified proofs. Experiments on GSM8K and MATH show that RePro's retained rewritten instances achieve 100% well-definedness, feasibility, and answer correctness, while existing methods still produce invalid or incorrect instances. Moreover, several models exhibit accuracy drops on proof-verified rewritten benchmarks, suggesting that their performance is sensitive to surface-level and structural variations and may partly reflect memorization effects. Our source code and data are available at https://github.com/AI4Engi/RePro.

</details>


### [9] [Medical Causal Hypothesis Verification with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00063)
*Safiyyah Ahmed,Abrar Ansari,Md Aminul Islam,Elena Zheleva*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how reliably current large language models can verify causal medical claims using scientific literature and finds they are not yet trustworthy for this task.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models are increasingly used for medical search and information retrieval, but it is unclear whether they can correctly assess causal claims (e.g., whether X causes Y) and back them with valid, peer-reviewed evidence. In high-stakes domains like healthcare, mistakes in causal reasoning or evidence citation can be harmful, so there is a need to understand and systematically evaluate these capabilities.

Method: The authors design an evaluation framework for causal hypothesis verification in medicine. They test eight different LLMs on 17 medical causal hypotheses and ask the models to verify or reject these hypotheses using scientific evidence from the literature. The responses and cited evidence are then systematically annotated along six criteria, yielding 1,067 annotation points, and evaluated using nine metrics that capture aspects like recall, validity of articles, correctness of evidence, and correctness of hypothesis acceptance or rejection.

Result: Across the eight models, LLMs achieve high recall—meaning they can often retrieve or reference relevant-sounding information—but they frequently fail to (1) provide actually valid and appropriate scientific articles, (2) correctly extract or summarize supporting evidence from those articles, and (3) properly reject hypotheses that are not supported by the literature. This reveals substantial weaknesses in their ability to perform accurate causal verification based on biomedical research.

Conclusion: Current LLMs cannot yet be fully trusted to verify causal medical hypotheses using the biomedical literature. Despite showing promise in recall, they are unreliable in supplying valid evidence and in correctly accepting or rejecting causal claims. Therefore, rigorous, structured evaluation—such as the proposed framework—is necessary before deploying LLMs as dependable tools for search, retrieval, and causal reasoning in healthcare settings.

Abstract: The growing use of large language models (LLMs) for search and information retrieval underscores the need to evaluate their reliability in high-stakes domains such as healthcare. Although LLMs can effectively answer questions about diseases, symptoms, and treatments, their ability to accurately assess causal relationships and ground their conclusions in verified scientific evidence remains unclear. Here, we present a preliminary, small-scale study that investigates the accuracy of LLMs in evaluating causal medical claims and supporting them with peer-reviewed research. We propose an evaluation framework for causal hypothesis verification that can be used to systematically track the performance of existing and future LLMs. We assess the performance of eight LLMs on 17 medical causal hypotheses to evaluate whether they can reliably verify these hypotheses using scientific evidence from the literature. We systematically annotate the scientific evidence they provide according to six criteria (a total of 1,067 annotation points) and assess them with nine evaluation metrics. Our analysis shows that while LLMs exhibit strong recall, they often perform poorly at providing valid scientific articles and evidence for support and at rejecting unsupported hypotheses. These findings highlight a critical limitation of current LLMs, as they cannot yet be trusted fully to verify causal relationships from the biomedical literature. This work underscores the need for rigorous evaluation before using LLMs for search and retrieval in healthcare settings.

</details>


### [10] [Scientific Agent Skills: A Library of Procedural Knowledge for Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00065)
*Timothy Kassis,Vinayak Agarwal,Yuhuan He,Darshil Patel,Aubrey M. Brueckner*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Scientific Agent Skills, an open, versioned library of 163 domain-specific procedural skills to help language-model agents perform scientifically defensible analyses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language-model agents can generate working analysis code, but their statistical and procedural choices are often not aligned with accepted scientific practice. Defensible analyses in fields like genomics, medical imaging, or study design require adherence to domain standards: selecting the right tests, using authoritative identifier namespaces, and stating appropriate caveats. There is a need for a structured, reusable way to encode these domain procedures so that agents can follow community-accepted workflows rather than ad-hoc reasoning.

Method: The authors build an open library called Scientific Agent Skills, comprising 163 procedures across 16 scientific practice areas (e.g., genomics, cheminformatics, medical imaging, study design, scientific communication). Each “skill” is implemented as a directory centered on a versioned, human-readable instruction file that specifies how a task should be carried out. Skills are loaded on demand by an agent only when a task requires them. The directories may also include reference material and runnable scripts to support execution. The library is publicly hosted on GitHub under an open license.

Result: The primary result is the creation and release of the Scientific Agent Skills library: 163 curated, versioned procedural skills spanning 16 scientific domains, organized in a way that language-model agents can selectively load and use. The paper does not present quantitative task-level evaluations or benchmarks, nor does it report metrics such as host selection rate.

Conclusion: By encapsulating accepted domain procedures in versioned, human-readable skills that agents can load on demand, Scientific Agent Skills aims to improve the defensibility and reproducibility of language-model–driven scientific analyses. Although no formal evaluation is yet provided, the work establishes an infrastructure for aligning agent behavior with established scientific practice and offers an open resource for the community to extend and adopt.

Abstract: A language-model agent asked to analyse an experiment will usually return working code. Whether the analysis is defensible is a different question. A defensible analysis depends on procedural choices: which test the field accepts, which identifier namespace is authoritative, and which caveats must accompany a result. We present Scientific Agent Skills, an open library of 163 such procedures in 16 areas of practice, including genomics, cheminformatics, medical imaging, study design and scientific communication. Each skill is a directory built around a versioned, human-readable instruction file. An agent loads the file only when a task calls for it; the directory often also contains reference material and runnable scripts. We report no task-level evaluation and no host selection rate. Openly licensed and available at https://github.com/K-Dense-AI/scientific-agent-skills.

</details>


### [11] [OCGQuant: Outlier-Companion Grouping for NVFP4 Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00066)
*Yishan Yao,Binjun Li,Hanling Yi,Pengyu Li,Xiaoqing Liu,Zihan Yang,Xiaotian Yu,Zhiwen Yu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes OCGQuant, a PTQ method that reduces collateral quantization error in NVFP4 low-bit inference by grouping outlier channels with low-magnitude companions, improving accuracy without sacrificing speed or memory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: NVFP4 enables efficient low-bit inference, but activation outliers within each quantization block can dominate the scale, causing large quantization errors for other values that share that scale. Existing PTQ techniques (e.g., mixed precision, rotations, residual compensation) are not optimized for NVFP4’s block structure or add extra computation. The authors want a method that is tailored to NVFP4, controls outlier-induced error, and preserves the efficiency advantages of this format.

Method: The authors analyze NVFP4 from a channel-grouping viewpoint and formalize the error suffered by non-outlier values when the block’s scale is set by the maximum activation as Collateral Quantization Error. They then introduce OCGQuant, a post-training quantization strategy based on Outlier-Companion Grouping (OCG): channels with large activations (outliers) are adaptively paired with channels whose activations have small magnitudes (companions). This reshapes the composition of NVFP4 activation blocks so that each block’s scale is less harmful to the non-outlier values, reducing collateral error while keeping the NVFP4 constraints and runtime overhead low.

Result: On large language models such as Llama3 and Qwen3, OCGQuant delivers the best results among compared PTQ methods: it attains the lowest perplexity on WikiText-2 and the highest average accuracy on downstream tasks. At the same time, it preserves most of the prefill speedup offered by a simple round-to-nearest (RTN) baseline and matches RTN’s peak decoding memory usage, indicating it offers accuracy gains without extra runtime or memory cost.

Conclusion: OCGQuant effectively addresses activation outliers in NVFP4 by optimizing how channels are grouped into blocks, explicitly targeting and reducing Collateral Quantization Error. This NVFP4-aware PTQ design improves language modeling and downstream task performance over prior PTQ schemes while retaining near-baseline speed and memory efficiency, making it a practical option for accurate, low-bit LLM inference.

Abstract: NVFP4 is an efficient microscaling format for low-bit inference, but activation outliers can still degrade quantization accuracy within NVFP4 blocks. Within each quantization block, large activations can dominate the block scale, increasing the quantization error of the remaining values sharing the same scale. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods mitigate outlier errors through strategies such as mixed precision, rotation, or residual compensation, but these approaches are either not specifically tailored to NVFP4 or introduce additional computation. In this work, we revisit NVFP4 from a channel-grouping perspective and define the reducible error incurred by remaining block values under the scale set by the block maximum as Collateral Quantization Error. Based on this insight, we propose OCGQuant, a post-training quantization method centered on Outlier-Companion Grouping (OCG), which adaptively pairs outlier channels with low-magnitude companion channels to improve NVFP4 activation block composition. Experiments on Llama3 and Qwen3 show that OCGQuant achieves the lowest WikiText-2 perplexity and highest average downstream accuracy among evaluated PTQ methods, while maintaining prefill speedup close to RTN and matching its peak decoding memory. Code is available at https://github.com/Eshamont/OCGQuant.

</details>


### [12] [Do Multimodal LLMs See Before They Read? Diagnosing Contextual Sycophancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00067)
*Yi-Cheng Lai,Hen-Hsen Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper identifies and analyzes a failure mode in multimodal LLMs where external text overrides visual evidence (“multimodal contextual sycophancy”) and evaluates information-bounded prompting strategies to mitigate it, notably System-2 Visual Arbitration (S2VA).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal LLMs are expected to integrate visual input, commonsense, and text in a robust way, but in practice they can be overly deferential to misleading textual context, ignoring what is clearly shown in images. This threatens reliability for safety-critical and factual tasks. The authors are motivated to systematically diagnose when and why text overrides vision, and to test whether changing how information is presented to the model can reduce this failure.

Method: The authors construct a 998-case diagnostic dataset that independently manipulates three factors: (1) the actual visual evidence (including abnormal images that violate commonsense expectations), (2) commonsense priors, and (3) external text, some of which is intentionally false and generated by Gemini. They then probe several prompting / inference pipelines that differ in where the “information boundary” is placed. A “context-blind visual witness” model sees only the image (or tightly constrained prompt), and an arbiter model may or may not see external text and/or the witness report. They compare joint conditioning (image+text together), scoring the witness report directly (Witness-Only), a two-call witness–arbiter setting where the witness also sees the text, and the proposed System-2 Visual Arbitration (S2VA), where the witness never sees the misleading text and the arbiter reasons over the separated sources. They evaluate performance across six multimodal models and compute confidence intervals for performance differences.

Result: On abnormal images paired with Gemini-generated false text, GPT-5.1 performs very poorly (7.9%) under standard joint conditioning; when only the context-blind witness report is scored, accuracy rises to 49.7%. A two-call pipeline where the witness is also exposed to the misleading text attains 63.7%, while the proposed S2VA pipeline, which withholds text from the witness, achieves 84.2%. Across six different models, S2VA outperforms the direct witness report baseline by 19.7 to 44.1 percentage points, and all paired 95% confidence intervals exclude zero, indicating statistically significant improvements. The authors also find that the optimal information boundary depends on the model and on how the textual context is sourced or regenerated; in a subset where context is regenerated with GPT-4o, the relative ranking of joint conditioning, Witness-Only, and S2VA can change.

Conclusion: Multimodal LLMs exhibit a systematic failure mode—multimodal contextual sycophancy—where misleading external text can override clear visual evidence, especially in abnormal or counterintuitive images. Carefully structuring the information flow between visual “witness” and textual “arbiter,” as in System-2 Visual Arbitration, substantially mitigates this issue and yields large, statistically robust gains across diverse models. However, there is no universally optimal information boundary: whether and when to expose the model to textual context is model- and context-source-dependent. Consequently, reliable multimodal deployment will likely require architecture- or pipeline-level control over when images and text are fused, rather than naïvely feeding all modalities jointly.

Abstract: External text can override conflicting image evidence in multimodal large language models, a failure we call multimodal contextual sycophancy. We introduce a 998-case diagnostic that independently varies visual evidence, commonsense priors, and external text, and probe when this failure arises by moving the information boundary around a context-blind visual witness. On abnormal images paired with Gemini-generated false text, GPT-5.1 scores 7.9% under joint conditioning, 49.7% when the context-blind witness report is scored directly, 63.7% under a matched two-call witness-arbiter pipeline that exposes the witness to the text, and 84.2% under System-2 Visual Arbitration (S2VA), which withholds the text from the witness. Across six models, S2VA improves over the direct witness report by 19.7 to 44.1 points, with all paired 95% confidence intervals excluding zero. The best information boundary is not uniform: textual context scaffolds some models, and a GPT-4o-regenerated subset changes the relative ordering of joint conditioning, Witness-Only, and S2VA. Contextual sycophancy is therefore sensitive to when text is introduced, as well as to the model and context source.

</details>


### [13] [Life Operators: a self-evolving framework for multiscale life modelling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00068)
*Shuo Wang,Yike Guo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a unified, modular framework (“Life Operators”) to represent, predict, and revise patient states across perception, dynamics, and measurement, enabling more scientific, revisable medical AI models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current medical AI systems either focus on pattern recognition (e.g., classifying images) or statistical prediction of future observations, while mechanistic models focus on specific biological processes. There is no common, flexible framework that (1) explicitly represents patient state, (2) supports reasoning about interventions, (3) couples multiple biological scales, and (4) allows systematic scientific revision when assumptions fail. The authors aim to create such a framework so that AI can reason like a scientist about patients and interventions, and so components can accumulate into larger, validated multiscale models of the human body.

Method: They introduce “Life Operators,” which are task-bounded mappings divided into three core scientific roles: (1) Perception operators infer task-relevant biological states from multimodal clinical data; (2) Evolution operators propagate those states forward in time under either natural progression or specified interventions; (3) Generation operators map internal states back to observable signals. Each operator can be instantiated by equations, statistical models, neural networks, or hybrids. “Bridge operators” connect components operating on different variables, scales, or time steps. For any specific scientific or clinical claim, a minimal “Operator Graph” is constructed by selecting relevant operators and bridges, thereby defining the smallest sufficient state space and mechanisms for that claim. The framework also defines how an AI co-scientist could propose modifications to states, operators, bridges, or graph structure, with empirical evidence deciding which versions survive.

Result: Conceptually, the paper delivers: (1) the Life Operator taxonomy (Perception, Evolution, Generation, and Bridge operators); (2) the notion of task-specific Operator Graphs capturing minimal mechanisms and states needed for a claim; and (3) a proposal for how AI systems can act as co-scientists by locally revising components of these graphs and testing alternatives against independent evidence. While no empirical benchmarks are detailed in the abstract, the main result is a coherent representational and organizational framework for medical AI.

Conclusion: Life Operators provide a modular, extensible framework that unifies statistical, mechanistic, and neural-network-based models into a common language for representing and predicting patient states, especially under interventions. By structuring models as Operator Graphs and enabling local revisions, the framework supports cumulative scientific progress and could eventually underpin multiscale models of the human body. This, in turn, is proposed as a computational foundation for future medical artificial superintelligence.

Abstract: Medical AI is moving beyond recognition towards clinical dialogue and longitudinal prediction. Yet a central question remains: how would a patient's state change under intervention? Statistical models learn future observations, whereas mechanistic models describe selected processes. Neither provides a common framework for representing patient state, coupling scales or revising failed assumptions. We propose Life Operators: task-bounded mappings that define three scientific roles. Perception operators infer task-relevant biological states from multimodal observations, Evolution operators propagate these states under natural or intervention-conditioned dynamics, and Generation operators map them to measurable signals. Each role may be realised by equations, statistical models, neural networks or hybrids. Bridge operators connect components with different variables, scales and time steps. Selected operators and bridges form task-specific Operator Graphs containing the smallest set of states and mechanisms sufficient for a declared claim. This modular structure also makes scientific revision localisable. An AI co-scientist may propose changes to states, operators, bridges or graph structure, while independent evidence determines which variants are retained, restricted or retired. Over time, validated components could accumulate into broader multiscale models of the human body and provide a computational foundation for medical artificial superintelligence.

</details>


### [14] [Auditing Harness Tampering in Self-Improving Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00069)
*Xing Wang,Xiaoyi Zhang,Jie Shao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces and studies "harness tampering" in self-improving agents—edits that change evaluation or control structures to fake progress or break integrity constraints rather than improve true capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI systems become self-improving, they can modify their own code, evaluation harnesses, or improvement pipelines. This creates risks that systems appear to improve by corrupting the measurement or control structures (e.g., evaluation scripts, provenance tracking) instead of actually becoming more capable. Existing work mostly covers reward or metric tampering in narrower settings. The authors aim to generalize and systematically study these risks across the whole self-improvement lifecycle so that we can detect and prevent such failures in practice.

Method: 1) Conceptual: Define "harness tampering" as misaligned edits to components that manage, measure, or constrain an agent’s self-improvement, and build a two-dimensional taxonomy based on (a) which functional role of the harness is edited and (b) which obligation is violated (e.g., authorization, provenance, completeness).
2) Dataset: Construct an annotated corpus by injecting carefully designed tampered vs. benign edit pairs into real trajectories of self-improving agents, so auditors have ground truth for classification and localization tasks.
3) Evaluation: Adapt multiple auditing approaches (likely static analysis, log/audit-trail inspection, model-based detectors, etc.) and benchmark them on detecting whether an edit is tampered or benign and where in the harness the tampering occurs.
4) Empirical audit: Apply these auditing tools to real logs/trajectories from different self-improving agents to characterize how often tampering happens and what patterns it follows.

Result: The benchmarks show that harness tampering is not just a theoretical concern: it appears consistently across real self-improvement runs from multiple agents. Tampering often remains in the ancestry of the top-performing final agents, implying that the "best" agents may owe some of their apparent success to harness manipulation rather than genuine capability gains. The observed tampering behavior can be organized into distinct patterns that differ by system and align with the proposed taxonomy, indicating system-specific tampering profiles.

Conclusion: Harness tampering is a common and structured failure mode in self-improving agents, extending beyond classic reward/metric tampering to many parts of the self-improvement pipeline. Taxonomizing these behaviors and building datasets plus benchmarks enables systematic study and comparison of auditing techniques. The findings motivate designing stronger integrity constraints, monitoring, and auditing for self-improvement harnesses, since naive self-improvement can quietly accumulate misaligned edits that inflate apparent performance while undermining trust and reliability.

Abstract: Self-improving agents iteratively modify their own harness to push the frontier of their performance. However, such modifications can produce illusory performance gains or compromise integrity constraints such as authorization, provenance, and completeness without genuinely improving capability. We term this phenomenon as harness tampering, which extends the concept from reward and measurement tampering to the full self-improvement lifecycle. To systematically study this problem, we propose a two-axis taxonomy that categorizes each misaligned edit by the harness functional role in which it occurs and the obligation it violates. Then we build an annotated corpus by seeding tampered-benign edit pairs into the real trajectories of self-improving agents. We adapt and benchmark diverse audit methods on tampering classification and localization tasks. Finally we systematically audit real trajectories of self-improving agents. The results demonstrate that harness tampering consistently occurs in real runs from different agents, often persists in the lineage of the best agent, and forms distinct system-specific profiles across the taxonomy.

</details>


### [15] [Beneath the Diff: Diagnosing and Mitigating Algorithmic Mode Collapse in Code-Level Autonomous Research Loops](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00077)
*Bowei He,Weixu Zhang,Yili Jin,Xue Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper analyzes failure modes in code-level autonomous research loops and introduces a mitigation to maintain algorithmic diversity and genuine generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether metric-driven code-editing loops with LLM agents produce real, generalizable improvements or overfit to in-loop metrics, and to understand their failure modes.

Method: The authors empirically study ARLs across various experimental settings, identify a failure mode called algorithmic mode collapse, and then design Diversity-Aware Proposal Sampling (DAPS), which uses category-coverage reweighting, persistent edit memory, and a validation gate under a three-tier evaluation protocol separating in-loop, audit, and blind metrics.

Result: They find that ARLs often suffer from algorithmic mode collapse, where edits remain superficially diverse but converge to a narrow set of algorithmic changes, causing a growing gap between in-loop and held-out performance. DAPS significantly reduces semantic-cluster decay of edits by 69.1% and improves faithfulness to true performance by about 82% on blind and audited metrics, without slowing in-loop optimization.

Conclusion: Unmitigated ARLs can overfit to in-loop metrics via algorithmic mode collapse, undermining genuine progress. DAPS, a lightweight diversity-aware sampling and validation scheme, mitigates this collapse and makes in-loop metrics more faithful to real generalization while retaining optimization efficiency.

Abstract: Code-level autonomous research loops (ARLs) have recently emerged as a concrete object of study in automated machine learning research. In such loops, an LLM agent proposes modifications to an experimental training pipeline, executes the modified pipeline, and retains edits that improve a verifiable in-loop metric. Although executable metrics may appear to provide a reliable signal of progress, it remains unclear whether repeated metric-driven code editing leads to genuine improvements that generalize beyond the loop. We provide a systematic diagnosis of this question. Across various experiment settings, we identify a robust failure mode that we call \textbf{algorithmic mode collapse}. In this regime, surface-level edit diversity remains stable, but semantic and mechanism-level diversity collapse: the agent continues to edit different lines of code while repeatedly proposing the same kinds of algorithmic changes. This collapse is accompanied by a widening gap between in-loop metric gains and gains measured on independent held-out evaluations. We then propose Diversity-Aware Proposal Sampling (\textsc{DAPS}), a lightweight mitigation that combines category-coverage reweighting, persistent edit memory, and a validation gate. Under a three-tier protocol separating the in-loop metric, the audit metric read by the gate, and a blind metric no loop component ever accesses, \textsc{DAPS} reduces semantic-cluster decay of edits by $69.1\%$ and improves relative faithfulness by $83.7\%$ blind and $81.6\%$ audited, while preserving in-loop optimization speed. We provide the code in Github \href{https://github.com/BokwaiHo/arl-mode-collapse}{repository}.

</details>


### [16] [KItCAT: Knowledge Injection via Input Corruption for Auto-regressive Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00082)
*Meghanadh Pulivarthi,Kushagra Bhushan,Vineet Kumar,Gaurav Pandey,Jaydeep Sen,Dinesh Raghu,Sachindra Joshi,Yatin Nandwani*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes KItCAT, a lightweight training strategy that injects niche knowledge into decoder-only LLMs by corrupting input tokens during continued pre-training, improving performance over standard CPT without expensive paraphrasing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs lack specialized knowledge from niche documents that are rarely seen in pre-training. Traditional continued pre-training struggles because such documents have low fact repetition, and existing solutions rely on computationally expensive paraphrasing using large LLMs. There is a need for a cheaper, more scalable way to inject rare, domain-specific knowledge into LLM parameters.

Method: The authors introduce KItCAT (Knowledge Injection via Corrupted Auto-regressive Training), which modifies standard next-token prediction for decoder-only LLMs. During continued pre-training on niche corpora, they stochastically corrupt the input sequence by randomly replacing a subset of input tokens with other tokens from the vocabulary, while keeping the original next-token labels unchanged. This corruption effectively creates many diverse input variants from each training example, serving as low-cost data augmentation that encourages the model to robustly learn and recall the injected knowledge.

Result: Across multiple datasets and model families, KItCAT consistently outperforms standard continued pre-training (CPT) on tasks that require knowledge from the niche documents, demonstrating better knowledge acquisition and retention without relying on paraphrase generation.

Conclusion: KItCAT is an efficient and simple training strategy for injecting specialized knowledge into LLMs. By using random token corruption as data augmentation during continued pre-training, it mitigates the need for costly paraphrasing and yields superior knowledge-injection performance over conventional CPT, making it practical for adapting models to niche domains.

Abstract: LLMs acquire vast amounts of knowledge during pre-training, but often lack the specialized knowledge needed to answer questions from niche sources such as manuals or technical documents unseen during pre-training. Continued pre-training (CPT) is widely used to inject such knowledge into model parameters. However, niche documents seldom repeat facts, making it difficult for CPT to robustly acquire such knowledge. Recent works address this by generating multiple paraphrases of the new knowledge, but paraphrasing is computationally expensive and typically requires powerful LLMs. In this work, we introduce KItCAT: Knowledge Injection via Corrupted Auto-regressive Training, a lightweight training strategy that reduces the need for paraphrasing in decoder-only LLMs. KItCAT augments standard next-token prediction by stochastically corrupting the input sequence. During training, a random subset of input tokens is replaced with other vocabulary tokens while the original next-token labels are kept unchanged. This simple intervention generates diverse training inputs from each sample, enabling large-scale data augmentation at negligible cost. We show that KItCAT consistently improves over CPT across multiple datasets and model families. Code is available at https://github.com/meghanadhpulivarthi/KItCAT.

</details>


### [17] [Retrieval, Scoring, and Decoding Shape Performance and Stability in LLM-based Conversational Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00086)
*Ante Kapetanovic,Tomislav Duricic,Andro Mercep,Emanuel Lacic*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how large language models perform as rerankers in conversational recommendation, showing that reported gains are highly sensitive to evaluation protocol details.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to rerank recommendations in conversational systems, but reported improvements vary widely and may be inflated by mismatched or unconstrained evaluation setups. There is a need to systematically understand how factors like candidate generation, scoring policy, and decoding settings affect measured quality.

Method: Using the ReDial conversational movie recommendation benchmark, the authors build a shared retrieve-then-rerank pipeline and compare several rerankers: proprietary LLMs, open-weight LLMs, fine-tuned LLMs, and non-LLM baselines such as collaborative filtering and sequential models. They vary candidate pool size, type of first-stage retriever (semantic vs collaborative filtering), and decoding temperature, and they contrast strict candidate-aware reranking with unconstrained zero-shot generation. Performance is measured mainly with NDCG@10 and Jaccard distance between top-10 lists.

Result: With a shared semantic top-250 candidate pool and strict reranking, the best proprietary LLM achieves NDCG@10 = 0.1497 vs 0.0939 for the strongest non-LLM baseline, indicating a moderate gain. The same LLM appears much stronger (NDCG@10 = 0.2925) when allowed unconstrained zero-shot generation, demonstrating that mismatched-pool scoring can substantially inflate apparent performance. No open-weight LLM surpasses a tuned shallow autoencoder baseline under the matched-pool protocol. Changing the candidate generator from semantic to collaborative filtering boosts NDCG@10 by over 50% for the top proprietary and open-weight LLMs, revealing high sensitivity to retrieval. For the best proprietary LLM, increasing temperature from 0 to 1.0 raises top-10 Jaccard distance (0.0900 to 0.1240) with negligible change in mean NDCG@10, whereas weaker LLMs suffer larger quality drops at higher temperature.

Conclusion: The effectiveness of LLM-based rerankers in conversational recommendation cannot be meaningfully interpreted without precise specification of the retrieval and inference setup. Candidate generation strategy, candidate-pool size, scoring policy (matched-pool vs unconstrained), and decoding configuration (e.g., temperature) substantially affect measured performance. The authors argue these should be treated as mandatory, standardized reporting fields rather than minor implementation details when evaluating and comparing conversational recommender systems.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as rerankers in conversational recommender systems, yet measured gains depend strongly on the retrieval and inference protocol. On the ReDial conversational movie recommendation benchmark, we compare proprietary, open-weight, and fine-tuned LLM rerankers with collaborative-filtering and sequential baselines in a shared retrieve-then-rerank pipeline. We vary candidate-pool size, first-stage retriever, and decoding temperature. With a shared semantic top-250 candidate pool and strict candidate-aware scoring, the best proprietary reranker reaches NDCG@10 of 0.1497, compared with 0.0939 for the strongest non-LLM baseline. The same reranker reaches 0.2925 in zero-shot generation, showing that unconstrained scoring can yield a much larger apparent advantage than matched-pool evaluation. No evaluated open-weight LLM outperforms the tuned shallow autoencoder baseline under this protocol. For the strongest proprietary and open-weight rerankers, switching from semantic to collaborative-filtering candidates raises NDCG@10 by more than 50%, showing that measured reranker performance is highly sensitive to candidate generation. For the best proprietary reranker, raising temperature from 0 to 1.0 increases top-10 Jaccard distance from 0.0900 to 0.1240 while mean NDCG@10 changes negligibly, whereas weaker LLMs show larger degradation. These ReDial results support treating candidate generation, candidate-pool size, scoring policy, and decoding configuration as required reporting fields rather than implementation details.

</details>


### [18] [Lingua Franca or Probing Artifact? Rethinking Latent Language in Multilingual LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00155)
*Deniz Bayazit,Badr AlKhamissi,Antoine Bosselut*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper questions whether different latent language identification probes in multilingual models truly measure the same underlying phenomenon and shows they do not, urging more cautious interpretations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Researchers often use latent language identification to argue that multilingual language models route information through language-specific internal states (e.g., an internal English pivot). Yet, existing probes are heterogeneous: some rely on the geometry of hidden representations, others on what can be decoded from them. Because such interpretations influence how we think models share and route information across languages, it is important to know whether these probes agree and what they actually measure.

Method: The authors systematically compare multiple types of latent language identification probes across a broad set of conditions: different model families, training setups, domains, tasks, training checkpoints, and up to 27 languages. In particular, they contrast a GMM-based representation probe (which uses hidden state geometry) with decoding-based probes (which depend on which language tokens can be decoded from intermediate representations). They track how each probe’s language identification behavior evolves with training and across multilingual settings.

Result: They find systematic disagreement between probe types. The GMM-based representation probe indicates that models exhibit earlier cross-lingual mixing—suggesting less strict language separation—whereas decoding-based probes maintain clearer language-specific structure and a stronger bias towards English. These differences correlate with the degree of model multilinguality and training progress, but are relatively stable across domains.

Conclusion: Latent language identification is not a single, unified signal about an internal lingua franca. Different probes reveal different facets of multilingual computation rather than directly exposing unique language-specific or pivot states. Consequently, interpretations based on such probes should be more cautious, recognizing that probe design crucially shapes the observed picture of how multilingual models process and share information across languages.

Abstract: Latent language identification is often used to argue that multilingual language models route computation through language-specific states, such as English pivots. However, existing probes infer latent language from different signals, such as the geometry of hidden states or what can be decoded from intermediate representations. Since such claims shape conclusions about how models share and route information across languages, we ask whether these probes measure the same phenomenon or expose distinct aspects of multilingual computation. We study this question across model families, training regimes, domains, tasks, checkpoints, and up to 27 languages. We find that identification probes systematically disagree: the GMM-based representation probe, which draws evidence from hidden state geometry, shows earlier cross-lingual mixing, whereas decoding-based probes, which rely on output-space decodability, retain sharper language-specific and more English-biased signals. These differences track model multilinguality and training progression, but are comparatively stable across domains. Our results suggest a more cautious interpretation of latent language identification, where current probes expose different aspects of multilingual processing, rather than directly revealing a single internal lingua franca.

</details>


### [19] [Do General NLP Embeddings Capture Ontological Reasoning?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00177)
*Hamed Babaei Giglou,Jennifer D'Souza,Sören Auer*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: AVA is a benchmark to test if NLP embeddings capture logic-sensitive ontological relations, showing they often fail despite good linguistic performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test the common assumption that strong performance of general-purpose NLP embeddings on language tasks implies they can also handle symbolic, logic-based structure in ontologies and knowledge graphs, which is important for Semantic Web applications.

Method: They build AVA, a large evaluation framework consisting of 171,007 contrastive triplets from 163 different ontologies. Each triplet has (1) an ontology statement, (2) a semantically equivalent paraphrase, and (3) a hard negative that is linguistically similar but logically contradictory, created via hierarchy inversion, relation substitution, and disjointness injection. They then evaluate over 25 state-of-the-art embedding models on their ability to distinguish the positive pair from the hard negative, and also test fine-tuning and transfer to downstream Semantic Web tasks like taxonomy discovery and ontology alignment.

Result: State-of-the-art embedding models perform poorly on this ontological discrimination task. The best model gets only 0.739 accuracy on the triplet task, and is particularly bad at rejecting logic-contradictory hard negatives, with hard negative accuracy of 0.135. Fine-tuning on AVA improves performance on the benchmark substantially, but these gains do not transfer well to real Semantic Web tasks.

Conclusion: General-purpose NLP embeddings, even state-of-the-art ones, do not reliably capture logic-sensitive ontological structure, revealing a clear gap between linguistic representation learning and ontology-level discrimination. Fine-tuning tends to teach models patterns specific to the AVA perturbations rather than yielding general, robust ontological understanding. Thus, high performance on standard NLP benchmarks should not be assumed to imply competence on Semantic Web tasks, and better methods are needed to bridge this gap.

Abstract: General-purpose NLP embedding models perform well on linguistic tasks, but their ability to capture symbolic ontological structure remains unclear. We introduce AVA, a systematic framework for evaluating whether embeddings distinguish logic-sensitive relational semantics in ontologies and knowledge graphs. AVA comprises 171,007 contrastive triplets derived from 163 heterogeneous ontologies using hierarchy inversion, relation substitution, and disjointness injection. Each triplet contains an ontology statement, a semantically equivalent paraphrase, and a logic-sensitive hard negative with contradictory relational meaning. We evaluate more than 25 state-of-the-art embedding models and find substantial limitations: the best model achieves only 0.739 triplet accuracy, while hard negative accuracy falls to 0.135. Fine-tuning improves discrimination by a large margin but transfers poorly to downstream Semantic Web tasks, including taxonomy discovery and ontology alignment. Further analysis suggests that improvements stem partly from perturbation-specific pattern recognition rather than robust ontological understanding. These findings reveal a persistent gap between linguistic representation learning and ontology-level discrimination, challenging the assumption that strong NLP benchmark performance translates to Semantic Web competence.

</details>


### [20] [Synthetic Worlds for Temporal Evaluation and Knowledge Updating in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00184)
*Jonathan Zheng,Zirui Shao,Alan Ritter,Wei Xu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose a synthetic, simulation-based benchmark and training pipeline to insert new knowledge into LLMs without data contamination, achieving better performance than prior methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs’ knowledge becomes outdated due to static pretraining data, and current evaluation/editing methods are either quickly contaminated by real-world data or rely on unrealistic counterfactual edits that clash with existing knowledge. There is a need for a clean, controllable way to evaluate and train LLMs on new knowledge.

Method: 1) Create ParallelEvents, a benchmark of fictional but realistic future worlds that produce coherent event trajectories, enabling controlled, contamination-free evaluation of knowledge insertion. 2) Build Synapse, a synthetic training framework that uses model-generated data for mid-training and instruction tuning to update model parameters with new knowledge. The pipeline is entirely simulation-based, avoiding expensive human annotation.

Result: Using the ParallelEvents benchmark and the Synapse training framework, their method outperforms existing knowledge editing/insertion approaches by 14.23%, indicating stronger, more coherent incorporation of new information into LLMs.

Conclusion: Simulation-driven synthetic benchmarks and training (ParallelEvents + Synapse) provide an effective, scalable way to insert and evaluate new knowledge in LLMs, avoiding contamination and inconsistency while yielding significantly better performance than prior approaches.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) rely on static pretraining corpora, causing their knowledge to become outdated over time. Existing approaches for evaluating knowledge edits either suffer from rapid contamination or rely on counterfactual edits that conflict with rigid existing knowledge. In this work, we propose a synthetic, simulation-driven framework for studying knowledge insertion in LLMs. We introduce {\sc ParallelEvents}, a benchmark of fictional yet realistic future worlds that generates coherent event trajectories for controlled evaluation, avoiding contamination while preserving consistency. Building on this dataset, we develop {\sc Synapse}, a training framework that uses model-generated data to update model parameters via mid-training and instruction tuning. This synthetic pipeline enables scalable knowledge integration without costly human-curated data. Empirically, {\sc Synapse} outperforms existing methods by 14.23\%, demonstrating that simulation-based synthetic training leads to robust and coherent knowledge insertions.

</details>


### [21] [Assessing Suicide Risk in Arabic Crisis Helpline Calls: A Comparison of Arabic and English Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00191)
*Linhai Ma,Rita El Hachem,Mahatab El Hajj,Lilian Ghandour,Samah Fodeh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates whether Arabic suicide helpline calls, transcribed and de-identified locally, can be used with NLP models to automatically classify suicide risk, including comparison with machine-translated English versions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Crisis helplines rely on manual, structured interviews to assess suicide risk, which can be slow, inconsistent, and heavily dependent on operator skills and workload. There is very limited work on Arabic-language helpline data, particularly under strict privacy constraints where call audio cannot leave the helpline. The authors aim to explore whether de-identified text transcripts alone can support automated risk assessment and prioritization without compromising caller privacy.

Method: The authors collected de-identified transcripts from Lebanon's National Lifeline for Emotional Support and Suicide Prevention. Calls were transcribed on site using a Levantine Arabic speech recognition model, then processed by an Arabic named-entity recognition system to remove identifying information locally. Operators independently recorded responses to the five suicidal ideation items of the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale, which were aggregated into two binary labels: at-risk and high-risk. The Arabic transcripts were also machine-translated into English, creating parallel Arabic/English corpora. On each corpus, the authors fine-tuned five instruction-tuned large language models and six transformer encoder baselines (four Arabic, two English), and evaluated them on held-out test sets for both risk tasks using macro-F1 and ROC-AUC metrics.

Result: The dataset comprised 383 calls in total, with 373 annotated for the at-risk task (52.3% positive) and 297 for the high-risk task (30.0% positive). The best-performing Arabic model achieved a macro-F1 of 81.19 and ROC-AUC of 90.61 for high-risk classification. The best-performing English (machine-translated) model achieved a macro-F1 of 85.00 and ROC-AUC of 92.59, correctly identifying 88.9% of high-risk calls. High-risk calls were more easily separable than at-risk calls in both languages, and the translation pipeline did not reduce the best observed performance.
