Conclusion: Automated suicide risk classification is feasible using de-identified Arabic helpline transcripts, with no need to transmit audio outside the helpline, thus preserving caller privacy. High-risk cases can be detected with strong performance that may justify operator-facing decision support tools, whereas lower-severity suicidal ideation remains more challenging to classify reliably. Machine translation to English can be used without degrading top-level performance, potentially enabling the use of a broader ecosystem of English-language NLP models.

Abstract: Crisis helplines assess suicide risk through structured interviews, a process that is slow and dependent on operator training and workload. Natural language processing could support risk assessment and call prioritization, but almost no work addresses Arabic-language helpline calls or operates within the privacy constraints of real helpline data. We analysed de-identified transcripts from Lebanon's National Lifeline for Emotional Support and Suicide Prevention. Audio never left the helpline: calls were transcribed on site with a speech recognition model for Levantine Arabic, and an Arabic named-entity recognition model removed identifying information locally. Only the de-identified transcripts were shared with the research team. Operators recorded the five suicidal ideation items of the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale, which we combined into two binary outcomes: at-risk and high-risk. We also machine-translated the transcripts into English, giving a paired Arabic/English comparison. On each corpus, we fine-tuned five instruction-tuned large language models alongside six transformer encoder baselines (four Arabic, two English) and evaluated all models on a held-out test set. We included 383 calls: 373 for the at-risk task (52.3% positive) and 297 for the high-risk task (30.0% positive). The best Arabic model reached a macro-F1 of 81.19 and a ROC-AUC of 90.61 on high-risk; the best English model reached 85.00 and 92.59, identifying 88.9% of high-risk calls. In both languages, high-risk calls separated more cleanly than at-risk calls, and translation to English did not reduce the best observed performance. Suicide risk can be classified from de-identified Arabic transcripts without sending audio outside the helpline. The high-risk results support further testing as an operator-facing tool; lower-severity ideation proved the harder case.

</details>


### [22] [Uncovering and Mitigating Aggregation-Induced Reward Hacking in Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00213)
*Yu Yuan,Yaoyou Fan,Lili Zhao,Guangting Zheng,Kai Zhang,Lu Pan,Ke Zeng,Qi Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper identifies a reward-hacking failure mode caused by naively scalarizing multiple rewards in RL fine-tuning of LLMs and proposes an adaptive weighting method, AMRP, that improves balance across rewards and downstream performance across several tasks and RL algorithms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL fine-tuning of large language models increasingly uses multiple reward dimensions (e.g., rule adherence, task quality, learned preferences) combined via fixed-weight scalarization. This scalarization can cause reward hacking, where optimization is biased toward easier or denser rewards, trapping policies in suboptimal behaviors and preventing convergence to better-balanced solutions. The authors aim to diagnose this failure mode and develop a simple, general way to adapt aggregation weights during training so that all reward dimensions are appropriately optimized.

Method: The authors introduce Adaptive Multi-Reward Projection (AMRP), an online algorithm that dynamically adjusts the aggregation weights assigned to each reward dimension during RL training. AMRP monitors three signals per reward dimension: (1) relative shortfall (how far that reward is from desired or observed best values), (2) reward volatility (instability or noisiness), and (3) recent progress (change in reward over time). It increases the weight for lagging, unstable, or stagnant dimensions and decreases it for dimensions that appear saturated or already performing well. This reweighting is applied on top of existing RL algorithms such as GRPO, GDPO, and PPO without changing their core updates, making AMRP a lightweight extension.

Result: On several LLM fine-tuning settings—structured reasoning tasks, citation-grounded generation, and open-ended alignment using GRPO—the AMRP method yields more balanced reward profiles across dimensions and improves downstream task performance compared with both fixed-weight scalarization and other dynamic-weighting baselines. The approach also shows good compatibility and effectiveness when used with alternative RL algorithms (GDPO and PPO), suggesting it is robust to the underlying optimizer.

Conclusion: Static scalarization of multiple rewards in RL fine-tuning can itself induce reward hacking by collapsing distinct reward profiles into a single scalar and favoring easier dimensions, which harms overall task performance. By adaptively reallocating weights based on shortfall, volatility, and progress, AMRP better balances optimization pressure across reward dimensions, leading to improved alignment and task outcomes. The method is lightweight, algorithm-agnostic, and empirically effective across tasks and RL algorithms, offering a practical way to mitigate multi-reward failure modes in LLM training.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning fine-tuning of large language models increasingly adopts multiple reward dimensions, including verifiable rules, task-specific evaluators, and learned reward models, to provide richer supervision across diverse capabilities. These dimensions are commonly scalarized with fixed aggregation weights. We identify a failure mode in which aggregation itself induces reward hacking: static projection aliases qualitatively different reward profiles into a single scalar, steering optimization toward whichever dimensions are easiest, densest, or systematically favored by the reward signal. Over training, this traps the policy in suboptimal profiles and prevents convergence to better-balanced ones that would yield higher task performance. To address this, we propose Adaptive Multi-Reward Projection (AMRP), a lightweight online method that reallocates aggregation weights using three signals, relative shortfall, reward volatility, and recent progress, increasing pressure on lagging, unstable, or stagnant dimensions while relieving saturated ones. Across structured reasoning, citation-grounded generation, and open-ended alignment under GRPO, AMRP consistently improves reward-profile balance and downstream performance over fixed and dynamic weighting baselines; it also remains effective with GDPO and PPO, supporting compatibility across RL algorithms. Our code is available at https://github.com/yyhappier/AMRP.git.

</details>


### [23] [LLM-as-a-Demographic: Whom Sociodemographic Prompting Helps, and Whom It Hurts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00222)
*Daniela Occhipinti,Andrea Piergentili,Marco Guerini*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how well large language models (LLMs) used as judges reproduce the label distributions of different demographic annotator groups, and finds that “neutral” judges reflect White, college-educated perspectives and that demographic prompting tends to pull model judgments toward majority groups and away from minorities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as automatic judges for subjective tasks (e.g., offensiveness, preference ratings). In these settings, there is no single ground truth, and annotators from different sociodemographic groups systematically disagree. It is therefore crucial not only to measure judge accuracy, but also to understand whose perspectives and label distributions an LLM reproduces, and whether demographic prompting can reliably align model behavior with specific groups, especially minorities.

Method: The authors evaluate 23 open-weight LLMs on three subjective labeling tasks and compare their predicted label distributions to those of real human annotator groups. They test three prompting conditions: (1) no demographic specification, (2) single-attribute demographic profiles (e.g., gender, race, age, education), and (3) intersectional profiles combining these attributes. They analyze how closely model predictions match the empirical distributions for specific demographic groups and compare base versus instruction-tuned models to identify sources of systematic alignment or bias.

Result: (1) LLM judges prompted without any demographic information are not neutral; instead, their output distributions most closely match those of White, college-educated annotators. (2) When explicitly conditioned on sociodemographic profiles, models do not symmetrically align with all groups: demographic prompting tends to move predictions toward majority-group distributions and away from minority-group distributions, with the strongest effects on offensiveness judgments and with intersectional profiles exacerbating misalignment for minorities. (3) Comparing base and instruction-tuned models suggests that instruction tuning is a key contributor to this asymmetric behavior, likely embedding majority perspectives more strongly.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that LLM judges, even when used in a seemingly neutral way, implicitly privilege majority (White, college-educated) perspectives. Demographic conditioning via prompting does not reliably recover minority-group label distributions and can even worsen misalignment, especially in sensitive tasks like offensiveness detection and under intersectional prompts. Because instruction tuning appears to encode these asymmetric behaviors, practitioners should be cautious when using sociodemographic prompting to approximate group-level judgments or to serve minority groups; naïve demographic conditioning may systematically move predictions away from the very groups it is intended to represent.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges for subjective tasks, where annotators disagree and the relevant question is not only how accurate a judge is, but whose judgments it reproduces. Sociodemographic prompting conditions the judge on an annotator's demographic profile to align its judgments with the corresponding group's. We test whether this alignment emerges distributionally, comparing the predicted label distributions of 23 open-weight LLMs on three subjective tasks against those of real annotator groups, under three conditions: no demographic information, single-attribute profiles, and intersectional profiles over gender, age, race, and education. Three findings emerge. First, a judge prompted with no demographics is not perspective-neutral: models best reproduce the judgments of White, college-educated annotators. Second, demographic conditioning is asymmetric: it moves the judge toward majority groups and away from minority groups, most strongly on offensiveness, where intersectional profiles amplify the harm. Third, by comparing base and instruct models we identify instruction-tuning as a possible source of the asymmetry. Demographic conditioning should therefore be used with caution to estimate group judgments: conditioning moves predictions away from the reference distributions of the minority groups the method is often invoked to serve.

</details>


### [24] [Bridging Lexical Divergence: LLM-Assisted, Cost-Efficient, Zero-shot Scientific Entity Linking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00228)
*Md Rasel Khondokar,Qiao Qiao,Farjana Sultana Samia,Nhat Le,Yuepei Li,Qi Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Sci-ZSEL, a zero-human-annotation framework for scientific domain entity linking that selectively generates and filters LLM-based aliases and shows improved performance, especially when lexical overlap is low.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific domain entity linking suffers from low lexical overlap between mentions and entity names and from specialized terminology that is not covered by general-domain pretrained models. Many domains also lack expert-annotated data, making in-domain fine-tuning difficult and motivating a zero-human-annotation solution.

Method: The authors propose Sci-ZSEL, which (1) selectively invokes an LLM to generate entity aliases to keep computation manageable, (2) uses an ontology-aware filter to remove aliases that semantically drift toward neighboring ontology entities, and (3) uses the remaining aliases to build pseudo-labeled mention–entity pairs for fine-tuning an entity linking model. They also construct and release a new animal science EL benchmark with low lexical overlap, linked to three livestock trait ontologies.

Result: Across five benchmarks, Sci-ZSEL significantly outperforms non-fine-tuned baselines, is particularly effective on mentions with low lexical overlap to entity names, and achieves the best performance in most settings when combined with existing curated synonyms.

Conclusion: Sci-ZSEL provides an efficient, zero-human-annotation approach to scientific entity linking that addresses low lexical overlap and domain-specific terminology by selective LLM alias generation and ontology-aware filtering. It improves EL performance, especially on challenging low-overlap mentions, and the newly released animal science benchmark supports evaluation in such settings.

Abstract: Scientific domain entity linking (EL) differs from general domain EL because mentions and entity names often lack lexical overlap. Another challenge is that specialized terminology is used in the scientific domain, which is rarely encountered in models pretrained on general domains. Therefore, models trained on general domains transfer poorly to scientific domains. To address this, in-domain fine-tuning is the natural remedy. However, many scientific domains lack expert-annotated data, motivating the need for a zero-human-annotation approach. Existing zero-shot methods heavily rely on LLMs to generate aliases across entire mention corpora, which incurs substantial computational cost, and those methods provide no mechanism to filter out noise from LLMs. To address these challenges, we propose Sci-ZSEL, a framework that selectively generates entity aliases with an LLM to control computational cost, and applies an ontology-aware filter to remove aliases that semantically drift toward ontology neighbors. Then, filtered aliases are used to construct pseudo-labeled mention-entity pairs for fine-tuning. To enable evaluation of EL under low lexical overlap, we also release a new animal science EL benchmark linked to three livestock trait ontologies, where mentions and entities exhibit substantially lower lexical overlap than in existing benchmarks. Across five benchmarks, Sci-ZSEL outperforms the non-fine-tuned baseline, is most useful on nonoverlapping mentions, and combining it with curated synonyms gives the best performance in most settings.

</details>


### [25] [LOOMSUM:Weaving Quantitative and Narrative Evidence for Faithful Long Text-Table Summarization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00241)
*Meng Zhou,Wenhao You,Wei Yuan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces LOOMSUM, a training-free framework for more faithful summarization of long documents with both text and tables, and a new evaluation metric (TGF) to measure table-grounded faithfulness at the claim level.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Summarizing long documents that mix narrative text and tables is hard because important information is distributed across modalities. Existing summarizers may state individually correct numbers and analyses but mismatch them—linking a right number to the wrong interpretation—leading to summaries that are quantitatively plausible but analytically unfaithful. There is a need for methods that not only ground individual facts in tables but also preserve the correct analytical relations between them, along with metrics that can diagnose these specific failures.

Method: The authors propose LOOMSUM, a training-free summarization framework that: (1) extracts atomic, source-grounded evidence from both tables and text; (2) explicitly links numeric facts derived from tables to their supporting narrative analyses; and (3) plans the discourse structure of the summary before generating it. In parallel, they introduce Table-Grounded Faithfulness (TGF), a claim-level evaluation metric decomposed into three components: Numeric Grounding (are numbers grounded in the table?), Analysis Support (is the analytic statement supported?), and Relation Consistency (are relations between quantities and analyses preserved?).

Result: On two text–table summarization benchmarks, FINDSum and USTT, LOOMSUM improves analytical faithfulness compared to baselines while preserving strong overall summarization quality. Human evaluations show that the individual components of TGF correlate positively with the corresponding human judgments of faithfulness. Additionally, the Relation Consistency sub-metric aligns better with human judgments about relational correctness than general factuality metrics, indicating that explicit cross-modal linking addresses errors where correct numbers are paired with incorrect analyses.

Conclusion: The study concludes that for long text–table summarization, it is not enough to ground each fact individually in the source; systems must also explicitly maintain the relations between quantitative facts and their narrative interpretations. LOOMSUM demonstrates that a training-free pipeline focused on atomic evidence extraction, cross-modal linking, and discourse planning can enhance analytical faithfulness. The proposed TGF metric, especially its Relation Consistency component, provides a more diagnostic and human-aligned way to evaluate table-grounded summarization faithfulness than generic factuality metrics.

Abstract: Long documents often distribute important information across extensive narrative passages and multiple tables, making faithful summarization particularly challenging. Existing methods may generate individually supported quantitative facts and analytical statements yet associate them incorrectly, producing quantitatively plausible yet analytically unfaithful summaries. In this work, we propose LOOMSUM, a training-free framework that extracts source-grounded atomic evidence, explicitly links table-derived facts with supporting narrative analyses, and plans the discourse structure before generation. We also introduce Table-Grounded Faithfulness (TGF), a claim-level metric that separately evaluates Numeric Grounding, Analysis Support, and Relation Consistency. Experiments on the text--table summarization benchmarks FINDSum and USTT show that LOOMSUM improves analytical faithfulness while maintaining strong summarization quality. Human evaluation finds positive component-level associations with the corresponding human judgments. Our Relation Consistency metric further shows stronger agreement with human relation judgments than generic factuality metrics, indicating that explicit cross-modal linking helps reduce errors in which supported quantities are paired with incorrect narrative interpretations. Together, these findings show that faithful long text--table summarization requires not only grounding individual facts, but also preserving the relations between them.

</details>


### [26] [NSIDDx: A Design Framework for Neuro-Symbolic, Practitioner-First Differential Diagnosis in Low-Resource Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00256)
*Aarav Singh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Neuro-symbolic LLM pipeline for safer rare-disease diagnosis in low-resource clinical settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based diagnostic systems look good on standard benchmarks but fail on rare or atypical real-world cases, often giving confident but unverifiable answers that resist clinician questioning. There is a need for systems that remain reliable, transparent, and usable in low-resource clinical environments, especially for rare diseases.

Method: The authors propose NSIDDx, a neuro-symbolic framework for differential diagnosis that explicitly treats the clinician as an active reasoning partner. The pipeline combines an LLM with structured symbolic reasoning components: ternary symptom encoding (present/absent/unknown), contradiction detection between model hypotheses and structured findings, audit strings that expose the reasoning chain, and a mechanism for practitioner override. The system runs offline on consumer hardware and is evaluated as an LLM+rare-disease-RAG pipeline on two patient cohorts, focusing on rare and clinically uncommon presentations.

Result: In open-ended testing on clinically uncommon cases, standard LLM+RAG diagnostic setups produce confident responses that are often not verifiable against clinical evidence and resist correction. The NSIDDx framework demonstrates that incorporating neuro-symbolic methods, structured symptom encodings, and explicit clinician control can mitigate these issues and support more interrogable and auditable diagnostic reasoning, though large-scale validation is still pending.

Conclusion: Headline benchmark accuracy for LLM-based diagnostic tools is insufficient to guarantee safe clinical use, especially in rare-disease contexts. Diagnostic NLP systems should be designed as clinician-in-the-loop tools with explicit support for interrogation, contradiction handling, transparency, and override, and must function in low-resource settings. The authors summarize their proposal as five design principles for such systems and call for prospective clinical studies to validate their framework at scale.

Abstract: LLM-based diagnostic systems achieve high semantic accuracy on benchmarks, but open-ended evaluation on clinically uncommon presentations reveals a systematic gap between headline accuracy and verifiable clinical reliability. We evaluate an LLM+rare-disease-RAG pipeline across two cohorts and show that the paradigm produces confident outputs that are frequently unverifiable and systematically resistant to clinician interrogation. We present NSIDDx (Neuro-Symbolic Integrated Differential Diagnosis System), a design framework arguing that DDx systems in low-resource settings must treat the clinician as an active reasoning agent. We instantiate this through a neuro-symbolic pipeline with ternary symptom encoding, contradiction detection, audit strings, and practitioner override - running offline on consumer hardware. We distill five design principles for clinician-in-the-loop clinical NLP and invite the prospective studies needed to validate the claim at scale.

</details>


### [27] [Slow to See, Slow to Suppress: Understanding the Effects of Modality in Context-Memory Conflicts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00293)
*Athulith Paraselli,Etha Tianze Hua,Ellie Pavlick*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how vision-language models resolve conflicts between new contextual information and their stored factual knowledge, revealing asymmetric biases toward context for text entities and toward parametric memory for visual entities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand and characterize how multimodal models, specifically vision-language models, reconcile discrepancies between information provided at inference time (in-context) and knowledge stored during training (parametric memory), which is important for reliability, controllability, and safe deployment of such models as they become more multimodal and retrieval-augmented.

Method: The authors create scenarios with deliberate conflicts between contextual information and the model’s parametric knowledge for entities presented either in text or in images. They then probe the model’s responses to measure whether it follows the new context or defaults to its stored knowledge, analyze the asymmetry between modalities, and relate it to representational alignment timing across modalities. They also test interventions like chain-of-thought prompting and increasing visual context to see how these factors influence conflict resolution.

Result: They find that VLMs show asymmetric biases: they usually follow in-context information when the entity appears in text, but default to their parametric (trained) knowledge when the entity appears in images. This asymmetry is linked to late representational alignment between modalities; visual entity resolution takes longer, so the mechanisms that would suppress default factual recall are less effective, yielding more parametric answers. Chain-of-thought prompting does not significantly reduce this asymmetry, while adding more visual information in the context does have a measurable effect.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that VLMs do not treat conflicting information uniformly across modalities; instead, they show a systematic, modality-dependent bias in how they reconcile context with parametric memory. This highlights challenges for building consistent, controllable multimodal and retrieval-augmented systems, and suggests that architectural and training choices affecting cross-modal alignment and visual context richness are crucial levers for improving behavior in context-memory conflict scenarios.

Abstract: We investigate how vision-language models (VLMs) handle context-memory conflicts; that is, situations in which the model is given information in context that differs from what was stored parametrically during training. We document asymmetric biases: models tend to prefer in-context information about entities which appear in text, but prefer parametric information about entities which appear in images. We relate this asymmetry to the late representational alignment across modalities, showing that the longer processing time associated with resolving visual entities prevents the suppression of the model's usual factual recall mechanism, thus resulting in more parametric answers. Chain-of-thought reasoning does not appear to resolve the gap, but increasing the amount of visual information in the context does show an effect. These results illustrate the complexity of ensuring consistent behavior as models become increasingly multimodal and retrieval-augmented.

</details>


### [28] [Toward Workflow-Aware Benchmarking for Healthcare NLP Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00296)
*Junyi Yao,Baichuan Li,Zihao Zheng,Jiayu Long*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Proposes an episode-level evaluation protocol for healthcare LLM agents that better reflects real workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of healthcare LLM agents mostly use static QA or one-shot generation, which fail to capture longitudinal interactions, interruptions, and human handoffs typical in clinical workflows. There is a need for a more realistic, workflow-aware, and reproducible evaluation framework that can bridge the gap between static benchmarks and real-world deployment.

Method: Designs an episode-level evaluation protocol with a five-field episode schema and explicit separation of evidence used by the model, the agent, and the simulated workflow. Defines annotation and scoring guidelines for three key aspects: maintaining state continuity over time, ensuring evidence traceability, and deciding when to escalate to a human. Instantiates this protocol into four concrete task templates: documentation update, evidence retrieval, patient messaging, and triage handoff.

Result: Provides a concrete, reusable protocol and four task templates that can be used to systematically evaluate healthcare NLP agents at the episode level, considering longitudinal context and escalation costs. Establishes metrics and annotation guidelines but does not report clinical outcome improvements.

Conclusion: The proposed protocol offers a reproducible intermediate evaluation layer between simple static benchmarks and full prospective workflow studies. It allows more realistic assessment of healthcare LLM agents’ behavior over episodes, especially regarding state management, evidence use, and escalation decisions, with an explicit cost-sensitive view of missed versus unnecessary escalations, without making claims about direct clinical outcome impact.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly proposed for healthcare tasks such as clinical documentation, evidence retrieval, patient messaging, and care coordination. Yet many evaluations remain limited to static medical question answering or one-shot generation, under-representing longitudinal state, interruptions, and human handoffs. We introduce an episode-level evaluation protocol for healthcare NLP agents. The protocol separates evidence across model, agent, and simulated-workflow behavior; specifies a five-field episode schema; and defines annotation and scoring for state continuity, evidence traceability, and escalation decisions. It is instantiated as four task templates: documentation update, evidence retrieval, patient messaging, and triage handoff. The protocol does not claim to measure clinical outcomes or deployment value. Instead, it supplies a reproducible intermediate evaluation layer between static benchmarks and prospective workflow studies, with an explicit cost-sensitive treatment of missed versus unnecessary escalation.

</details>


### [29] [Emotional Labor Strategy Preferences in LLM Personas](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00310)
*Mohammad Saim,Tianyu Jiang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper tests whether large language models (LLMs), when given carefully specified personality profiles, show personality-based preferences for emotional labor strategies across everyday social situations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work links personality traits to emotional labor strategies (surface acting, deep acting, genuine expression), but nearly all of it relies on human self-report in workplace contexts. It is unknown whether LLMs can reproduce these personality-driven patterns, and whether persona conditioning meaningfully shapes their behavior in diverse, non-occupational social scenarios. This gap limits both our understanding of LLMs as social simulators and our ability to model emotional labor beyond traditional survey methods.

Method: The authors build a novel dataset of 500 everyday social events, each mapped to three behavioral responses representing surface acting, deep acting, and genuine emotional expression. They select 50 fictional characters from a large personality repository and derive two types of personality profiles for each: (1) observer-rated bipolar adjective composites and (2) in-character self-report items. Five different LLMs are prompted to choose among the three emotional labor strategies in all scenarios under both persona-profiling approaches. The authors then analyze strategy preferences, link them to Big Five traits (especially Conscientiousness and Emotional Stability), and use entropy-based measures to quantify how strongly persona information shapes model outputs and how this varies across models and emotional contexts.

Result: Across models, choices skew toward deep acting over surface acting and genuine expression. Personality traits, particularly higher Conscientiousness and Emotional Stability, robustly predict a stronger preference for deep acting strategies. Entropy analyses show that persona injections significantly and systematically affect LLM outputs, with the strength and pattern of this influence differing by model architecture and by the emotional content of the scenario.

Conclusion: LLMs equipped with psychometrically grounded personas exhibit systematic, personality-consistent preferences in emotional labor strategies, mirroring human trait–strategy associations found in psychology. Deep acting emerges as the dominant strategy, especially for conscientious and emotionally stable personas. Persona information demonstrably and reliably shapes model behavior, supporting the use of LLMs as tools for simulating personality-linked emotional labor in everyday social situations and highlighting model-specific differences in sensitivity to persona conditioning.

Abstract: Emotional labor is the effortful management of emotional displays to meet social or professional expectations. Personality traits have been correlated with emotional labor strategies, yet research on this link relies almost exclusively on self-report scales administered only in occupational settings. We investigate whether large language models injected with psychometrically grounded personas reproduce these personality-driven selection patterns across everyday social scenarios. We construct the first emotional labor strategy dataset of 500 socially situated events, each offering three behavioral choices corresponding to surface acting, deep acting, and genuine expression. We source 50 fictional characters from a large-scale personality repository and profile each through two parallel tracks: observer-rated bipolar adjective composites and in-character self-report items. Five LLMs evaluate all scenarios under both persona conditions. We find that models align more towards deep acting, and that Conscientiousness and Emotional Stability consistently predict this preference. Entropy analysis confirms that persona reliably influences the output and varies across models and emotions.

</details>


### [30] [Latent Mechanisms of Language Control in Multilingual Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00325)
*Ryo Mitsuhashi,Sabri Boughorbel,Majd Hawasly*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Study compares three methods to identify and control language-specific latent directions in multilingual LLMs to reduce unintended code-switching.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multilingual LLMs often code-switch unintentionally, which can harm usability, controllability, and evaluation. The authors aim to find which internal latent dimensions control output language so that generation can be steered reliably across languages.

Method: They analyze cross-layer transcoders in multilingual LLMs (Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-4B) and compare three strategies for selecting language-controlling latents: (1) ValSel, which chooses latents based on activation magnitudes associated with specific languages; (2) FreqSel, which selects latents that are frequently active for a given language; and (3) AnnSel, which uses an LLM to annotate and select latents based on textual descriptions of their language behavior. They build two multilingual benchmarks that reliably trigger code-switching across seven languages, then run targeted interventions on the selected latents to test how well each method can steer the generation language. They also perform knock-out analyses to see how disjoint or overlapping the selected latent sets are and how each subset affects behavior.

Result: All three selection methods can effectively steer the generation language, mitigating code-switching. FreqSel performs best overall in terms of language control strength and reliability, while AnnSel provides interpretable latent subsets by linking them to explicit language annotations. Knock-out experiments show that the selected latent subsets are largely non-overlapping yet each functional, implying multiple redundant language-control mechanisms rather than a single dominant direction in representation space.

Conclusion: Language-controlling latents in multilingual LLMs can be identified and manipulated using several selection strategies, allowing effective control over output language and reduction of unintended code-switching. The existence of multiple, non-canonical language directions suggests redundancy in how models represent language identity, and FreqSel emerges as a strong practical method, with AnnSel adding interpretability. The released benchmarks, code, and data support further research on mechanistic understanding and control of multilingual behavior.

Abstract: Multilingual large language models can exhibit unintended code-switching -- unnecessarily alternating between languages during generation. We present a comparative study of three methods that identify language-controlling latents in cross-layer transcoders: activation value-based selection (ValSel), activation frequency-based selection (FreqSel), and LLM-generated latent annotation-based selection (AnnSel). To evaluate the efficacy of these methods in identifying language-controlling latents, we introduce two multilingual benchmarks that exhibit code-switching for fine-grained analysis of language steering across seven languages. Through targeted intervention experiments on Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-4B, we find that all three methods effectively manipulate generation language, with FreqSel achieving the strongest overall performance, while AnnSel offering interpretable latent selection through explicit language annotations. A knock-out analysis suggests the methods select non-overlapping but each-functional latent subsets, indicating redundancy rather than a single canonical language direction. Code and data can be found at https://github.com/rm-3284/Latent-Mechanism-Multilingual.

</details>


### [31] [The Curse of Multilinguality in Lexical Normalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00329)
*Saman Rahbar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how the number of languages jointly trained in a single lexical normalization model affects per-language accuracy, and finds that training on fewer languages (often 1–4) outperforms training on many (up to 12) for a fixed-capacity model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lexical normalization of noisy user-generated text is important for downstream NLP tasks. Since labeled data is scarce for most languages, practitioners often train one shared multilingual model instead of many monolingual ones. However, it is unclear whether adding more languages to a fixed-capacity model always helps or whether there is a limit beyond which performance degrades. The paper is motivated by this gap in understanding how multilingual joint training scales with the number of languages for the task of lexical normalization.

Method: The authors use a single fixed-capacity character-level neural model and a benchmark containing twelve different languages. They systematically vary the number of languages that are jointly trained—from purely monolingual training up to training on all 12 languages at once—and measure per-language lexical normalization accuracy. They also run a control experiment where the total amount of training data is held constant while increasing the number of languages, to disentangle data size effects from capacity competition. Finally, they analyze whether typological distance between languages can predict the ideal number of co-trained languages for each target language.

Result: They observe a clear “curse of multilinguality”: per-language accuracy is highest when each language is trained with only a small number of other languages (often 1–4). As more languages are added to the shared model, accuracy for each individual language declines steadily and substantially, dropping by around 40% when all twelve languages are trained together. In the control setting with fixed total training data, the decline in accuracy begins earlier and is even more severe, supporting the view that languages are competing for limited model capacity. The exploration of typological distance finds no robust predictive rule for how many co-training languages are ideal for a given language; any apparent correlations depend heavily on just a couple of languages and do not generalize.

Conclusion: For compact, fixed-capacity lexical normalization models, jointly training on many languages can be harmful: a smaller multilingual grouping, or even near-monolingual training, can yield much better normalization accuracy than pooling all languages together. The key issue appears to be competition for limited model capacity rather than simply the amount of data. Typological distance does not provide a reliable guide for grouping languages, so practitioners should be cautious about indiscriminately training a single model on a large set of languages and instead consider smaller, task-specific language groupings.

Abstract: Lexical normalization rewrites the noisy, non-standard words that fill user-generated text (tmrw, u, gr8) into their standard forms. Because labelled data is scarce for most languages, a popular shortcut is to train a single model on many languages at once. We ask a simple question: how many languages should such a model be trained on? Using one fixed-capacity character-level model and twelve languages from a standard benchmark, we vary the number of jointly trained languages from one to twelve and measure per-language accuracy. We find a clear curse of multilinguality: accuracy is highest when a language is trained with only a few others, often just one to four, and then falls steadily and substantially, dropping by about forty percent as the rest are piled on. A control that holds the total amount of training data constant makes the decline arrive sooner and fall further, which points to competition among the languages for one fixed-size model rather than to how much data is available. We also test whether a language's typological distance from the others predicts its ideal number of co-training languages, and find no dependable rule: any apparent relationship rests on a couple of languages and does not hold up. For compact normalization models, less can be more: a few languages beat pooling everything into a single model.

</details>


### [32] [Topic Matching in the Wild: Benchmark and Lessons from Real-World ASR Transcripts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00330)
*Saman Rahbar,Xiliang Zhu,Irvin Cardoza,David Rossouw*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper builds and benchmarks a dataset and models for detecting topic relevance of noisy call center utterances, showing lightweight LLM matchers with natural language topic descriptions work best.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-time agent-assist systems in contact centers need to reliably detect when a customer utterance is relevant to one of many predefined topics, but the input (ASR transcripts of spontaneous phone conversations) is noisy and hard to process. There is a lack of systematic study and benchmark datasets for this practical problem, motivating the authors to curate a labeled dataset and evaluate different matching approaches.

Method: The authors curate a human-annotated dataset of topic-utterance relevance judgments from real call-center ASR transcripts. They then implement and compare three types of topic-utterance matching models: (1) a regex-based baseline system, (2) zero-shot sentence-embedding based encoders, and (3) Gemini-based lightweight LLM matchers. They also examine two formats for representing topics: concise keyphrases versus more detailed natural language descriptions. They run empirical experiments across these combinations to benchmark performance.

Result: Experiments show that lightweight LLM-based matchers significantly outperform both regex-based and sentence-embedding-based models, particularly when topics are represented with rich natural language descriptions rather than short keyphrases. This demonstrates the advantage of LLMs' contextual understanding in handling noisy, unstructured ASR data.

Conclusion: For real-time topic relevance detection in noisy call-center ASR transcripts, lightweight LLM matchers paired with natural language topic descriptions provide superior accuracy over traditional regex and zero-shot embedding approaches. The work also contributes a human-annotated dataset and benchmark setup for further research on this task.

Abstract: In contact centers, real-time agent-assist tools determine, for each of many predefined topics, whether a live customer utterance is relevant and display a coaching card to the agent when it is. The input is noisy and challenging: ASR(Automatic Speech Recognition) transcripts of spontaneous phone conversations, which can be unclear, repetitive, and mostly lack punctuation. To systematically study this real-world task, we curate a human-annotated topic-utterance judgments dataset sourced from real call-center transcripts. We compare three types of matchers: a regex-based baseline, zero-shot sentence embedding encoders, and Gemini-based LLM matchers. In addition, two types of topic representations are studied in our benchmark:keyphrases and natural language description. Our empirical experiments highlight the superior performance of lightweight LLM matchers over embedding and regex models when equipped with natural language descriptions.

</details>


### [33] [Two locked tests of phase-structure features for transition prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00335)
*Abraham Chachamovits*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Two pre-registered tests found no predictive benefit of adding phase-derived features to a rotary attention model for classifying commitments vs contradictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To empirically test a theoretical claim that phase structure in rotary attention yields additional predictive power, specifically for distinguishing commitment from contradiction endpoints, beyond a baseline model without phase-derived features.

Method: Study 1: Freeze an existing contradiction-category prediction pipeline, add a PC-2 phase-derived feature, and conduct a sealed, pre-specified primary comparison against the baseline using AUROC on 1,136 eligible cases. Study 2: On open blocks b0-b4 (1,415 transitions) develop 15 layer treatments (modifications involving phase structure) evaluated via 20x5 grouped cross-validation folds; advancement required a conjunctive rule: positive PC-2 mean-repeat increment, positive increment in at least 4/5 seed blocks, and positive mean of those five differences.

Result: Study 1: The AUROC improvement from adding PC-2 was +0.00087 with a 99% interval including zero and far below the +0.05 advancement threshold; the model failed to advance. Study 2: None of the 15 layer treatments satisfied the conjunctive advancement criteria (no consistent positive PC-2 effect across blocks).

Conclusion: Across two pre-registered empirical tests, phase-derived features based on PC-2 did not provide the pre-specified level of predictive improvement for commitment vs contradiction classification. The official outcome is that there is no confirmed ranking lift from the proposed phase structure under the locked rules, though the underlying theoretical paper remains unwithdrawn.

Abstract: A published theoretical account of phase structure in rotary attention was subjected to two pre-specified empirical tests of whether phase-derived features improve prediction of a commitment or contradiction endpoint over a baseline that does not receive those features. Study 1 froze a contradiction-category pipeline and scored a sealed primary comparison of PC-2 against baseline. On 1,136 eligible cases the paired AUROC difference was +0.00087. The 99% interval included zero, and the difference did not reach the pre-specified threshold of +0.05. Advancement was not passed. Study 2 developed fifteen layer treatments on open blocks b0-b4 only (1,415 transitions, 20x5 grouped folds). A locked conjunctive rule required a positive PC-2 mean-repeat increment, a positive increment on at least four of five seed blocks, and a positive mean of those five differences. No treatment advanced. The official selection is null. The theoretical paper is not withdrawn. The extra ranking lift was not found under the rules locked in advance.

</details>


### [34] [From Tool Use to Technological Agency: LoopCAT as a Local-First, Open-Source Tool for Translation Technology Education](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00344)
*Gokhan Dogru,Adrià Martín Mor*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces LoopCAT, a local-first translation environment, and an educational framework to teach translation technologies and evaluative judgment, without yet claiming learning outcome evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Translation students must not only use translation tools but also critically evaluate and shape the technological options and outputs these tools provide. Existing tools often lack transparency and pedagogical structure to foster workflow competence, evaluative judgement, and technological agency in one integrated setting.

Method: The authors describe the design and implementation of LoopCAT, drawing on its repository history, code inspection, and verification of a specific development build. They outline system components (local storage, translation memories, terminology, QA, document exchange, optional AI connections) and propose a pedagogical framework organized around four modes of student participation. They specify concrete teaching artifacts: a six-session sequence, UI-localization assignment, placeholder example, and assessment rubric. They distinguish verified capabilities and checks from proposed educational uses and offer a protocol for future classroom evaluation.

Result: LoopCAT has been implemented as an Apache-2.0-licensed, local-first CAT tool with multilingual UI catalogs (English, Catalan, Turkish) and support for translation memories, terminology, QA, document handling, and AI integrations. The authors deliver a structured framework for using LoopCAT in translator education and clearly separate what is technically realized from what is still hypothetical regarding learning outcomes. They also document the current validation status of the software build and package checks.

Conclusion: LoopCAT offers an inspectable, open, and pedagogically structured environment where students can practice operating translation workflows, evaluating outputs, inspecting and configuring mechanisms, and making bounded interventions in translation technology. The paper positions LoopCAT as a testbed for studying how translation decisions interact with data, interfaces, and rules but stresses that the effectiveness of these activities for improving judgment, transfer, or participation awaits empirical validation through classroom studies.

Abstract: Translation students need to learn both how to use translation technologies and how to judge the choices those technologies make available. This article presents LoopCAT, an Apache-2.0-licensed, local-first computer-assisted translation environment co-created with OpenAI Codex using GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6, and proposes a framework connecting workflow competence, evaluative judgement, and technological agency. The account draws on repository history, implementation inspection, and the verification records of an identified development build. LoopCAT combines local project storage, translation memories, terminology, quality assurance, document exchange, and optional connections to local or hosted AI services. Its English, Catalan, and Turkish interface catalogs also make the application itself available as teaching material: students can translate English UI strings into another language, review the existing automatically generated target drafts, import their revisions, and test the interface. We organize these opportunities around four forms of participation: operating a workflow, evaluating outputs, inspecting and configuring mechanisms, and making or defending a bounded intervention. A six-session sequence, a UI-localization assignment, a placeholder example, and an assessment rubric specify how teachers could use the framework. The paper separates implemented capabilities from proposed educational benefits; it reports no new student-learning outcomes. It distinguishes the latest package checks from earlier regression evidence and sets out a protocol for classroom evaluation. LoopCAT provides an inspectable setting for teaching how translation decisions interact with data, interfaces, and software rules. Whether these activities improve judgement, transfer, or participation remains an empirical question.

</details>


### [35] [Detecting Hidden Behaviors in LLMs via Activation-matched Finetuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00351)
*Robin Haselhorst,Lucie Flek,Florian Mai*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes an unsupervised method, activation-matched finetuning, to detect hidden or backdoored behaviors in large language models without knowing the trigger or target behavior in advance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models may contain covert behaviors such as backdoors, sleeper agents, sandbagging, or topic-specific censorship that only activate under narrow conditions, and existing detection methods often require knowing the trigger or having labeled data. There is a need for a general, unsupervised way to discover such hidden behaviors without prior knowledge of what to look for.

Method: The authors introduce activation-matched finetuning. They take a suspect model and a benign, publicly available anchor model, then finetune the anchor so that its internal activations match those of the suspect model on a small, benign training corpus. This causes the anchor to learn the suspect’s normal (benign) computation, but not any hidden behavior that only appears in a sparse trigger region of the input space. At evaluation time, they compute a residual score for each prompt based on the difference between the activation-matched anchor and the suspect model; unusually large residuals indicate that the suspect model is doing something atypical, flagging potential trigger prompts and their semantic neighbors.

Result: Across both third‑party and custom-trained models, activation-matched finetuning reliably exposes the presence of hidden behaviors, successfully identifying trigger prompts and nearby inputs that cause anomalous computation. The method works without any supervision about triggers or targets. In experiments with a defense-aware attacker that attempts to hide the behavior from this detector, the attack fails to fully suppress the detection signal without degrading or removing the hidden behavior itself.

Conclusion: Activation-matched finetuning offers a practical, unsupervised mechanism for defenders to detect backdoors and other covert behaviors in language models without prior knowledge of the specific trigger or malicious behavior. Because attempts to evade this detection either fail or substantially weaken the hidden behavior, the method appears robust to natural, adaptive attackers and is a promising tool for LLM safety auditing.

Abstract: Large language models can hide hidden behaviors that activate only under narrow conditions, such as backdoor triggers, sleeper-agent deployment cues, sandbagging, or topic-conditioned censorship. Such behaviors are difficult to detect without prior knowledge what to look for. We present activation-matched finetuning, an unsupervised detection method that assumes no knowledge of the trigger or the target behavior. Given a suspect model and a publicly available anchor, we finetune the anchor to reproduce the suspect's activations on a small benign corpus, and score each evaluation prompt by the residual between the two models. Since no benign corpus covers the sparse trigger region, the reference learns the benign computation but not the hidden behavior. Therefore, trigger prompts -- and, crucially, their semantic neighbors -- incur a large residual that signal the presence of unusual behavior to the defender. Testing our method across third-party models and custom models, activation-matched finetuning surfaces hidden behavior reliably. Furthermore, we empirically consider a natural defense-aware attack and showcase that it fails to suppress our detection method without sacrificing the behavior itself.

</details>


### [36] [Neurosymbolics for Data Engineering: Achieving Long Context Token Reduction Without Finetuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00367)
*Vishvesh Bhat*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They add a new neurosymbolic layer to existing LLMs that both boosts logical/Text-to-SQL reasoning without finetuning and cuts long-context compute from quadratic toward linear by symbolic selection/compression of relevant tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are used for data engineering tasks like Text-to-SQL and spreadsheet automation but suffer from (1) limited reasoning accuracy without expensive finetuning/RLHF, and (2) quadratic time and memory cost for long-context inference, which makes large-context applications slow and costly.

Method: Propose a drop-in neurosymbolic layer that can be inserted into existing Transformer backbones. The layer performs symbolic reasoning over intermediate representations to better handle logical structure and, for long contexts, symbolically identifies and compresses the most relevant contextual information so that the downstream Transformer processes a reduced, more focused sequence.

Result: On reasoning benchmarks such as BIRD-CRITIC and LiveSQLBench, the new layer yields an average accuracy improvement of 85% without any task-specific finetuning or RLHF. For long-context tasks, token usage is reduced by over 50%, and empirical effective time complexity is reduced from O(n^2) to approximately O(n) on some tasks.

Conclusion: A neurosymbolic layer can simultaneously improve finetuning-free reasoning performance for data engineering tasks and alleviate the quadratic computational bottleneck of long-context Transformers, making LLMs more reliable and cost-effective for real-world data engineering workloads.

Abstract: Large Language Models are increasingly deployed for sophisticated data engineering tasks such as generating structured queries from natural language, Text-to-SQL, and automating complex spreadsheet operations. However, maximizing their utility demands both higher finetuning-free accuracy and solutions to the computational bottleneck imposed by the Transformer architectures inherent quadratic (On2) time complexity. This paper introduces a novel drop-in neurosymbolic layer designed to seamlessly integrate into existing LLM backbones enhancing logical reasoning and mitigating long-context resource consumption. On the reasoning front, the layer immediately and significantly improves performance yielding an average accuracy increase of 85% across rigorous benchmarks including BIRD-CRITIC and LiveSQLBench, critically achieving these gains without any task specific finetuning or RLHF. Concurrently, we repurpose this approach to address the severe computational strain of long context inference. By leveraging symbolic processing to prioritize and compress relevant contextual information the layer reduces the effective token usage by over 50% and brings the effective time complexity down from O(n2) to approximately O(n) on certain long context tasks. This dual impact approach not only makes LLMs substantially more reliable for data engineering but also drastically reduces the computational pressure on inference chips, making long context tasks more manageable and cost effective.

</details>


### [37] [Removable and Irreducible: A Token-Cost Ledger for the Multilingual Tokenization Tax](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00378)
*Madhulatha Mandarapu,Sandeep Kunkunuru*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper analyzes why non-English texts incur higher token and compute costs in large language models and decomposes this “token tax” into removable and intrinsic components using an information-theoretic framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models use more tokens and thus more quadratic attention compute for non-English, especially non-Latin scripts, creating inefficiency and inequity. The authors want to know how much of this extra cost is due to poor tokenization (representation) versus inherent information content of the language, and to give a principled accounting of these costs.

Method: They frame tokenization as a source coding problem, relating sequence length to Shannon entropy and vocabulary size. Using parallel data (FLORES-200 across eight languages), they construct a token-cost ledger that decomposes token usage into coding redundancy, residual slack, intrinsic content, and a grapheme-to-phoneme term. They train script-matched tokenizers on small data (1,012 sentences) and design constructed codes to approach the information-theoretic floor, then compare token and implied attention costs to a production tokenizer.

Result: Production tokenizers use up to 8.9× more tokens for some Indic scripts than for English on the same content. Script-matched codes trained on only 1,012 sentences can remove a median 64% of this excess token cost, and an information-theoretic “script-fair” floor shows intrinsic content differences across languages are under 6%. A constructed code removes 98% of redundancy on a controlled source, and the measured token tax can correspond to up to 79× higher attention compute. They provide an open harness implementing their ledger and experiments.

Conclusion: Most of the non-English “token tax” is representational, not due to inherent information differences between languages. Better, script-aware tokenization and coding schemes can remove a large portion of the excess token and compute cost, though the work is explicitly about compute/memory accounting, not model quality. The authors contribute a unified ledger to separate removable from intrinsic costs and tools for further investigation, while acknowledging open questions around orthography’s role and performance impacts.

Abstract: Large language models pay a well-documented tax on non-English text: the same content costs several times more tokens, and because attention is quadratic in sequence length, far more compute. We ask how much of this tax is removable. Framing the token layer as source coding -- transformer compute is monotone in sequence length, whose per-atom floor is the Shannon rate $H/\log_2 V$, an object already applied to tokenizers in prior work -- we assemble a token-cost ledger that splits each language's cost, at fixed parallel content, into a removable coding redundancy, a residual coding slack, an intrinsic-content term, and an orthogonal, irreducible grapheme-to-phoneme term that governs the multimodal rather than the text cost. On FLORES-200 across eight languages, a production tokenizer costs up to $8.9\times$ more tokens for Indic scripts than for English; a script-matched code trained on $1,012$ sentences removes a median $64\%$ of that excess (bootstrap 95\% CI $[0.638, 0.647]$), and a script-fair information floor shows the intrinsic content differs by under $6\%$ -- the tax is representational, not informational. A constructed code removes $98\%$ of a controlled source's redundancy, and the token tax implies up to $79\times$ attention cost. We are explicit about scope and failure: this is compute-and-memory accounting, not a model-quality claim; we neither measure nor claim the cross-lingual direction of the orthographic term; and our matched code is a conservative small-data demonstration. We contribute the unifying ledger, the removable-versus-intrinsic attribution, and an open one-command harness.

</details>


### [38] [Late Transformer Layers Recode Syntax Canonically: Evidence from Greek Scrambling and Cross-Layer Generalisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00416)
*Christos Nikolaos Zacharopoulos,Revekka Kyriakoglou,Chara Tsoukala,Théo Desbordes*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that in Greek-tuned LLMs, late transformer layers actively recode non-canonical word orders into canonical ones, rather than simply losing syntactic information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While prior probing work shows that syntactic structure is decodable in early and middle transformer layers, it is unclear what happens to that syntactic information in later layers. The authors aim to determine whether late layers merely lose syntactic detail or instead transform it into a different representational format, focusing on word-order alternations in Modern Greek.

Method: The authors use cross-layer generalisation probing on three large language models fine-tuned on Greek. They evaluate models with tightly controlled minimal sentence pairs involving object-relative clauses in Modern Greek, contrasting canonical SVO and non-canonical VSO orders with matched propositional content. Probes are trained on late layers (20–31) to distinguish canonical vs. non-canonical sentences and then tested on each early layer individually. They analyze transfer accuracy and probe coefficient signs across layers, applying cluster-based correction for statistical testing.

Result: When probes trained on late layers are applied to early layers, they show below-chance transfer performance (cluster-corrected p<0.01), misclassifying 99.3% of non-canonical VSO sentences as canonical SVO. Around layer 22, probe coefficients systematically reverse sign, indicating that the representational axis distinguishing canonical vs. non-canonical orders has been flipped in late layers. This pattern implies an active recoding toward canonical word-order representations rather than mere degradation of syntactic information.

Conclusion: Late transformer layers in Greek-tuned LLMs do not simply lose syntactic information; instead, they undergo a representational format change that effectively recodes non-canonical word orders toward canonical SVO-like representations. This goes beyond the known decline in syntactic decodability and suggests that late layers implement a directed normalization or canonicalization step. The authors also propose that this recoding pattern yields concrete, testable predictions for human EEG/MEG decoding using the same stimuli, and they release code and materials for further study.

Abstract: Probing studies have established that syntactic information is decodable in early and middle transformer layers, but what happens to that information in later layers remains poorly understood. We apply a cross-layer generalisation analysis to three Greek-tuned large language models evaluated on tightly controlled minimal pairs: object-relative constructions in Modern Greek, where canonical (Subject-Verb-Object; SVO) and non-canonical (Verb-Subject-Object; VSO) orders differ only in within-clause word order, while preserving propositional meaning. When a probe trained on late layers (20-31) is tested on each early layer individually, it produces below-chance transfer (cluster-corrected, p<0.01), classifying 99.3% of non-canonical sentences as canonical. Probe coefficients reverse sign around layer 22, indicating a directional recoding toward the canonical form rather than simple information loss. These findings characterise a representational format change in late transformer layers that goes beyond the well-established decline in syntactic decodability, and they generate a directly testable prediction for human EEG and MEG decoding studies using the same stimuli. Code and stimuli are publicly available on OSF.

</details>


### [39] [(V)LMs generalize beyond surface co-occurrence: Evidence from cross-modal number agreement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00443)
*Zach Studdiford,Kanishka Misra*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper tests whether vision-language models (VLMs) learn abstract grammatical number rules rather than just memorizing word co-occurrences, by training them on novel nouns whose number is signaled only visually or only linguistically, and finds they can generalize number knowledge cross-modally, suggesting genuine abstraction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a debate about whether large language models (LLMs) and related systems truly learn abstract grammatical rules (like singular vs. plural) or merely track surface co-occurrence statistics between specific words (e.g., “cats are” vs. “cat is”). Text-only tests cannot resolve this, because textual cues to number are pervasive and tightly coupled to particular lexical items. To probe abstraction more rigorously, the authors exploit multimodal models that can take visual input, asking whether such models can infer and generalize grammatical number when the crucial evidence comes only from the visual modality instead of from text co-occurrences.

Method: The authors use vision-language models and introduce pairs of novel nouns by adding new embeddings for them. During training, they update only these new embeddings, leaving the rest of the model fixed, which isolates how the model incorporates new lexical items. They construct different learning conditions: in some, grammatical number (singular vs. plural) can be diagnosed only from visual information; in others, it is disambiguated via textual cues. They then assess: (1) behavioral generalization (whether the model uses correct number morphology with the new nouns), (2) representational dynamics (how the internal embeddings and activations evolve and encode number), and (3) causal mechanisms (e.g., via interventions or ablations to see which components support number generalization). They compare performance and internal representations across the visual-only vs. text-cue conditions.

Result: The vision-language models show substantial cross-modal generalization of grammatical number. Even when number is learned from purely visual cues, models can appropriately apply singular/plural distinctions in linguistic contexts, and vice versa. The internal representations and mechanisms involved in handling number appear similar across the conditions where number is learned from visual vs. textual cues. Analyses of representations and causal roles of components indicate that number information is encoded and used in ways that do not merely mirror direct word-level co-occurrence statistics.

Conclusion: The findings indicate that vision-language models, as statistical learners, are capable of forming abstract representations of grammatical number that generalize beyond simple surface co-occurrence patterns. The similar internal treatment of number learned from linguistic vs. extra-linguistic (visual) cues suggests that these models perform abstraction-like computations, supporting the view that they can go beyond rote memorization of lexical patterns and exhibit behavior compatible with genuine rule-like generalization.

Abstract: Language models learn about grammatical number primarily from co-occurrence, and show frequency effects as a result---sometimes taken to indicate that they do not learn abstract ``rules'', and are instead dependent on specific lexical items. Testing generalization with text stimuli alone cannot settle this debate, since distributional cues (is/are, this/these) easily give number away. We instead use cross-modal generalization as a tool to investigate abstractions in LMs that can also accept visual inputs (VLMs), restricting the evidence that diagnoses number to an extra-linguistic modality. We teach VLMs pairs of new nouns by adding new embeddings and only updating them during learning, comparing conditions where number is diagnosed by visual cues alone against ones where it is disambiguated by text. Across behavior, representational dynamics, and causal mechanisms, we find non-trivial evidence for cross-modal generalization across both exposure conditions, and that linguistic vs. extra-linguistic cue conditions are treated in similar ways in the internal mechanisms of the model. This suggests that statistical learners like VLMs can generalize beyond surface-level co-occurrence and show genuine abstraction-compatible behavior.

</details>


### [40] [Location-Aware Language Models via Secondary Embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00454)
*Gokul Srinivasagan,Munir Georges*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They add lightweight geo-spatial signals (lat/long + special masking) to existing language model embeddings, greatly improving spatial understanding with minimal retraining and no tokenizer changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard pretrained transformers are weak at representing geo-locational semantics (e.g., understanding places, distances, and spatial relations) because they only see place names as ordinary tokens without explicit geographic grounding. This leads to poor performance on tasks requiring spatial reasoning or place-aware understanding, despite strong performance on common NLP benchmarks.

Method: They introduce a model-agnostic input augmentation scheme that: (1) associates place names with their latitude and longitude; (2) injects these structured geographic signals into the input representations of a pretrained model without altering the tokenizer; and (3) applies a location-focused masking strategy during training to force the model to align textual place representations with their real-world spatial relationships. The approach is lightweight and only requires a brief additional training phase on top of existing models.

Result: Experiments show that the augmented models achieve significantly better geo-spatial alignment and understanding of spatial entities, while retaining similar performance to the original models on standard NLP benchmarks like GLUE. The approach works consistently across different pretrained architectures and model sizes, and the added training cost is small (on the order of minutes).

Conclusion: Injecting simple, structured geographic signals and using targeted masking can effectively make pretrained language models geo-spatially aware without expensive retraining or architectural changes. This yields better spatial representations with minimal overhead and no loss on general NLP tasks, and the technique is broadly applicable across model types and scales.

Abstract: Pretrained transformer-based language models achieve strong performance across a wide range of NLP tasks but remain limited in encoding geo-locational semantics, leading to suboptimal representations of place names and spatial entities. In this work, we propose a lightweight, model-agnostic approach for injecting geo-spatial awareness into pretrained embeddings without modifying the tokenizer or requiring costly retraining. Our method augments input representations with structured geographic signals by combining location names with their corresponding latitude and longitude, and employs a location-focused masking to better align textual representations with real-world spatial relationships. This design allows the model to incorporate geo-spatial context while preserving existing semantic and syntactic knowledge. Experimental results demonstrate substantial improvements in geo-spatial alignment while maintaining comparable performance on standard NLP benchmarks such as GLUE. The method is computationally efficient, requiring only minutes of additional training, and generalizes across multiple model architectures and scales.

</details>


### [41] [Toppling the Hierarchy in Byte-level Language Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00463)
*Lukas Edman,Alexander Fraser*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies why hierarchical byte-level language models struggle with precise character manipulation compared to pure byte-level models, identifying byte-level attention as the key factor and highlighting a trade-off between efficiency and character-level understanding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the popularity of byte-level models that use hierarchical structures for efficiency, they often fail at tasks requiring exact character-level control. The paper aims to understand the root cause of these failures and to clarify how architectural choices affect character-level capabilities.

Method: The authors compare state-of-the-art hierarchical byte-level models (which downsample bytes to words and then upsample back) to pure byte-level models on character manipulation tasks. They also perform ablations of transformer layers, separating attention and feed-forward components, to isolate which parts of the architecture are responsible for character-level behavior.

Result: Pure byte-level models consistently outperform hierarchical byte-level variants on tasks involving character manipulation. The ablation studies show that byte-level attention, rather than feed-forward components or hierarchical processing, is the main driver of strong character-level behavior.

Conclusion: Hierarchical byte-level architectures introduce an inherent limitation in fine-grained character understanding, even though they are more computationally efficient. Byte-level attention is crucial for strong character-level manipulation, implying a fundamental trade-off between efficiency and precise character modeling in current hierarchical designs.

Abstract: This work examines recent byte-level models and their failure to perfectly manipulate characters. State-of-the-art byte-level models use a hierarchical structure, starting at the byte level, downsampling to the word level, and then upsampling back to bytes. While this improves training and inference efficiency, we find that the hierarchical design itself limits character-level understanding, with pure byte-level models consistently outperforming hierarchical variants on character manipulation tasks. Ablating transformer layers into attention and feed-forward components further reveals that byte-level attention is the primary mechanism driving this behavior. Together, our results provide an explanation for the character-level failures of hierarchical byte models and establish a clear trade-off between computational efficiency and fine-grained character understanding.

</details>


### [42] [TRIS: A Tri-Layer Retrieval Integrity Sieve Against Knowledge Poisoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00470)
*Muhaimin Bin Munir,Akib Jawad Ononto,Nazia Shehnaz Joynab,Bhavani Thuraisingham,Latifur Khan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Tri-Layer Sieve, a middleware defense that protects Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems from poisoning attacks by filtering and validating retrieved documents across three complementary layers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG systems rely heavily on retrieved documents, which are implicitly trusted. Adversaries can inject a small number of carefully crafted passages into the corpus that dense retrievers over-select, causing large language models to generate attacker-specified, incorrect answers. Existing systems lack robust, practical defenses against such retrieval-stage poisoning, particularly under black-box and white-box (e.g., HotFlip) settings.

Method: The authors design Tri-Layer Sieve, a three-stage middleware defense that operates between retrieval and generation: (1) cross-embedding-space clustering with an independent judge model to identify and downweight outlier or suspicious passages, (2) structural filtering to detect trigger-payload artifacts within documents (e.g., segments that appear optimized to trigger the model then deliver malicious content), and (3) LLM consistency verification to check whether candidate evidence is consistent across multiple perspectives/queries and with the model’s own expectations. The defense leverages the fact that a single poisoned document must simultaneously satisfy retrieval geometry, internal trigger-payload structure, and generation influence, making it vulnerable to detection when examined through these diverse lenses.
