They evaluate with Contriever retrieval (k=50) and consider both black-box poisoning (PoisonedRAG) and white-box attacks (HotFlip), plus paraphrased, architecture-aware adversaries.

Result: On Natural Questions, HotpotQA, and MS-MARCO with Contriever (k=50), Tri-Layer Sieve reduces black-box attack success rate from 67.0/87.0/64.0% to 3.0/14.0/4.0%. It mitigates white-box HotFlip attacks on NQ from about 74% ASR down to 27.8% when Layer 3 (consistency verification) is enabled. The defense also drives the mean reciprocal rank (MRR) of poisoned documents to 0.000, meaning they effectively never appear among top-ranked results, and restores clean-task accuracy from heavily degraded 13–33% under attack back up to 58–76%. Against an adaptive adversary that paraphrases triggers to bypass structural filters, enabling the consistency layer still halves ASR (32.0% → 15.0% on NQ) and improves clean accuracy by 18 points, at an additional latency cost of roughly 16–19 seconds per query in live retrieval settings.

Conclusion: Tri-Layer Sieve is an effective practical middleware defense for RAG systems against data poisoning at the retrieval stage. By combining cross-embedding clustering, structural trigger-payload analysis, and LLM-based consistency checking, it exploits the inherent fragility of poisoned documents, which must satisfy multiple incompatible constraints. The approach substantially reduces attack success rates and restores accuracy across various datasets and attack regimes, including adaptive adversaries, at the cost of moderate added latency, demonstrating a viable path toward more robust RAG deployments.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds large language models in external corpora, but implicit trust in retrieved documents creates a critical attack surface: PoisonedRAG shows that a handful of crafted passages can dominate dense retrieval and steer generation toward attacker-chosen answers. We present the Tri-Layer Sieve, a middleware defense that sanitizes retrieved evidence through cross-embedding-space clustering with an independent judge model, structural filtering of trigger-payload artifacts, and LLM consistency verification. The design exploits a key weakness of retrieval-stage poisoning: a single document must satisfy one embedding geometry, one internal Trigger-Payload structure, and one generation objective - rarely all three simultaneously, a fragility that persists even against an adaptive attacker who paraphrases around it. On Natural Questions, HotpotQA, and MS-MARCO with Contriever retrieval (k=50), the Sieve reduces black-box Attack Success Rate from 67.0/87.0/64.0% to 3.0/14.0/4.0%, mitigates white-box HotFlip attacks from ~74% to 27.8% on NQ with Layer 3 enabled, and drives poisoned-document MRR to 0.000, while restoring clean accuracy from 13-33% under attack to 58-76%. Under an architecture-aware adversary who paraphrases triggers to evade the structural filter, enabling the consistency layer halves adaptive ASR (32.0% to 15.0% on NQ) while raising clean accuracy by 18 points, at an added latency of ~16-19 s/query under live retrieval.

</details>


### [43] [Exploring Collaboration between a language and a non-language agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00474)
*Harini S,Somesh Singh,Yaman K Singla,Rajiv Ratn Shah,David Doermann,Balaji Krishnamurthy*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces LLAMIA-Bench and LLAMIA to study and improve collaboration between LLMs and non-language agents (a chess engine), showing that directly internalizing latent states outperforms textual verbalization and avoids a growing 'verbalization debt.'


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs are used to orchestrate specialized agents, many of the strongest domain agents (e.g., chess engines, robots) are non-linguistic. Current integration requires translating their continuous states into text, which may be lossy and limit performance. The authors want to understand if this verbalization is a fundamental bottleneck and how to enable tighter, more efficient collaboration between LLMs and non-language agents.

Method: They design LLAMIA-Bench, six collaborative chess tasks that require an LLM and a chess engine to work together, covering behavioral imitation, state assessment, and natural-language explanation. They propose latent state internalization, where the non-language agent's continuous internal representations are projected into the LLM’s token sequence as learned state tokens, which are dynamically re-encoded as the game state changes. They compare this approach to standard textual verbalization across model scales (4B–14B parameters) and tasks.

Result: Across all LLAMIA-Bench tasks, latent state internalization consistently outperforms verbalized integration. The performance gap, termed 'verbalization debt,' grows over training and remains even as model size increases. A single 14B-parameter model, LLAMIA, trained with latent state internalization, matches or surpasses specialized task models and strong frontier LLMs (e.g., GPT-5.1 with tool access) on all benchmark tasks and shows better out-of-distribution generalization, where task-specific finetuned models fail.

Conclusion: Textual verbalization of non-language agents’ internal states is a significant bottleneck for LLM-agent collaboration, leading to an accumulating 'verbalization debt.' Directly internalizing latent states as learned tokens within the LLM enables tighter integration, better performance, and stronger generalization. LLAMIA-Bench provides a controlled setting (chess) to study these effects, and LLAMIA demonstrates that a single model can effectively integrate with a strong non-linguistic agent and outperform both verbalized approaches and large frontier models.

Abstract: LLMs are increasingly deployed as orchestrators that coordinate specialized subagents to solve complex tasks through natural language. However, in many important domains like game playing and robotics, the strongest available agents are not language models. Integrating non-language agents with LLMs would require \emph{verbalization}: compressing their rich continuous representations into sparse textual summaries at each interaction step. To study whether verbalization constitutes a bottleneck, we introduce \textsc{LLAMIA-Bench}, a suite of six diverse collaborative chess tasks spanning three facets: behavioral imitation, state assessment, and natural-language explanation. Each task instantiates a well-established chess problem that neither the LLM nor the chess engine can solve alone. To solve LLM collaboration with non-language agents, we introduce \emph{latent state internalization}, which projects the subagent's continuous representations directly into the LLM's token stream as learned state tokens, with dynamic re-encoding as actions advance the environment state. Comparing internalization to verbalized integration, our experiments reveal a consistent \emph{verbalization debt}: the performance gap widens throughout training and persists as the LLM scales from 4B to 14B parameters. A single 14B model, \textsc{LLAMIA}, trained with latent state internalization, matches or exceeds task specialists and frontier models including GPT-5.1 with tool access across all benchmark tasks, and generalizes out-of-distribution where task-specific finetunes collapse

</details>


### [44] [Are Near-Tied LLM Rankings Robust to Family-DIF-Guided Benchmark Recomposition?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00482)
*Qiaoyuan Zheng,Yiqu Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that small performance differences between language models on leaderboards (under 1 percentage point) are often unstable and can flip depending on which test items are included.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Leaderboard culture in language modeling often treats very small score differences as strong evidence that one model is better than another. However, benchmarks are made of many heterogeneous items, and models from different "families" (e.g., architectures, training regimens, or owners) may have specific strengths and weaknesses on subsets of items. The authors want to know: (1) how much model rankings depend on the specific composition of benchmark items, and (2) whether near-ties on leaderboards are trustworthy indicators of real performance differences across model families.

Method: The authors use item-level response data from five different language-model benchmarks and apply a spectral approximation to multidimensional item-response theory (MIRT) without using explicit family labels. They split models into two owner-disjoint halves. In one half, they identify items that exhibit low residual differential item functioning (low-DIF) across model families, meaning items whose behavior is relatively stable and not biased toward particular families. They then construct frozen subtests with source- and difficulty-balanced weights from these low-DIF items. These subtests are used to score models in the other half. As a control, they create matched-random subtests of identical length and difficulty distribution. They compare model rankings using: (a) the full benchmark, (b) the low-DIF weighted benchmark, and (c) the matched-random subtests, focusing on how many model pairs within one percentage point of each other swap order between these conditions. They also pre-specify and run population perturbations and check replication of item–family residual signatures across the owner folds.

Result: Across benchmarks, global rankings based on full benchmarks and low-DIF subtests remain highly correlated (Kendall’s τ_b around .900–.948). However, for four out of five benchmarks, between about 31% and 47% of cross-family model pairs that were within one percentage point on the full benchmark reverse order when scored on the low-DIF subtests. These reversal rates are 16.9–28.6 percentage points higher than those observed in matched-random subtests, and these excesses are statistically significant at p = .001. The fifth benchmark does not show a reliable excess over random (−0.9 percentage points, p = .689). The instability pattern remains under all pre-specified perturbations to the model population. Moreover, the residual item–family interaction patterns ("signatures") are reproducible between the two owner-disjoint halves, indicating that these effects are systematic rather than noise. No model family enjoys a consistent advantage across all benchmarks.

Conclusion: Even when overall benchmark rankings of language models appear stable, near-tie orderings (within ~1 percentage point) are often fragile and can flip depending on which items are included in the evaluation, especially across different model families. Many small leaderboard gaps therefore lack robustness to benchmark composition. The authors argue that claims based on sub-one-point leaderboard differences should be accompanied by evidence that those orderings are robust to changes in test composition (e.g., via low-DIF or similar analyses), and that benchmark design and interpretation should explicitly account for item-level and family-specific effects.

Abstract: Small leaderboard gaps are often interpreted as evidence that one language model is better than another, but their sign may depend on which benchmark items are included. We test this using item-level responses from five benchmarks and a family-label-free spectral approximation to multidimensional item-response theory (MIRT). In owner-disjoint folds, one owner half identifies items with low residual differential item functioning across model families (low-DIF); the resulting frozen, source- and easiness-balanced weights score models in the other half, while equally short matched-random subtests control for generic subtest variation. Full-benchmark and low-DIF rankings remain strongly correlated ($τ_b=.900$--$.948$). Yet in four of five benchmarks, 30.9--47.1\% of cross-family pairs initially within one percentage point reverse order, exceeding their matched-random medians by 16.9--28.6 percentage points (all $p=.001$). The fifth benchmark shows no reliable excess ($-0.9$ points, $p=.689$). The pattern survives all pre-specified population perturbations, and residual item--family signatures replicate across owner halves; however, no family shows a consistent advantage across benchmarks. Thus, globally stable rankings can still leave individual near-tie orderings sensitive to benchmark composition, and sub-one-point leaderboard gaps should be accompanied by evidence that the implied ordering is composition-robust.

</details>


### [45] [EvoFlint: An Evolutionary Atlas of Multi-Turn LLM Vulnerabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00487)
*Feitong Qiao,Liren Peng,Shiming Ren,Aishwarya Jadhav,Arghavan Bahadorinejad,Marinette Chen,Muhan Zhang,Abdulaziz Suria,Gennevi Lu,Anish Das Sarma*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes EvoFlint, an evolutionary quality-diversity search framework for multi-turn red-teaming of language models, focusing on discovering and organizing diverse attack strategies rather than just generating successful attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing frontier language models can still be manipulated via multi-turn conversations even when they block harmful single-turn prompts, and current automated red-teaming mainly seeks isolated successful attacks without systematically mapping failure modes.

Method: The authors frame multi-turn red-teaming as a search problem and design EvoFlint, where attack strategies are phased conversation plans evolved via LLM-based mutation and crossover. A Pareto fitness function balances attack success rate and peak harm severity, while a risk-indexed archive uses novelty search with local competition on strategy embeddings to maintain diversity. A generation-level memory stores insights about the target model and conditions further strategy generation.

Result: On the HarmBench-test benchmark, EvoFlint achieves notable attack success rates against several target models: 35.8% on Claude Sonnet 4.6, 59.7% on GPT-5.4, 94.3% on Qwen3-32B, and 98.7% on GPT-4o (baseline), demonstrating its effectiveness in uncovering multi-turn vulnerabilities.

Conclusion: EvoFlint produces a structured, risk-organized archive of multi-turn attack strategies, revealing which harm categories each target model’s safety training covers or misses, and showing that quality-diversity evolutionary search is a powerful paradigm for systematic multi-turn red-teaming.

Abstract: Frontier language models that refuse harmful single-turn prompts often comply when the same intent is reached gradually over many turns, making multi-turn attacks one of the least understood failure modes of large language models. Most automated red-teaming methods treat this as a generation problem: produce attacks that break the model. We argue it is better framed as a search problem: discover, organize, and iteratively refine a diverse archive of attack strategies, producing a structured map of how a target model fails rather than a list of one-off successes. We introduce EvoFlint, which applies evolutionary quality-diversity search to multi-turn red-teaming. Attack strategies are phased conversation plans, not raw prompts, and are evolved through LLM-driven mutation and crossover. A Pareto fitness over attack success rate and peak severity preserves selection signal from near-miss attacks. A risk-indexed archive runs novelty search with local competition over strategy description embeddings inside each cell, maintaining diversity without committing to a predefined style taxonomy. A generation-level memory accumulates target-model insights across the population and feeds them back into strategy generation. On the HarmBench-test split, EvoFlint reaches attack success rates of 35.8% on Claude Sonnet 4.6, 59.7% on GPT-5.4, and 94.3% on Qwen3-32B, alongside 98.7% on the older GPT-4o included as a baseline reference. The resulting archive, organized by risk category, exposes for each target which categories of harm its safety training has and has not covered.

</details>


### [46] [MemeBridge: A Dataset for Benchmarking and Mitigating the Bidirectional Cultural Gap in Meme Interpretation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00491)
*Hangxiao Zhu,Suliu Qin,Zhuoyan Li,Ming Jiang,Yu Zhang,Meng Xia*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces MemeBridge, a dataset for evaluating and improving cross-cultural meme understanding between U.S. and Chinese participants, and shows that fine-tuning LLMs on it improves cross-cultural meme interpretation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-cultural communication via memes is difficult because memes are culturally dense and ambiguous, and existing LLM benchmarks lack the necessary cultural context for accurate interpretation. There is also a need to understand not just how another culture interprets content, but how one culture (incorrectly) anticipates the other’s misunderstandings.

Method: The authors build MemeBridge, a curated dataset of U.S.-originated memes annotated through a multi-stage crowdsourcing pipeline. They collect two perspectives: Chinese participants’ actual interpretations of U.S. memes and U.S. participants’ expectations of how others might misunderstand them. They validate data with human agreement checks and GPT-based classification, and annotate each meme with sentiment, emotion, cultural significance, and knowledge type. They then probe multiple LLMs on the dataset and fine-tune models using MemeBridge.

Result: They find that U.S. participants’ anticipated misunderstandings of memes by other cultures are often inaccurate, showing asymmetries in cultural understanding. Existing LLMs trained in different cultural contexts show partial but limited cross-cultural meme understanding, struggling with more complex interpretations. Fine-tuning on MemeBridge leads to improved model performance on cross-cultural meme interpretation tasks.

Conclusion: MemeBridge provides a richer, bidirectional benchmark for evaluating cross-cultural comprehension, especially of culturally dense content like memes. The dataset exposes human and model asymmetries in cross-cultural perspective-taking and demonstrates that culturally grounded training data can substantially enhance LLMs’ cross-cultural interpretive capabilities.

Abstract: Communicating across cultures is inherently challenging, especially through culturally dense and ambiguous formats like memes. While people expect large language models (LLMs) to hold promise for bridging such gaps, existing benchmark datasets often fail to capture the cultural context necessary for accurate interpretation. To address this, we introduce MemeBridge, a curated dataset centered on U.S.-originated memes, designed to capture two complementary perspectives: (1) how Chinese participants interpret these memes, and (2) how U.S. participants anticipate how people from other cultures might misunderstand them. Here, context refers to implicit cultural knowledge, including background beliefs, norms, and shared assumptions that shape meme comprehension. The dataset was constructed via a multi-stage crowdsourcing pipeline with rigorous validation, including human agreement checks and GPT-based classification verification. Each meme is annotated with sentiment, emotion, cultural significance, and knowledge type, providing rich supervision for downstream tasks. Notably, we observe that the anticipated misunderstandings from U.S. participants are often inaccurate, highlighting the asymmetries in cultural understanding and the challenges of adopting perspectives beyond one's own. This bidirectional framing, which focuses on both expression and perception, enables more nuanced benchmarking of cross-cultural comprehension. Our probing of multiple LLMs reveals that while models developed in different cultural contexts exhibit partial cross-cultural understanding, they often struggle with sophisticated interpretations. By contrast, fine-tuning with MemeBridge improves model performance, underscoring the value of culturally grounded resources for training and evaluating LLMs in globally diverse settings.

</details>


### [47] [Human-Anchored Factuality Evaluation with Strategic Annotation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00494)
*Yu Wang,Craig Erickson,Kevin Small*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a human-anchored factuality evaluation framework that efficiently combines LLM judge predictions with selectively sampled human annotations using a failure-space analysis–guided policy, improving the effective sample size over standard sampling strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based factuality judges are scalable but systematically biased compared to humans, often under- or over-estimating factual accuracy. Since human annotation is expensive, there is a need for methods that can correct or account for these biases using only a small number of human labels, while still obtaining statistically valid estimates of factual accuracy across large datasets.

Method: The authors formulate factuality evaluation under a limited human-annotation budget. They analyze structured failure modes driving misalignment between LLM judges and humans—such as incomplete evidence, temporal mismatch, unverifiable claims, and rubric misalignment—and introduce a factuality-specific annotation policy design pipeline based on failure-space analysis (FSA). FSA identifies and uses diverse predictive signals of judge-human disagreement to design sampling policies that selectively query humans on examples most informative for correcting judge bias, instead of relying only on uncertainty-based sampling or uniform sampling.

Result: On an internal reference-based factuality system (AutoFA) and the RAGTruth benchmark, judge predictions alone substantially underestimate human-annotated factual accuracy. Using the FSA-guided annotation policy, the authors achieve more efficient use of human labels, with effective sample size gains of 40.3% on AutoFA and 27.1% on RAGTruth versus uniform and uncertainty-driven baselines.

Conclusion: Structured misalignment between LLM factuality judges and human annotators cannot be addressed by simple uncertainty-based sampling. By explicitly modeling failure modes via failure-space analysis and using them to guide selective human annotation, one can obtain more accurate and statistically efficient human-anchored factuality estimates, significantly improving annotation efficiency under limited budgets.

Abstract: LLM-based factuality judges provide scalable evaluation signals, but their metrics are often systematically biased relative to human judgments. We study human-anchored factuality evaluation under limited annotation budgets, where judge predictions on the full dataset are combined with human labels on a small selectively sampled subset to obtain statistically valid estimates. The efficiency of this approach depends critically on which examples receive human annotation: in factuality evaluation, judge-human misalignment is not driven solely by low confidence, but also by structured failure modes such as incomplete evidence, temporal mismatch, unverifiable claims, and rubric misalignment. To exploit this structure, we introduce a factuality-specific annotation policy design pipeline that uses failure-space analysis (FSA) to derive diverse predictive signals for modeling human-judge misalignment. On an internal reference-based factuality evaluation system (AutoFA) and RAGTruth, where judge-predicted estimates substantially underestimate human-annotated factual accuracy, our FSA-guided policy improves annotation efficiency over uniform sampling and uncertainty-driven baselines, achieving effective-sample-size gains of 40.3% on AutoFA and 27.1% on RAGTruth.

</details>


### [48] [Beyond Token Positions: Safety Alignment Across Denoising Steps in Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00495)
*Guoli Wang,Haonan Shi,Tu Ouyang,An Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper analyzes how diffusion-based LLMs handle safety refusals during the denoising process and proposes a decoding method, RAEC, that locks in strong early refusal signals to improve safety without much harming utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion LLMs generate text via iterative denoising rather than standard left-to-right decoding, which changes how and when safety-relevant tokens (like refusals) appear. Existing safety analyses and defenses are mostly designed for autoregressive LLMs, leaving a gap in understanding and controlling safety behavior specific to dLLMs. The authors want to understand where and when refusal behavior arises during the denoising trajectory, and to leverage that to design a light-weight, training-free safety control method.

Method: The authors inspect diffusion LLMs under harmful prompts by logging intermediate token distributions and token commitments at each denoising step and position in the output. They quantify where (positions in the sequence) and when (steps in the denoising schedule) refusal-related tokens appear, and how early commitments influence the final outcome. Based on this, they design Refusal-Aware Early Commitment (RAEC), a decoding strategy that detects strong, persistent refusal signals at early denoising steps and forcibly commits them to the final output, rather than allowing later steps to overwrite them. They then evaluate RAEC on benchmarks such as LLaDA and Dream, comparing attack success rates and utility against baseline decoding.

Result: The analysis reveals that refusal signals in dLLMs are concentrated at early denoising steps and in leading positions of the generated response, and that early-committed tokens have disproportionate influence on the final safety behavior. The authors find that both the specific denoising step at which refusal tokens appear and the persistence of those commitments are key predictors of safe versus unsafe outputs. With RAEC, they empirically demonstrate a reduction in attack success rates on harmful prompts while mostly preserving the helpfulness/utility of the model on benign prompts, across LLaDA and Dream benchmarks.

Conclusion: Safety behavior in diffusion-based LLMs is tightly linked to early denoising dynamics and early token commitments, particularly at the beginning of the generated sequence. By tracing these dynamics, the authors show that enforcing early, persistent refusal tokens via the RAEC decoding method can significantly strengthen safety alignment with minimal cost to utility. This positions RAEC as a simple, training-free mechanism to improve the robustness of dLLMs against harmful prompt attacks and highlights the importance of step-wise, position-aware analysis for safety in diffusion generation paradigms.

Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text through iterative denoising rather than left-to-right decoding. This generation paradigm introduces two axes that can influence safety alignment: when tokens are generated during denoising and where they appear in the response. In this paper, we measure dLLM safety behavior under harmful prompts by tracing intermediate token distributions and commitment decisions throughout denoising. Our analysis shows that refusal signals are concentrated in early denoising steps and leading response positions, and the tokens committed early can strongly shape the final safety outcome. Our measurements further show that the denoising step and persistence of refusal-token commitment are important for understanding dLLM safety. Based on these findings, we propose Refusal-Aware Early Commitment (RAEC), a simple training-free decoding method that commits persistent refusal signals from early steps. Experiments on LLaDA and Dream show that RAEC reduces attack success rates while largely preserving utility. The code is available at https://github.com/Glresearch1/RAEC.

</details>


### [49] [The Interlingua Hypothesis: LLMs Translate via a Latent Task-agnostic Feature Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00515)
*Jacob Brinton,Jannik Brinkmann,Mark Crovella,Aaron Mueller*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes and tests the “interlingua hypothesis” that LLMs translate via a shared latent feature space rather than language-pair-specific mechanisms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs outperform strong supervised MT systems, but it is unclear what internal mechanisms they use for translation. Recent interpretability work suggests LLMs rely on massively multilingual latent feature representations, motivating the question of whether a shared interlingual space underlies translation.

Method: They formulate the interlingua hypothesis and investigate it through three empirical analyses: (1) modeling BLEU variance across language pairs to see if it can be explained by language-specific competence without pairwise interaction terms; (2) causal analysis of model components to test whether the same components matter for both monolingual and translation tasks; and (3) fine-tuning experiments comparing monolingual data vs aligned parallel documents to quantify how much translation improvement can be recovered from purely monolingual fine-tuning.

Result: (1) Variation in BLEU scores across language pairs is largely predictable from language-specific abilities, with minimal need for pair-specific effects; (2) Many components of the model that affect monolingual performance are also causally important for translation; and (3) Fine-tuning on monolingual data recovers a large fraction of the translation gains that would be achieved with parallel, aligned data.

Conclusion: The evidence from BLEU variance modeling, causal component analysis, and fine-tuning experiments converges to support the interlingua hypothesis: LLMs perform translation by encoding inputs into and decoding outputs from a shared multilingual latent space. This perspective offers a conceptual framework for interpreting LLM translation behavior and implies that improving general multilingual representations and monolingual abilities can directly benefit translation performance without requiring language-pair-specific modeling.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated improved machine translation performance over strong supervised baselines. This raises questions as to what mechanisms underlie how LLMs perform machine translation between languages. Motivated by recent interpretability findings--namely, that LLMs use massively multilingual latent feature representations to perform language modeling--we propose the interlingua hypothesis. The hypothesis holds that language models translate by reading a source sentence into a latent feature space, and generate a target sentence by reading from the latent feature space. We show three lines of evidence in support of this hypothesis: (1) variance in BLEU across language pairs is largely predictable from language-specific competences with no language pair-specific interaction terms; (2) many model components are causally influential in both monolingual tasks and translation tasks; and (3) fine-tuning on monolingual data recovers a large proportion of translation improvements relative to fine-tuning on aligned documents. Together, these provide convergent evidence in support of the interlingua hypothesis, and suggest new ways of understanding and improving how LLMs can be leveraged to perform translation tasks.

</details>


### [50] [Skill Following: Evaluating Actual Skill Use in Retrieval-Enabled LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00549)
*Seonghyeon Cho,Chanjun Park*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose a new metric (RAE) to accurately measure whether LLM agents actually benefit from using retrieved external skills on the specific tasks where retrieval occurs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM agents using external tools/skills rely on aggregate metrics that compare tasks with and without retrieval, mixing different task sets. This introduces selection bias: tasks that trigger retrieval may be inherently harder or different, so an overall performance lift with retrieval does not prove that retrieval helps on the tasks where it is actually used. The authors want a clean, unbiased measure of the real value of retrieval on those exact tasks, and to test whether current systems truly use skills effectively rather than just appearing to perform better in aggregate.

Method: They formalize an ability called Skill Following (SF): how well a model can benefit from a retrieved skill when it chooses to use one. To measure SF, they define the Retrieval-Invoked Actual-Use Effect (RAE). RAE compares outcomes on the same tasks under two execution modes: skill-enabled (the model can retrieve and use skills) versus skill-disabled (the model cannot use them). Crucially, RAE conditions only on tasks where, in the skill-enabled setting, the agent actually decided to retrieve a skill. This creates a matched evaluation at the task level, isolating the causal effect of skill use. They apply RAE to 17 different LLMs on coding (e.g., MBPP+) and mathematical benchmarks, analyzing performance differences between the two modes and contrasting RAE with standard aggregate retrieval metrics.

Result: Across coding and math domains, many models show a positive aggregate retrieval lift—overall performance appears better when retrieval is available. However, when measured with RAE on the subset of tasks where retrieval actually occurred, several models exhibit negative RAE: their performance on those tasks is worse with skills enabled than with skills disabled. On the MBPP+ coding benchmark, multiple models that look improved at the system level are in fact harming their accuracy on the very instances where they choose to retrieve skills. This reveals a discrepancy between standard aggregate evaluations and true skill-use effectiveness.

Conclusion: Aggregate averages and standard retrieval-lift metrics can be misleading indicators of tool-use proficiency in LLM agents because they conflate task difficulty and selection effects. The proposed RAE metric directly measures whether using retrieved skills helps or hurts on the specific tasks where retrieval is invoked, providing a cleaner estimate of Skill Following. Their experiments show that many current LLMs often misuse retrieval—hurting performance on retrieved tasks despite seemingly positive system-wide gains. The work argues that future evaluation of tool-using LLMs should adopt RAE-style, task-matched metrics to accurately assess and improve actual skill-use behavior.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external skills, yet standard evaluations obscure whether retrieving these skills actually helps. Aggregate metrics often compare retrieved versus non-retrieved tasks, introducing severe selection bias and failing to isolate the true effect of skill use. To measure this actual-use capability-which we formalize as Skill Following (SF)-we introduce the Retrieval-Invoked Actual-Use Effect (RAE). RAE computes the same-task outcome difference between matched skill-enabled and skill-disabled executions, conditioned exclusively on tasks where the agent actively retrieved a skill. Evaluating 17 LLMs across coding and mathematical domains, we uncover a stark evaluation paradox: models frequently show positive aggregate retrieval lift but negative RAE. On MBPP+, multiple models that appear to benefit system-wide actually harm their own performance on the exact tasks where retrieval occurred. These findings demonstrate that aggregate averages can create a misleading illusion of tool-use proficiency, whereas RAE directly measures whether the retrieval-to-answer pipeline genuinely rescues more outcomes than it harms.

</details>


### [51] [Same Semantics, Different Outcome: On the Modality Robustness of Multimodal LLMs under Knowledge Conflict](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00550)
*Jungyeon Lee,Yejin Yoon,Taeuk Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that multimodal large language models treat the same evidence inconsistently depending on whether it is text, image, or both, especially when this evidence conflicts with their internal knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand and quantify how reliably multimodal LLMs use contextual evidence across different modalities (text vs. image) when that evidence disagrees with what the model has learned parametrically.

Method: The authors evaluate 13 multimodal LLMs on two datasets specifically constructed to create conflicts between contextual evidence (text passages, rendered images of those passages, or both) and the models' parametric knowledge. They measure which modality the models trust under conflict, analyze behavior patterns, and run experiments in multimodal retrieval-augmented generation and adversarial attack scenarios. They also test interventions including prompting strategies, representational steering, supervised fine-tuning, and direct preference optimization.

Result: They find that models are not modality-robust: (1) models are more willing to accept context that contradicts their parametric knowledge when that context is provided as an image than when it is provided as text; (2) when contradictory text and image are both present, the modality the model follows is unstable and depends on arbitrary factors like input order, model choice, and dataset. This instability measurably harms multimodal RAG performance and enables adversarial exploits. Most mitigation techniques fail, with only supervised fine-tuning offering moderate gains.

Conclusion: Current multimodal LLMs inconsistently integrate textual and visual evidence, especially under knowledge conflict, leading to brittle and exploitable behavior in practical applications. Simple fixes are largely ineffective, so the inconsistency should be treated as a fundamental challenge requiring attention throughout model training and design.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly provided with contextual evidence in heterogeneous forms: as a text passage, as a rendered image of the same passage, or as both together. However, it remains unclear how consistently these surface forms are processed, especially when the evidence conflicts with the model's parametric knowledge. We study modality robustness under knowledge conflict across 13 MLLMs and two datasets, and find them far from robust. (1) Contrary to common belief, models favor a context that contradicts parametric knowledge more readily in image form than in text form; (2) when a contradicting text and image are presented together, the preferred modality is essentially arbitrary, varying with input order, model, and dataset. We further demonstrate that this instability has practical consequences: it degrades performance in multimodal RAG and can be exploited by adversarial attacks. To alleviate this brittleness, we examine several simple techniques---prompting, steering, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and direct preference optimization; the majority prove ineffective, whereas SFT achieves moderate success. We therefore call for greater awareness of this inconsistency and argue that it is fundamental, demanding attention at multiple training stages.

</details>


### [52] [EM^2Mem: Event-Centric Multimodal Memory for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00551)
*Yijun Chen,Yaqi Zheng,Yanya Li,Boyi Xiao,Buqiang Xu,Shuofei Qiao,Jizhan Fang,Xinle Deng,Yunzhi Yao,Xuehai Wang,Liuxin Zhang,Hui Li,Huajun Chen,Shumin Deng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Event-centric multimodal memory (EM^2Mem) improves long-video QA by binding heterogeneous evidence to event anchors for compact, aligned retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal memories for long-video QA store captions, frames, transcripts, summaries, or graph facts as isolated, modality-specific fragments. At inference, language models must re-align these fragments temporally and across modalities under limited context windows, making attribution difficult and inefficient. There is a need for a memory representation that is directly generation-ready, with cross-modal and temporal alignments baked in.

Method: The paper introduces EM^2Mem, an event-centric multimodal memory framework where memory cells are indexed by events rather than by raw fragments. During memory construction, heterogeneous evidence—multimodal records (video, audio, text), temporal context, graph-linked relations, semantic facts, and provenance—is bound to event anchors and stored in unified event-indexed cells. At query time, the system retrieves compact evidence bundles grounded in these multimodal events, instead of independent modality-specific fragments, enabling more efficient and faithful generation.

Result: On three long-video QA benchmarks, EM^2Mem outperforms the strongest memory baseline by 2.0, 2.4, and 3.7 accuracy points respectively. It also improves strict event-level Top-5 evidence recall by 7.0 points, and significantly boosts efficiency: per-query latency is reduced by a factor of 4.67, and total inference token usage decreases by 63.66%.

Conclusion: Event-centric multimodal memory provides a more generation-ready and attribution-friendly representation for long-video QA than fragment-based approaches. By aligning and binding heterogeneous evidence to event anchors during memory construction, EM^2Mem yields better accuracy, higher quality event-level evidence retrieval, and substantial gains in efficiency, making it a promising direction for scalable multimodal reasoning systems.

Abstract: Multimodal memory offers a scalable interface for long-video question answering, but existing methods often retrieve captions, frames, transcripts, summaries, or graph facts as isolated fragments. Although searchable, such fragments are not generation-ready: language models must reconstruct cross-modal and temporal alignments at inference time, when context is limited and attribution is difficult. We propose EM^2Mem, an event-centric multimodal memory framework that binds heterogeneous evidence to event anchors during memory construction. Each event-indexed memory cell aligns multimodal records, temporal context, graph-linked relations, semantic facts, and provenance, enabling compact evidence readout over grounded multimodal events rather than modality-specific fragments. Across three long-video QA benchmarks, EM^2Mem improves average accuracy over the strongest memory baseline by 2.0, 2.4, and 3.7 points, improves strict event-level Top-5 evidence recall by 7.0 points, and reduces per-query latency by 4.67 times and total inference tokens by 63.66% (The code will be integrated into https://github.com/zjunlp/LightMem).

</details>


### [53] [Enoki: Efficient Multi-Level Hallucination Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00581)
*Elisei Rykov,Timur Ionov,Nikolay Ivanov,Maksim Savkin,Maksim Makarenko,Alexander Panchenko,Vasily Konovalov,Julia Belikova*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Enoki, an Open IE-based framework that detects hallucinations from LLMs at both claim and span levels using a shared representation of text-anchored relational facts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hallucinations in LLM outputs are a major obstacle for using them in high-stakes applications. Existing detectors are siloed: claim-level methods reason over discrete factual claims but don’t precisely localize errors in text, while span-level methods highlight problematic spans but lack interpretable, structured factual units. Bridging these two views typically requires expensive multi-step LLM pipelines or complex alignment between claims and text spans. The authors are motivated to create a unified, efficient framework that supports both granular localization and interpretable verification without heavy overhead.

Method: The authors propose Enoki, an Open Information Extraction framework that converts generated text into text-anchored relational facts (subject–relation–object tuples with span links). These facts are then automatically verified against external evidence. Facts deemed unsupported are projected back onto the originating text spans, enabling detection of hallucinations at both the claim level and the span/entity level using a single shared representation. Enoki is designed to be flexible: it can use LLM-based, encoder-based, or rule-based extractors, all interfacing through the same Open IE abstraction to trade off accuracy against computational cost.

Result: Experiments show that Enoki performs on par with strong existing claim-level hallucination detection systems while requiring fewer computational resources, and it outperforms baselines on finer-grained span- and entity-level localization tasks. This demonstrates that the shared Open IE representation can effectively support multi-level hallucination detection, providing both interpretability and precise localization.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that Enoki successfully unifies claim-level verification and span-level localization of hallucinations via a common Open IE representation of text-anchored relational facts. This reduces the need for complex, multi-stage pipelines and alignment procedures, while remaining competitive or superior in accuracy and more efficient in resource usage. The authors also contribute EnokiQA, a new dataset that jointly annotates claim-level verification and span-level localization, facilitating future research on multi-granularity hallucination detection.

Abstract: Ensuring factuality remains a critical challenge for deploying LLMs in high-stakes settings. Existing hallucination detectors usually operate at a single level: claim-level methods provide interpretable factual units, while span-level methods localize unsupported text. Bridging these views is costly, as LLM-heavy pipelines require multiple decomposition and verification calls, and modular systems need additional claim-to-span alignment. We propose Enoki, an Open Information Extraction framework for multi-level hallucination detection. Enoki extracts text-anchored relational facts, verifies them against evidence, and projects unsupported facts back to hallucinated spans. This shared representation enables claim-level verification and span-level localization without requiring separate alignment. Enoki supports LLM-based, encoder-based, and rule-based extraction regimes, balancing accuracy and inference cost through a common interface. Experiments show that Enoki remains competitive with strong claim-level systems while using fewer resources and achieves superior performance on fine-grained span- and entity-level localization. We also release EnokiQA, a dual-granularity dataset with aligned claim-level verification and span-level localization annotations.

</details>


### [54] [Quit While You're Ahead: Quit for Efficient Candidate Generation in Machine Translation Reranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00588)
*Guangyu Chen,Boxuan Lyu,Hidetaka Kamigaito,Kotaro Funakoshi,Manabu Okumura*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Quit, an early-stopping strategy that speeds up NMT reranking while keeping translation quality nearly unchanged.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reranking methods like MBR decoding and QE reranking improve NMT output quality but significantly increase inference latency, especially because both reranking computation and candidate generation are expensive. Existing speed-up approaches focus only on MBR and on the reranking step, neglecting QE reranking and leaving candidate generation as a bottleneck. There is a need for a unified method that accelerates the full generation–reranking pipeline without harming translation quality.

Method: The authors frame candidate generation as a sequential decision-making process under uncertainty. They propose Quit (Quantifying Uncertainty for Incremental Termination), which incrementally generates candidate translations and applies reranking after each increment. Quit monitors the estimated quality of the best candidate and stops generating new candidates once this top estimated quality value stabilizes according to some uncertainty-based criterion, effectively performing early stopping for both candidate generation and reranking. The approach is applied to both MBR decoding and QE-based reranking.

Result: On three different NMT models and 19 language pairs, Quit achieves substantial end-to-end speedups. For MBR decoding, it yields a 1.47–2.66× acceleration, and for QE-based reranking, a 3.43–4.12× acceleration. These gains are obtained while keeping translation performance within predefined equivalence margins compared to the full reranking baselines, meaning quality degradation is negligible or statistically insignificant.

Conclusion: Quit provides an effective early-stopping mechanism for NMT reranking pipelines, targeting both candidate generation and reranking computations. By treating candidate generation as a sequential decision under uncertainty and stopping when the best candidate’s estimated quality stabilizes, Quit significantly reduces inference time for both MBR and QE reranking without meaningfully sacrificing translation quality. This suggests that uncertainty-aware incremental termination can be a powerful general strategy for accelerating reranking-based systems.

Abstract: Reranking methods, such as Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) decoding and Quality Estimation (QE) reranking, are widely used in modern neural machine translation (NMT) to select an output from a set of candidate hypotheses. However, the performance gains come at the cost of high inference latency. Existing acceleration methods target MBR decoding and reduce only reranking computation, leaving QE reranking unaddressed and candidate generation---which can be the larger computational bottleneck---largely untouched. In this work, we propose Quit (Quantifying Uncertainty for Incremental Termination), a novel early-stopping strategy for the entire generation--reranking pipeline. Viewing candidate generation as a sequential decision under uncertainty, Quit incrementally generates and reranks candidates, stopping when the highest estimated quality in the candidate set stabilizes. Comprehensive experiments on three NMT models across 19 language pairs show that Quit yields end-to-end speedups of $1.47$--$2.66\times$ for MBR and $3.43$--$4.12\times$ for QE reranking while preserving translation quality within prespecified equivalence margins.

</details>


### [55] [Investigating Assistant Bias in LLM User Simulators Using a Role Vector](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00608)
*Daeheon Jeong,Yoonjoo Lee,Eugene Choi,Sinie van der Ben,Juho Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies and mitigates ‘assistant bias’ in LLM-based user simulators by analyzing internal activations to separate user and assistant roles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based user simulators are used to evaluate autonomous agents cheaply and at scale, but they behave too much like helpful assistants, not like realistic users who may be frustrated, disengaged, or uncooperative. This mismatch threatens the validity of agent evaluations, and existing prompt-based role-playing does not remove the bias because it is rooted in model training. The authors aim to understand, at the representation level, how this assistant bias arises and how user-like behavior is encoded in the model.

Method: The authors analyze the internal activations of an LLM when it processes dialogues from both user and assistant perspectives. By contrasting these activations, they derive a ‘user role vector’ that captures the direction in representation space corresponding to user behavior as opposed to assistant behavior. They then manipulate activations along this direction to see how it affects generated behavior, and study how this interacts with role prompts and user profiles in simulation settings.

Result: They find that (i) the user direction is clearly identifiable in the activation space, and pushing activations along this direction elicits behaviors that look more like real users and are distinguishable from assistant-like traits; and (ii) activating this user role is correlated with more realistic simulations and can be further strengthened by steering, but excessive steering can lead to exaggerated user behaviors and can overpower individual user profiles encoded elsewhere in the model.

Conclusion: Assistant bias is structurally encoded in LLM representations, but a distinct, manipulable user-role direction also exists. This means user behavior in LLM-based simulators can be analyzed and controlled at the representation level rather than only via prompts, enabling more realistic user simulations while highlighting a trade-off between realism and preserving individual user profiles.

Abstract: LLM-based user simulators are increasingly used to evaluate autonomous agents at scale, in place of costly human evaluations. Despite this promise, these simulators exhibit "assistant bias," a tendency to cooperate and pursue task goals. They rarely reproduce the frustration or disengagement that real users exhibit, compromising evaluation validity. Prior work outlines that this bias is baked in during model training, which role-playing prompts fail to override. We analyze this bias from model activations, extracting a user role vector by contrasting how the model represents user versus assistant perspectives on the same dialogue. We observe two findings: (i) the user direction is identifiable in activations, elicits user-like behaviors, and captures characteristics distinct from assistant traits; and (ii) although user-role activation associates with simulation realism and steering strengthens it, it can exaggerate user behaviors and override individual user profiles. Together, our findings provide a representation-level analysis of LLM user simulators, confirming that assistant bias is structurally identifiable and that user behavior can be directionally analyzed.

</details>


### [56] [Trust Your Guide Only When Certain: Uncertainty-Aware Sparse Alignment at Inference Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00624)
*Zeen Zhu,Zhuo Li,Weiyang Guo,Liye Zhao,Haibing Di,Yequan Wang,Jing Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper identifies a mismatch in current inference-time alignment methods that use weak supervisors at every decoding step, and proposes TUSA, a sparse, trust-based arbitration mechanism that only intervenes when the supervisor is confident and the token is important, improving both safety and helpfulness while cutting about half of alignment steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing inference-time alignment methods rely on lightweight (weak) supervisors to guide LLM outputs at every generation step. However, these weak supervisors tend to have high uncertainty (entropy) over most tokens, meaning their forced, dense interventions can override correct base-model reasoning, lower utility, and be inefficient. There is a need to reduce unnecessary or harmful interventions while preserving or improving safety.

Method: The authors first empirically analyze the entropy and intervention patterns of weak supervisors used in inference-time alignment, revealing that they are uncertain over most tokens. They then propose TUSA (Trust-based Uncertainty Sparse Alignment), which introduces an uncertainty-aware arbiter. This arbiter decides whether to apply the supervisor’s intervention at each decoding step based on two criteria: (1) the supervisor’s confidence (low entropy or high trust) in its guidance, and (2) the semantic salience or importance of the current token. Only when both conditions are satisfied does TUSA intervene; otherwise, it defers to the base model. This creates a sparse and dynamic arbitration mechanism instead of continuous oversight.

Result: Across multiple LLMs and benchmark tasks, TUSA is shown to skip roughly 50% of the alignment interventions compared to dense baselines, while improving safety and utility. Specifically, it increases safety preference scores by up to 15.6% and general preference (helpfulness) rates by up to 12.0% relative to the dense intervention approach. These results indicate that selective, high-confidence interventions can be more effective than always-on alignment.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that the standard paradigm of dense, step-wise supervision with weak supervisors is structurally flawed due to pervasive supervisor uncertainty. By reframing alignment as a dynamic arbitration problem and intervening only when supervision is both confident and semantically necessary, TUSA achieves better safety and helpfulness with fewer intervention steps. This demonstrates that sparse, trust-based inference-time alignment can outperform continuous oversight and provides a more efficient and robust path for steering LLM behavior.

Abstract: A prominent paradigm in inference-time alignment employs lightweight supervisors to steer Large Language Models (LLMs). Through empirical analysis, we identify a structural mismatch in this paradigm: weak supervisors exhibit pervasive high entropy across the vast majority of tokens, yet prevailing dense intervention approaches mandate supervision at every decoding step. This leads to frequent low-confidence interventions that can disrupt valid base-model reasoning and incur substantial utility costs. To resolve this, we propose TUSA (Trust-based Uncertainty Sparse Alignment). Moving away from continuous oversight, TUSA reframes alignment as a dynamic arbitration process, introducing an uncertainty-aware arbiter that authorizes intervention only when two conditions are met: the supervisor is confident and the token is semantically salient. This mechanism effectively filters out uncertainty-driven noise and redundant supervision. Extensive experiments across multiple models and benchmarks show that TUSA consistently improves both safety alignment and general helpfulness. By bypassing approximately 50% of alignment steps, it not only enhances safety preference by up to 15.6%, but also boosts general preference rates by up to 12.0% compared to the dense baseline, demonstrating that selective, high-precision alignment can outperform continuous supervision.

</details>


### [57] [ExpArt-KG: Artwork Image Description Generation through Iterative Exploration of Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00629)
*Yuta Kato,Shintaro Ozaki,Kazuki Hayashi,Yusuke Sakai,Hidetaka Kamigaito,Katsuhiko Hayashi,Taro Watanabe*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They enhance large vision-language models with a retrieval-augmented framework that iteratively pulls facts from a knowledge graph to generate more detailed, accurate image explanations, demonstrated on a new art-domain KG.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing large vision-language models can caption images and answer visual questions, but they struggle to capture rich, precise factual relations between entities and concepts in an image (e.g., detailed art-historical or domain knowledge). Simply scaling models or naive retrieval is inefficient and may add noise. There is a need for a method that injects just the necessary external factual knowledge to improve explanation quality without excessive retrieval cost, especially in domains where images have clear mappings to entities, such as artworks.

Method: They propose a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework that tightly couples an LVLM with a knowledge graph. The process alternates between (1) generating partial answers or explanation segments from the LVLM and (2) retrieving relevant facts from the knowledge graph. A correctness-judgment component evaluates whether the current explanation is adequately supported or needs more information, guiding further retrieval and generation. To evaluate and ground this process, they build ExpArt-KG, a knowledge graph focused on artworks, where links between images and KG entities are unambiguous. The system is compared with baselines that perform a fixed number of retrieval iterations, measuring explanation detail, quality, and retrieval cost.

Result: On the ExpArt-KG benchmark, their alternating generate-and-retrieve framework produces artwork explanations that contain more detailed factual content than standard LVLM outputs and baselines. At the same time, by using correctness judgments to stop retrieval when sufficient facts have been gathered, it reduces the number of knowledge-graph queries compared with approaches that always iterate a fixed number of retrieval steps, while preserving comparable overall generation quality.

Conclusion: Integrating LVLMs with a knowledge graph via an adaptive, correctness-guided RAG loop yields more informative and accurate image explanations at lower retrieval cost than fixed-iteration baselines. The new ExpArt-KG resource provides a clean testbed for artwork-focused image explanation, and the proposed framework demonstrates an effective way to combine visual understanding with structured factual knowledge for richer multimodal reasoning.

Abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) achieve strong performance on image-grounded text generation and visual question answering. However, it remains difficult for them to comprehensively and accurately describe the factual relations among the entities and concepts associated with the objects depicted in an image. In this work, we propose a framework that efficiently exploits factual information from a knowledge graph via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), with the goal of enabling LVLMs to generate detailed and accurate image explanations. Specifically, our method alternates between answer generation and knowledge-graph retrieval, and controls the search using a correctness judgment, thereby acquiring the necessary and sufficient factual information efficiently. We also construct a knowledge graph for the artwork domain (ExpArt-KG), in which the correspondence between images and entities is unambiguous. Applying the proposed method to this knowledge graph, we show experimentally that it improves the level of detail of artwork explanations and reduces the retrieval cost of external knowledge while maintaining generation quality comparable to that of iterating a fixed number of times.

</details>


### [58] [Creative Generation via Multi-Agent Debate: Does Debate Suppress Diversity?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00683)
*Tien Anh Nguyen,Khanh-Binh Nguyen,Van Dai Do,Svetha Venkatesh,Hung Le*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Creative-MAD, a modification of Multi-Agent Debate to better support creative generation by preserving diversity among debating agents, thus achieving both high output quality and greater diversity across runs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Multi-Agent Debate improves quality on factual and reasoning tasks but tends to converge on similar answers, which is harmful for creative tasks that require diverse outputs across independent runs. There is a need to understand and address the trade-off between convergence for quality and divergence for creativity.

Method: The authors theoretically analyze the relationship between within-session agent diversity and across-run output diversity, proving that intra-session diversity is necessary for diverse final outputs. Based on this, they design Creative-MAD with two mechanisms: (1) Cognitive Lens Assignment, which assigns each agent a distinct, stable cognitive mode to prevent identity drift; and (2) Embedding-based Peer Selection, which restricts each agent’s debate context to the most semantically distant peers to resist majority pull. They then implement this framework and evaluate it on multiple creative-generation benchmarks.

Result: Across four creative benchmarks, Creative-MAD increases both lexical diversity (variety of word choices and phrasing) and semantic diversity (variety of ideas and meanings) of generated outputs, while maintaining the high quality typically achieved by standard Multi-Agent Debate.

Conclusion: Maintaining diversity among debating agents is crucial for producing diverse creative outputs across runs. By anchoring agents in distinct cognitive modes and controlling which peer arguments they see, Creative-MAD successfully balances quality and diversity, making debate-style multi-agent methods more suitable for creative generation tasks.

Abstract: Creative generation tasks, such as narrative writing and scientific ideation, demand both high-quality outputs and distinct responses across independent runs to maximize exploration. Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) has shown strong quality gains on factual and reasoning tasks, making it a natural candidate for creative generation. However, we find its convergence-driven design actively suppresses output diversity across independent runs, creating an inherent trade-off with creative tasks. We theoretically show that preserving diversity among agents within each debate session is a necessary condition for achieving diverse outputs across independent runs. Building on this finding, we propose Creative-MAD, which introduces two synergistic interventions to sustain agent divergence. Specifically, Cognitive Lens Assignment counters identity drift by anchoring each agent to a distinct and persistent cognitive mode, while Embedding-based Peer Selection counters majority pull by limiting each agent's context to its most semantically distant peers. Experiments across four creative benchmarks demonstrate that Creative-MAD significantly enhances both lexical and semantic diversity while maintaining MAD's output quality.

</details>


### [59] [Visual Framing for News Stance Detection via Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00685)
*Dahyun Lee,Jiyoung Han,Kunwoo Park*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes VFStance, a method that uses visual framing via image generation to make implicit news stances more explicit, improving article-level stance detection and user perception of stance signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Article-level news stance detection is difficult because stances are often implicit, subtly expressed through framing, and embedded in long, complex news texts. Existing methods struggle to capture these nuanced and indirect cues, which limits the reliability of automated stance detection systems used to support trustworthy media environments.

Method: The authors introduce VFStance, a stance detection framework that incorporates visual framing by generating images that correspond to the stance in the article. These visual representations surface implicit stance cues, making them more explicit for the model. They evaluate VFStance against existing stance detection methods and also conduct a controlled user study in a snippet-based news consumption scenario to test whether the visualized stance cues help humans perceive stance more clearly.

Result: Experimental evaluations show that VFStance outperforms existing stance detection methods, and ablation or comparative analyses confirm that the visual framing component significantly contributes to these gains. The user study with 200 participants in a snippet-based news scenario further shows that the images produced by VFStance make stance signals more visually salient to readers.

Conclusion: Leveraging visual framing via image generation is an effective way to expose implicit stance cues in news articles, improving automatic stance detection performance and helping human users better perceive stance in short news consumption contexts. VFStance thus has potential applications beyond automated stance classification, such as enhancing transparency and user awareness of stance in media consumption tools.

Abstract: Article-level news stance detection aims to identify the perspective of news articles toward social issues. Despite advances in stance detection and its importance for trustworthy media environments, news articles pose distinct challenges because their stances are often implicit, subtly conveyed through journalistic framing, and embedded in long, structurally complex texts. To address these challenges, we introduce VFStance, which leverages visual framing to make implicit stance cues more explicit via image generation. In evaluation experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of VFStance over existing methods and the contribution of visual framing to its performance. Finally, a controlled user study (N=200) in a snippet-based news consumption setting further demonstrates that VFStance can make stance signals visually salient and highlights its potential use beyond automated stance detection.

</details>


### [60] [SCoNE: Selective Context-aware Neuron Editing for Robust Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00689)
*Chaewon Kim,Seo Yeon Park*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SCoNE is a training-free method to make RAG more robust to noisy retrieved documents by editing specific context-aware neurons in the FFN, improving QA performance without extra inference cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG systems often retrieve a mix of relevant and irrelevant documents. LLMs are easily distracted by the noise, which causes hallucinations and degraded performance. Existing fixes may need fine-tuning, extra modules, or inference-time overhead. The motivation is to make RAG robust to retrieval noise in a lightweight, training-free way.

Method: They propose SCoNE (Selective Context-aware Neuron Editing), which identifies FFN neurons that are both (1) highly attributed to the model’s outputs and (2) show strong variability across different input contexts. These are treated as context-aware neurons. SCoNE then selectively strengthens these neurons through a model editing procedure. The method needs only a small mining set, avoids fine-tuning, and does not change the inference-time architecture or cost.

Result: On multiple knowledge-intensive QA benchmarks and with two different LLM backbones, applying SCoNE improves robustness to noisy retrieval and yields better performance than strong baseline approaches designed to handle retrieval noise or improve RAG.

Conclusion: Selective editing and strengthening of context-aware FFN neurons can significantly improve RAG robustness to noisy retrieved documents, without training or inference overhead. SCoNE offers a practical way to reduce hallucinations and improve QA quality in RAG systems.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is highly sensitive to retrieval noise: when retrieved documents mix informative and irrelevant context, LLMs are easily distracted, leading to hallucinations. To overcome this, we propose SCoNE (Selective Context-aware Neuron Editing), a training-free model editing approach that improves retrieval noise robustness by selectively strengthening context-aware FFN neurons that are identified by both high attribution and high cross-input variability. SCoNE requires only a small number of mining samples, no fine-tuning, and no inference-time overhead. Across various knowledge-intensive question-answering benchmarks and two LLM backbones, SCoNE consistently outperforms competitive baseline methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/HYU-ARK-Lab/SCoNE.

</details>


### [61] [A Certificate-Producing Cascade for Equational Implication: The SAIR EQT2 Stage 2 Solver](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00706)
*Haobo Ma,Wenlin Zhang,Manuel Israel Cázares*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A Python-based solver addresses the SAIR Mathematics Distillation Challenge by determining implication between magma identities and producing Lean-checkable certificates, achieving full coverage on public benchmarks without language-model calls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The challenge requires automated reasoning about equational theories (magma identities) with verifiable certificates in Lean. Existing methods may not provide fully checkable certificates, may rely on untrusted components, or may not handle the specific structure of the competition. The paper aims to build a compact, fully specified, and practically effective solver that fits the competition’s constraints and provides reliable, reproducible results tied to immutable ledgers.

Method: The authors implement a single-file Python solver organized as a cheapest-first search cascade. For disproving implication (false branch), it uses: (1) coefficient tests over structured algebra families, (2) bounded finite-model search, (3) an explicit central-groupoid counterexample, and (4) several infinite-carrier witnesses. For proving implication (true branch), it uses a proof-producing ordered unit superposition procedure featuring Knuth–Bendix ordering, bidirectional demodulation, indexing, memoized substitution, and anytime size deepening. All search results are kept outside the trusted base: successful proofs are replayed as small Lean terms, and countermodels are independently rechecked by the official Lean judge.

Result: The frozen solver is a 189,504-byte Python file with a specified SHA-256 hash, ensuring its immutability. In local experiments against judge revision 2848228, it produced accepted certificates for all 1,889 rows of the six public datasets without using language models. Additional tests show exact agreement on 800 Stage 1 evaluation problems, 100 accepted rows from the canonical Marathon manifest (without tokens), and 200 accepted rows from a hosted playground. All these are regression and playground measurements, not official leaderboard results.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that a compact, fully specified Python solver can reliably solve all currently public instances of the SAIR Mathematics Distillation Challenge on Equational Theories, producing Lean-checkable certificates using a mix of model search and proof search. The authors emphasize reproducibility and verifiability via immutable result ledgers and do not claim completeness or superiority over other systems, instead presenting a robust baseline aligned with the competition’s requirements.

Abstract: The SAIR Mathematics Distillation Challenge on Equational Theories asks a solver to classify whether one magma identity implies another and, for either verdict, to return a certificate accepted by a deterministic Lean judge. We present a single-file solver organized as a cheapest-first cascade. Its false branch combines coefficient tests over structured algebra families, bounded finite-model search, an explicit central-groupoid witness, and several infinite-carrier witnesses. Its true branch is a proof-producing ordered unit superposition procedure with Knuth-Bendix ordering, bidirectional demodulation, indexing, memoised substitution, and anytime size deepening. Search results remain outside the trusted base: successful derivations are replayed as small Lean terms, and countermodels are rechecked by the competition judge.
  The frozen solver is a 189,504-byte Python file with SHA-256 f2392533c9f4c03b.... In local runs through official judge revision 2848228, it produced accepted certificates for all 1,889 rows of the six public sets with no language-model calls. Separate measurements recorded full agreement on the 800 published Stage 1 evaluation-distribution problems, 100 accepted rows in the canonical Marathon manifest without tokens, and 200 accepted rows in the hosted playground. These are regression and playground measurements, not a leaderboard result and not evidence about a hidden set. All quantitative claims are tied to immutable result ledgers; the paper makes no completeness or comparative-superiority claim.

</details>


### [62] [Can Large Language Models Forecast What Researchers Study Next?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00747)
*Fenghai Li,Zihan Tang,Haofei Yu,Yining Zhao,Jiaxuan You*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces IdeaForecastBench, a benchmark to test whether models can forecast future research papers from past literature, comparing several LLM setups and a learned forecaster on multiple metrics and diagnostics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models can generate research ideas, but existing evaluations of novelty or feasibility at the time of generation do not show whether these ideas actually anticipate directions the community will later pursue. There is no standard way to measure a system’s ability to forecast future research from current literature. The authors aim to fill this gap by creating a benchmark that quantifies how well models can predict which ideas later appear as published work.

Method: The authors build IdeaForecastBench as a rolling, time-split benchmark: for each of 624 episodes across 52 research topics, a system is given community literature only up to a temporal cutoff and must output up to five ranked research ideas. These ideas are later matched against papers that appear after the cutoff. They standardize a retrieve-then-judge protocol and report results with two independent judges (mainly GPT-4.1-mini). They evaluate five different ways of compressing the literature history and apply them across several LLM backbones (GPT-4.1, Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Qwen3.5-9B), and also test a learned Mode-Decomposition Forecaster (MDF). Performance is assessed with metrics like Hit@5 and Precision@5, along with outcome-blind breadth assessments, threshold studies, and judge diagnostics to understand limitations of equating realization with precise anticipation.

Result: Using the primary GPT-4.1-mini judge, summarizing the literature (Summary) consistently outperforms a direct approach (Direct) on Hit@5 and Precision@5 for all four model backbones. Qwen2.5 models outperform GPT-4.1 on the benchmark, whereas Qwen3.5 underperforms GPT-4.1. Outcome-blind evaluation shows that Qwen2.5 tends to propose broader, more wide-ranging forecasts, although the contribution of this breadth to its better scores cannot be precisely quantified. Threshold and judge analyses reveal that interpreting a later-realized paper as a precise anticipation of an earlier idea is nuanced and limited by judging and matching procedures.

Conclusion: IdeaForecastBench establishes a standardized task and evaluation protocol for research idea forecasting—predicting which research directions a community will later pursue based on past literature. Summarizing prior work before forecasting appears consistently beneficial, and different LLM families vary meaningfully in forecasting performance and breadth. However, the work also underscores that realizing a paper similar to a suggested idea does not straightforwardly equate to exact anticipation, encouraging careful interpretation of forecasting metrics. The benchmark is intended as a shared resource for further study of how and how well models can anticipate future research developments.

Abstract: Large language models increasingly generate research ideas, yet judging their novelty or feasibility at generation time does not establish whether they anticipate subsequent work. We introduce IdeaForecastBench to evaluate research idea forecasting. Given a community's literature up to a cutoff, a system produces up to five ranked ideas, which are evaluated against later papers. The benchmark comprises 624 rolling episodes across 52 topics, with a fixed retrieve-then-judge protocol and separately reported results from two judges.
