We compare five history-compression strategies across GPT-4.1, Qwen2.5-7B/14B, and Qwen3.5-9B, together with a learned Mode-Decomposition Forecaster (MDF). Under the primary GPT-4.1-mini judge, Summary improves on Direct in Hit@5 and Precision@5 across all four backbones. Qwen2.5 scores above GPT-4.1, whereas Qwen3.5 scores below it. An outcome-blind assessment finds that Qwen2.5 produces broader forecasts, but does not identify how much breadth contributes to its advantage. Threshold and judge diagnostics further clarify the limits of interpreting realization as precise anticipation. IdeaForecastBench provides a common task for studying which research ideas a community subsequently pursues and how reliably this outcome can be measured.

</details>


### [63] [Measuring Optimal Transport in Transformer Depth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00748)
*Alexandre Quemy*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether token representations in Transformer models evolve across layers in a way that approximates an optimal transport map over the vocabulary embedding cloud.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To better understand the internal dynamics of Transformer models by testing if the layer-to-layer evolution of token embeddings follows a principled geometric rule, specifically optimal transport, which would imply cost-efficient, structured movement of the entire vocabulary’s representation cloud through depth.

Method: They model the set of token representations at each layer as a point cloud in representation space and compare the actual layer-to-layer movement to an optimal transport (OT) plan. Using Pythia-160m and Pythia-410m, they compute exact assignments between consecutive layer clouds, estimate a sampling floor, calibrate their metrics on couplings known to be OT-optimal, and decompose the transport cost into a global shift of the cloud and token-specific displacements.

Result: At the final layer, token movements in both models closely follow the OT map: Pythia-410m achieves essentially optimal transport cost, while Pythia-160m is slightly above optimal. At the first layer, movements deviate substantially from OT behavior. For intermediate layers, only two of ten single-layer transitions can be reliably assessed on cost, but aggregating multiple layers shows that the cloud moves at nearly optimal cost. The agreement with OT at the last layer is much lower at initialization (0.64) and increases with training (to 0.86).

Conclusion: Transformer representations evolve with depth in a way that, especially in later layers and when aggregated across several layers, approximates an optimal transport map over the token cloud, and this structure strengthens as training progresses. Early layers do not follow OT closely, suggesting that optimal-transport-like organization is an emergent property of training and is more characteristic of deeper representational transformations.

Abstract: A transformer carries each token's state from layer to layer, and the whole vocabulary carried together forms a cloud that moves with depth. We ask whether a trained network moves this cloud the way optimal transport would: at the cheapest cost, and along the map that pairs each token with its optimal destination. We measure both on Pythia-160m and Pythia-410m, with an exact assignment between consecutive layer clouds, a measured sampling floor, calibration on couplings known to be optimal, and a split of the cost into the common shift of the cloud and the token-specific moves. At the last layer, both models move their tokens where the optimal-transport map sends them, at the optimal cost for Pythia-410m and slightly above it for Pythia-160m. At the first layer they do not. In between, single layers can be judged on cost at only two of ten transitions, and blocks of several layers move the cloud at close to the optimal cost. The agreement at the last layer is much weaker at initialisation (0.64 against 0.86) and grows with training.

</details>


### [64] [Joint Training Is Not Enough: Conditioned Cross-Granularity Training for Multimodal Document Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00756)
*Chengguang Gan,Yunhao Liang,Hanjun Wei,Qinghao Zhang,Shiwen Ni*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Study tests whether fine-grained (span-level) and coarse (document-level) tasks mutually reinforce when trained in one multimodal document understanding model; finds standard joint training mostly fails, while a conditioned-training setup often helps both levels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate the Mutual Reinforcement Effect (MRE): can one model benefit from learning both span-level field extraction and document-level classification simultaneously in multimodal document understanding? Prior work assumed mixed joint training helps, but this had not been rigorously tested, especially across different document types and with carefully constructed annotations.

Method: Construct Doc-MRE, an annotation layer linking span-level field extraction labels with four document-level facet labels, created via a three-LLM-judge committee under preregistered protocols and validated by blind re-annotation. Use three corpora (two receipt datasets including CORD and WildReceipt, plus a scanned business forms corpus). Compare three regimes: (1) single-task training for each granularity, (2) mixed joint training on both tasks, and (3) conditioned training where, during training only, the gold output for one granularity is inserted into the prompt for the other. Define a reinforcement predicate in advance: a regime reinforces if it outperforms the corresponding single-task model on both tasks at a fixed training recipe. Run additional controls with byte-identical prompts but shuffled or neutral conditioning content to disentangle the effects of prompt content vs format. Probe models to test whether document-level information is decodable under each regime.

Result: Mixed joint training does not reinforce on any corpus at the main evaluation scale: on CORD it underperforms both single-task models; on the other two corpora it trades off performance between fine and coarse tasks rather than improving both. Conditioned training shows mutual reinforcement on two of the three corpora (CORD and the forms corpus), with measurable gains especially on document-level facets (+4.8 and +11.0 points respectively) and smaller but directional gains on span-level extraction (+0.5 and +7.2). On WildReceipt, conditioned training still avoids being beaten by any alternative on both sides, but it leads to a tradeoff rather than strict reinforcement. Control experiments show that shuffling the conditioning content breaks document-level improvements while mostly preserving span-level performance, and a neutral-content control reproduces fine-level gains on WildReceipt (due to prompt structure) but yields no clear benefit on the other datasets. On the forms corpus, mixed and neutral regimes collapse to predicting the majority document label for all test cases, while conditioned training recovers a realistic distribution of labels. Probing reveals that relevant information is decodable across all regimes and does not become clearly more decodable under conditioning.

Conclusion: Standard mixed joint training across span- and document-level tasks does not produce the hypothesized Mutual Reinforcement Effect in multimodal document understanding and can even hurt performance. A more constrained conditioned-training scheme, where one task’s gold outputs condition the other only during training, can yield mutual gains on both granularities for some corpora and prevents pathological label collapse, particularly on coarse document-level tasks. However, benefits are dataset-dependent, sometimes driven more by prompt structure than semantic conditioning content, and do not correspond to a clearly increased decodability of task-relevant information inside the model, suggesting that reinforcement mechanisms may be subtle and architecture- or dataset-specific.

Abstract: The Mutual Reinforcement Effect (MRE) asks whether a fine, span-level and a coarse, document-level task help each other when one model handles both. We test it in multimodal document understanding on three corpora, two of receipts and one of scanned business forms, comparing single-task, joint and conditioned training, which puts one granularity's gold output in the other's prompt during training only. We build Doc-MRE, an annotation layer pairing gold field extraction (point) with four document-level facets (line), from a three-judge LLM committee under a pre-registration, validated by blind re-annotation. One predicate, fixed in advance: at a shared recipe, a regime reinforces if it beats the matched single-task model on both granularities. Mixed joint training, the arrangement prior MRE work assumes, reinforces on no corpus at the main scale: it is below both single-task models on CORD and trades one granularity for the other on the two others, as single-task tuning does. Conditioned training reinforces on two of the three, CORD (+0.5 point, +4.8 line) and the forms corpus (+7.2 point, +11.0 line), resolvably on the coarse side and directionally on the fine one, and trades on WildReceipt; at that recipe no alternative measurably beats it on either side anywhere. Two byte-identical-prompt controls separate content from format: shuffled conditioning destroys the coarse-side skill but costs the fine side far less, and a neutral-content control reproduces the whole fine-side gain on WildReceipt, which is therefore prompt structure but buys nothing resolvable on the other two. On the forms corpus conditioning buys collapse avoidance: mixed training and the neutral control both assign the majority semantic label to all 50 test documents; only conditioning recovers the gold distribution. Probes find the information decodable under every regime with no resolvable increase under conditioning.

</details>


### [65] [Compile, Don't Memorize: A Context Compilation Architecture (CCA) for In-Context Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00759)
*Jinhu Qi,Minda Hu,Wentao Zhang,Weiqiang Jin,Yanyu Chen,Junli Wang,Irwin King*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes Context Compilation Architecture (CCA), which compiles long natural-language task descriptions into a structured intermediate representation with explicit rules and output specs, then uses verifiers and correction loops to improve LLM performance on rule-heavy in-context learning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs struggle with long, rule-dense in-context learning tasks where missing a single rule fails the whole task. Current approaches rely on a one-shot “read-and-reason” forward pass that jointly handles extraction, planning, generation, and self-checking, leading to brittleness and low pass rates on strict benchmarks. The authors want to reduce this brittleness and understand whether explicit context compilation can systematically improve performance compared to existing long-context strategies like gist retrieval and multi-agent self-play.

Method: They introduce the Context Compilation Architecture (CCA), which first compiles a long prose context into a typed intermediate representation (IR) with fixed slots: rules (must_do, must_not, conditional), output_spec, available_tools, and data_profile. This compilation is performed once per context. Downstream, CCA uses executable verifiers derived from the IR and a violation-gated correction loop: candidate answers are checked against the IR, violations are detected, and the model iteratively corrects its outputs. They evaluate CCA on CL-bench (1,899 tasks) across four open-base LLMs and compare against vanilla prompting and long-context baselines ReadAgent-P and Ctx2Skill.

Result: On CL-bench, CCA outperforms vanilla prompting and both long-context baselines across all four base models. For example, it increases Kimi K2.5’s accuracy from 15.4% to 21.4%, with improvements especially strong on rule-dense categories where many fine-grained constraints must be followed simultaneously. The method thus yields consistent and meaningful gains on challenging, detail-sensitive ICL tasks.

Conclusion: Explicitly compiling natural-language contexts into a structured IR and coupling this with verifiers and correction loops can substantially reduce the brittleness of LLMs on long, rule-heavy in-context learning tasks. CCA provides a generally applicable harness that improves performance over existing long-context strategies across models and is particularly effective when many precise rules must be respected. The approach suggests that separating context understanding from answer generation is a promising direction for robust ICL systems.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly handle in-context learning (ICL) tasks where a long, novel context defines the rules, knowledge, and output schema for a series of questions. On benchmarks that grade against every detail of the context, even strong open-weights models pass only 12-16% of tasks: a single overlooked rule fails the whole response. We argue this brittleness is structural: the dominant "read-and-reason" paradigm asks the model to extract, plan, generate, and self-verify in one forward pass. We therefore ask whether explicit context compilation can fix it, how it compares to existing long-context strategies (gist retrieval, multi-agent self-play), and where the resulting harness benefit holds across task structure and model scale. We propose the Context Compilation Architecture (CCA), whose central novelty is a typed intermediate representation (IR) with fixed slots (rules.{must_do, must_not, conditional}, output_spec, available_tools, data_profile) into which any prose context is compiled once; executable verifiers and a violation-gated correction loop follow as downstream consequences. On CL-bench (1,899 tasks across 4 open base models), CCA outperforms vanilla prompting and two long-context baselines (ReadAgent-P, Ctx2Skill) on every base model, lifting Kimi K2.5 from 15.4% to 21.4% with gains concentrated on rule-dense sub-categories. Code and cached completions are available at https://github.com/TonyQJH/cca-emnlp2026.

</details>


### [66] [A Unified Mechanistic Analysis of Knowledge- and Safety-Based Refusals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00760)
*Yuri Son,Seunghee Kim,Hyuhng Joon Kim,Taeuk Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how large language models internally decide to refuse answering, comparing refusals due to lack of knowledge (KR) vs safety policy violations (SR), and finds they share a common initial mechanism but diverge in later layers into epistemic vs normative justifications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although language models often give similar refusal responses whether they lack knowledge or must enforce safety, prior work has analyzed these two refusal types separately. It is unclear whether they rely on the same internal mechanisms or distinct pathways, which matters for interpretability, control, and improving refusal behavior. The paper aims to fill this gap with a systematic, joint analysis.

Method: The authors construct a new dataset of 213 contrastive quadruples that jointly probe knowledge-based and safety-based refusals. They analyze internal representations across layers of LLMs to detect directions associated with refusal, examine transfer between KR and SR signals, and study where and how the model specializes into type-specific mechanisms related to uncertainty/knowledge vs safety/policy.

Result: They find a shared refusal direction that underlies both KR and SR, showing that the mechanisms overlap but are not identical. The overlap is asymmetric: internal signals learned for safety-based refusal transfer strongly to knowledge-based refusal, but knowledge-based signals transfer less effectively to safety-based contexts. Type-specific features appear mainly in higher layers: KR aligns with representations of uncertainty and knowledge, while SR aligns with safety and policy features.

Conclusion: Refusal in LLMs follows a commit-then-specify process. An early, shared mechanism first decides to refuse, then later, type-specialized features determine whether the justification is epistemic (knowledge/uncertainty) or normative (safety/policy). This explains both the commonality and divergence in KR and SR behavior and informs future work on steering and interpreting refusals.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly trained to decline queries that fall outside their knowledge (knowledge-based refusal, KR) or violate safety policies (safety-based refusal, SR). Although KR and SR result in superficially similar responses, they have largely been studied in isolation, leaving open whether they share an underlying mechanism. We address this gap with a systematic study on a new dataset of 213 contrastive quadruples that jointly probe both refusal types. We find that KR and SR are governed by overlapping yet distinguishable mechanisms. Both share a refusal direction, yet the overlap is asymmetric: SR signals transfer more strongly to KR than the reverse. Type-specific specialization emerges mainly in upper layers, with KR aligning with uncertainty- and knowledge-related representations and SR with safety- and policy-related ones. We thus characterize refusal as a commit-then-specify process: a shared initial mechanism commits to refusing, then type-specific features in later layers specify whether the grounds are epistemic or normative.

</details>


### [67] [Instella-MoE Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00791)
*Jiang Liu,Sudhanshu Ranjan,Prakamya Mishra,Yonatan Dukler,Gowtham Ramesh,Jialian Wu,Ximeng Sun,Wen Xie,Chaojun Hou,Vikram Appia,Zhenyu Gu,Zicheng Liu,Emad Barsoum*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Instella-MoE is a 16B-parameter, fully open Mixture-of-Experts language model optimized for efficiency on AMD GPUs, achieving strong benchmark performance and releasing all artifacts for reproducible research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To build an efficient, high-performing, and fully open Mixture-of-Experts language model that competes with existing open and open-weight models, while enabling transparent and reproducible research, especially on AMD Instinct hardware.

Method: They design a sparsely activated MoE architecture with 16B total parameters and 2.8B active per token, introducing Gated Multi-head Latent Attention and FarSkip-Collective connectivity for efficiency. The training pipeline is multi-stage: pre-training, mid-training, long-context extension, supervised fine-tuning with feedback-driven data curation, direct preference optimization, and reinforcement learning with Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation. The model is trained from scratch on AMD Instinct MI300X and MI325X GPUs and evaluated on standard pre-training and post-training benchmarks.

Result: Instella-MoE attains an average score of 76.7 on standard pre-training benchmarks, surpassing prior fully open models like OLMo-3-7B, SmolLM3-3B, and OLMoE-1B-7B. At similar active-parameter scales, it remains competitive with open-weight MoE and dense models such as Moonlight-16B-A3B and Qwen3.5-4B. After post-training, the Think checkpoint scores 73.2 on instruction-following, reasoning, math, coding, and chat benchmarks, outperforming both fully open and open-weight peers with comparable or larger active parameters.

Conclusion: Instella-MoE demonstrates that a carefully designed, sparsely activated MoE architecture, combined with a comprehensive multi-stage training pipeline and system-level optimizations, can yield an efficient and competitive open model. By releasing weights, configs, data mixtures, and training code, the work establishes Instella-MoE as a strong, fully open foundation for future MoE research and reproducible LLM development, particularly on AMD GPU hardware.

Abstract: In this work, we introduce Instella-MoE, a fully open Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model with 16 billion total parameters and 2.8 billion active parameters per token, trained entirely from scratch on AMD Instinct MI300X and MI325X GPUs. Instella-MoE combines a sparsely activated MoE design with architectural and system-level innovations, including Gated Multi-head Latent Attention (Gated MLA) and FarSkip-Collective connectivity, enabling efficient large-scale training and inference. The model is developed through a multi-stage pipeline comprising pre-training, mid-training, long-context extension, supervised fine-tuning with feedback-driven data curation, direct preference optimization, and reinforcement learning with Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation. Instella-MoE achieves an average score of 76.7 across standard pre-training benchmarks, outperforming prior fully open models including OLMo-3-7B, SmolLM3-3B, and OLMoE-1B-7B, while remaining competitive with open-weight MoE and dense baselines at comparable active-parameter scales, including Moonlight-16B-A3B and Qwen3.5-4B. After post-training, our final Think checkpoint achieves an average score of 73.2 across instruction-following, reasoning, math, coding, and chat benchmarks, outperforming both fully open and open-weight models with comparable or larger active parameter counts in our evaluation. To support transparent and reproducible research, we release the complete Instella-MoE model flow, including model weights, training configurations, data mixtures, and training code. Together, these contributions establish Instella-MoE a strong, fully open foundation for efficient, high-performing MoE models and reproducible research.

</details>


### [68] [SFAD: Speculative Factuality-Aware Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00796)
*Guanqiao Chen,Di Wang,Lijie Hu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A new speculative decoding framework (SFAD) improves contextual faithfulness of LLMs while keeping or improving inference efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for improving contextual faithfulness in LLMs either double inference cost (contrastive decoding) or require heavy post-training with reinforcement learning, making them impractical for efficient, knowledge-intensive applications.

Method: They build ConFide, a fine-grained preference dataset with atomic perturbations, and train a context-faithful draft model using Direct Preference Optimization. At inference, they introduce Epistemic Friction to detect hallucinations by measuring distributional tension weighted by model certainty, and Asymmetric Logit Steering to adjust the target distribution via residual-based logit injection only when friction is high; otherwise normal speculative decoding is used.

Result: SFAD significantly improves contextual faithfulness and achieves a 2.48x speedup in inference compared with baselines in experiments.

Conclusion: Speculative decoding can be augmented with targeted hallucination detection and logit steering to provide both higher contextual faithfulness and faster inference, offering a practical solution for deploying more reliable LLMs in knowledge-intensive settings.

Abstract: As one of the most critical challenges in large language models, contextual faithfulness directly determines their reliability in knowledge-intensive applications. This task is particularly challenging as it requires balancing factual consistency with generation efficiency. Contrastive decoding methods require dual forward passes (with and without context) to compare model outputs, doubling inference computational overhead, while post-training alignment demands extensive reinforcement learning with substantial computational overhead. To address this challenge, we present \textbf{SFAD}, a speculative decoding framework that enhances contextual faithfulness without inference degradation. We first construct \textbf{ConFide}, a preference dataset with fine-grained atomic perturbations, to train a context-faithful draft model via Direct Preference Optimization. During inference, Epistemic Friction detects potential hallucinations by quantifying distributional tension weighted by specialist certainty. When friction exceeds the threshold, Asymmetric Logit Steering refines the target distribution through residual-based logit injection; otherwise, standard speculation proceeds. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SFAD substantially improves faithfulness while achieving $2.48\times$ speedup, offering a practical solution for efficient LLMs.

</details>


### [69] [TEIDAN: A Multilingual Multiparty Dialogue Corpus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00802)
*Taiga Mori,Koji Inoue,Mikey Elmers,Divesh Lala,Tatsuya Kawahara*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduction of TEIDAN, a multilingual multimodal corpus of spontaneous three-party conversations in Japanese and English.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing corpora for multi-party interaction are limited: they often involve meetings, task-oriented or text-based interactions, acted scenarios, and rarely support cross-linguistic comparison of spontaneous face-to-face triadic discussions. There is a need for naturalistic, multilingual, multimodal resources for studying and modeling human-human and human-agent group conversation.

Method: The authors created TEIDAN, a corpus of three-party conversations in Japanese and English. They recorded groups of three participants discussing open-ended topics using individual pin microphones, a microphone array, and participant-facing cameras. They produced IPU-based transcripts for both languages, described the collection design, participants, recording setup, and transcription format, and computed corpus statistics. They also performed preliminary analyses to demonstrate possible research uses.

Result: TEIDAN currently contains multilingual (Japanese and English) multimodal recordings of spontaneous triadic conversations, with synchronized audio, video, and IPU-based transcripts. The paper reports descriptive statistics and initial analytic results that show patterns relevant to turn-taking, addressee recognition, and multimodal grounding.

Conclusion: TEIDAN is presented as a reusable corpus resource for research on multi-party human-human and human-agent interaction, especially in triadic, face-to-face, and cross-linguistic settings. The initial release includes Japanese and English, and the authors plan to expand it to additional languages. Preliminary analyses indicate its suitability for studying turn-taking behavior, identifying addressees, and exploring multimodal grounding.

Abstract: Multi-party interaction is a central setting for human communication and a necessary target for human-agent interaction systems that must participate in group conversation. Yet available corpora often focus on meetings, task-oriented interaction, text-based interaction, or acted scenarios, and fewer resources support cross-linguistic comparison of spontaneous face-to-face triadic discussion. This paper presents TEIDAN, a multilingual multimodal corpus that currently consists of Japanese and English three-party conversations. TEIDAN records groups of three participants discussing open-ended topics with individual pin microphones, a microphone array, and participant-facing cameras, and provides IPU-based transcripts for both language portions. Earlier studies used subsets of the Japanese portion for task-specific benchmarks in multi-party dialogue modeling; in contrast, this paper presents TEIDAN as a corpus resource spanning both Japanese and English, with planned expansion to additional languages. We describe the collection design, participants, recording setup, transcription format, and corpus statistics, and provide preliminary analyses to illustrate how TEIDAN can support research on turn-taking, addressee recognition, and multimodal grounding in human-human and human-agent interaction.

</details>


### [70] [TWIX: a Two-Stage Approach for End-To-End Named Entity Recognition and Relation Extraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00832)
*Marco Martinelli,Laura Menotti*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They introduce TWIX, an end-to-end two-stage IE pipeline that excels on the GutBrainIE benchmark for extracting entities and relations in the gut-brain axis domain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Due to the rapid increase in scientific literature, particularly in specialized domains like the gut-brain axis, there is a need for robust automatic information extraction systems to aid knowledge discovery and organization.

Method: They design TWIX, an end-to-end information extraction pipeline with three interconnected modules. Each module uses a two-stage framework to jointly tackle four subtasks in the GutBrainIE benchmark: NER, NERD, and RE (with two RE subtasks). The two-stage design likely separates candidate generation from refinement or disambiguation to improve performance.

Result: On both development and test splits of the GutBrainIE benchmark, TWIX significantly outperforms the provided baseline system and ranks first among all submitted systems on every subtask (NER, NERD, and both RE tasks).

Conclusion: A two-stage, modular end-to-end pipeline such as TWIX is highly effective for domain-specific information extraction; it yields substantial precision and recall improvements and sets a new state of the art on the GutBrainIE benchmark.

Abstract: The exponential growth of scientific publications calls for automatic Information Extraction (IE) systems to support knowledge discovery. In this context, the GutBrainIE benchmark evaluates Named Entity Recognition (NER), Named Entity Recognition and Disambiguation (NERD), and Relation Extraction (RE) systems in the gut-brain axis domain. We propose Two-stage Workflow for Information eXtraction (TWIX), an end-to-end IE pipeline featuring three interconnected modules, each leveraging a two-stage framework to solve all four GutBrainIE subtasks. Evaluation on the development and test sets shows that our method substantially outperforms the baseline by a wide margin, while also ranking first among all participant submissions across all subtasks. These results indicate that the proposed two-stage pipeline effectively improves both precision and recall in practical settings.

</details>


### [71] [Dense Process Supervision for Search Agents via Fact Utility Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00833)
*Rongzhi Zhu,Xiangyu Liu,Yi Liu,Shuo Zhang,Ruirui Zhang,Rui Wu,Tao Jiang,Zequn Sun,Wenhao Xu,Wei Hu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They improve reinforcement learning for search-based question answering by estimating the utility of intermediate facts and using that as dense rewards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RL with only outcome rewards struggles in search/QA tasks because it cannot accurately credit or blame intermediate reasoning steps, especially in multi-hop reasoning where many steps contribute to the final answer.

Method: They model the reasoning process as accumulating discrete evidence facts. From raw observations they extract structured facts into a fact store, cluster semantically equivalent facts, and use Bayesian estimation over multiple rollouts within each cluster to infer each cluster's posterior utility. These utilities are converted into dense step-level rewards used to train RL agents.

Result: On seven QA benchmarks (covering single-hop and multi-hop), their dense process supervision method achieves consistent performance gains over existing baselines that rely only on outcome rewards.

Conclusion: Fact-level utility estimation enables dense, step-level rewards that greatly improve credit assignment in RL for QA, particularly for multi-hop tasks, leading to better performance than outcome-based reward schemes.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for search agents typically relies on outcome rewards. However, it often fails to achieve effective credit assignment, due to the unclear value of intermediate steps. It is hard to separate their contributions from the final result. In this paper, we propose a dense process supervision method based on fact utility estimation, which models the reasoning process as the accumulation of discrete evidence facts. We first extract structured facts from raw observations and organize them into an explicit fact store. To support credit assignment, we then cluster semantically equivalent facts and infer the posterior utility of each fact cluster using Bayesian estimation over group rollouts. Finally, we convert the estimated fact utilities into dense step-level rewards to guide RL training. Experiments on seven single-hop and multi-hop QA benchmarks show that our method consistently outperforms existing baselines. Ablation studies validate clear relative improvements on multi-hop QA compared to outcome reward-only training.

</details>


### [72] [Staged Linguistic Seeding: Grounded Query Expansion for Verified-Unit QA in AI Contact Centers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00844)
*Hyeonseop Yoon,Jeong-Eun Park*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents an AI contact center QA system that only answers using a closed set of verified QA units, enhanced via staged linguistic seeding to boost retrieval accuracy under strict latency and safety constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional QA benchmarks and generative systems do not capture the strict latency and high cost of incorrect or unsupported answers in real-world AI contact centers, especially for voice hotlines. There is a need for a retrieval-based system that is both safe (avoids hallucinations) and effective (high recall) under deployment constraints.

Method: They build a contact-center QA system that responds exclusively with pre-verified QA units or routes to clarification/abstention/handoff. To improve retrieval, they propose staged linguistic seeding (SLS): (1) a human writes a world-grounded slot recipe per QA unit, (2) gpt-4.1-mini generates multiple query variants from the recipe, and (3) a light human review filters the generated variants. The enriched index supports low-latency inference via a single retrieval pass using various retrievers, without any query-time generation.

Result: On held-out query variants from two industrial domains, SLS significantly raises hybrid R@1 to 0.881 and 0.930, corresponding to +0.27 and +0.34 improvements, consistently across five different retrievers. Using the same gpt-4.1-mini generation budget, SLS outperforms doc2query by +0.20 and +0.32. Cross-provenance evaluation further indicates that SLS transfers well across different generated-query distributions. Additionally, by restricting answers to verified units, the system virtually eliminates unsupported generated content, reducing it from 7–13% to approximately 0%.

Conclusion: A verified-unit, retrieval-only QA architecture, combined with staged linguistic seeding for offline index enrichment, can meet real-world contact center constraints by significantly improving top-1 retrieval accuracy while effectively removing the surface for free-form hallucinations. The approach generalizes across domains and retrievers and is practical enough for industrial deployment, though the paper also notes and discusses negative results as part of its application-focused study.

Abstract: Customer-service QA in an AI contact center (AICC) runs under deployment constraints that benchmark QA misses: tight voice-hotline latency and a high cost for unsupported or wrong automatic answers. We deploy a system that answers only from a closed set of verified QA units: it returns a retrieved unit verbatim, or routes to clarify, abstain, or handoff. The index is enriched offline by staged linguistic seeding (SLS): a human authors a per-unit world-grounded slot recipe, gpt-4.1-mini renders it into variants, and a light human gate filters them. One methodology is reused across both domains, so inference stays a single retrieval pass with no query-time generation. On held-out query variants from two industrial domains, SLS lifts hybrid R@1 to 0.881/0.930 (+0.27/+0.34), with gains across all five retrievers tested. At the same gpt-4.1-mini generation budget, SLS beats doc2query by +0.20/+0.32, while cross-provenance evaluation provides additional evidence of transfer across generated-query distributions. Verified-unit answering also removes free-form generation's unsupported-content surface (7-13% versus approximately 0%). We report this as an application study, including negative results.

</details>


### [73] [Membership Inference in Fine-tuned Diffusion Language Models via Token-level Memorization Asymmetry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00873)
*Shengfang Zhai,Leo Marchyok,Yuling Shi,Huanran Chen,Yinpeng Dong,Jiaheng Zhang,Sanghyun Hong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies privacy risks in diffusion language models, discovers an asymmetry in how they memorize training tokens, and introduces a new metric (Q-Skew) that enables strong membership inference and PII-leakage attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion language models are becoming popular alternatives to autoregressive LMs because they support parallel generation and bidirectional context modeling, but their privacy risks are poorly understood compared to traditional LMs. The authors aim to rigorously characterize what, if anything, these models memorize about their training data and how that can be exploited for attacks.

Method: The authors first perform a theoretical analysis of the training dynamics of diffusion language models to uncover a phenomenon they call token-level memorization asymmetry, where different tokens or positions are memorized unevenly. Leveraging this insight, they design Q-Skew, a quantile-weighted skewness-based statistical indicator that, when computed from model outputs or internal scores, can distinguish training samples from non-members. They then evaluate Q-Skew as a membership inference attack on multiple fine-tuned DLMs and datasets, and also adapt it to scenarios involving PII extraction to test broader privacy leakage.

Result: Q-Skew consistently outperforms existing membership inference baselines across various DLM architectures and fine-tuning datasets, making it a more powerful attack tool. The token-level memorization asymmetry predicted by their theory is empirically observable, and the same Q-Skew signal can be used to improve or guide other privacy attacks, including extraction of personally identifiable information from models.

Conclusion: Diffusion language models exhibit a distinct form of token-level memorization that can be exploited for privacy attacks. The proposed Q-Skew metric effectively detects whether data points were in the training set and assists in PII leakage, demonstrating that DLMs have a significant, previously underappreciated privacy attack surface. This underscores the necessity of systematic, dedicated privacy evaluation and mitigation strategies for DLMs, not just for autoregressive LMs.

Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) have recently emerged as an alternative modeling paradigm to autoregressive LMs, offering advantages such as parallel generation and bidirectional context modeling. Despite growing interest in their generative capabilities, the privacy risks of DLMs remain underexplored. We identify a phenomenon termed token-level memorization asymmetry through theoretical analysis of diffusion training dynamics. Building on this finding, we propose Q-Skew, a quantile-weighted skewness-based indicator for membership inference on finetuned DLMs. Experiments across multiple fine-tuning datasets and models show that our method outperforms existing baselines. Moreover, we show that Q-Skew can also facilitate other privacy violations, such as PII extraction. Our findings reveal a previously underexplored privacy attack surface and highlight the need for systematic privacy evaluation of DLMs.

</details>


### [74] [Context-Grounding Gains Are Mediated by Pre-existing Machinery: Auditing GRPO, SFT, and DPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00925)
*Prakhar Gupta,Vaibhav Gupta*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how different post-training methods (GRPO, SFT, DPO) affect a language model’s ability to follow conflicting prompt evidence (grounding), finding that most grounding improvements come from reusing mechanisms already present in the base model rather than creating new ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language models often rely on memorized knowledge instead of information presented in the prompt, especially when the two conflict. While post-training methods (like RL-based GRPO, supervised fine-tuning, and preference-based DPO) are known to improve instruction-following, it is unclear whether they do so by building new grounding mechanisms or by strengthening existing ones. Understanding this distinction matters for designing more efficient and safer training pipelines and for knowing how far we can push grounding without changing model architecture.

Method: Starting from a single base checkpoint, the authors apply nine post-training procedures spanning GRPO variants, conflict-focused supervised fine-tuning (conflict-SFT), and DPO. Before any post-training, they estimate a “grounding direction” in representation space that corresponds to using prompt evidence over memorized knowledge. They then (1) measure grounding performance after each method, (2) compare across scales and model families, (3) use causal tracing / attention-head analysis to identify which attention heads support grounding, and (4) manipulate representations by adding or subtracting the estimated grounding direction to assess causality and shared mechanisms across methods. They also examine how a supervised warm start that increases rollout inclusion of the correct context answer affects subsequent GRPO gains.

Result: Across five GRPO variants, improvements in grounding are minor, even when the RL objective’s rewarded metric increases. Two GRPO variants replicated across seeds show effects that, via equivalence tests, are statistically bounded to be smaller than the gains from conflict-SFT. Conflict-SFT yields moderate improvements in grounding, while DPO pushes grounding performance close to ceiling on the distribution it is trained to match. Conflict-SFT and DPO are found to rely largely on the same causal attention heads already present in the base model. Representation interventions show that subtracting the base model’s grounding direction reduces both methods’ gains, whereas adding that direction to the base model recovers about 35% of DPO’s gain without detectable side effects. After a supervised warm start that increases the frequency with which rollouts contain the context answer, applying the same GRPO setup adds almost no additional grounding improvement.

Conclusion: Most of the observed grounding improvements from conflict-focused SFT and DPO can be explained by amplifying existing grounding machinery in the base model, not by learning qualitatively new mechanisms. GRPO, at least in the tested configurations, offers little extra grounding beyond what can be achieved with supervised methods, especially once a warm start is applied. Effective grounding thus appears to depend primarily on representational directions and attention heads already present before post-training, suggesting that future work should focus on better identifying and leveraging these pre-existing structures rather than relying solely on new RL-style objectives.

Abstract: Language models can ignore prompt evidence when it conflicts with memorized knowledge. Post-training can make models follow such evidence more reliably, but it is unclear whether these gains require new machinery or strengthen machinery already present. We compare nine post-training arms spanning GRPO, SFT, and DPO from one starting checkpoint, with key comparisons extended across scales and families. We estimate a grounding direction from that checkpoint before training. Across five tested GRPO variants, grounding gains are small. For the two variants replicated across seeds, equivalence tests bound their effects below the conflict-SFT gain even as the rewarded metric improves. Conflict-SFT improves grounding moderately, while DPO drives grounding near ceiling on its matched distribution. Conflict-SFT and DPO largely use the same causal attention-head set as the starting model. Subtracting the starting-model direction suppresses both gains, while adding it to the starting model recovers 35% of DPO's gain at a dose passing all stated side-effect checks. After a supervised warm start makes the context answer appear in more rollouts, the same GRPO recipe adds essentially no further grounding gain. In our setting, grounding gains largely depend on machinery already present in the starting model.

</details>


### [75] [DualStake: Dual-Path Confidence Calibration in Deep Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00935)
*Yinuo Xu,Yuwei Liang,Jianjie Cheng,Meng Wang,Yongcan Yu,Shuo Lu,Jian Liang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper addresses overconfidence in Deep Research agents by introducing stepwise confidence elicitation and a dual-path calibration method, DualStake, which jointly calibrates evidence and answer confidence to better reflect true uncertainty without hurting accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep Research agents perform multi-round retrieval and reasoning but exhibit unreliable and overconfident self-reported confidence, which harms user trust and makes it hard to know when they should abstain. There is a need to better understand and calibrate these confidence signals in a way that is compatible with existing Deep Research pipelines.

Method: The authors first augment Deep Research pipelines with explicit confidence elicitation after each retrieval step, distinguishing between Evidence Confidence (E-Conf, after final retrieval) and Answer Confidence (A-Conf, after answer generation). They empirically analyze the relationship between these signals and correctness, discovering that E-Conf is a stronger uncertainty indicator and strongly shapes A-Conf. Building on this, they design DualStake, a dual-path calibration method that introduces margin-clipped, confidence-dependent stake rewards to simultaneously align E-Conf and A-Conf with answer correctness. This training objective rewards calibrated confidence while explicitly preventing excessive push toward extreme confidence values.

Result: Across Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Qwen3-4B models evaluated on 8 question answering benchmarks, DualStake yields consistently better calibration of both evidence and answer confidence, as measured by standard calibration metrics, without degrading answer accuracy. This shows that the method makes the models’ confidence scores more trustworthy while preserving task performance.

Conclusion: The study concludes that evidence-level confidence elicited within the Deep Research process is a powerful signal for uncertainty and that answer confidence is heavily influenced by it. By leveraging these insights, the proposed DualStake calibration framework successfully aligns both confidence types with actual correctness, mitigating overconfidence and improving the reliability of Deep Research agents without sacrificing accuracy.

Abstract: Deep Research agents tackle knowledge-intensive tasks through multi-round retrieval and decision-oriented generation. However, these agents suffer from severe overconfidence, making their expressed confidence unreliable for user trust and downstream abstention. To address this, we augment the Deep Research pipeline with step confidence elicitation after each retrieval, building on the commonly used post-answer verbalized confidence. Interestingly, we find that Evidence Confidence (E-Conf), elicited after the final retrieval step, provides a stronger uncertainty signal than Answer Confidence (A-Conf), elicited after answer generation, and that A-Conf is largely shaped by E-Conf. Based on these findings, we propose DualStake, a dual-path calibration method that applies margin-clipped, confidence-dependent stake rewards to jointly align E-Conf and A-Conf with answer correctness while limiting extreme confidence optimization. Experiments on Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Qwen3-4B across 8 QA benchmarks demonstrate that DualStake consistently improves calibration without sacrificing answer accuracy. The code is available at https://github.com/FloXXXt/DualStake.

</details>


### [76] [A Dataset for Modeling Iterative Problem-Solving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00940)
*Fagun Patel,Sang T. Truong,Duc Q. Nguyen,Kazunori Fukuhara,Benjamin W. Domingue,Sanmi Koyejo,Nick Haber*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces CodeInsight, a large-scale dataset and benchmark for modeling how programmers iteratively solve problems via repeated code submissions and feedback, and compares different model families for predicting performance and understanding error/strategy dynamics over attempts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Iterative problem solving—by humans or agents—involves sequences of attempts, feedback, and revisions, but we lack large, fine-grained datasets and standardized benchmarks to study how performance changes (improves, plateaus, regresses) and how errors and strategies evolve across attempts. Programming courses with automated grading naturally generate rich logs of such iterative behavior, yet prior work has not fully leveraged them to systematically compare sequential and generative models as predictors of solver dynamics.

Method: The authors curate CodeInsight, a dataset of over 3 million C++ code submissions from 3,286 undergraduates across two introductory courses over two years, including test-case outcomes, timestamps, and source code. They construct a benchmark with a unified calibration-and-scoring protocol to evaluate several model classes: (1) parametric models, (2) sequential models, and (3) generative models. A key method is an adapted Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM) that uses discrete latent variables to track evolving solver characteristics. They also build an LLM-based predictor that, conditioned on context, generates full code submissions for each attempt, from which predictions are derived and failure modes analyzed.

Result: On the CodeInsight benchmark, the adapted RSSM achieves the best predictive accuracy on three of the four courses examined, outperforming other model types in forecasting solver performance over attempts. The LLM-based predictor shows lower predictive accuracy but can output complete code submissions at each step, allowing richer qualitative analysis of where and how it fails. An observed pattern is that higher coding proficiency in the generative model does not translate into better predictive performance of human solver behavior; instead, there is an inverse relationship in this setting.

Conclusion: The work provides a new large-scale dataset and benchmark for studying sequential learning and iterative problem solving in programming education. The adapted RSSM is currently the strongest predictor of performance trajectories, whereas LLMs, despite strong coding skills, are better interpreted as generative solvers conditioned on context rather than accurate simulators of human solver behavior. By releasing the dataset (on request) and code, the authors aim to catalyze future research on modeling learning dynamics, strategy shifts, and persistent errors across iterative attempts.

Abstract: Solving problems through repeated attempts is a sequential modeling task: at each step, the solver receives feedback and decides how to revise their solutions. Predicting whether performance improves, plateaus, or regresses across attempts is central to understanding any iterative problem-solving process in both human learners and autonomous agents. Beyond outcomes, modeling what errors persist and how strategies shift across attempts provides deeper insight into the mechanics of sequential learning. Studying these dynamics requires observing many solvers as they attempt, receive feedback, and revise. Programming courses with automated grading provide this setting, as students iteratively submit code to test suites and receive feedback on every attempt. We therefore curate CodeInsight, a large-scale dataset of over 3 million submissions from 3,286 undergraduates across 2 introductory C++ courses in 2 academic years, with test-case-level outcomes, timestamps, and source code. On this dataset, we build a benchmark that evaluates models spanning parametric, sequential, and generative traditions under a shared calibration-and-scoring protocol, including a Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM) adapted to track solver characteristics through discrete latent variables and an LLM-based predictor that generates explicit solutions. The adapted RSSM achieves the strongest predictive accuracy on three of the four courses. The LLM predictor is less accurate but produces full submissions at each attempt, enabling direct analysis of failure modes. We find that the model's coding proficiency is inversely related to predictive performance in this setting, with the LLM better understood as a generative solver conditioned on context rather than a faithful predictor of solver behavior. We publicly release our code and the dataset on request to facilitate future research.

</details>


### [77] [Calibration is the Bottleneck: An Action-Class Diagnostic of Multi-Turn Tool-Calling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00949)
*Kangjia Zhao,Jiajun Li,Haozhan Shen,Wei Chow,Linfeng Li,Hang Song,Lingdong Kong,Chen Zhi,Tiancheng Zhao,Songhua Liu,Jianwei Yin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose a diagnostic framework for multi-turn tool-calling LLMs that decomposes failures into miscalibrated action selection vs tool execution errors, revealing issues hidden by aggregate accuracy metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-turn tool-calling benchmarks report aggregate accuracy where open models now rival or beat closed models, but this single metric hides whether models are actually making context-appropriate decisions across different action types. There is a need to understand *how* models fail in multi-turn interactions—whether they choose the wrong type of action or execute the chosen action poorly—and to expose problems that current state-graders and metrics cannot see.

Method: They define a four-way action space for each turn—TOOL_CALL, ASK (ask user), REFUSE, CONFIRM—and introduce an action-class-oriented diagnostic that computes both standard accuracy and a new quantity, Gold Action Recall (GAR), which upper-bounds accuracy if the model were perfectly calibrated over the gold action class. They then analyze when accuracy exceeds GAR (indicating grading artifacts that hide miscalibration) and when GAR is much larger than accuracy (pinpointing execution failures within TOOL_CALL). They apply this diagnostic to a range of tool-calling LLMs on multiple multi-turn benchmarks, and study how simple context-only perturbations affect calibration and accuracy across different model families and perturbation mechanisms.

Result: The diagnostic shows that action-class miscalibration is a major hidden failure mode across evaluated models and is often invisible to standard state-based graders, leading to overly optimistic aggregate accuracy—especially for models heavily trained on tool use. Their framework separates such models from those that better choose context-appropriate actions. They further find that calibration is highly sensitive to context-only perturbations, with the same perturbation improving accuracy for some model families (up to +11.5 percentage points) while harming others (down to -21.0 percentage points), and that the impact varies with how the perturbation is implemented.

Conclusion: Aggregate accuracy on multi-turn tool-calling benchmarks is insufficient and can be misleading because it masks distinct error modes and grading artifacts. Evaluations should include action-class-level diagnostics—especially the GAR-based analysis—to reveal whether models are choosing the right type of action and where execution within TOOL_CALL actually fails. This richer analysis better characterizes model behavior, exposes miscalibration, and clarifies differences between model families.

Abstract: Multi-turn tool calling is a core evaluation scenario for large language model (LLM) agents. On public tool-calling benchmarks, open-weight models now approach or even surpass closed-source frontier models in aggregate accuracy. However, this metric averages over many different multi-turn situations and obscures whether progress is balanced across them. We propose an action-class-oriented diagnostic framework that decomposes multi-turn failures into two orthogonal modes: action-class miscalibration and action-execution failure. The framework operates over a four-class action space (TOOL_CALL/ASK/REFUSE/CONFIRM) and introduces a self-revealing upper bound Acc <= GAR (Gold Action Recall); the two modes show up as bound violation (Acc > GAR, exposing state-grader masking of miscalibration) and large bound slack (GAR >> Acc, localizing execution failure within TOOL_CALL). We validate it on a panel of tool-calling models across multiple multi-turn benchmarks. Across our panel, the diagnostic reveals action-class miscalibration as a substantial failure mode the state grader cannot see. This gap inflates standing for heavily tool-trained families, which our diagnostic separates from families with context-appropriate action choice. Calibration is reshapable through context-only perturbations, but the reshape is heterogeneous: a single perturbation moves accuracy in opposite directions across families (up to +11.5 vs -21.0 pp on the same scenario), and its effect further depends on the perturbation mechanism. We argue that multi-turn tool-calling evaluations should supplement aggregate accuracy with action-class diagnostics that expose what the model actually does in each scenario.

</details>


### [78] [PersianAnonymizer: Evaluating LLM-Labeled Training for Efficient NER-based Anonymization in Persian](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00958)
*Mohammad Hossein Shalchian,Mostafa Amiri,Amir Mahdi Sadeghzadeh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper builds a compact Persian NER model for anonymizing customer chats, supervised by different LLM-generated annotations, and finds that zero-shot OSS labeling leads to the best downstream performance and very fast, cheap deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industrial Persian customer-service chats contain sensitive personal information and must be anonymized before use, but running large LLMs for real-time or large-scale anonymization is too slow and costly. There is also a lack of strong, domain-specific NER models and labeled data in Persian. The authors aim to leverage LLMs as labelers to cheaply generate supervision and then distill that into a small, efficient NER model suitable for production anonymization.

Method: The authors use three instruction-tuned LLMs (DeepSeek-V3-0324, GPT-OSS-120B, and Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507) to annotate Persian chats with entity spans via a shared JSON schema, creating four labeled corpora (OSS_ZeroShot, Qwen_ZeroShot, Qwen_FewShot, DeepSeek_FewShot) that differ in labeler and prompting regime (zero-shot vs few-shot). For each corpus, they train a MatinaRoberta-based token classification NER model and evaluate on a test set using token-level precision, recall, and F1 (overall and by class). They also introduce Label Coverage Recall (LCR), measuring how many true non-O tokens are at least detected as some entity, and analyze cross-labeler agreement using tokenwise Venn diagrams. Finally, they benchmark the latency of LLM-based annotation on H200 GPUs versus the trained NER model on a single RTX 3090 for labeling the entire test set.

Result: Among the NER models trained on different LLM-generated corpora, the model trained on OSS_ZeroShot supervision attains the highest macro-F1 and LCR, indicating both better per-class balance and stronger overall entity coverage. The distilled NER model can process a 40,000-message test set in about two minutes on a single consumer-grade RTX 3090 GPU, while LLM-based labeling is much slower and more resource-intensive on H200 hardware. Cross-labeler analysis shows differing behaviors among LLM labelers, which explains the variance in downstream NER performance.

Conclusion: Using an open-source LLM in a zero-shot setting to generate initial annotations provides surprisingly strong supervision for training a compact MatinaRoberta-based NER model for Persian chat anonymization. The resulting model achieves high-quality entity detection, particularly in terms of macro-F1 and label coverage, while being orders of magnitude faster and cheaper to run than the original LLM labelers. This demonstrates a practical and scalable distillation pipeline for anonymizing large volumes of Persian industrial chat data and suggests that careful selection of LLM labelers and prompting strategies is crucial for effective low-resource NER distillation.

Abstract: We target practical anonymization of Persian customer chats by training a compact NER model from LLM-labeled supervision and selecting the best labeler for deployment. We compare three instruction-tuned LLMs: DeepSeek-V3-0324, GPT-OSS-120B, and Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507, to produce span annotations under a shared JSON protocol, yielding four corpora (OSS_ZeroShot, Qwen_ZeroShot, Qwen_FewShot, DeepSeek_FewShot). A MatinaRoberta-based token-classifier is trained per corpus and evaluated with token-level Precision/Recall/F1 (overall and per-class). We also report Label Coverage Recall (LCR), the proportion of gold non-O tokens predicted as non-O, and quantify cross-labeler behavior via a token-level Venn on test annotations. Finally, we contrast test-set annotation latency of the LLMs on H200 nodes with the trained NER's test-time labeling on a single RTX 3090. Results show that supervision from OSS_ZeroShot yields the strongest macro-F1 and LCR, while the resulting NER labels an entire 40K-message test set in approximately 2 minutes on one consumer GPU. This establishes a practical path to high-quality, low-cost anonymization for Persian industrial data.

</details>


### [79] [Disclosure-Gated User Simulation for Companion-Agent Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00982)
*Yao Liu,Yu He*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They fix over-cooperative LLM user simulators in benchmarks by adding a learned disclosure gate that conditions how much information the simulated user reveals on the system’s behavior, and show this changes rankings in meaningful but stable ways.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current scalable evaluation often uses LLMs to simulate users, but these simulated users are unrealistically cooperative. Systems can “game” such benchmarks by just asking more questions instead of actually engaging users well. The authors want a principled way to make simulated users control their information disclosure based on how the companion agent behaves, and to verify that this change affects rankings meaningfully without breaking benchmark stability.

Method: They design a disclosure gate: a five-level internal ladder of information access, mapped onto three observable depth layers. They create a specification of how the gate should behave, then build a training corpus with a synthetic branch (explicit gating labels and behaviors) and a real branch (human-like speech and reactions). They train an LLM-based user simulator to implicitly learn gating behavior from the synthetic branch while learning natural language from the real branch, without telling it the gate level at runtime. They run ablations (e.g., removing or altering gating), audits, human studies, and negative controls. They test sensitivity by running multiple systems under test on CompanionBench, comparing rankings and score scales with and without explicit gate labels, and comparing against alternative simulators (including a frontier model prompted as a simulator).

Result: When gate labels are removed at inference but the simulator has learned the gating behavior, system rankings on the benchmark change more than run-to-run noise, showing the gate meaningfully affects evaluation, but individual system scores remain statistically stable. The best simulator candidate meets two criteria: order-preserving rankings and scale-stable absolute scores. This simulator’s leaderboard correlates at 0.993 with the original CompanionBench simulator. Other candidate simulators fail: e.g., simply prompting a frontier model as the user simulator leaves rankings nearly unchanged but increases all scores, masking a systematic bias if one only inspects rankings.

Conclusion: A disclosure gate that conditions user-simulator information release on agent behavior is a crucial, load-bearing part of realistic companion-agent evaluation. When properly specified and trained, it yields evaluations that are sensitive to agent quality while preserving ranking order and score scale, and can be implemented in a way that closely matches existing benchmarks. Relying on naïvely prompted large frontier models as user simulators risks silently inflating scores without changing rankings, which can mislead benchmark users. The authors provide a full formalization, empirical analysis, and a validated simulator implementation for CompanionBench.

Abstract: Using a large language model to play the user is now standard in scalable evaluation. It has a repeatedly diagnosed failure: the simulated user is excessively cooperative, so a system under test can score by the sheer number of questions it asks rather than by making the user willing to speak. We answer with a disclosure gate conditioning information release on the companion agent's behaviour: its state is a ladder of five ordered gates, merged onto three observable depth layers. We specify, ablate, and audit it, and train a user simulator against that specification. Gating behaviour is learned from the training corpus's synthetic branch, while the real branch supplies how people speak and react; after training, the simulator need not be told at runtime which gate each item sits behind. The gate is a load-bearing component of the environment: on the English corpus of a published companion-agent benchmark (CompanionBench), once training no longer states per example which gate each item sits behind, the largest rank displacement across 12 systems under test exceeds the noise band set by re-running that environment under a new seed, while per-system scores show no detectable change. We state two acceptance criteria: a ranking must be order-preserving, and absolute scores must be scale-stable. Of the candidates we examine, only one passes both -- the simulator we release -- and its leaderboard correlates at 0.993 with the benchmark's original simulator. By contrast, prompting a frontier model as the simulator barely moves the ranking while shifting every score upward -- a shift invisible to anyone checking the ranking alone. The environment we specify is the one that benchmark already used. That publication describes the mechanism in about four hundred words, and we supply what it lacked: specification, ablations, human studies, negative controls, and downstream sensitivity analysis.

</details>


### [80] [Inspicio: Open-Vocabulary, LLM-Based Sense Retrieval for Historical Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00998)
*Michele Ciletti*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Inspicio, an open-vocabulary LLM-based pipeline that links words in historical and low-resource languages to English WordNet synsets without needing a prior sense inventory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most word sense disambiguation methods require a pre-existing sense inventory and word-to-sense mapping in the source language, assumptions that fail for historical and low-resource languages whose WordNets are incomplete or missing. The authors aim to enable sense-level semantic analysis in such settings by leveraging English WordNet as a universal target without requiring source-language lexical resources.

Method: They design Inspicio, a retrieval-based pipeline. For each token occurrence in context, an instruction-tuned LLM generates (i) two English translations of the sentence, (ii) several candidate dictionary-style definitions of the target word in that context, and (iii) candidate English lemmas. These artifacts are then fed into a hybrid retrieval module that: (a) computes dense similarity between generated definitions and Open English WordNet synset glosses via sentence embeddings, (b) performs sparse lexical matching between candidate lemmas and WordNet lemmas, and (c) applies Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) to re-rank synsets, balancing relevance and diversity. They systematically vary the LLM and sentence-embedding model in a 6×6 grid to study configuration effects.

Result: On a new manually annotated dataset of Latin and Ancient Greek perception verbs, plus portions of the PREMOVE dataset and diachronic Italian data, the best Inspicio configuration achieves 96% Recall@50 on the perception-verb test set. Ablation shows that each component (translations, definitions, lemma suggestions, dense/sparse retrieval, MMR) yields measurable improvements. The method remains competitive on out-of-domain and cross-lingual evaluation scenarios.

Conclusion: LLM-generated translations, contextual definitions, and lemmas can effectively mediate between low-resource or historical source texts and a high-resource sense inventory like Open English WordNet. Inspicio offers a practical open-vocabulary WSD solution that does not require source-language WordNets or sense mappings, performs strongly on challenging historical-language benchmarks, and generalizes reasonably well across domains and languages.

Abstract: Word Sense Disambiguation has advanced rapidly for English and a handful of well-resourced modern languages, but it continues to assume the existence of a sense inventory and a word-to-sense mapping in the source language (Navigli, 2026). These assumptions break down for most historical and low-resource languages, whose dedicated WordNets are either incomplete or still under construction. We present Inspicio, an open-vocabulary retrieval pipeline that links tokens in context to synsets of the Open English WordNet (McCrae et al., 2020) without requiring any source-language inventory or mapping. For each occurrence, an instruction-tuned LLM produces two English translations of the surrounding sentence, a small set of candidate dictionary-style definitions, and a few candidate English lemmas. These outputs drive a hybrid retrieval step that combines dense definition-synset similarity, sparse lemma matching, and Maximal Marginal Relevance re-ranking. We evaluate the pipeline across a 6x6 grid of LLMs and sentence-embedding models on a new bilingual set of manually annotated Latin and Ancient Greek perception verbs, on a subset of PREMOVE dataset (Farina, 2025), and on a diachronic sample of Italian. The best configuration reaches 96% Recall@50 on the perception-verb test set, with each component contributing measurable gains, and remains competitive in the out-of-domain and cross-lingual settings.

</details>


### [81] [Right Frame, Wrong Rule: Cultural Cues Expose the Financial Knowledge Gap They Were Meant to Close](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00999)
*Rania Elbadry,Ahmed Heakl,Saeed Almheiri,Fan Zhang,Muhra AlMahri,Xueqing Peng,Mohsinul Kabir,Shuyao Wang,Yi Han,Saadeldine Eletter,Duzhen Zhang,Preslav Nakov,Yuxia Wang,Fajri Koto,Zhuohan Xie*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper analyzes how language models choose between multiple valid normative frameworks, focusing on Islamic finance, and shows that cultural cues strongly influence framework choice but not necessarily correctness within that framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand and evaluate how language models behave in settings where multiple normative frameworks (e.g., Islamic vs. conventional finance) could apply, and to expose failures that are hidden by standard, simpler evaluations that only test whether the model picked the 'right side'.

Method: They define a four-way taxonomy that separates (1) which normative framework the model chooses from (2) whether the answer is correct within that framework. Using Islamic finance as a testbed, they probe twelve models across two languages and fifty demographic/cultural signals, manipulating cultural cues to see how they affect framework selection and within-framework accuracy.

Result: Cultural cues significantly shift which normative framework models select, and there are large framework-specific accuracy differences, especially for non-frontier models. Under strong Islamic cues, large open-weight models choose the Islamic framework 97% of the time, but 57–66% of those Islamic-framework answers are wrong. Thus a simpler two-choice metric would misleadingly indicate near-perfect alignment while masking large competence failures.

Conclusion: Evaluations that only check whether a model picked the 'intended' normative side are insufficient. The authors propose that models may implicitly route toward frameworks where they are more competent, and that cultural cues can reveal competence gaps across frameworks. This supports (but does not yet test) a competence-conditioned routing hypothesis and motivates richer, framework-aware evaluation methods for normative pluralism settings.

Abstract: When a question has valid answers under different normative frameworks, a language model must decide which framework to use and whether it can answer correctly within it. We call this setting normative pluralism and study it in Islamic finance using a four-choice taxonomy that separates framework selection from within-framework correctness. This separation reveals the stereotype trap: a cultural cue steers a model toward one framework, but the model selects an incorrect answer within that framework. Across twelve models, two languages, and fifty demographic signals, cultural cues change framework selection and reveal substantial differences in accuracy, especially among non-frontier models. Under the strongest signal, large open-weight models select the Islamic framework 97% of the time. A two-choice evaluation would report near-perfect alignment, although 57--66% of those selections are incorrect. These findings motivate, but do not directly test, the competence-conditioned routing hypothesis: models may favor frameworks where they are more accurate, while cultural cues may expose framework-specific competence gaps.

</details>


### [82] [Phrase-Localized Language-Contrastive Guidance: Training-Free Localized Accent Control for Code-Switching Text-to-Speech](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01016)
*Che Hyun Lee,Sangkwon Park,Donghun Kang,Dongwook Lee,Youngho Cho,Heeseung Kim,Sungroh Yoon*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They introduce a training-free inference method to make code-switched TTS speak each language segment with its correct native accent rather than the primary language accent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing cross-lingual TTS systems handle code-switching poorly: when a foreign phrase appears inside a main-language utterance, it is usually pronounced with the main language’s accent, reducing naturalness and intelligibility. Training data and fine-tuning for every language combination is expensive, and current systems often leak accents across languages and hurt speaker identity.

Method: They propose Phrase-Localized Language-Contrastive Guidance (LCG), an inference-time framework for diffusion-style TTS. Instead of using a single language embedding/guidance across the entire utterance, LCG assigns different language guidance to different text regions (phrases) so that each part is generated under its own language condition. To determine phrase boundaries for code-switched segments without external alignment tools, they introduce a self-attention probing technique that inspects model attention patterns to automatically locate where each language segment starts and ends. The approach is training-free: no fine-tuning or auxiliary models are required, and it operates purely at inference.

Result: On multiple language pairs and code-switching scenarios, LCG consistently improves the perceived nativeness of the foreign-language phrase, reduces accent leakage between languages, and maintains overall speaker identity and naturalness. The improvements are robust across diverse language combinations.

Conclusion: Localized, language-specific guidance during inference, coupled with self-attention-based phrase boundary detection, can substantially improve the accent correctness of code-switched phrases in cross-lingual TTS without extra training or models. This shows that better use of existing model internals at inference can address code-switching accent problems efficiently.

Abstract: Current speech synthesis struggles with code-switching, which mixes a foreign language phrase into a primary language utterance, causing the phrase to be spoken with the primary language's accent rather than its native one. We propose Phrase-Localized Language-Contrastive Guidance (LCG), a training-free inference framework that restores a native accent to code-switched phrases in cross-lingual text-to-speech. LCG replaces the single language guidance applied across the whole utterance with a separate guidance for each region, so each part is guided by its own language. To choose where to apply this localized guidance, we propose a self-attention probing technique that finds the phrase boundaries without external alignments. Together, these components generate speech in which each region carries the accent of its own language, requiring no fine-tuning or auxiliary models. Across diverse language pairs, LCG robustly increases the nativeness of the code-switched phrase while suppressing accent leakage, and preserving overall speaker identity and naturalness.

</details>


### [83] [PCoMoE: Shifting MoE Inference from Monolithic Expert Selection to Fine-Grained Path Composition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01024)
*Ziyan Gan,Fangxin Liu,Chenyang Guan,Junjie Wang,Ning Yang,Haomin Li,Xiang Li,Siran Yang,Jiamang Wang,Lin Qu,Zongwu Wang,Li Jiang,Haibing Guan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PCoMoE is a path-compositional MoE inference framework that decomposes experts into finer-grained paths, prunes low-value path combinations, and exploits reusable sub-expert structures to speed up inference while improving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern MoE LLMs only activate a subset of experts per token, but inference is still constrained by treating each expert as an indivisible unit. This coarse-grained design fixes the optimization granularity too early and leaves redundant intra-expert computation unoptimized, limiting speed and efficiency improvements.

Method: PCoMoE reformulates MoE computation at the path level rather than whole experts.
