It introduces: (1) a path-level formulation that decomposes expert computation into finer-grained paths, (2) a compatibility-aware, layer-wise pruning strategy to remove low-value path combinations without hurting consistency across layers, and (3) a hardware-friendly execution engine that identifies and reuses shared sub-expert structures while keeping overhead bounded.

Result: On evaluated MoE LLMs, PCoMoE delivers up to 1.31× end-to-end inference speedup and at the same time improves model accuracy by up to 10%, showing both efficiency and quality gains over standard expert-level MoE execution.

Conclusion: By moving from coarse expert-level selection to fine-grained path composition, PCoMoE exposes and exploits intra-expert redundancy, enabling faster and more accurate MoE inference. The framework demonstrates that path-level structuring and pruning, combined with hardware-aware execution, can surpass traditional whole-expert abstractions in both performance and accuracy.

Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures scale Large Language Model (LLM) capacity efficiently by activating a sparse subset of experts per token. However, modern MoE inference remains heavily constrained by the rigid, whole-expert abstraction. Existing frameworks manage, schedule, or prune experts as atomic execution units, which fixes the optimization boundary too early and leaves fine-grained intra-expert computational redundancy underexplored. In this work, we present PCoMoE, a path-compositional execution framework that shifts MoE inference from coarse-grained expert selection to fine-grained path composition. PCoMoE incorporates a path-level formulation of expert computation, a compatibility-aware layer-wise pruning strategy to suppress low-value path combinations, and a hardware-friendly execution engine to exploit reusable sub-expert structures under strictly bounded overheads. Experimental results demonstrate that PCoMoE achieves up to a 1.31x end-to-end inference speedup while enhancing model accuracy by 10%. The code is available at https://github.com/gzyyy0/PCoMoE

</details>


### [84] [Lagged Coupling: Internal Representations Become Readable Before They Become Causal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01048)
*Xining Xun*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that language models internally encode a variable in a way that is easily readable by linear probes long before (and much more strongly than) that variable becomes causally effective for model behavior or steerable interventions, a phenomenon they call lagged coupling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Probing studies often assume that if a variable is linearly decodable from a model’s internal activations, then it is functionally used and potentially steerable. The authors want to test this assumption rigorously across scales and training steps, and to understand the developmental relationship between internal representations and their causal influence on behavior.

Method: They analyze the Pythia model suite (160M–12B parameters) at eight training checkpoints across four task families. For a chosen target variable, they: (1) train linear probes on the residual stream to measure internal readability (AUROC), (2) measure behavioral readability (how well the same variable can be inferred from model outputs), and (3) perform causal interventions by steering activations along the probe direction to test causal efficacy. They quantify representation headroom along the probe direction and compare it to the magnitude and impact of causal write-in, run pre-registered statistical tests for scaling and onset hypotheses, and replicate on OLMo‑2.

Result: Linear probes can reliably read the target variable from very early training (around step 1,000) at all scales, with near-perfect AUROC (≥0.99) from the first checkpoint. However, steering along that probe direction almost never has a causal effect on model behavior: in 43 of 48 model–checkpoint combinations, interventions are null-equivalent, sometimes even counterproductive, with only one isolated positive effect that is not robustly resolved. Behavioral readability emerges later than internal readability and shifts later in training as model scale increases. Representation headroom along the probe direction grows dramatically (up to 57×) with scale and training, but causal write-in remains under 0.11% of that headroom. Pre-registered tests on scale and time of onset are inconclusive (INDETERMINATE), and OLMo‑2 replication shows similar but weaker patterns.

Conclusion: Internal decodability of a variable is not a reliable indicator that it is behaviorally used or steerable. There is a systematic lagged coupling between representation formation and causal readout: models learn to represent variables in their activations early and strongly, but the mechanisms that causally use these representations for behavior consolidate much more slowly and sometimes barely at all. This cautions against interpreting probe accuracy as evidence of control or alignment and highlights a developmental bottleneck where read-before-write dynamics dominate. Replication on another model suite supports the robustness of this pattern.

Abstract: Across the full Pythia suite (160M-12B, eight checkpoints, four task families), a linear probe can read a target variable from the residual stream as early as step 1,000 at every scale -- yet steering along that same reading direction remains null-equivalent in 43 of 48 model-checkpoint cells. Internal readability systematically outruns causal efficacy, and the lag does not shrink with scale. We call this structure lagged coupling and decompose it into three dissociable tracks: (i) internal readability, saturated (AUROC >= 0.990) from the first checkpoint everywhere; (ii) behavioral readability, which develops gradually and progressively later at larger scales (12B reaches 0.909 only at the final checkpoint); (iii) causal efficacy, almost always null-equivalent, occasionally counterproductive early, with one isolated positive pulse (12B, step 8,000, z = +2.49) our grid cannot resolve. The ordering is dominantly read-before-write (11/11 units, no inversion). Representation headroom along the probe direction grows up to 57x with training and scale while causal write-in stays below 0.11% of headroom -- the variable is increasingly written into the representation and increasingly ignored by the readout. Under a fully pre-registered protocol, both single-onset hypotheses resolve INDETERMINATE (scale slope +0.24, 95% CI [-0.60, +0.87]; time vote 3:3) -- a disciplined negative explained by the three-track decomposition. A pre-registered OLMo-2 replication preserves the direction at attenuated magnitude. Our results caution against inferring steerability from probe accuracy and establish a developmental bottleneck: representation formation reliably outpaces causal readout consolidation.

</details>


### [85] [OUTLETS: Output-Length Prediction from Speculative Decoding Backbones](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01068)
*Weihuang Wen,Yingying Liu,Yichuan Liu,Wenqi Zeng,Li Zhou,Chumin Sun,Jie Sun,Tianshu Yu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Paper tackles LLM serving latency caused by variable, heavy-tailed output lengths by predicting output length using speculative decoding representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM outputs have highly variable and heavy-tailed lengths, making it hard to provision resources and schedule clusters efficiently. Existing output-length predictors either rely on external proxy models that add latency and are inaccurate, or internal shallow probes that do not capture enough information from model states. There is a need for a method that is both efficient and accurate for length prediction during inference.

Method: Observe that speculative decoding frameworks (e.g., EAGLE-3) already compute rich draft decoder latent representations. Propose OUTLETS, which repurposes these draft representations as a trajectory-aware length predictor by attaching a lightweight regression head, leveraging information produced anyway for speculative decoding. Evaluate MAE vs existing methods and integrate predictions into scheduling policies under saturated disaggregated serving.

Result: OUTLETS achieves lower mean absolute error (MAE) for output-length prediction compared to evaluated baselines while adding minimal computational overhead when speculative decoding is already in use. In serving simulations, using OUTLETS predictions allows standard schedulers to prioritize shorter requests and better balance load, leading to a 34.8% reduction in P99 latency for short requests under saturated conditions.

Conclusion: By exploiting the latent structure present in speculative decoding backbones, it is possible to build efficient and accurate output-length predictors for LLM serving. OUTLETS demonstrates that such predictors can be used with existing scheduling policies to significantly reduce tail latency, improving responsiveness for short queries without introducing substantial additional overhead.

Abstract: The heavy-tailed distribution of output lengths in Large Language Model (LLM) serving poses major challenges for resource provisioning and cluster scheduling. Although output-length prediction can mitigate these issues, existing approaches have key drawbacks: external proxy models add substantial latency and often have limited fidelity, whereas internal state-based methods are efficient but rely on shallow probes of current model states. We identify a structural connection between speculative decoding (SD) and length prediction: latent representations produced by the draft decoder in advanced frameworks (e.g., EAGLE-3) encode signals that are predictive of generation length. Building on this insight, we introduce OUTLETS (Output-Length Prediction from Speculative Decoding Backbones), which repurposes the speculative backbone as a trajectory-aware length predictor. When its draft representations are already computed for speculative decoding, OUTLETS adds only a lightweight regression head and achieves lower MAE than the evaluated methods. Under saturated disaggregated serving, OUTLETS predictions enable standard scheduling policies to prioritize shorter requests and distribute requests more evenly across decoding instances, reducing short-request P99 latency by 34.8%.

</details>


### [86] [Post-hoc Alignment of LLM-judges to Human Judgment Distribution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01073)
*Sebastian Steindl,Nikos Voskarides,Alberto Gasparin,Diego Marcheggiani*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how well large language models acting as judges (LLMaJ) can match not just single ground-truth labels but full distributions of human judgments, and introduces NAPHA, a post-hoc alignment method that significantly improves matching these human judgment distributions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLMaJ evaluations mostly compare model judgments against aggregated hard labels, ignoring human label variation that reflects differing human opinions and uncertainty. There is growing interest in using this variation (soft labels/HJDs) for better evaluation and alignment, but we lack a systematic understanding of how well LLMs capture these distributions and methods to improve their performance on this task.

Method: The authors systematically benchmark LLM-judge performance on predicting both hard labels and soft-label human judgment distributions across five diverse datasets. They measure how closely LLM outputs match these distributions, then propose NAPHA, a post-hoc alignment framework. NAPHA assigns each instance to an entropy class based on the uncertainty/diversity of human judgments, and routes it to specialized lightweight alignment models trained per entropy class to adjust the LLM’s output distribution toward the empirical human judgment distribution.

Result: They find that LLMs generally perform close to humans at predicting hard labels but perform poorly on predicting soft-label distributions. Applying NAPHA consistently improves the alignment between LLM output distributions and human judgment distributions across different base LLMs and all evaluated datasets, with especially large gains on high-entropy (high-disagreement) instances. Oracle experiments show that if entropy class assignment were more accurate, NAPHA’s improvements would be even larger, highlighting entropy prediction as a key bottleneck.

Conclusion: LLMs used as judges can approximate consensus labels but fail to capture the nuanced distribution of human opinions, especially in ambiguous or controversial cases. Incorporating entropy-aware post-hoc alignment via NAPHA significantly improves soft-label prediction, particularly for high-entropy items where modeling diverse human perspectives matters most. Future gains hinge on better modeling or predicting entropy classes, suggesting that uncertainty-aware and distributional evaluation should become standard in LLMaJ research and practice.

Abstract: The LLM-as-a-judge (LLMaJ) framework offers a cost-effective and reproducible solution for automatic evaluation. However, current evaluation practices typically compare LLMaJ judgments against aggregated ground-truth labels, overlooking the valuable information contained in Human Label Variation (HLV). Inspired by an increasing line of work that proposes to leverage HLV, we systematically study LLMaJ performance on predicting both a single, aggregated ground truth hard-label and unaggregated soft-labels that represent Human Judgment Distributions (HJD). Our results across five diverse datasets reveal that while LLMs achieve near human-level performance at hard-label prediction on most tasks, they exhibit poor performance when predicting soft-labels. To address this limitation, we propose NAPHA (eNtropy-Aware Post-Hoc Alignment), a simple yet effective lightweight post-hoc alignment method that matches the LLM distribution to the HJD by first assigning an instance to a discrete entropy class and then routing it to specialized, trained alignment models. We find that NAPHA consistently improves soft-labels prediction across base LLM models and datasets, with particularly strong gains on high-entropy instances where capturing diverse human perspectives is most critical. We also show via oracle experiments that improving entropy class prediction can substantially enhance NAPHA's practical effectiveness.

</details>


### [87] [StateSwap: Probing Support-Elimination Hidden States in Multiple-Choice Questions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01081)
*Chao Gao,Haijiang Liu,Qiyuan Li,Caicai Guo,Frank van Harmelen,Jinguang Gu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies why large language models answer the same multiple-choice question inconsistently under different prompt framings, using a dual-framing protocol and a special [STATE] token to probe and intervene on internal activations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand and reduce inconsistencies in large language model answers to the same question when it is framed differently (support-oriented vs elimination-oriented), and to link these behavioral differences to specific internal representations.

Method: The authors design a dual-framing protocol where prompts differ only in being support-oriented or elimination-oriented while targeting the same evaluation. They append an untrained special token [STATE] whose residual-stream activation is used as an intervention handle. They analyze the [STATE] activations across layers, test their separability between framings, and perform activation swapping and mean-difference steering to study behavioral effects and layer-wise responses.

Result: They find that support- and elimination-oriented framings produce separable [STATE] activations that are concentrated in intermediate layers. Swapping [STATE] activations between the two framings systematically flips or changes the model’s predictions and increases agreement across framings. Mean-difference steering directions derived from their dual-framing contrast produce more bounded, controlled layer-wise effects than generic contrastive activation addition directions under their protocol.

Conclusion: Prompt framing differences correspond to distinct, behaviorally relevant internal representations localized in intermediate layers. Intervening via a dedicated [STATE] token can systematically steer model predictions and reduce framing-based inconsistencies, and dual-framing-derived steering directions offer a more controlled way to manipulate internal computation than standard contrastive activation addition.

Abstract: Large language models often answer the same multiple-choice question inconsistently when it is posed under support-oriented and elimination-oriented framings. We investigate whether these discrepancies arise from different internal representations induced by the two framings. We introduce a dual-framing protocol with minimally varied prompts that use either support- or elimination-oriented framing while keeping the evaluation target fixed. To probe the internal computation, we append an untrained special token, [STATE], and treat its residual-stream activation as an intervention interface. Across both models, the two framings induce separable [STATE] activations concentrated in intermediate layers. Swapping these activations between paired prompts systematically changes predictions and improves cross-framing agreement, providing intervention-based evidence that the activations are behaviorally relevant. Beyond instance-level substitution, mean-difference steering directions derived from the dual-framing contrast exhibit more bounded layer-wise responses than matched contrastive activation addition directions under the evaluated protocol.

</details>


### [88] [Beyond Magnitude: Contrastive Routing for Modular Mixture-of-Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01100)
*Nikolaos Xiros,Dimitrios Damianos,Maria-Eleni Zoumpoulidi,Leon Voukoutis,Vassilis Katsouros,Georgios Paraskevopoulos*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Proposes a new routing mechanism for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models that uses contrastive signals against an EMA reference, leading to better expert specialization and improved zero-shot performance with small compute/parameter overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard MoE routing uses token representations dominated by features shared across all tokens, which prevents experts from specializing effectively. The authors aim to design a routing scheme that focuses on discriminative, low-dimensional subspaces aligned with meaningful linguistic structure to improve zero-shot reasoning without large computational costs.

Method: They introduce the Contrastive Routing Mechanism (CoRM). Instead of routing based on the absolute hidden state of a token, they compute a contrastive representation by comparing each token to an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of the layer’s hidden states. Each expert has its own projection that scores a token by the gap between its affinity to the token and its affinity to the shared EMA reference. Routing then selects experts based on these contrastive scores, yielding routing boundaries more aligned with linguistic structures, and they integrate CoRM into standard Top-k MoE architectures with modest overhead.

Result: CoRM concentrates routing information into a low-dimensional, highly separable subspace, resulting in routing decisions that better reflect linguistic structure than standard Top-k MoE. Empirically, on nine zero-shot reasoning benchmarks, CoRM improves average zero-shot accuracy by +0.67 to +1.69 percentage points for Top-1 and +1.38 to +1.77 percentage points for Top-2 routing, with only 2.9% more parameters and 2.6% more FLOPs per token compared to baseline MoE models.

Conclusion: Contrastive routing via CoRM enables more linguistically meaningful expert specialization in MoE architectures, leading to consistent zero-shot accuracy gains with minimal increases in parameters and computation. This suggests that rethinking routing as a contrastive operation against a shared EMA reference is a promising direction for enhancing MoE efficiency and effectiveness.

Abstract: In current Mixture-of-Experts architectures, routing is performed based on representations dominated by structure shared across all tokens, limiting expert specialization. We show that contrasting each token against an Exponential Moving Average of the layer's hidden states, rather than routing on absolute magnitude, concentrates the routing signal onto a low-dimensional, highly separable subspace. Building on this, we propose the Contrastive Routing Mechanism (CoRM), which scores each expert by the gap between its affinity for the incoming token and its affinity for this shared reference state, interpreted through a distinct per-expert projection. The resulting experts have routing boundaries that align with linguistic structure significantly more than the Top-k baseline. Our experiments show that CoRM improves average zero-shot accuracy by +0.67 to +1.69 points (Top-1) and +1.38 to +1.77 points (Top-2) over standard Top-k MoE baselines on nine zero-shot reasoning benchmarks, at the minimal cost of 2.9% added parameters and 2.6% added FLOPs per token.

</details>


### [89] [When Modality Gap Reduction Fails: Prediction-Level Hubness in CLIP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01103)
*Shota Sato,Hajime Kiyama,Tosho Hirasawa,Mamoru Komachi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper explains why reducing the CLIP image–text modality gap does not always improve zero-shot accuracy, identifying a new failure mode called prediction-level hubness where predictions concentrate on a few classes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many methods aim to reduce the representation gap between image and text modalities in CLIP, assuming this will improve cross-modal alignment and downstream performance. Empirically, however, decreasing the average image–text gap sometimes leads to worse zero-shot classification accuracy. The authors are motivated to understand and systematically explain this discrepancy, focusing on how gap correction affects the downstream decision process in zero-shot classification rather than just average alignment metrics.

Method: The authors analyze zero-shot CLIP classification from the perspective of the decision structure: choosing the class whose text prototype is most similar to an image embedding. They use linear gap correction as an analytically tractable example to study how modifying embeddings affects relative similarities among class prototypes and decision margins. They then conduct experiments on multiple datasets, applying both linear and learning-based gap correction methods, and measure both zero-shot accuracy and the concentration of predictions across classes to quantify prediction-level hubness.

Result: They show theoretically and empirically that modality gap correction can change the relative decision structure among classes, causing predictions to collapse onto a small subset of classes—what they term prediction-level hubness. Across datasets and methods, cases where gap correction hurts zero-shot accuracy are consistently associated with increased prediction concentration. Thus, a smaller average modality gap does not guarantee better accuracy and can even harm it by distorting class-wise decision margins.

Conclusion: Reducing the image–text modality gap in CLIP should not be evaluated solely by average alignment metrics. Because gap correction can reconfigure the downstream decision structure and induce prediction-level hubness, it may degrade zero-shot accuracy despite improving average alignment. The paper argues that future gap correction methods must explicitly consider their impact on prediction structure—such as class-wise margins and prediction concentration—to reliably improve CLIP’s zero-shot performance.

Abstract: Reducing the modality gap between image and text representations in CLIP is widely expected to improve cross-modal alignment and downstream performance. However, a smaller average image-text gap does not necessarily lead to consistent accuracy gains. We analyze this mismatch from the perspective of the decision structure in zero-shot classification, i.e. selecting the most similar class-text prototype for an input image. Zero-shot accuracy depends not only on average image--text alignment, but also on class-wise decision margins. Using Linear correction as an analytically tractable case, we show that modality gap correction can alter the relative decision structure among classes and cause predictions to concentrate on a small subset of classes. We refer to this output-space failure mode as prediction-level hubness. Furthermore, experiments across multiple datasets show that accuracy degradation under gap correction is consistently associated with increased prediction concentration, both for Linear correction and for learning-based correction methods. This provides a systematic explanation of why modality gap reduction does not consistently improve CLIP zero-shot accuracy from the perspective of downstream decision structure. Our results suggest that gap correction should be evaluated not only by average alignment, but also by its impact on downstream prediction structure.

</details>


### [90] [ClinTraceBench: Source-Verifiable Longitudinal Clinical Reasoning over EHR-Derived Dialogues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01111)
*Huimin Wang,Zhengyi Zhao,Yutian Zhao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces ClinTraceBench, a benchmark to evaluate whether compact patient history representations used in clinical LLM assistants preserve crucial longitudinal information for reasoning over multi-visit trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical LLM assistants need to reason over long, multi-visit patient histories, but practical systems compress these histories (via retrieval, summaries, timelines, agentic memory) to fit context and cost constraints. It is unknown whether such compression preserves key longitudinal signals (e.g., multi-visit trends, relations) required for safe clinical reasoning. The authors aim to systematically measure the impact of different history representation strategies on clinical question-answering performance.

Method: They construct ClinTraceBench: 385 verified dialogues derived from MIMIC-IV with event-level provenance, organized into nine task types (T1–T9), and validated via a multi-level (L0–L4) deterministic process plus L5 human audit achieving 98.92% agreement. They pose 6,271 questions and evaluate eight history-representation strategies (no context, last-visit-only, full-context, dense retrieval with BGE-M3, two compression schemes including LLM summaries, and two agentic memory systems Mem0 and A-Mem) across four LLM backbones (DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o-mini, Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.6), resulting in 32 configuration cells and 200,672 model predictions. They also design a controlled T3 injection probe to test whether compressed representations retain specific relational attributions.

Result: The evaluation uncovers four main findings: (SP4) In a controlled T3 relation-injection probe, even when the key attribution sentence is present before constructing the compressed memory, Mem0, A-Mem, and LLM summarization recover only 0–5.3% of the injected positive relations, revealing severe relation loss due to compression. (SP1) Compressed strategies perform worse on tasks involving multi-visit trend aggregation and cross-patient comparisons, indicating an "aggregation tax" from compression. (SP2) Having full patient context vs. blind/no context yields large performance gains, with blind-to-full accuracy gaps from +29.8 percentage points (GPT-4o-mini) up to +62.7 pp (Haiku). (SP3) The rate of model abstention does not increase monotonically with context length, suggesting complex interactions between context size and uncertainty behavior. Economically, under full-context access, the smaller Haiku backbone lies on the Pareto frontier and cost-dominates Sonnet ($25.76 vs. $106.21) while achieving comparable or better performance, challenging the assumption that larger backbones always win.

Conclusion: Compact history representations commonly used to scale clinical LLM assistants can severely degrade the longitudinal and relational information needed for accurate clinical reasoning, especially for multi-visit and cross-patient tasks. Full-context access substantially improves performance, and compression induces both relation loss and an aggregation tax, which current agentic memory and summarization methods fail to avoid. Moreover, within realistic cost constraints, smaller but well-performing backbones (e.g., Haiku) can dominate larger ones under full-context setups, overturning the "bigger is better" heuristic. ClinTraceBench provides a standardized benchmark to study and improve history representations for safe, cost-effective clinical LLM systems.

Abstract: Clinical LLM assistants must reason over multi-visit patient trajectories, yet whether the compact history representations used to scale them---retrieval, structured timelines, LLM summaries, agentic memory---preserve the longitudinal signal clinical reasoning needs has not been measured. We introduce ClinTraceBench: 385 MIMIC-IV-derived verified dialogues with event-ID provenance, a nine-task taxonomy (T1--T9), and L0--L4 deterministic + L5 human-audit validation (98.92\% agreement). We evaluate eight history representation strategies---a no-context floor, \textit{last-visit-only}, \textit{full-context}, BGE-M3 \textit{dense-retrieval}, two compression schemes, and two agentic-memory systems (\textit{Mem0}, \textit{A-Mem})---across four backbones (DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o-mini, Haiku~4.5, Sonnet~4.6) on 6{,}271 questions: 32 cells, 200{,}672 predictions. Four findings: (SP4) a controlled T3 injection probe isolates compression-induced \textit{relation} loss---with the attribution sentence present \textit{before} construction, \textit{Mem0}, \textit{A-Mem} and \textit{llm-summary} still recover only 0--5.3\% of the injected positives; (SP1) compressed strategies pay an aggregation tax on multi-visit trends and cross-patient comparisons; (SP2) the blind-to-full gap spans $+29.8$~pp (GPT-4o-mini) to $+62.7$~pp (Haiku); (SP3) abstention scales non-monotonically with context length. On the Pareto frontier Haiku dominates Sonnet under \textit{full-context} (\$25.76 vs.\ \$106.21), inverting the ``biggest backbone wins'' heuristic.

</details>


### [91] [EDRAC: Benchmarking Arabic Dialect Reading Comprehension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01113)
*Noor Abo Mokh,Kirill Chirkunov,Teresa Lynn,Nizar Habash,Reham Marzouk,Malik H. Altakrori,Younes Samih,Muhammed Abu Odeh,Nour Rabih,Rahaf Alshahrani,Hamad Alshehhi,Hamdan Al-Ali,Muhra Almahri,Besher Hassan,Mohamed Anwar,Abed Alhakim Freihat,Preslav Nakov,Alham Fikri Aji*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents EDRAC, a large-scale benchmark for machine reading comprehension and generative QA in five major Arabic dialects, built from spoken interactions and used to evaluate Arabic-centric and multilingual LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dialectal Arabic is under-resourced for machine reading comprehension and QA, and existing benchmarks mainly target Modern Standard Arabic or multiple-choice formats, lacking realistic coverage of naturally spoken dialects. This resource gap hinders progress on dialectal Arabic NLP and accurate evaluation of dialectal QA systems.

Method: The authors construct EDRAC, a benchmark consisting of 499 passages from naturally occurring spoken interactions across five major Arabic dialects (Egyptian, Moroccan, Emirati, Syrian, and Saudi) and 4,977 QA pairs. The QA pairs are created using a human–LLM collaborative pipeline that includes iterative question generation, LLM-as-a-judge assessment of quality, and final human verification. They then benchmark Arabic-centric and multilingual LLMs on this dataset using both lexical and semantic evaluation metrics.

Result: The evaluation of various Arabic-centric and multilingual LLMs on EDRAC shows notable discrepancies between semantic answer quality and how well the answers preserve dialectal characteristics. This indicates that current automatic metrics fail to fully capture dialectal fidelity in generated responses.

Conclusion: EDRAC constitutes the first large-scale dialectal Arabic MRC and generative QA benchmark drawn from realistic spoken content across multiple dialects. It exposes limitations in existing evaluation metrics for dialectal Arabic generation and offers a challenging, realistic testbed to drive future research in dialectal Arabic NLP and more dialect-sensitive evaluation methods.

Abstract: Dialectal Arabic (DA) remains under-resourced compared to Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), particularly for machine reading comprehension (MRC) and question answering (QA). Existing Arabic QA benchmarks primarily focus on formal written MSA or multiple-choice QA, with limited coverage of naturally spoken dialects. Here, we aim to bridge this gap. We introduce EDRAC, the first large-scale benchmark for dialectal Arabic machine reading comprehension (MRC) and generative QA, covering five major dialects: Egyptian, Moroccan, Emirati, Syrian, and Saudi Arabic. EDRAC contains 499 passages derived from naturally occurring spoken interactions and 4,977 corresponding QA pairs generated through a human--LLM collaborative pipeline combining iterative generation, LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, and human verification. We benchmark Arabic-centric and multilingual LLMs on EDRAC using lexical and semantic metrics. Our results reveal substantial gaps between semantic answer quality and dialectal fidelity, highlighting the limitations of existing evaluation metrics for dialectal Arabic generation. EDRAC provides a realistic and challenging MRC benchmark for future research on dialectal Arabic NLP.

</details>


### [92] [Overfitting Mitigation via Singular Value Decomposition in Minimum Bayes Risk Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01135)
*Riza Setiawan Soetedjo,Yusuke Sakai,Hidetaka Kamigaito,Katsuhiko Hayashi,Taro Watanabe*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose SVD-MBR, a denoised variant of Minimum Bayes Risk decoding that reduces metric overfitting by low-rank approximating the metric utility matrix.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard MBR decoding often overfits to the chosen evaluation metric: it can boost that metric while harming performance on others, because it treats noisy, metric-specific scores as ground truth. This limits the reliability and generality of MBR in text generation tasks.

Method: Treat the pairwise utility (metric score) matrix over sampled hypotheses as a noisy signal, and apply Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to compute a low-rank approximation. Keep only the top-k singular components to capture shared consensus across hypotheses while filtering out metric-specific noise, then perform MBR decoding using this denoised matrix. Compare behavior across different metric types (neural vs surface-based).

Result: SVD-MBR regularizes MBR decoding, preventing extreme over-optimization of the chosen metric and delivering better overall performance across multiple generalized evaluation metrics. Experiments show clear gains when using neural evaluation metrics, whose score matrices exhibit strong low-rank structure; in contrast, surface-level metrics show weaker benefits due to noisier, less low-rank score patterns.

Conclusion: Viewing metric scores as a noisy low-rank signal and denoising them with SVD produces more robust MBR decoding. Neural metrics are particularly well-suited to this approach, as they encode a clear consensus structure that SVD can exploit, while surface-level metrics lack such structure and thus benefit less from SVD-MBR.

Abstract: Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) decoding enables high-quality text generation by selecting the hypothesis that maximizes a utility metric over sampled pseudo-references. However, it is highly susceptible to metric overfitting: it can irregularly inflate the chosen utility metric at the direct expense of other unoptimized evaluation metrics. To mitigate this, we introduce SVD-MBR, which frames the pairwise utility matrix as a noisy information signal. By computing a low-rank approximation via Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and retaining only the top-$k$ components, we effectively decouple true consensus from metric noise. Experiments demonstrate that SVD-MBR successfully regularizes decoding, yielding substantial gains across a range of generalized metrics. Furthermore, we reveal that this denoising is metric-dependent: neural metrics encode a robust low-rank consensus ideal for SVD, whereas surface-level metrics struggle to separate signal from metric noise.

</details>


### [93] [Does task decomposition improve automatic NLG evaluation?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01139)
*Sebastian Steindl,Nikos Voskarides,Alberto Gasparin,Diego Marcheggiani*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates whether breaking evaluation prompts into smaller sub-tasks actually improves LLM-as-a-judge performance and finds that decomposition itself brings no real gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-as-a-judge is popular for cheap, reference-free NLG evaluation, and recent work claims that decomposing the judging task into simpler subtasks improves reliability and correlation with humans. However, these claims have not been systematically and fairly tested against non-decomposed baselines, and confounding factors like using human labels for training have not been clearly separated from the effect of decomposition itself.

Method: The authors systematically compare LLM-as-a-judge methods with and without task decomposition across multiple NLG datasets. They control for factors such as training data, especially the use of human labels, and construct a fair baseline that does not use decomposition. They then measure performance, likely via correlation with human judgments or similar metrics, to isolate the effect of decomposition.

Result: They observe no significant performance gains from using task decomposition compared to the fair non-decomposed baseline. The improvements reported in prior decomposition-based LLMaJ work are largely explained by the use of human labels as training data, rather than by the decomposition design. Furthermore, in settings where human labels are available, a non-decomposed LLMaJ setup can reach performance comparable to human annotators.

Conclusion: Task decomposition, by itself, does not improve LLM-as-a-judge performance for NLG evaluation when compared to a carefully controlled non-decomposed baseline. Reported gains in earlier work mainly stem from leveraging human-labeled training data. When such labels exist, a straightforward, non-decomposed LLM-as-a-judge approach can already match human annotator performance, questioning the necessity and benefit of complex decomposition schemes.

Abstract: The LLM-as-a-judge (LLMaJ) framework has emerged as a promising solution for cheap, reproducible, reference-free Natural Language Generation (NLG) evaluation. Prior work seeks to improve LLMaJ by decomposing evaluation tasks into simpler sub-tasks. In this work, we systematically compare LLMaJ methods with and without decomposition on multiple NLG datasets. We find no evidence that LLMaJ with task decomposition leads to performance gains over a fair baseline that does not use decomposition. Instead, we find that previously reported performance gains in decomposition-based LLMaJ stem from using human labels as training data, and not task decomposition itself. Also, we find that, when human labels are available, LLMaJ without using task decomposition can perform comparably to human annotators.

</details>


### [94] [Subword Segmental BabyLMs: Learning to Tokenise for Sample-Efficient Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01151)
*Francois Meyer*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces subword segmental language models that learn tokenisation during training and shows they improve sample efficiency and zero-shot performance in the BabyLM 2026 Challenge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard language model training uses a fixed, precomputed subword tokeniser, which may not be optimal for data efficiency, especially in low-resource settings like the BabyLM Challenge. The authors want to investigate whether learning the tokenisation jointly with the language model can yield better representations and performance, particularly under strict data constraints.

Method: They propose two new models: SubSegGPT, a decoder-only autoregressive LM that learns subword segmentation jointly with pretraining; and SubSegDeBERTa, an encoder-based masked language model that jointly learns to generate and tokenise masked words. Both models are trained under the Strict and Strict-small data regimes of the BabyLM Challenge. The models dynamically induce subword units during training instead of relying on a fixed tokeniser, and the authors analyse how these learned segmentations evolve over time.

Result: In the Strict track, SubSegDeBERTa is their best-performing system, yielding notable improvements in zero-shot evaluation compared to baselines. In the Strict-small track, SubSegGPT performs best and surpasses standard tokenisation-based baselines. Empirically, the learnable tokenisers lead to better sample efficiency for BabyLM pretraining.

Conclusion: Jointly learning subword tokenisation and language modelling can be more sample-efficient than using a fixed tokeniser, especially in data-constrained regimes like BabyLM. The learned segmentations converge toward subword units that strike a balance between aligning with morphology and maintaining sufficiently fine-grained segmentation, suggesting that this inductive bias is beneficial for downstream performance.

Abstract: In the standard LM training pipeline, subword tokenisation is applied as a preprocessing step. Subword segmental language modelling is an alternative paradigm in which tokenisation is learned during training, allowing the model to discover subword units that optimise its training objective. In this paper, we present our submission to the 2026 BabyLM Challenge, for which we develop two new subword segmental LMs: SubSegGPT and SubSegDeBERTa. SubSegGPT is a decoder-only model that learns tokenisation during autoregressive pretraining. SubSegDeBERTa is an encoder-based model that jointly learns to generate and tokenise masked words. We train both for the Strict and Strict-small tracks. Our top submission to Strict is SubSegDeBERTa, which achieves notable gains in zero-shot evaluation. Our top submission to Strict-small is SubSegGPT, which outperforms tokenisation-based baselines. Our results show that learnable subword tokenisation can improve sample-efficiency for BabyLM pretraining. We analyse the subword learning dynamics of our models and find that tokenisation gradually converges on subword units that balance morphological alignment and fine-grained segmentation.

</details>


### [95] [LLMPEDIA: Browsing, Verifying, and Comparing the Parametric Encyclopedic Knowledge of LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01182)
*Muhammed Saeed,Simon Razniewski*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMPEDIA systematically extracts and audits language models’ internal knowledge to expose gaps between benchmark scores and real-world factual reliability, providing a live, browsable encyclopedia of model claims and their verification status.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks like MMLU suggest frontier LLMs are nearly solved on many tasks, but they only measure performance on a narrow, human-curated question set. This creates availability bias: models are evaluated only on what benchmark designers thought to ask, ignoring most of the models’ parametric knowledge and hallucinations. The authors want a way to directly inspect and quantify what models "know" at scale, including unsupported or unverifiable assertions, and to make this gap between benchmarks and real-world reliability visible and explorable.

Method: The authors query three major LLM families (GPT-5-mini, DeepSeek-V3.2, Llama-3.3-70B) without any external retrieval to recursively elicit and materialize about 1.3 million article-style pieces from their parametric memory. They then sample atomic claims from these generated articles using a stratified sampling strategy, and audit each claim against Wikipedia plus a curated set of web sources. Each claim is labeled as supported, refuted, or insufficient evidence, following an earlier factuality framework. They compute factuality rates from a uniform random sample, and they build a live web interface that exposes every article, claim, evidence, and verdict via stable URLs, with multiple one-click views for exploration, cross-model comparison, and guided topic drill-down.

Result: From a uniform random sample of claims, only 68.4% are supported by external evidence, over 21 percentage points lower than the models’ performance on MMLU. About 30.5% of claims are labeled as having insufficient evidence: they are assertions that no current benchmark asks about and that even large reference sources like Wikipedia cannot clearly confirm or refute. This demonstrates a substantial coverage and verification gap between benchmarked performance and the broader space of model-generated factual claims. The authors also release LLMPEDIA, a live online encyclopedia of audited LLM claims with interactive views for browsing and comparison across models and personas.

Conclusion: High benchmark scores substantially overstate language models’ reliability as knowledge sources because benchmarks probe only a small, curated subset of possible questions. By directly sampling and auditing models’ parametric knowledge at scale, LLMPEDIA shows that factual support is significantly lower than benchmark scores and that a large fraction of claims fall into an "insufficient evidence" gray zone. The work argues that understanding and improving LLM factuality requires moving beyond fixed test sets to open-ended, claim-level auditing and providing transparent, publicly browsable resources like LLMPEDIA that expose models’ true knowledge frontier and gaps.

Abstract: Flagship language models appear saturated on benchmarks like MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021), scoring above 90% - yet benchmarks test only what the experimenter thought to ask, the availability bias of fixed question sets. LLMPEDIA makes this bias measurable and browsable. We recursively materialized ~1.3M articles from three model families' parametric memory (GPT-5-mini, DeepSeek-V3.2, Llama-3.3-70B) without retrieval, then audited a stratified sample of atomic claims against Wikipedia and a curated web stack, coloring every claim supported, refuted, or insufficient (Saeed and Razniewski, 2026). On a uniform random sample the true rate is 68.4% - more than 21 pp below MMLU - with 30.5% of claims insufficient: assertions no benchmark probes and the world's largest encyclopedia cannot adjudicate - long-tail knowledge or plausible hallucination, the evidence cannot tell - extending to free text the coverage gap GPTKB established for triples (Hu et al., 2025). The resulting live, open encyclopedia lets visitors inspect this frontier one claim at a time through five one-click views - link-traversal exploration, claim-level factuality, cross-model and political-persona comparison, and a guided topic drill-down - each page, claim, and verdict at a stable URL. LLMPEDIA is live at https://llmpedia.net

</details>


### [96] [PersuaRL: Reinforcement Learning-Driven Multi-Expert Selection for Persuasive Dialogue Generation in Insurance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01188)
*Rohan Kirti,Akash Ghosh,Aryan Vats,Niladri Ghosh,Shipra Shriparn,Roshni Ramnani,Anutosh Maitra,Sriparna Saha*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces InsureDial, a motor insurance persuasion dialogue dataset, and PersuaRL, a reinforcement learning framework that makes LLM-based agents more persuasive and context-aware, outperforming baselines on multiple datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based conversational agents are widely used in domains like insurance but remain weak at persuasive, context-sensitive dialogue where trust and clarity are crucial. There is a need for domain-specific resources and methods that systematically enhance persuasiveness beyond factual correctness, particularly in complex decision-making scenarios such as motor insurance.

Method: The authors build InsureDial, a specialized dataset of persuasive motor insurance dialogues capturing domain-specific strategies. They then propose PersuaRL, a reinforcement learning framework where an LLM-driven agent interacts with multiple expert modules (each embodying different persuasive strategies). PersuaRL learns to adaptively explore, choose, and coordinate these strategies based on the evolving dialogue context, optimizing for persuasion quality via RL signals. They evaluate using automatic metrics, human judgments, and qualitative analysis on InsureDial and another persuasion benchmark.

Result: PersuaRL generates responses judged to be more persuasive and contextually appropriate than baseline systems on both InsureDial and an additional persuasion dialogue dataset. Across automatic metrics and human evaluations, PersuaRL consistently outperforms comparison models in persuasion effectiveness and dialogue quality.

Conclusion: Specialized datasets like InsureDial and RL-based control over strategy modules can substantially improve the persuasive capabilities of LLM-powered dialogue agents in sensitive, trust-dependent domains such as insurance. The proposed PersuaRL framework effectively coordinates multiple persuasion strategies according to context, leading to more effective and appropriate persuasive conversations than standard baselines.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are revolutionizing digital communication by powering conversational agents deployed across domains such as customer service, digital sales, and insurance. These agents, built on LLMs, can understand user input, retrieve relevant information, and generate coherent responses. However, while they excel at factual communication, they often lack the ability to engage in truly persuasive, context-sensitive dialogue, especially in domains like insurance, where trust and clarity are critical. Building on this need within the insurance domain, our work focuses on improving the persuasiveness of digital agents, aka LLMs. To support this, we introduce InsureDial, a Persuasive Insurance Dialogue dataset, designed to capture the nuances of persuasive communication specific to motor insurance interactions. We introduce PersuaRL, a reinforcement learning-based framework that equips LLM-driven dialogue agents with the ability to adaptively explore, select, and coordinate strategies across multiple expert modules, guided by the evolving dialogue context, to achieve more effective persuasion. We conduct extensive automatic human and qualitative evaluations on two benchmark persuasion dialogue datasets, including our InsureDial. Our evaluations consistently demonstrate that PersuaRL outperforms baseline, generating contextually appropriate and highly persuasive responses.

</details>


### [97] [CaRL-EM: Cost-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Entity Matching with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01195)
*Chaohui Guo,Michel Klein,Zhisheng Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They introduce CaRL-EM, a reinforcement-learning controller that orchestrates LLM calls for entity matching in a cost-aware, sequential, multi-candidate setting, achieving better quality-cost trade-offs than prior LLM-based methods across benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based entity matching methods are strong but have two key limitations: (1) they usually treat candidate pairs independently or rely on rigid, manually designed matching pipelines, which is ill-suited for realistic scenarios where an entity must be matched among multiple candidates; and (2) they largely ignore inference cost, which is critical when LLMs are used at scale. There is a need for a flexible, adaptive controller that can reason over candidates sequentially and explicitly balance match quality against computational cost.

Method: They formulate LLM-based entity matching with candidate sets as a cost-aware sequential decision-making problem. They propose CaRL-EM, a reinforcement learning-based controller that, given the current state (anchor record, its candidate set, and accumulated cost), selects among a set of abstract operators (Match, Compare, Select, Decide) and among different LLM capacities. The controller is trained to maximize an objective that trades off matching quality and inference cost. Because it operates over abstract operators rather than specific prompts or models, the learned policy can be reused with different LLM backends at inference time without retraining.

Result: On 7 benchmark datasets, CaRL-EM learns policies that allocate inexpensive versus expensive LLM operations depending on task difficulty and candidate ambiguity. It demonstrates robust zero-shot transfer to diverse datasets and domains not seen during training. Across all evaluations, CaRL-EM attains a consistently better trade-off between prediction quality and inference cost than strong LLM-based baselines and hand-crafted pipelines, achieving equal or higher accuracy/F1 with lower total LLM cost.

Conclusion: CaRL-EM shows that viewing LLM-based entity matching as a cost-aware sequential decision process and controlling LLM usage via reinforcement learning yields flexible, transferable, and cost-efficient matching. The abstraction layer between the controller and concrete LLMs allows the same learned policy to be reused with different backends, making the approach practical for deployment in varied environments while maintaining strong accuracy-cost performance.

Abstract: Entity matching (EM) requires fine-grained contextual understanding and domain knowledge. Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can serve as strong matchers across domains, but most methods either make independent pairwise decisions or rely on manually designed composite pipelines, thus lacking flexibility in realistic multi-candidate settings. At the same time, they typically ignore inference cost at scale. We formulate LLM-based EM with candidates as a cost-aware sequential decision problem and propose CaRL-EM, a reinforcement learning controller that manages LLM operations. Given the state of an anchor record, its candidate set, and the cost, CaRL-EM adaptively chooses among different operators (Match/Compare/Select/Decide) and model capacities to maximize a quality-cost objective. The policy interacts with abstract operators, allowing the same controller to be reused with different underlying LLM backends at inference time without retraining. Experiments on 7 benchmarks show that CaRL-EM (i) learns to dynamically plan the usage of inexpensive and expensive operators based on task complexity, (ii) achieves robust zero-shot transfer across diverse datasets and domains, and (iii) consistently achieves a better quality-cost trade-off than strong LLM-based baselines and manually designed pipelines, yielding a lower inference cost at comparable or higher quality.

</details>


### [98] [Towards AI-Assisted Clinical Trial Matching: Practical Considerations, Multicenter Evaluation, and Real-World Deployment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01202)
*Yin Fang,Qiao Jin,Shubo Tian,Lauren He,Maya Geer,Noor Naffakh,Ryan Huu-Tuan Nguyen,Zifeng Wang,Jimeng Sun,Charalampos S. Floudas,James L. Gulley,Kamilia Moalem,Catarina Martins Maia,Amanda Nottke,Juan W. Valle,Melinda Bachini,Lourdes Rocha-Nussbaum,Kari Ramage,Nikita Curry,Megan Barnes,Mandy Mansaray,Darlene Gabeau,Craig E. Grossman,Heath Skinner,Michael Burczynski,NIH-TrialBench Consortium,Zhiyong Lu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces TrialGPT 2.0, an AI-assisted system that recommends oncology clinical trials for patients, demonstrating improved trial matching efficiency and increased access to trial opportunities in real-world workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many oncology clinical trials fail or are delayed due to insufficient patient enrollment, partly because clinicians lack efficient tools to identify appropriate trials tailored to individual patients and local workflow constraints. Existing AI systems mainly assess eligibility and are rarely deployed or evaluated in real-world oncology settings, creating a gap between algorithmic trial matching and practical clinical use.

Method: The authors developed TrialGPT 2.0, an AI-assisted clinical trial recommendation system that not only screens eligibility but also prioritizes which trials are most relevant to a patient’s current clinical needs and local workflow priorities. The system generates structured, transparent explanations for expert review. They evaluated TrialGPT 2.0 using retrospective multicenter cohorts of 288 oncology cases and through a six-month prospective deployment embedded in a precision oncology tumor board. They also created NIH-TrialBench, a clinician-authored benchmark dataset of 126 synthetic patient vignettes across 11 NIH Institutes and Centers for reproducible evaluation.

Result: In retrospective evaluation, TrialGPT 2.0 retrieved at least one clinician-recommended trial in its top 10 suggestions for about 91% of 288 cases and reduced clinician screening time by 55%. In the six-month prospective tumor board deployment, the system identified additional clinical trial options not found by the existing workflow, increasing patient access to trial participation opportunities by 90.9%. The NIH-TrialBench dataset was produced as a public benchmark resource for trial-matching systems.

Conclusion: TrialGPT 2.0 shows that AI can be successfully integrated into real-world oncology workflows to support clinical trial matching, substantially improving clinician efficiency and uncovering overlooked trial opportunities. The accompanying NIH-TrialBench dataset enables standardized, reproducible evaluation of trial recommendation systems. Collectively, the work suggests that AI-assisted trial matching can help expand and accelerate enrollment in cancer clinical trials.

Abstract: Clinical trials are essential for advancing cancer care and drug development, but many fail because of insufficient patient enrollment. While there is growing interest in using AI to support patient recruitment, existing systems largely perform eligibility assessment alone and have rarely been evaluated in real-world oncology workflows. Here we present TrialGPT 2.0, an AI-assisted clinical trial recommendation system designed for real-world deployment. Rather than asking only whether a patient may qualify, the system also assesses which trials warrant further consideration given the patient's current clinical needs and local workflow priorities, and provides structured, inspectable explanations for expert review. Importantly, we evaluated TrialGPT 2.0 retrospectively and prospectively across multiple oncology-focused settings, spanning government, academic cancer-center, patient-advocacy, and NIH referral workflows. In retrospective multicenter cohorts comprising 288 cases, TrialGPT 2.0 retrieved at least one clinician-recommended trial in its top 10 recommendations for approximately 91% of cases while reducing clinician screening time by 55.0%. In a six-month prospective evaluation embedded in an active precision oncology tumor board, TrialGPT 2.0 contributed additional trial opportunities missed by the routine workflow, expanding patient access to clinical trial participation by 90.9%. To support scientific reproducibility, we also introduce NIH-TrialBench, a clinician-authored dataset comprising 126 diverse synthetic patient vignettes and matching scenarios from 11 NIH Institutes and Centers. Together, these results support the value of AI to assist clinical trial matching by improving clinician efficiency and identifying frequently overlooked trial opportunities, ultimately helping to expand and accelerate accrual to cancer trials.

</details>


### [99] [Ready to Speak: Aligning LLMs for TTS-Friendly Text Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01246)
*Thibaut Thonet,Jos Rozen,Laurent Besacier*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They adapt large language models so that their text is naturally suitable for text-to-speech, using preference alignment instead of post-processing rewrites.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although current LLMs output text that reads well, it often sounds unnatural or hard to follow when spoken by TTS systems. Existing solutions usually rely on separate rewriting or formatting modules, which adds complexity and may degrade quality. The authors want LLMs to directly produce speech-friendly text, avoiding extra steps and making conversational agents more effective when used with voice interfaces.

Method: They formulate TTS-friendly generation as a preference alignment problem: given pairs of TTS-friendly and TTS-unfriendly responses, they train LLMs to prefer the friendly ones. They build two preference datasets, CORA and Recipe, that contain such paired examples in different domains. For optimization, they evaluate the Feature-aware Sampling and Tuning (FaST) framework, which uses interpretable features instead of a black-box reward model, and compare it with several standard alignment baselines. For evaluation, they design a suite combining: (1) a pattern-based heuristic metric to automatically detect TTS-friendly patterns, (2) a TTS-to-ASR pipeline where generated text is synthesized and then transcribed to measure how well it survives speech, and (3) a MUSHRA listening test with human raters to assess subjective quality and TTS-friendliness.

Result: Across experiments on the new datasets and evaluation suite, the FaST framework outperforms baseline alignment methods in balancing TTS-friendliness with general helpfulness of the responses. The various evaluation metrics, including the heuristic pattern-based metric, the TTS→ASR scores, and human MUSHRA ratings, show strong correlation with each other.

Conclusion: Directly aligning LLMs to generate TTS-friendly text is effective and preferable to post-hoc rewriting. The Feature-aware Sampling and Tuning approach provides the best overall tradeoff between spoken delivery quality and informational helpfulness, and the proposed heuristic metric serves as a reliable, efficient proxy for more expensive TTS-based and human evaluations of TTS-friendliness.

Abstract: Current Large Language Models (LLMs) are primarily optimized for written text, often producing outputs that are grammatically correct and helpful yet poorly suited for spoken delivery via Text-to-Speech (TTS). In this work, we study how to make LLMs natively generate TTS-friendly text, which we frame as a preference alignment problem: instead of relying on downstream rewriting modules, we directly align LLMs to generate text optimized for spoken delivery. We introduce two preference datasets spanning different target domains, CORA and Recipe, which contain paired TTS-friendly and TTS-unfriendly responses. We further propose an evaluation suite combining a pattern-based heuristic metric, a TTS$\to$ASR evaluation pipeline, and a MUSHRA listening study with human judges. Our experiments compare the recently proposed Feature-aware Sampling and Tuning (FaST) framework -- leveraging interpretable features instead of a black-box reward model -- against an array of alignment baselines on the TTS-friendly generation task. Notably, we found that FaST achieves the best overall tradeoff between TTS-friendliness and helpfulness across various settings. We also identified a strong correlation between our different metrics, highlighting the ability to reliably assess TTS-friendliness via an efficient heuristic.

</details>


### [100] [From Base Rollouts to RL Reasoning: A Budgeted Search Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01274)
*Wenhe Sun,Cunxiang Wang,Zijun Yao,Yixin Cao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates how reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves reasoning in language models, focusing on whether RL creates new reasoning capabilities or better exploits existing ones through search and decoding strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While RLVR has been shown to improve reasoning performance in language models, it is unclear whether these improvements stem from genuinely new capabilities learned by the model or simply from more efficient exploration of reasoning trajectories that the base model already had access to but rarely sampled. Clarifying this distinction is important for understanding what RL is doing, for transferability across models, and for designing more efficient inference-time search strategies without full RL retraining.

Method: The authors propose a Unified Decoding Framework (UDF) that represents various decoding and search strategies—such as token-level sampling, beam search, tree search, and sequence-level resampling—within a common, budgeted operating space. They use this framework to compare base models and their RLVR-finetuned counterparts (from SimpleRL-Zoo) under matched compute budgets on reasoning benchmarks (Math500, AIME, GPQA, IFEval). They then seek structured mappings from RL operating points to base-model operating points, focusing on how many samples (budget N) are needed by the base model to match RL performance. They identify and fit a Budgeted Operating-Point Transition Rule (BOPTR), expressed as N_Base ≈ α N_RL^β, and evaluate how well this rule recovers RL performance across models, benchmarks, and settings, including out-of-distribution tests (new models, benchmarks, and cases without RL checkpoints or RL supervision).

Result: They find that for multiple models and benchmarks, the base model’s performance curve under search can approximate the RL model’s default-policy performance when scaled by the BOPTR relation N_Base ≈ α N_RL^β. On Qwen2.5-7B, BOPTR yields the lowest transfer error among non-oracle rules, around 3–3.5 percentage points, and this finding is replicated across seeds. The rule generalizes to ten models from four model families, to additional benchmarks not used for fitting, and even to settings without an RL checkpoint or without any RL supervision, with transfer errors generally in the 3–5 percentage point range. These empirical regularities suggest that much of the RL performance gain can be matched by appropriately adjusting the base model’s search budget and decoding strategy, rather than requiring fundamentally new reasoning abilities.

Conclusion: The study concludes that, for the RLVR recipe and model cohort examined, RL’s reasoning gains can largely be interpreted as improved sampling efficiency—an internalized search process that steers the model toward high-quality reasoning trajectories that the base model could, in principle, reach via more extensive search. The Budgeted Operating-Point Transition Rule (BOPTR) offers a compact description of how to trade off search budget between base and RL models to approximate RL performance. However, the authors emphasize that these findings are descriptive, not proof of parameter-level equivalence, and they document where the patterns fail. UDF and BOPTR are proposed as behavioral diagnostics for understanding and comparing RL-tuned and base models, and for potentially replacing some RL benefits with smarter inference-time search in base models.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves language-model reasoning, but how these gains relate to inference-time decoding and search remains unclear. Does RL create reasoning the base model lacks, or shift the rollout distribution toward trajectories it can already reach but rarely samples? We study this behaviorally with a Unified Decoding Framework (UDF), which expresses token-level sampling, beam-like search, tree search, and sequence-level resampling as executable policies over a shared budgeted operating space, scored post hoc with pass@$k$, self-consistency, best-of-$N$, and first-finish success. Using paired Base/RL checkpoints from SimpleRL-Zoo, we ask whether an RL default-policy curve can be approximated by a structured path of Base operating points. On Math500, AIME, GPQA, and IFEval, the pass@$k$ recovery path follows a Budgeted Operating-Point Transition Rule (BOPTR), $N_{\mathrm{Base}} \approx αN_{\mathrm{RL}}^β$, with benchmark-conditioned exponents. On Qwen2.5-7B, BOPTR gives the lowest transfer error among the non-oracle rules we test, 3.41 pp (95% CI [2.32, 5.53]); a three-seed replication gives 3.07 $\pm$ 0.39 pp. The rule extends to ten models across four families (3.28 to 4.87 pp on checkpoints added after fitting), to four benchmarks it was never fitted on (5.03 pp vs. 4.44 pp in fit), and holds without an RL checkpoint for the target model (4.19 pp) or without RL supervision of any kind (5.08 pp). These results support a qualified internalized-search reading: under the recipe we test, much of the measured RL gain corresponds to a change in sampling efficiency toward operating points the base model can already reach under search. We treat the scaling patterns as descriptive of this recipe and cohort, report where they break down, and use UDF and BOPTR as behavioral diagnostics rather than evidence of parameter-level equivalence.

</details>


### [101] [Some Emotions Run Deeper: Layer-wise Probing and Causal Intervention in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01279)
*Tian Fang,Gaël Guibon,Davide Buscaldi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper analyzes how and where large language models represent emotion information across layers, and how this varies with different text sources and model families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand whether the layer depth at which emotional information becomes accessible in LLMs is an intrinsic property of the models or is influenced by the nature of the input text, especially given that prior work typically used a single corpus and did not control for variation in emotional explicitness and contextualization.

Method: The authors evaluate eight 1B–9B open-weight LLMs from the Llama, Qwen, and Granite families using three emotion datasets that differ in explicitness and context (Twitter, Reddit, autobiographical narratives). They apply layer-wise probing, offline feature scaling, online forward-pass interventions targeting probe-identified layer bands, transfer analyses of these bands across datasets and emotion categories, and an early-exit classifier guided by probe-selected representations.

Result: They observe that the optimal probing layer for emotion prediction systematically shifts with the corpus, from early layers for explicit, local emotion (e.g., Twitter) to deeper layers for more contextualized narratives, and that this ordering is robust even after matching label-length distributions. Forward interventions on probe-selected layer bands degrade emotion classification performance 5–6 percentage points more than random bands, with statistical significance. The selected layer bands also generalize across datasets and emotion labels, indicating shared affective substrates. Finally, using probe-selected early-exit representations yields an average 6.9 percentage point improvement over using full-depth exits for emotion prediction.

Conclusion: Emotional information in LLMs is not localized at a fixed depth but depends systematically on the nature of the input corpus, with more contextualized expressions relying on deeper layers. Probe-identified layer bands appear causally and robustly involved in emotion representation, are partially shared across emotions and domains, and can be exploited to build more efficient, accurate early-exit emotion classifiers.

Abstract: Emotion is expressed in text along a wide spectrum, from surface lexical cues to inferences entangled with content. Most layer-wise analyses of emotion in LLMs use a single corpus, leaving open whether the depth at which emotion becomes accessible is a property of the model or also of the text source. We investigate this across three datasets spanning different degrees of explicitness and contextualization in emotion expression (Twitter posts, Reddit comments, and autobiographical narratives) and eight 1B--9B open-weight LLMs from the Llama, Qwen, and Granite families. We combine layer-wise probing with offline feature scaling and online forward interventions, transfer analyses, and an early-exit classifier. We find that (i) the best probing layer shifts systematically across corpora, from input-adjacent layers to over half model depth, and this ordering persists after matching label-by-length-bin distributions; (ii) across the evaluated settings, forward-pass interventions on probe-selected bands reduce test accuracy by 5--6 points more than same-width random bands ($q < 0.01$); (iii) selected bands transfer across datasets and emotion categories, suggesting partially shared affective information rather than strictly per-emotion substrates; and (iv) probe-selected early-exit representations outperform full-depth exits by $6.9$ percentage points on average.

</details>


### [102] [Explore Before Committing: Hypothesis-Guided Search for Deep Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01294)
*Ruochen Zhou,Zhengyu Chen,Luan Zhang,Siyang Gao,Yee Whye Teh,Shiqi Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper identifies a common failure mode in deep-research agents that follow a single search trajectory and proposes HypoSearch, a method that uses lightweight hypotheses and branched exploration to improve accuracy and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep-research agents typically follow a single evolving search trajectory when using tools, which can cause them to prematurely commit to a misleading direction when facing multiple plausible paths early in the search. This leads to path-reinforcement and reduced performance. The authors aim to understand and mitigate this failure mode.

Method: The authors perform trajectory-level analysis of tool-using deep-research agents to characterize their failure modes and the behaviors of successful trajectories. Based on these insights, they introduce HypoSearch: the agent first generates lightweight hypotheses as soft search hints, then explores these hypotheses through bounded, independent search branches, and finally compares the evidence gathered in each branch before committing to a final direction or answer. They also conduct a pilot supervised fine-tuning (SFT) study that leverages these behavioral signals to curate compact training trajectories.

Result: HypoSearch is evaluated on four deep-research benchmarks using three different backbone models. It consistently outperforms single-trajectory search and standard parallel search baselines. For example, on the BC-small benchmark, HypoSearch improves Qwen3.5-122B performance from 46.7 to 60.0 while using fewer tool calls than running five independent trajectories. The SFT pilot study suggests that using the identified behavioral signals can help construct compact training data and reduce performance degradation compared to using unfiltered trajectories.

Conclusion: Single-trajectory search in deep-research agents is prone to premature commitment and self-reinforcing errors when multiple plausible directions exist early on. Successful behavior involves grounding exploration in concrete candidates and flexibly shifting directions. HypoSearch operationalizes these behaviors via hypothesis-driven, branched exploration and evidence comparison, leading to more accurate and efficient tool use across benchmarks. Moreover, these behavioral patterns can guide data curation for supervised fine-tuning, suggesting a path toward more robust training and deployment of deep-research agents.

Abstract: Deep-research agents answer complex questions by interacting with search and browsing tools, yet they often search along a single evolving trajectory. Our trajectory-level analysis reveals a common failure mode in which the agent may encounter an early search state with several plausible directions, but follow one direction before collecting enough comparative evidence. Once this happens, subsequent tool calls tend to reinforce the same path, increasing the chance of failure when the initial direction is misleading. We further find that successful trajectories reduce this risk through two behaviors: grounding vague exploration in concrete candidates and shifting directions when the current path is weak or incomplete. Based on these findings, we propose HypoSearch, which generates lightweight hypotheses as soft search hints, explores them through bounded independent branches, and compares branch-level evidence before commitment. Across four deep-research benchmarks and three backbone models, HypoSearch consistently outperforms single-trajectory search and standard parallel baselines, improving Qwen3.5-122B from 46.7 to 60.0 on BC-small while using fewer tool calls than five independent trajectories. A pilot supervised fine-tuning study further shows that these behavioral signals can curate compact training trajectories and reduce degradation from unfiltered data.

</details>


### [103] [Exploring Sparse Autoencoders in Text-Based Causal Confounding Adjustment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01322)
*Mian Zhong,Katherine A. Keith,Anjalie Field*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a sparse autoencoder-based pipeline to construct text representations for causal adjustment that balance bias reduction and variance control, showing improved performance over alternatives and highlighting challenges with more realistic multi-label confounding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Causal inference with text data requires adjusting for confounding information embedded in high-dimensional text. Existing representations face a tradeoff: rich enough to capture confounders for unbiased estimation, yet compact/sparse enough to maintain overlap and low variance in finite samples. There is a need for methods that explicitly address this tradeoff and provide interpretable, testable adjustments.

Method: The authors employ sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to learn high-dimensional but sparse representations of text. They then design a causal adjustment pipeline that iteratively selects a minimal subset of SAE features using conditional independence tests, aiming to retain only those features necessary for confounding control. They compare these representations to alternative text encodings in semi-synthetic experiments with both binary and multi-label confounders.

Result: In standard semi-synthetic setups with binary confounders, SAE-based representations outperform other methods in terms of lower bias and better confidence interval coverage when estimating causal effects. The sparsity and interpretability of SAE features also facilitate falsification checks.
