In a more complex semi-synthetic setting where multi-label data serve as unobserved confounders, the authors find that common off-the-shelf adjustment strategies struggle, indicating limitations of existing approaches.

Conclusion: Sparse autoencoders, coupled with an iterative conditional independence-based feature selection pipeline, offer an effective and interpretable approach for constructing text representations for causal adjustment. They can better navigate the tradeoff between preserving confounding information and maintaining overlap/low variance in simpler confounding scenarios, but more work is needed to robustly handle realistic, multi-label confounding structures, as current off-the-shelf methods show weaknesses there.

Abstract: In many settings, studying causal questions based on text data requires adjusting for confounding information within texts. Yet there is a tradeoff in constructing text representations for adjustment: they must be sufficiently large and/or dense to preserve the confounding variables necessary for unbiased effect estimation, but sufficiently small and/or sparse to satisfy finite-sample overlap and yield low-variance estimates. To address this tradeoff, we turn to sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and propose a novel causal adjustment pipeline that iteratively selects a minimal set of SAE features via conditional independence tests. We find that SAE representations achieve better adjustments (lower bias and and higher coverage) than alternative representations in standard semi-synthetic evaluations with binary confounders, and their interpretability offers opportunities for falsification. We also introduce a more realistic semi-synthetic evaluation that uses multi-label data as the unobserved confounders and find off-the-shelf adjustment methods require increased investigation for these more complex settings. Code: https://github.com/mianzg/sae-text-confounder

</details>


### [104] [VerTox: Verifiable Reward-Guided Corpus Poisoning Against Neural Ranking Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01325)
*Zhiqi Huang,Vivek Datla,Zhichao Xu,Puxuan Yu,Vivek Srikumar,Alfy Samuel*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how vulnerable modern neural ranking models are to corpus poisoning attacks and introduces VerTox, a verifiable RL-based framework to generate highly effective adversarial documents that corrupt rankings and harm RAG systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural ranking models are central to search engines and RAG pipelines, but the rise of LLMs makes it easy to generate fluent, deceptive text at scale. It is unclear how robust ranking models are when attackers inject a small set of malicious documents into the corpus. Existing work has not thoroughly examined or optimized such corpus poisoning attacks against state-of-the-art ranking and embedding models, nor their concrete impact on downstream RAG applications.

Method: The authors formulate corpus poisoning as a verifiable reward-guided reinforcement learning problem (RLVR). They design a reward that explicitly captures both ranking distortion (making adversarial documents outrank target documents) and factual corruption (misleading or contradicting correct information). Using this shaped reward, they fine-tune compact LLMs into adversarial text generators that can produce poisoning documents. The framework, named VerTox, optimizes generation so that the resulting documents are both effective at manipulating rankers and remain natural and difficult to detect (e.g., via low perplexity).

Result: VerTox achieves near-perfect attack success rates, with generated adversarial documents often ranking above their intended targets across multiple major neural ranking architectures and even a proprietary commercial embedding model. The adversarial documents are fluent and exhibit low perplexity, suggesting that standard quality or anomaly metrics will not easily flag them. In downstream evaluations on a RAG pipeline, these factually corrupted adversarial documents significantly degrade system performance, showing practical end-to-end impact beyond isolated ranking benchmarks.

Conclusion: Neural ranking models and RAG systems are highly vulnerable to corpus poisoning attacks powered by LLM-based text generation. By casting poisoning as a verifiable RLVR problem, VerTox can systematically train compact LLMs to generate small amounts of adversarial content that strongly distort rankings while remaining fluent and hard to detect, and that meaningfully harm downstream applications. This highlights an urgent need for more robust ranking architectures, detection methods, and defenses against LLM-enabled poisoning in real-world retrieval systems.

Abstract: Neural ranking models have become core components of modern information retrieval systems and important building blocks of AI systems such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines. However, their robustness remains insufficiently understood in the presence of large language models (LLMs), which can generate fluent and deceptive content at scale. This work investigates the vulnerability of neural ranking models to corpus poisoning attacks, in which an adversary injects a small number of maliciously crafted documents into the corpus to distort ranking behavior. We propose VerTox, the first framework to formulate corpus poisoning as a verifiable reward-guided reinforcement learning (RLVR) problem. By explicitly coupling ranking distortion with factual corruption through specialized reward shaping, we fine-tune compact LLMs into adversarial generators. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves near-perfect attack success rates, producing adversarial documents that frequently rank higher than target documents across major neural ranking architectures, as well as a proprietary commercial embedding model. The generated adversarial documents are fluent and exhibit low perplexity, making them difficult to detect. Furthermore, by explicitly encouraging factual corruption, our adversarial documents significantly degrade the performance of a downstream RAG application.

</details>


### [105] [Probing Factual Knowledge Transfer with Training Data Interventions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01341)
*Romina Oji,Marc Braun,Marcel Bollmann,Marco Kuhlmann,Jenny Kunz*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies whether multilingual language models truly transfer factual knowledge between languages or mostly rely on target-language data, finding that genuine cross-lingual fact transfer is quite limited.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is growing interest in multilingual language models and assumptions that knowledge learned in a high-resource language (like English) transfers to low-resource languages. However, existing evaluations often cannot clearly distinguish true knowledge transfer from memorization of target-language training data or use of superficial heuristics. A more controlled and intervention-based approach is needed to measure how much factual knowledge actually transfers across languages.

Method: The authors start with an English-pretrained language model and then continue pretraining it on Persian text. They systematically remove specific factual triples from the Persian training data at different granularities (e.g., sentence-level co-occurrence removal) to prevent the model from encountering these facts in Persian. They build SIFT, a dataset of 500 subject–relation–object triples over 20 relations, separating facts about globally prominent versus Persian-related entities. They then evaluate the model with native Persian cloze-style prompts, using both easy (random) and harder negative candidate sets, to measure whether facts originally learned in English appear in the model’s Persian outputs after continued pretraining without access to those facts in Persian.

Result: The experiments show that, under the strictest fact-removal setting, most facts that the model learned in English do not appear to transfer into Persian: successful cross-lingual factual transfer is rare. They also find that removing only sentence-level co-occurrences in Persian is not enough to eliminate the fact signal, indicating that facts can still be inferred from remaining context. Furthermore, using easy, randomly chosen negative candidates artificially inflates measured transfer, because the model can rely on shallow associations rather than true factual recall; performance drops substantially with a more challenging candidate set. Finally, the frequency of entities in the source language matters greatly: Persian-related facts, which are much less frequent in English, hardly transfer at all into Persian.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that genuine cross-lingual factual knowledge transfer in multilingual language models is far more limited than commonly assumed. Many previously reported successes may largely reflect memorization from target-language data or exploitation of simple heuristics rather than true transfer of facts learned in another language. Effective evaluation requires strong data interventions, careful negative candidate design, and attention to source-language entity frequency, especially for low-resource or culturally specific knowledge.

Abstract: Do multilingual language models transfer factual knowledge across languages during continued pretraining, or do they mostly recall facts learned directly from the target-language data? To answer this question more reliably, we propose an intervention-based framework: starting from an English-pretrained model, we continue pretraining on Persian data from which specific facts have been systematically removed at varying levels of granularity. We construct SIFT, a resource of 500 triples across 20 relations, stratified by the cultural origin of each fact's subject into general (globally prominent) and Persian-related entities, designed for both systematic fact removal from training data and evaluation, with natively written Persian cloze templates. Our results show that fact transfer is very limited: under the strictest removal condition, a large majority of English-acquired facts fail to transfer into Persian. We further show that sentence-level co-occurrence removal is insufficient to eliminate fact signal, and that easier (randomly selected) negative candidate sets substantially inflate apparent transfer by rewarding shallow associative heuristics, while performance on a harder candidate set that allows for less reliance on heuristics is much lower. Finally, we show that source-language entity frequency has a large influence, with Persian-related facts, which are orders of magnitude rarer in the English corpus, hardly transferring.

</details>


### [106] [CHARM: Character Hallucination for Multicultural Role Play Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01352)
*Sunkyung Han,Nahyeon Park,Gaeun Seo,Seunghyun Yoon,JinYeong Bak*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces CHARM, a benchmark for evaluating how well role-playing LLMs respect characters’ knowledge boundaries, and finds hallucinations are mainly due to failure to comply with known boundaries rather than failure to recognize them.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of role-playing LLMs detect hallucinations but do not separate whether the model: (1) fails to realize that a question is outside a character’s knowledge, or (2) realizes this but still answers incorrectly. This distinction is crucial for understanding and fixing hallucinations, especially when LLMs role-play characters with limited temporal or fictional knowledge. There is also a need for a culturally diverse, validated benchmark covering characters from multiple regions to study potential cultural biases in these failures.

Method: The authors build CHARM, a multicultural benchmark of 40 real and fictional characters from five cultural-linguistic regions, with validation by native speakers/reviewers. They design abstention-enabled multiple-choice questions targeting two boundary types: Temporal (distinguishing what the character could know in their historical era vs modern facts) and Cross-Universe (facts outside the character’s narrative or historical universe). They introduce a two-stage evaluation: (1) Boundary-Awareness—asking models explicitly whether a query is in-scope for the character; (2) Boundary-Compliance—testing whether models abstain when asked to answer concrete out-of-scope questions. They then evaluate six LLMs and re-ask the same questions without role-play constraints to detect “parametric overrides” where the model clearly knows the fact but should suppress it in character.

Result: Across six LLMs, most character hallucinations stem from Boundary-Compliance failures, not lack of Boundary-Awareness. Models often explicitly recognize that a question exceeds the character’s knowledge but still provide factual answers that break character. Many such cases are confirmed as parametric overrides: when not role-playing, the model correctly knows the answers and this knowledge overrides role constraints. The authors also find systematic cultural variation in these failures, aligning with uneven representation of characters and regions in the models’ training knowledge.

Conclusion: Role-playing hallucinations in LLMs are mainly due to models’ inability to comply with known knowledge boundaries rather than ignorance of those boundaries. LLMs store factual knowledge and often cannot suppress it when it conflicts with a character’s epistemic limits, leading to out-of-character answers. Cultural imbalances in model training data further influence where these failures occur. Addressing hallucinations in role-play will therefore require mechanisms that enforce boundary compliance and mitigate parametric overrides, as well as attention to cultural representation in training and evaluation.

Abstract: Role-playing large language models (LLMs) are expected to adopt a character's style while also respecting that character's knowledge boundaries. Prior evaluations detect character hallucination but rarely distinguish whether errors arise from failure to recognize a boundary or from failure to comply despite recognition. We introduce CHARM, a multicultural benchmark of 40 real and fictional characters drawn from five cultural-linguistic regions, and validated by native reviewers. It probes two boundary types, Temporal (historical vs. modern) and Cross-Universe (entities outside a character's narrative or historical universe), using abstention-enabled multiple-choice questions. We propose a two-stage evaluation that separates Boundary-Awareness (explicit recognition that a query is out of scope) from Boundary-Compliance (abstention when answering concrete questions). Evaluations across six LLMs show that hallucination is driven predominantly by compliance failures. Models frequently acknowledge that a query lies outside the character's knowledge yet still provide factual, out-of-character answers. By re-posing the same questions to the target character, we confirm that a large fraction of these cases are verified parametric overrides; the model stores the relevant fact but fails to suppress it. We also observe systematic cultural variation in these failures, consistent with imbalances in how characters from different regions are represented in model knowledge.

</details>


### [107] [Where the Verifier Fails: A Category-Level Audit of Reward Signals in RLVR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01354)
*Esther Xin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper analyzes and stress‑tests automatic verifiers used in RL with verifiable rewards and math benchmarks, showing that much of their error comes from brittle handling of benign formatting like whitespace and punctuation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automatic verifiers map free‑form mathematical answers to binary rewards and are heavily used in RLVR and benchmark evaluation. Prior work noted that a verifier failed on about 6% of its own ground‑truth answers, vaguely attributing this to LaTeX parsing issues, but without identifying exactly which answer patterns were problematic. The paper aims to precisely decompose and localize these verifier failures to understand where reliability breaks down and how severe the problem is across commonly used systems.

Method: The authors apply metamorphic testing to verifiers instead of to models. They construct mathematically equivalent variants of answers—certified rewrites that are guaranteed to preserve semantic meaning—then feed these to four widely used verifiers. Because the variants are provably equivalent, any rejection is a definite false negative that needs no human review. They categorize the types of variants (e.g., whitespace, punctuation, LaTeX structure) and run large‑scale experiments, yielding 307,420 verifier verdicts to measure failure rates per category and per verifier configuration.

Result: (1) Self‑validation (a verifier accepting its own ground truth) varies dramatically from 53.8% to 95.2% even on identical inputs, with a 41.3‑point spread; two configurations of the same library disagree on nearly half of the input pairs (49.9%). (2) Errors are not evenly distributed over parsing cases; instead, 93.0% of contract‑violating failures under the default LaTeX configuration stem from trivial formatting issues—whitespace and punctuation—where features like a trailing period or newline dominate the error budget. (3) Distinguishing rejection from execution failure shows that verifiers with similar overall error rates can fail for qualitatively different reasons, and that a benchmark numeric cascade silently accepts off‑by‑one wrong answers in a scale‑dependent way (0% acceptance for magnitudes below 10^4, increasing to 100% at or above 10^4), driven by a scale‑invariant relative tolerance.

Conclusion: Automatic verifiers commonly used in RLVR and math benchmarks are far less robust and consistent than aggregate self‑acceptance numbers suggest. A large share of false negatives stems from superficial formatting differences like whitespace and punctuation, and different verifier implementations with comparable headline error rates can fail for very different underlying reasons, including systematically accepting certain incorrect answers. Therefore, reliance on these verifiers for evaluation and reward in RL must be reconsidered, and more robust, well‑characterized verification pipelines are needed.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and standard benchmark evaluation both rely on an automatic verifier that turns a free text answer into a binary reward. Prior work reports that one evaluation harness accepts only about 94% of its own ground truth answers, blaming LaTeX parsing. That is an aggregate: it does not say which answer forms consume the error budget. We supply the decomposition. We apply metamorphic testing to the verifier rather than the model, generating certified equivalent answer variants, that is, rewrites that preserve mathematical meaning by construction, so that any rejection is a provable false negative needing no human adjudication. We then measure rejection per answer category across four widely used verifiers over 307,420 verdicts. We find three things. (1) Self validation ranges from 53.8% to 95.2% on identical inputs, a spread of 41.3 points. The published figure describes one implementation, not the task; two configurations of the same library disagree on 49.9% of pairs. (2) The residual is not spread across parsing categories but concentrated in whitespace and punctuation, which account for 93.0% of in contract failures for the default LaTeX configuration. A trailing period or newline dominates the budget. (3) Separating rejection from execution failure shows that verifiers with similar aggregate error fail for opposite reasons, and that a reference numeric cascade accepts off by one wrong answers as a step function of magnitude, from 0% below 10^4 to 100% at or above, because its relative tolerance is scale invariant.

</details>


### [108] [Separating Syntax from Language: A Mechanistic Account of Translation in Multilingual LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01356)
*Mikhail Sonkin,Tanja Baeumel,Daniil Gurgurov,Josef van Genabith,Simon Ostermann*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that multilingual LLMs perform translation in multiple modular stages, with a distinct intermediate step where target-language syntax is formed before surface word realization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although multilingual LLMs are strong machine translators, it is not well understood how they internally transform representations between languages. Prior work argued for a separation between language-agnostic conceptual representation and language-specific production, but it remained unclear whether further substructure exists within the production stage, especially concerning syntax vs. surface form.

Method: The authors create controlled multilingual datasets that tease apart cross-linguistic word-order differences. They apply causal interventions (e.g., manipulating internal activations) and probing methods to examine how internal representations evolve during translation. They analyze attention heads to determine which ones are responsible for syntactic transformations versus language-specific surface realization.

Result: They find that models first form a representation of the target-side word order before encoding the specific surface form of the target language. They identify individual attention heads that are selectively responsive to syntactic transformations (word-order changes) and largely invariant to which language is being produced, indicating a language-agnostic syntactic process.

Conclusion: Translation in multilingual LLMs is more modular than previously recognized. Beyond the previously proposed separation between conceptual meaning and language-specific production, there is an additional independent stage where target-language syntactic structure is committed to. Different functional components (e.g., attention heads) implement these stages, with some specializing in syntax and others in surface language realization.

Abstract: Multilingual large language models (mLLMs) achieve strong performance in machine translation, yet our understanding of the mechanisms by which they transform representations from one language to another remains incomplete. Prior work suggests that translation decomposes into separable processes within an mLLM, where conceptual content is first represented independently, followed by a production into language-specific form. In this work, we show that translation is even more modular than previously assumed and that the output language production in translation processes is actually further separable into a syntax and a surface language process. We construct controlled multilingual datasets that isolate cross-linguistic differences in word-order and use causal interventions and probing to track how representations are transformed during translation. We find that models first construct target-side word-order before realizing the target language surface form. We identify individual attention heads that are selectively sensitive to syntactic transformations while remaining largely invariant to language identity. These results establish the commitment to a syntactic structure as an independent stage in translation, extending prior decompositions and showing how translation is implemented by functionally different components within mLLMs.

</details>


### [109] [Investigating Linear Probe Robustness to Linguistic Register, Medical Specialty, and Corpus Shifts in Medical QA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01361)
*Nishant Mishra,Ameen Abu-Hanna,Iacer Calixto*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies whether linear probes on LLM hidden states that distinguish true vs. false medical QA answers remain reliable under controlled input shifts, finding robustness to writing style and specialty but notable degradation across different medical QA corpora.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on ‘truth directions’ in LLM representations reports conflicting results on how well these directions generalise across datasets and input forms. These studies often change multiple factors simultaneously (e.g., style, topic, and dataset), making it unclear what actually causes performance drops. In safety and evaluation, we need to know if a single forward-pass truth probe is robust to realistic variation in how users phrase medical questions, or if it is entangled with artefacts of specific benchmarks.

Method: The authors construct a controlled benchmark from 500 MedQA questions, each rewritten into four distinct registers (textbook, patient, clinical note, colloquial), and labelled with medical specialties. They pair this with two other medical exam corpora, MedMCQA and MMLU-medical, to test cross-dataset transfer. They train linear classifiers (linear probes) on hidden states from four open-weight LLMs (2–8B parameters) to distinguish correct from incorrect answers and then systematically evaluate how probe AUROC changes when varying (1) writing style, (2) clinical specialty, and (3) corpus, holding the others fixed where possible. They also test robustness with an alternative text generator and with human-written patient questions.

Result: Probes exhibit small performance degradation when only writing style changes (about 0.10 AUROC drop on held-out facts) and even smaller sensitivity to medical specialty (about 0.03 AUROC). However, when transferring across corpora, probe performance decreases much more: by about 0.12 AUROC on MMLU-medical and about 0.21 AUROC on MedMCQA, roughly twice the gap observed for style changes. The robustness to register is replicated using a different generator and is observed on real, human-written patient queries, confirming that the effect is not an artefact of a particular paraphrasing model.

Conclusion: Within the medical domain, LLM hidden states appear to encode a relatively stable ‘truth direction’ that generalises across writing styles and specialties, enabling linear probes to flag factual errors from a single forward pass. However, the direction does not fully generalise across different medical QA corpora, suggesting that the probe partially captures dataset-specific structures or artefacts, not purely underlying medical truth. Thus, linear truth probes have real but limited robustness, and evaluations should distinguish style and domain shifts from deeper corpus shifts when assessing their reliability.

Abstract: Linear classifiers trained on hidden states of a large language model (LLM), linear probes, can flag factual errors from a single forward pass. Geometrically, that implies that true and false statements separate along a stable direction in hidden state space, i.e., the truth direction. Prior work disagrees on whether this generalises across input shifts, but the disagreement is hard to interpret because cross-dataset probe transfer experiments confound several kinds of input change at once. We isolate three such variables in medical question-answering (QA): writing style (register), domain (medical specialty), and corpus (dataset). We build a benchmark using 500 MedQA entries, each rewritten into four styles (textbook, patient, clinical note, colloquial), annotated with clinical specialty, and grouped with two other exam corpora, MedMCQA and MMLU-medical, for cross-dataset evaluation. Probing four open-weight LLMs (2--8B), we find that the truth direction is largely robust to writing style (mean $Δ_\text{register} \approx 0.10$ AUROC on held-out facts) and to medical specialty ($Δ_\text{specialty} \approx 0.03$), but degrades unevenly across corpora: by $0.12$ AUROC on MMLU-medical and by $0.21$ on MedMCQA, roughly twice the register gap. The register result replicates with a second generator and carries over to human-written patient questions. The truth direction is therefore largely stable within the medical domain but breaks under some corpus shifts, and question format does not explain the break, which suggests that the signal a linear probe recovers is partly bound to dataset structure rather than to medical knowledge alone.

</details>


### [110] [How Correct Is Your Answer? A Semantic Correctness Framework for Open QA Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01369)
*Elitsa Yotkova,Violeta Kastreva,Petar Velkov,Hristo Boyanov,Dimitar Dimitrov,Ivan Koychev,Preslav Nakov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a new taxonomy, datasets, and a context-aware NLI-based metric (CAP) for more fine-grained and reliable evaluation of open-ended QA by LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing metrics for evaluating open-ended QA either rely on surface similarity or undifferentiated judgments, failing to capture nuanced error types (e.g., hallucinations, incompleteness, overgeneration) and the many valid surface forms of correct answers. This creates a bottleneck for accurately measuring LLM performance.

Method: 1) Define a semantic correctness taxonomy with eight ordered classes for open-ended QA answers, distinguishing types of correctness and error (e.g., fully correct, verbose-but-correct, hallucinated, contradictory, incomplete). 2) Construct two datasets: CAP-Correctness (8.8k open-ended QA examples annotated with correctness classes) and CAP-Statements (11k question-answer pairs rewritten into declarative statements for NLI). 3) Propose CAP (Context-Aware Precision), a reference-based evaluation metric that converts QA into statements and uses bidirectional NLI with respect to question-conditioned statements, enforcing a monotonicity protocol to test whether metric scores align with the taxonomy ordering. 4) Empirically compare CAP to existing judgment- and similarity-based metrics under this protocol.

Result: CAP better aligns with the proposed correctness taxonomy than established baselines under a monotonicity testing protocol, showing improved ability to respect the intended ordering of semantic correctness classes. The released datasets (CAP-Correctness and CAP-Statements) enable more fine-grained evaluation and training of NLI models tailored to open-ended QA evaluation.

Conclusion: A taxonomy-based, NLI-driven approach can more reliably evaluate open-ended QA than traditional similarity or coarse judgment metrics. CAP and the associated datasets provide reusable tools for distinguishing qualitatively different correctness and error types, improving the evaluation of modern LLM-generated answers.

Abstract: Reliable evaluation of open-ended question answering remains a bottleneck for measuring answer correctness of modern LLMs. Unlike multiple-choice tasks, free-form answers may be correct in many surface forms and may fail in qualitatively different ways, including incompleteness, contradiction, overgeneration, and endorsement of false premises. Existing judgment-based and similarity-based metrics often collapse these distinctions. We address this gap with three reusable contributions. First, we introduce a semantic correctness taxonomy that assigns open-ended answers to eight ordered classes, separating verbose-but-correct answers from those contaminated by hallucinated content. Second, we release CAP-Correctness, an 8.8k-example benchmark spanning widely used QA datasets, and CAP-Statements, an 11k-example dataset for converting question-answer pairs into declarative statements for natural language inference (NLI) training and statement-based evaluation. Third, we introduce CAP (Context-Aware Precision), a reference-based metric that scores question-conditioned statements using bidirectional NLI. Under a monotonicity protocol testing whether metrics respect the taxonomy's intended ordering, CAP outperforms established baselines.

</details>


### [111] [Behaviorally Effective LoRA Writes Are Sparse and Structured](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01374)
*Haruto Sato,Yuki Tanaka,Ren Nakamura,Aoi Kobayashi,Mei Ito*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates where and how LoRA adapters store behavioral information, showing that effective updates are sparse, structured, and highly concentrated.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard LoRA constrains updates to a fixed low rank but does not clarify which parameters actually drive behavior. The authors want to directly study the geometry and sparsity of behaviorally relevant LoRA updates and whether they are more structured than the raw low-rank form suggests.

Method: They introduce Learned-Basis LoRA: first train an unconstrained adapter, then convert its learned write columns into a module-wise orthonormal basis, freeze this basis, and continue training in this constrained space. They perform exact switches between unconstrained and constrained training, same-state continuations under different write subspaces, no-retraining projection tests into various bases (learned vs random vs PCA), and a series of sparsification/ablation tests including per-module top-k subsets, global ranking of directions, and single-direction ablations across modules.

Result: Swapping from unconstrained to learned-basis LoRA preserves held-out accuracy and nearly exactly reconstructs the original writes (≤0.25% relative Frobenius error). Continuations from the same checkpoint diverge under different write subspaces, demonstrating that the geometry of the write space is a causal factor. Projecting into the learned space preserves useful behavior whereas random and PCA control spaces lose it. Behaviorally relevant signal is highly concentrated: per-module top-k continuation is optimal at very small k (2 or 4) across multiple datasets and seeds; globally top-ranked 16/32 directions beat random subsets; and individual late q_proj, o_proj, and down_proj directions can have disproportionately large behavioral impact.

Conclusion: LoRA updates that matter for behavior live in a sparse, structured, low-dimensional subset of directions rather than being diffusely spread across the nominal low-rank space. The learned write basis captures this structure and defines a meaningful geometric state variable for training. This has implications for understanding and controlling model behavior, enabling more targeted and parameter-efficient interventions via a small number of high-impact directions in specific attention and MLP projections.

Abstract: Low-rank adaptation fixes the rank of the update, but it does not identify which parts of a trained
  write actually carry behavior. We study that question directly and show that behaviorally effective
  LoRA writes are sparse, structured, and far more concentrated than the raw low-rank parameterization
  suggests.
  We use Learned-Basis LoRA, a learned-basis continuation recipe, to expose that structure. The recipe
  warms up an unconstrained adapter, converts its learned write columns into a module-wise orthonormal
  basis, freezes that basis, and continues training inside the constrained parameterization. Across 14
  exact switches from unconstrained to constrained form, held-out accuracy is unchanged at the
  conversion step and reconstructed write matrices differ by at most 0.25% relative Frobenius error.
  Same-state continuation then shows that the same trained checkpoint develops differently under
  different write subspaces, establishing write geometry as a causal state variable. A no-retraining
  projection test shows that useful write signal stays inside the learned write space and largely
  disappears from random or frozen-activation PCA controls.
  The concentration pattern is strong at both local and global scales. Across GSM8K, MathQA, and AQuA,
  per-module top-k continuation reaches its optimum at k in {2, 4} in all twelve seed-level cases we
  test. A stricter global ranking test shows that learned top-16 and top-32 subsets outperform matched
  random subsets, especially on GSM8K/Qwen and MathQA/Qwen. Single-direction ablations further reveal a
  sparse set of late q_proj, o_proj, and down_proj components with outsized behavioral impact.

</details>


### [112] [Polish ModernBERT: The Long and Short of Polish Language Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01379)
*Michał Perełkiewicz,Sławomir Dadas,Rafał Poświata,Małgorzata Grębowiec*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Polish ModernBERT, a family of efficient, long-context Polish encoder-only Transformers that outperform previous Polish BERT/RoBERTa-style models on a wide range of tasks, including new long-context benchmarks, while using fewer parameters and resources.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Polish encoder models are mostly based on older BERT/RoBERTa-style architectures and struggle with long-context inputs in terms of performance and efficiency. There is a need for a modern, resource-efficient Polish encoder that can handle long sequences (up to 8K tokens) and perform well across diverse discriminative and retrieval tasks, including those requiring legal and human-rights reasoning.

Method: The authors adapt the ModernBERT pretraining recipe to Polish through staged selection experiments. They design a family of four encoder-only models (Base and Large, each with 512-token and 8K-token context variants). They pretrain these models and evaluate them on 30 tasks, including a newly released long-context benchmark spanning legal topic classification, ideological decision-direction prediction, factual-consistency assessment over literary plot summaries, and human-rights violation assessment. They also compare against matched Polish RoBERTa-8K baselines and measure efficiency (memory and latency) in representative inference setups, as well as performance on a Polish retrieval benchmark for sub-300M-parameter encoders.

Result: Polish ModernBERT achieves the best overall performance among evaluated Polish encoders, with average scores of 83.99 (Base-8K) and 85.11 (Large-8K) across 30 tasks. On long-context tasks, the 8K variants substantially outperform matched Polish RoBERTa-8K baselines, improving from 67.47 to 77.15 at Base scale and from 75.88 to 78.49 at Large scale. The Base-8K model attains these gains with 22% fewer parameters than the RoBERTa-8K baseline (149M vs. 190M). Efficiency tests show lower peak memory usage and latency than Polish RoBERTa in both 512-token and 8K-token settings. Additionally, Polish ModernBERT-8K-Base obtains the best score on a Polish retrieval benchmark among encoders under 300M parameters.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that Polish ModernBERT provides a new state-of-the-art family of Polish encoder-only Transformers, combining stronger performance, better long-context handling, and higher computational efficiency than existing BERT/RoBERTa-style Polish encoders. The newly introduced long-context benchmark and released models establish a more capable and practical foundation for Polish discriminative, representation-learning, and retrieval tasks, particularly in domains like law, literature, and human-rights analysis.

Abstract: Encoder-only Transformers remain effective for discriminative and representation-learning tasks, yet Polish encoders still largely rely on BERT/RoBERTa-style architectures. We introduce \textbf{Polish ModernBERT}, a family of four Polish encoders available at Base and Large scales, each with 512-token and 8K context variants. We adapt the ModernBERT pretraining recipe through staged selection experiments and release a long-context benchmark covering legal topic classification, ideological decision-direction prediction, factual-consistency assessment over literary plot summaries, and human-rights violation assessment. Across 30 tasks, Polish ModernBERT achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated Polish encoders, reaching 83.99 and 85.11 for the Base-8K and Large-8K models, respectively. On long-context tasks, the 8K variants improve over matched Polish RoBERTa-8K baselines from 67.47 to 77.15 and from 75.88 to 78.49 at the Base and Large scales, respectively. The Base-8K model achieves this gain with 22\% fewer parameters (149M vs.\ 190M). Efficiency measurements in representative inference setups show lower peak memory usage and latency than matched Polish RoBERTa baselines in both 512-token and 8K settings. Polish ModernBERT-8K-Base additionally achieves the best result on a Polish retrieval benchmark among the evaluated encoders below 300M parameters.

</details>


### [113] [InSight: A Benchmark for Agentic Claim Verification in Interactive Visualizations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01383)
*Maeve Hutchinson,Syed Mahbubul Huq,Mohammad Albinhassan,Radu Jianu,Aidan Slingsby,Pranava Madhyastha*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduces InSight, a benchmark to test AI agents on verifying natural-language claims by interactively exploring dynamic data visualizations, not just static images.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most vision-language benchmarks use static images and single-turn QA, but real-world data analysis is interactive and dynamic: evidence may be hidden, split across multiple linked views, or revealed only through user-driven interactions. There is a need for a benchmark that captures these epistemic and interactional demands to properly evaluate agentic reasoning over visual data analysis interfaces.

Method: The authors build InSight, a large benchmark with 21,349 natural-language claims extracted from human-written analytical narratives. Each claim is grounded in a fully interactive, web-based visualization environment. Agents must operate as interactive agents, navigating and manipulating these interfaces to collect visual evidence and decide if each claim is supported, refuted, or unverifiable. The benchmark logs and treats interaction traces (clicks, navigation, filtering sequences, etc.) as proxies for the reasoning process, enabling fine-grained evaluation of how models search for and integrate evidence.

Result: Using InSight, the authors evaluate state-of-the-art models/agents and show that performance on interactive claim verification is still far from solved. Models struggle to robustly navigate complex interactive visualizations, locate all relevant evidence, and correctly categorize claims, indicating a significant gap between current capabilities and the demands of real-world data analysis tasks.

Conclusion: Interactive claim verification over visualizations is a challenging, largely unsolved problem for current models. InSight provides a rigorous benchmark that captures the dynamic, agentic nature of real data analysis, enabling both performance measurement and process-level auditing via interaction traces. The benchmark is publicly released to spur further research on interactive, reasoning-driven vision-language agents.

Abstract: Vision Language Models have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in interpreting static visual artifacts, but modern data analysis is inherently dynamic, requiring the active interrogation of interactive environments. Existing benchmarks are predominantly constrained to static imagery and one-shot question answering and fail to capture the epistemic demands of this domain, where evidence is frequently occluded, distributed across linked views, or conditionally revealed through user agency. In this paper, we introduce InSight, a benchmark for agentic claim verification over interactive visualizations. The dataset consists of 21,349 claims derived from human-authored analytical narratives and grounded in fully interactive web-based environments. Agents must navigate these environments to determine whether a natural language claim is supported, refuted or not verifiable given the available evidence. Unlike traditional evaluations, InSight treats interaction traces as intrinsic proxies for reasoning, enabling a rigorous audit of how models seek and synthesize visual evidence. We evaluate state-of-the-art models, revealing that interactive verification remains a non-trivial challenge. We release InSight at https://github.com/maevehutch/insight.

</details>


### [114] [When Tokenization is Secretly Output Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01386)
*Tanja Baeumel,Josef van Genabith,Simon Ostermann*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper argues that tokenization in autoregressive language models is not just input preprocessing but effectively defines the supervision signal and task, with output tokenization strongly influencing performance, training dynamics, and internal representations, especially for numeric reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing work shows tokenization matters for model performance, but it is usually treated as a low-level preprocessing detail. There is no principled explanation of why different tokenizations change behavior, and most evaluation papers do not even report the numeric tokenization they use, despite comparing models trained under different tokenization schemes. The authors want to explain and empirically probe how tokenization shapes what the model is supervised to learn, particularly in numeric reasoning tasks.

Method: They reframe tokenization as part of the output supervision in autoregressive models and design controlled experiments on numeric reasoning where they decouple input tokenization from output tokenization. By varying output granularity while holding other factors constant, they analyze how this affects task performance, training dynamics, and model internals (representations), and they complement this with a survey of 120 recent *CL papers on numeric reasoning to assess how tokenization is reported and compared in practice.

Result: The experiments show that output tokenization, not input tokenization, primarily drives differences in performance, learning dynamics, and internal representations for numeric reasoning. These effects are consistent with the view of tokenization as output supervision. The survey finds that only about 10% of numeric reasoning papers report numeric tokenization, while 69% compare models across differing tokenization (and thus supervision) regimes without acknowledging this difference.

Conclusion: Tokenization in autoregressive language models should be understood as defining the supervision signal and effectively changing the task, not just as an input preprocessing choice. Output tokenization, in particular, shapes what the model must learn in each forward pass and thus its capabilities and internal representations. Consequently, model comparisons across different tokenization strategies may partly reflect different underlying tasks rather than pure differences in ability. The authors propose that viewing tokenization as output supervision offers a principled account of tokenization effects and should inform future model design and evaluation practices, including transparent reporting of tokenization schemes.

Abstract: Tokenization in language models is treated by default as an input preprocessing decision. We argue that this framing is incomplete: in autoregressive models, tokenizer granularity determines what the model must resolve in a single forward pass, and therefore the supervision signal it receives. This affects both the difficulty of the learning problem and the representations that emerge inside the model. We test this in a controlled experiment on numeric reasoning with a novel decoupling of input and output tokenization. As the output supervision view predicts, differences in task performance, training dynamics, and model internals are induced by output tokenization and largely invariant to input tokenization. This may matter in practice, because models with different tokenization strategies differ not only in input representation but in the task they were trained on. Comparisons between models may thus partly reflect task definition rather than ability. A survey of 120 recent *CL papers on numeric reasoning confirms that this is rarely acknowledged: only about 10% report the numeric tokenization of the models they evaluate, while 69% compare across tokenization, and thus supervision, regimes without reporting it. While prior work documents that tokenization consistently affects model performance, there is no principled account of why. We argue that framing tokenization as output supervision provides that account.

</details>


### [115] [From Rollouts to Recipes: Self-Contained Post-Training for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01422)
*Yifei Li,Lingling Zhang,Muye Huang,Zihan Ma,Jiashuai Liu,Jun Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Self-Routing is a post-training framework for large language models that adaptively chooses how to optimize each sample based on the model’s own rollout correctness and confidence, improving mathematical reasoning performance over uniform and fixed training strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard post-training of large language models uses a single, uniform optimization recipe for all training samples (e.g., the same loss, same update rule), even though the model exhibits diverse behaviors and learning states across samples. Some samples are already solved confidently, some are wrong but high-signal, and others are noisy or low-signal; treating them identically can waste compute and even harm performance through unnecessary or misdirected updates. The authors aim to exploit the model’s own rollouts (correctness and confidence) to identify sample-specific learning states and adapt the training strategy per sample, without relying on external teachers, extra labels, or expensive additional sampling.

Method: They introduce Self-Routing, a behavior-conditioned post-training framework in which each training sample is dynamically routed to one of several optimization paths based on the model’s own rollout behavior: (1) GRPO (a gradient-based reinforcement-style objective) for certain behavior states, (2) on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) when consolidating the model’s own good behaviors is beneficial, (3) explicit regularization when updates risk overfitting or instability, and (4) skipping when the sample is low-signal or already stable. The routing decision is driven by rollout-level signals: whether the model’s answer is correct and how confident it is, forming behavior states that determine the optimization type applied to that sample. The framework is designed to be plug-and-play on top of existing post-training pipelines and uses no external teachers, no extra annotations, and no extra sampling beyond standard rollouts.

Result: On mathematical reasoning benchmarks using Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 model backbones, Self-Routing yields consistent performance gains over several baselines: (a) uniform GRPO (same objective for all samples), (b) uniform on-policy self-distillation, (c) fixed mixtures of objectives, and (d) simpler, less expressive routing heuristics. Empirical analyses show that the routing decisions evolve during training, with more samples being skipped or regularized once they become stable or low-signal, and more focus placed on high-signal, informative examples. This leads to better use of training compute and reduces detrimental or redundant parameter updates.

Conclusion: Behavior-conditioned, sample-wise routing based on rollout correctness and confidence is an effective strategy for post-training large language models. Self-Routing improves mathematical reasoning performance without the need for external supervision or extra data, and it automatically shifts training effort away from low-signal or already-converged samples. The dynamic routing distribution observed over training suggests that adaptive objective selection at the sample level is a promising direction for more efficient and effective post-training of large language models.

Abstract: Post-training large language models usually applies a single training recipe to all samples, even though the model's own rollouts reveal different sample-level learning states. We propose Self-Routing, a behavior-conditioned post-training framework that uses rollout correctness and confidence to decide how each sample should be optimized. Depending on its behavior state, a sample is routed to GRPO, on-policy self-distillation, regularization, or skipping, allowing training to adapt without external teachers, extra annotations, or additional sampling. Experiments on mathematical reasoning across Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 backbones show that Self-Routing consistently improves over uniform GRPO, uniform OPSD, fixed mixtures, and simpler routing baselines. Further analyses show that the routing distribution changes over training and reduces unnecessary updates on low-signal or already stable samples.

</details>


### [116] [GlossoGen: Emergent Language in Complex Multi-Agent LLM Interactions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01491)
*Elias Stengel-Eskin,Newton Sander,Carlos Bonetti,Sasha Boguraev,James Bowler,Hale Sirin,Simon Kirby*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces GlossoGen, a platform to study how languages emerge and evolve between interacting LLM agents, showing that they can develop efficient, compositional but human-incomprehensible languages and exhibit cumulative cultural evolution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM agents increasingly interact with each other rather than only with humans, their communication systems may drift or evolve in ways that matter for safety, monitoring, and our theoretical understanding of LLMs. Existing work has limited support for complex, realistic multi-agent scenarios and does not systematically examine which conditions lead to language emergence, evolution, and transmission among LLMs. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a controlled environment to observe and analyze language evolution among LLM agents.

Method: The authors build GlossoGen, a platform for multi-agent language evolution experiments, and within it design the SaveVeyru scenario, where multiple LLM agents have partial information and must coordinate under time or performance pressure. They systematically vary key factors such as efficiency pressure, model size/strength, and the presence of a postmortem phase in which agents can reflect and agree on conventions. They then analyze the emergent communication protocols for compositionality, morphological productivity, deviation from standard English priors, and learnability by new agents of varying strengths. They also compare conditions for language emergence vs. conditions for language transmission to naïve agents.

Result: The experiments show that LLM agents do indeed develop novel languages when repeatedly interacting in the SaveVeyru scenario. These emergent languages are compositional and morphologically productive yet diverge sufficiently from English that humans cannot easily interpret them. Language emergence critically depends on: (1) pressure toward efficient communication, (2) sufficiently strong underlying models, and (3) a postmortem stage where agents align on conventions. For transmission, they find that new agents can acquire these languages from exposure alone, actively shaping their learning strategies. Importantly, while stronger models are needed to create new languages, weaker models can successfully learn and use an already emerged language.

Conclusion: The study concludes that current LLMs are capable of cumulative cultural evolution in their communication systems: languages emerge, become more structured and efficient, and can be transmitted and further developed across generations of agents, including mixed populations of stronger and weaker models. This mirrors a hallmark property previously attributed only to humans. The findings raise both opportunities and concerns: interacting LLMs may autonomously develop increasingly sophisticated but opaque communication protocols, challenging monitoring and safety, while offering a testbed for theories of language evolution and cultural transmission.

Abstract: The growing rate at which LLM agents interact with one another raises key questions about language evolution in multi-LLM-agent settings, with implications for safety and monitorability as well as for linguistic accounts of LLMs. To address these questions, we introduce GlossoGen, a novel platform for studying multi-agent language evolution in complex scenarios. Within GlossoGen, we build the SaveVeyru scenario, which requires agents with partial information to communicate under pressure. We find that language evolution does occur between LLM agents, that the resulting languages are compositional and morphologically productive, and that they deviate from the LLMs' English prior in ways that render them incomprehensible to humans. Moreover, we identify several qualities essential to this evolution: pressure towards efficiency; the strength of the models backing the agents; and access to a "postmortem" stage in which agents can agree on linguistic conventions. Importantly, we observe that different conditions govern the transmission of language to new agents. Specifically, we find that agents learn new languages from usage alone, take an active role in this learning, and that while stronger models are required for novel language emergence, weaker models can learn an existing language once it has emerged. Taken together, our results indicate that current LLMs have the potential for cumulative cultural evolution -- previously attested only in humans -- with mixed populations of agents developing capacities that go beyond their lowest common denominator.

</details>


### [117] [Knowledge Distillation During Mid-Training Favors Reasoning over Factual Recall](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01532)
*Jacqueline He,Howard Yen,Shuyue Stella Li,Margaret Li,Hanqing Zeng,Yinglong Xia,Benyu Zhang,Zhuokai Zhao,Qiang Zhang,Pang Wei Koh,Luke Zettlemoyer,Wen-tau Yih*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies why standard logit-based knowledge distillation behaves differently at different stages of language model training and proposes a new mid-training distillation objective, Switch Distillation, that better balances reasoning and factual recall.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard forward KL knowledge distillation from a stronger teacher to a smaller language model is widely used, but its effects across different training stages are poorly understood. Empirically, practitioners see that models can gain reasoning skills yet sometimes lose factual recall or learn it more slowly, especially in mid-training. The authors want to understand this stage-dependent behavior, particularly when using post-trained teachers, and to design a distillation method that improves reasoning and knowledge-intensive abilities without hurting or delaying factual recall acquisition.

Method: The authors run controlled experiments comparing standard next-token prediction (NTP) versus forward Kullback-Leibler (KL) logit distillation from post-trained teachers at different stages: pre-training and mid-training on curated corpora. They analyze how distillation impacts reasoning, factual recall, knowledge and commonsense across training. They measure teacher confidence with predictive entropy and study its asymmetry across data domains (procedural vs knowledge-intensive) and relative to the student’s evolving knowledge state. Based on these insights, they design Switch Distillation, a mid-training objective that selectively applies distillation only on tokens where the teacher is confident (low predictive entropy) and uses standard cross-entropy loss elsewhere, using teacher entropy as a lightweight routing signal.

Result: The experiments show that forward KL distillation with post-trained teachers helps both reasoning and factual recall during early pre-training compared to pure NTP, but during mid-training it continues improving reasoning while actually slowing the acquisition of factual recall. Analysis ties this to teachers being more confident on procedural data while students already have low-entropy factual knowledge, leading to an imbalance when always following the teacher. Switch Distillation, which conditions on teacher confidence, consistently outperforms baseline distillation objectives across various teacher sizes. Compared with standard NTP, it yields 1.61–1.71x reasoning performance and 1.13–1.19x knowledge/commonsense performance during mid-training while preserving 96.7–96.8% of factual recall. After post-training, Switch Distillation closes the factual recall gap and still maintains 1.25–1.32x gains in reasoning and 1.13–1.20x in knowledge/commonsense relative to NTP.

Conclusion: Forward KL logit-based knowledge distillation from post-trained teachers has stage-dependent effects: it benefits both reasoning and factual recall early in pre-training but later harms the rate at which factual recall is acquired, even as reasoning continues to improve. This arises from a mismatch between teacher confidence across domains and the student’s evolving knowledge state. By selectively distilling only where the teacher is confident and defaulting to cross-entropy elsewhere, Switch Distillation corrects this imbalance. It provides stronger reasoning and knowledge/commonsense performance while largely preserving factual recall during mid-training and fully recovering factual recall after post-training, establishing it as a superior distillation strategy for training smaller LMs from larger teachers.

Abstract: Logit-based knowledge distillation (KD) is used to train smaller language models (LMs) via supervision from stronger teachers, but whether its benefits are consistent across training stages remains unclear. Through controlled experiments, we find that forward Kullback-Leibler (KL) distillation--the standard KD formulation--with post-trained teachers behaves fundamentally differently during mid-training, an intermediate phase of self-supervised learning on curated corpora. Surprisingly, while forward KD simultaneously improves reasoning and factual recall during pre-training relative to standard next-token prediction (NTP), it instead slows factual recall acquisition during mid-training despite continued reasoning gains. We trace this stage dependence to an asymmetry in teacher confidence across data domains and the student's evolving knowledge state: teachers are more confident on procedural than knowledge-intensive data, while students acquire low-entropy factual knowledge earlier in training. To mitigate this imbalance, we propose Switch Distillation, a simple mid-training objective that distills on tokens where the teacher is confident, using teacher predictive entropy as a lightweight routing signal, and otherwise falls back to cross-entropy. Switch Distillation consistently outperforms existing distillation objectives across teacher sizes. Relative to standard NTP, it achieves 1.61-1.71x the reasoning performance and 1.13-1.19x the knowledge and commonsense performance while preserving 96.7-96.8% of factual recall. Crucially, these benefits persist after post-training: Switch Distillation closes the factual recall gap while maintaining 1.25-1.32x and 1.13-1.20x gains in reasoning and knowledge and commonsense, respectively.

</details>


### [118] [SDARE-Bench: Evaluating Large Language Models on Conversational Stigma Detection and Response in Dyadic and Group Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01548)
*Stephanie Fong,Yiwen Jiang,Zimu Wang,Hongxi Yang,Yaling Shen,Hiu Weh Naomi Chow,Heung Ying Lai,Xiangyu Zhao,Qingyang Xu,Zhongxing Xu,Jiahe Liu,Guilherme C. Oliveira,Vincent Lee,Zongyuan Ge,Dominic Dwyer*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces SDARE-Bench, a benchmark to test how well LLMs detect and respond to stigma in conversation-like settings, revealing substantial safety vulnerabilities, especially under group pressure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large Language Models are widely used for advice and social decision-making, yet there is little systematic evaluation of how they handle stigma-related content, particularly in realistic conversational and group contexts. Existing benchmarks are static and do not capture audience effects or multi-party dialogue, leaving a critical safety and ethics gap.

Method: The authors construct SDARE-Bench, a scenario-based benchmark with 1,138 dyadic (one-to-one) queries and 1,388 group dialogue scenarios, including specially designed group-pressure conditions. They evaluate 8 different LLMs on two tasks: (1) stigma detection (identifying components of stigma in input), and (2) open-ended response generation (measuring stigma expression, resistance to stigma, and realism of advice). Model responses are assessed using a classifier trained on 1,392 human-annotated responses to detect stigma-related behaviors.

Result: Across 8 tested LLMs, models perform poorly at identifying stigma components, especially in group dialogue scenarios. In generative tasks, models express more stigma, show weaker resistance to stigmatizing content, and produce more unrealistic advice in group settings than in dyadic interactions. Under constructed group-pressure conditions, models’ stigma expression rates rise dramatically, reaching an average of 97.5% across models.

Conclusion: SDARE-Bench exposes a systematic safety weakness in current LLMs: their tendency to inadequately detect and to reproduce or amplify stigma, particularly in socially complex, group conversational settings and under social pressure. The benchmark highlights the need for improved training, safety alignment, and evaluation methods that explicitly consider stigma, conversational dynamics, and audience effects.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in advice seeking and decision making that may affect social judgements. Despite stigma's profound effects on people and communities, benchmarks remain scarce. Existing general-domain evaluations typically rely on static prompts and fixed-format tasks, overlooking conversational contexts and audience effects in everyday communication. To address these gaps, we introduce SDARE-Bench, the first scenario-based benchmark evaluating both stigma detection and open-ended response generation in LLMs, comprising 1,138 dyadic queries and 1,388 group dialogue. Empirical results across 8 LLMs consistently demonstrate poor identification of stigma components, especially in group dialogues. In open-ended response generation, stigma expression was substantially higher in group settings than in dyadic, with weaker resistance to stigma and more unrealistic advice. Responses were evaluated using a classifier trained on 1,392 human annotated responses. In constructed group pressure settings, stigma expression rates further increased to a striking average of 97.5%. Our findings identify stigma response as a recurring LLM safety vulnerability, especially in socially complex conversational contexts.

</details>


### [119] [A systematic Approach to constructing a Chance-and-Risk Matrix for Semiconductor Supply Chains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01563)
*Ema Salkić,Alexander Fichtl,Philipp Ulrich,Hans Ehm,Marta Bonik,Georg Groh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They build an automated LLM-based pipeline that turns semiconductor firms’ public disclosures into a structured, ranked knowledge graph of risks and opportunities, achieving high validity and reasonable agreement with human experts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Semiconductor supply chains are increasingly risky due to geopolitical issues, geographic concentration, and fast technology changes, but there is no scalable, continuous system that mines public corporate disclosures for structured, prioritized risk and opportunity intelligence. Existing approaches are manual, fragmented, or not tailored to the semiconductor context, creating a gap for decision-makers who need timely, comparable risk information across firms and along the supply chain.

Method: The authors design an end-to-end pipeline that: (1) automatically retrieves public corporate documents for semiconductor companies; (2) uses large language models to extract descriptions of risks and opportunities from these documents; (3) structures the extracted information into a knowledge graph that connects each risk/opportunity item to its category, source documents, and related events; (4) performs entity and item deduplication/merging; and (5) ranks all items using a three-layer scoring scheme that combines: (a) an initial algorithmic formula, (b) an LLM-based relevance adjustment, and (c) final expert validation. They then apply this pipeline to five semiconductor companies spanning different positions in the value chain.

Result: When applied to five semiconductor companies, the pipeline yields 76,207 scored risk and opportunity items. An independent validation finds that 92.6% of sampled items are valid (i.e., correctly extracted and categorized). The automatically generated rankings of risks and opportunities correlate substantially with expert rankings, with average Spearman correlations of 0.55 for risks and 0.72 for opportunities. Analysis of the resulting cross-company matrices highlights trade restrictions as the most prominent shared risk across the sampled firms.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that an LLM-driven, end-to-end pipeline can reliably and at scale extract, structure, and prioritize risk and opportunity intelligence from public corporate disclosures in the semiconductor industry. The high validity rate and substantial alignment between automated and expert rankings suggest that such systems can support continuous, cross-company risk monitoring. The knowledge-graph and ranking framework reveals systemic issues—such as trade restrictions—as dominant shared risks, indicating that this approach can help stakeholders better understand and manage supply chain vulnerabilities and strategic opportunities.

Abstract: Semiconductor supply chains face escalating risks from geopolitical tensions, geographic concentration, and rapid technological shifts, yet no scalable system continuously extracts, structures, and prioritizes risk intelligence from public corporate disclosures. We present an end-to-end pipeline that retrieves corporate documents for semiconductor companies and uses large language models (LLMs) to extract the risks and opportunities they describe. It organizes these into a knowledge graph linking each item to its category, sources, and related events, then merges duplicates and ranks them with a three-layer mechanism combining an algorithmic formula, an LLM relevance adjustment, and expert validation. Applied to five companies across the value chain, the pipeline produces 76,207 scored items, of which an independent check finds 92.6% valid. The automated rankings match expert judgment at an average Spearman correlation of 0.55 for risks and 0.72 for opportunities, and the resulting matrices identify trade restrictions as the dominant cross-company risk.

</details>


### [120] [From Confusion to Clarity: Confusion-Aware Retrieval and Knowledge Injection for Text Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01564)
*Manish Gupta,Chaitanya Giri,Jayasimha Talur*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a framework that helps large language models better distinguish between many similar labels in large taxonomies, using confusion analysis, label expansion, and rule generation, without fine-tuning, and with benefits transferable to smaller models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models are weak at fine-grained classification when many labels are semantically similar and domain-specific, because pre-training does not encode these subtle distinctions. Existing top-K retrieval narrows the candidate labels but does not help the model choose correctly between very similar ones, leading to frequent confusions in large taxonomies.

Method: The authors introduce a three-stage framework: (1) identify pairs of labels that the LLM often confuses; (2) for each instance, expand the retrieved candidate set to explicitly include these confusable labels; and (3) automatically generate targeted, human-interpretable rules that highlight key differences between similar labels and provide this guidance to the LLM during classification. The approach is fully prompt- and retrieval-based, requiring no model fine-tuning, and the derived rules can be reused with other, typically smaller, models.

Result: On three datasets with large taxonomies (WOS, Flipkart, LEDGAR), the method improves Macro F1 by up to 10.0 percentage points over baselines that rely only on top-K retrieval. When the generated rules are transferred from a stronger model to smaller models (2B–20B parameters), these smaller models gain up to 11.5 percentage points in Macro F1, demonstrating effective cross-model transfer of the rules.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling and correcting label confusions via expanded candidate sets and targeted rule generation significantly boosts LLM performance on large-label-space classification, without any fine-tuning. The learned rules are portable and can substantially enhance cheaper, smaller models, making the framework practical and cost-effective for real-world taxonomy classification tasks.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) struggle to classify text into taxonomies with many semantically similar labels, as the distinctions are domain-specific and not captured by pre-training. To handle large label spaces, a common approach retrieves top-$K$ candidate labels by embedding similarity and prompt the LLM to choose among them. However, top-$K$ retrieval reduces the number of candidates but does not help the model tell similar ones apart. When two similar labels both appear as candidates, the model lacks the signal to choose correctly between them. We propose a framework that (1) identifies which label pairs the model struggles to distinguish, (2) expands the candidate set to include confusable labels, and (3) generates targeted rules to differentiate between similar candidates. The framework requires no fine-tuning, and the generated rules transfer to smaller, cheaper models. On three benchmarks (WOS, Flipkart, LEDGAR), our approach improves Macro F1 by up to 10.0pp over retrieval baselines, with smaller models (2B--20B) gaining up to 11.5pp via cross-model transfer.

</details>


### [121] [From Production Traffic to Post-Training: Building a Self-Hosted LLM That Covers the Corporate Request Mix](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01572)
*Olga Tsymboi,Dmitrii Stoianov,Ramil Latypov,Danil Taranets,Daniil Dryabin,Mikhail Gashkov,Viktor Zelenkovskiy,Aleksandr Fida,Gleb Alektorov,Nikita Gulyakov,Arthur Babkin,Aleksandr Medvedev,Pavel Gein,Anatolii Potapov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents a method to consolidate traffic from many enterprise applications onto a single self-hosted LLM while improving quality and reducing serving cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprises constrained by data residency must self-host LLMs. As they adopt new models without retiring old ones, their GPU resources become fragmented across many models, increasing cost and operational complexity. The authors aim to collapse this fragmented fleet into a single, higher-quality model that can serve diverse use cases efficiently.

Method: They analyze production errors along three key axes—instruction following, function-calling, and internal task distribution—and construct stratified offline benchmarks aligned with real traffic, evaluated via deterministic verifiers or calibrated LLM judges. Instead of joint optimization, they train three separate GRPO (a policy optimization method) expert models, one per axis, to avoid cross-domain reward interference. They then merge these experts using a two-stage SLERP (spherical linear interpolation) procedure. For each axis, they define domain-specific reward functions that reveal and address distinct failure modes: semantic collapse, over-calling, and verbosity hacking.

Result: The consolidated model, in non-reasoning mode, outperforms a baseline that is about seven times larger in total parameters on internal and public benchmarks: on their in-house Arena (69.6 vs. 65.8), instruction following (0.85 vs. 0.83), and function-calling (0.79 vs. 0.77). It also improves general dialogue benchmarks. Operationally, this single model absorbs 50% of the platform’s traffic—116 million requests per month—at significantly lower serving cost.

Conclusion: By decomposing quality improvement into orthogonal axes, training specialized GRPO experts, and merging them via SLERP, enterprises can replace a fragmented fleet of self-hosted LLMs with one consolidated model that delivers better performance at lower cost and scales to large internal traffic volumes.

Abstract: Data-residency constraints force enterprises to self-host LLMs, but continuous adoption of newer models without decommissioning their predecessors expands the serving fleet, fragmenting a finite GPU pool. We consolidate traffic from over 200 internal applications onto a single model by closing quality gaps identified through production error analysis along three axes: instruction following, function-calling, and internal task distribution. Quality is tracked by offline benchmarks stratified to production traffic and scored by deterministic verifiers or calibrated LLM judges. Rather than optimising all objectives jointly, which introduces cross-domain reward interference, we train a separate GRPO expert per axis and merge them via two-stage SLERP. Each expert's reward exposes a distinct failure mode, namely semantic collapse, over-calling, and verbosity hacking, each requiring a domain-specific fix. In non-reasoning mode the recipe surpasses a ${\sim}7\times$ larger by total parameters baseline on the in-house Arena with 69.6 to 65.8, instruction following with 0.85 to 0.83, and function-calling with 0.79 to 0.77, while lifting general dialogue benchmarks. The model absorbs 50% of platform traffic, 116M requests per month, at a fraction of the serving cost.

</details>


### [122] [Scaling Near-Optimal SFT-RL Annotation Budget Allocation from Small to Large LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01573)
*Jingtan Wang,Arun Verma,Xiaoqiang Lin,Zhengyuan Liu,Nancy F. Chen,Daniela Rus,Bryan Kian Hsiang Low*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how to optimally split a fixed human annotation budget between supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) when post-training large language models, and shows that a wide range of SFT/RL ratios perform near-optimally and that this “near-optimal region” found on small models transfers reliably to larger models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In LLM post-training, practitioners must decide how much limited annotation budget to allocate to supervised fine-tuning versus RL (e.g., preference-based training). Current guidance is ad hoc: prior work only notes coarse patterns like SFT being better in low-data regimes, offers no principled framework for budget allocation, and does not clarify whether SFT/RL tradeoffs found on small models generalize to larger ones. This uncertainty leads to expensive trial-and-error on large models. The paper aims to provide a systematic, scalable way to choose SFT vs RL data under realistic annotation constraints.

Method: The authors formalize budget allocation between SFT and RL as a problem of identifying a near-optimal region rather than a single best ratio.
