They define this region as all SFT/RL allocations whose performance lies within a chosen tolerance (e.g., 2–10%) of the global optimum. They empirically map out this region across multiple tasks, model scales, and post-training schemes (including preference-based off-policy RL and reward-supervision on-policy RL). They then study how the size and position of this region change with model scale and with asymmetric annotation costs between SFT and RL data, and test whether the near-optimal region identified on small proxy models transfers to larger target models.

Result: Across evaluated setups, the near-optimal SFT/RL region is empirically large even for small performance tolerances, and becomes wider as model size increases. The approximate shape and location of this region generalize well from smaller proxy models to larger target models, meaning that ratios that are near-optimal on small models remain near-optimal on large ones. This transfer holds consistently across different tasks, model families, and both preference-based off-policy and reward-supervision on-policy RL. Additionally, when annotation costs differ between SFT and RL data, the effective near-optimal region shifts in predictable ways in SFT/RL space, reflecting the cost asymmetry.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that practitioners do not need to identify a single precise SFT/RL allocation to achieve good performance in LLM post-training. Instead, there typically exists a broad, scale-robust near-optimal region of SFT/RL budget splits. Because this region can be reliably estimated using small proxy models and then transferred to large models, one can avoid exhaustive, expensive sweeps at large scale. The study also shows that differences in annotation costs between SFT and RL mainly reweight this region rather than eliminating it, providing a practical, principled framework for choosing SFT vs RL data allocations under realistic budget constraints.

Abstract: How to divide a fixed annotation budget between supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) during LLM post-training remains an open problem. Existing work characterizes only broad trends (e.g., SFT dominates in low-data regimes), lacks a principled allocation framework, and does not examine whether the optimal ratio transfers across model sizes. We frame this problem in terms of near-optimality: rather than seeking a single optimal SFT-RL ratio, we characterize the near-optimal region, the set of allocations within a specified tolerance of peak performance. Empirically, this region is wide even for small tolerances (2-10%), widens with model scale, and transfers reliably from small proxy models to large target models. This yields a practical strategy: small proxy-model experiments suffice to identify a transferable near-optimal region, eliminating the need for exhaustive large-scale search. Our results hold consistently across tasks, model families, and both preference-based off-policy and reward-supervision on-policy RL methods. We further analyze how the asymmetry in annotation costs between SFT and RL data shifts the near-optimal region.

</details>


### [123] [Closing Cost-Quality Gap in Document VLMs: Difficulty-Aware Data Curation and Quality-Adjusted Deployment Economics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01575)
*Maksim Evdokimov,Matvey Ivanov,Dmitrii Tsiupin,Olga Tsymboi,Anatolii Potapov,Aleksandr Ivanov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper introduces a cost-efficient, high-quality document-understanding system based on a Mixture-of-Experts vision-language model (VLM) that significantly reduces annotation costs compared to humans and existing open-source models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Structured data extraction from massive volumes of documents in regulated industries is expensive due to limitations of bespoke OCR pipelines, privacy constraints that block external models, and the high serving cost of quality open-source VLMs.

Method: The authors design a 35B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts VLM with only 3B parameters active per inference. It is fine-tuned on proprietary production data plus open-domain documents selected via a Difficulty-Aware pipeline that emphasizes layout diversity, fact-extractability, and agreement across models. The system is optimized to fit training on a single H100 GPU and to serve diverse document workflows through prompting.

Result: The proposed model outperforms all deployable (non-reasoning) baseline models, including some up to 10x larger, on document-understanding quality. Cost analysis that factors in confirmation and correction costs (estimated from production telemetry) shows that the system cuts expected costs by over 80% compared to human annotation and by more than 50% versus the best competing open-source VLM; larger baselines are too expensive to be practical.

Conclusion: A carefully designed Mixture-of-Experts VLM, trained with a difficulty-aware data curation pipeline, can deliver state-of-the-art document-understanding performance at a fraction of the cost of both human annotation and existing open-source models, making large-scale, privacy-compliant deployment economically viable in regulated industries.

Abstract: Extracting structured fields from hundreds of millions of documents annually remains costly in regulated industries: bespoke OCR cascades cover only a fraction of workflows, privacy rules preclude external models, and existing open-source VLMs that clear quality thresholds cost more to serve than human annotation. We present a deployed document-understanding system built on a Mixture-of-Experts VLM (35B total, 3B active), fine-tuned on in-house production data mixed with open-domain documents curated by a Difficulty-Aware pipeline for layout diversity, fact-extractability, and cross-model consistency. Fitting on a single H100 and serving heterogeneous workflows via prompting, the model leads all deployable (non-reasoning) baselines up to an order of magnitude larger. A quality-adjusted cost analysis, with confirmation and correction costs calibrated from production telemetry, shows it reduces expected costs by over 80% against the human baseline and by more than 50% against the best competing open-source model, while larger baselines remain economically unviable.

</details>


### [124] [StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01591)
*Ke Yang,Chenglong Wang,Michel Galley,Chandan Singh,Jeevana Priya Inala,ChengXiang Zhai,Jianfeng Gao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: StudentSim is a framework for building per-student AI simulators that more faithfully imitate individual learners and their reactions to tutoring, outperforming strong LLM and domain baselines across chess, ESL writing, and math.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Adaptive AI tutors need to tailor guidance to each learner, but it is expensive and slow to gather enough real-student interaction data to learn which instructional strategies work for whom. Existing student simulators either track student state but cannot handle rich guidance (e.g., explanations, corrections), or use LLM role-play that is fluent but not faithful to the target student’s competence. There is a need for student models that are both behaviorally accurate and sensitive to tutor guidance so they can be used to efficiently evaluate and train tutoring strategies.

Method: The authors propose StudentSim, a two-stage training framework. First, they do pooled training over data from many students to learn a general model of learner behavior in a domain. Then they perform per-student specialization (fine-tuning or adaptation) using the sparse records of each individual student to obtain an individualized simulator. These simulators are designed to both reproduce the student’s responses and update those responses when given tutor guidance. They also introduce StudentSimEval, an evaluation protocol/dataset of 60 students across three domains—chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics—based on public, de-identified learner logs. StudentSimEval defines two metrics, behavioral fidelity (F), quantifying how closely the simulator matches a student’s actual responses, and guidance responsiveness (R), capturing how much the simulator changes appropriately when tutor guidance is provided. Competing methods, including GPT-5.4 role-play and Maia2 in chess, are trained and evaluated under the same conditions.

Result: Across all three domains, StudentSim surpasses GPT-5.4 on both behavioral fidelity and guidance responsiveness. In the chess domain, StudentSim achieves F=0.51 and R=0.91, outperforming GPT-5.4 (F=0.23, R=0.72) and the strong chess learner model Maia2 (F=0.45, R=0.27). As a demonstration, they use StudentSim as a reward model to train a tutoring policy with reinforcement learning. The resulting chess tutor is rated by expert humans as more accurate, better guided, and more personalized than both a non-RL baseline tutor and a tutor trained using a GPT-5.4-based simulator as the reward model.

Conclusion: StudentSim offers a practical way to convert sparse logs of individual students into high-fidelity, guidance-sensitive simulators that can stand in for real learners when testing or training AI tutors. The StudentSimEval benchmark shows that the approach yields simulators that both imitate real students closely and react appropriately to instructional guidance, outperforming a strong general-purpose LLM and domain-specific baselines. Furthermore, using such simulators as reward models can measurably improve the quality and personalization of AI tutors, suggesting a scalable path to optimizing tutoring strategies without requiring large volumes of new human-student experiments.

Abstract: AI tutors are most useful when they adapt to each student's strengths, weaknesses, and preferred guidance, but evidence about which guidance works for which student is sparse, slow, and costly to collect from real learners. Student simulators can provide this signal as a proxy, yet existing approaches are limited: state-tracking models fit student behavior but struggle to process explanations or corrections, while LLM role-play follows guidance fluently but does not reliably match the competence of the student being imitated. We present StudentSim, a training framework that turns sparse per-student data into individualized simulators through pooled training followed by per-student specialization. The resulting simulators both mirror a student's own responses and update them under tutor guidance. We also introduce StudentSimEval, a standardized protocol covering 60 students across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics, using public learner datasets with de-identified records shared for research. StudentSimEval measures behavioral fidelity (F), or how well a simulator matches a student's responses, and guidance responsiveness (R), or how readily it updates under tutor guidance, with all methods fit and evaluated on the same records. Across all three domains, StudentSim outperforms GPT-5.4 on both metrics. In chess, StudentSim reaches F=0.51 and R=0.91, compared with 0.23 and 0.72 for GPT-5.4 and 0.45 and 0.27 for Maia2. As a proof of concept, using StudentSim as a reward model for tutor reinforcement learning produces a chess tutor that expert humans rate as more accurate, better-guided, and more personalized than a no-RL baseline and a tutor trained against a GPT-5.4 simulator reward. Code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/StudentSim.

</details>


### [125] [The Rise of Verbal Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01597)
*Kshitij Tayal,Arun Sharma,Genta Indra Winata,Anirban Das,Sambit Sahu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes and organizes the paradigm of Verbal Reinforcement Learning, where natural language serves as feedback to shape language agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As language agents become more capable, natural language is increasingly used not just for interaction but as a rich feedback signal that can convey goals, preferences, and causal structures. However, existing work is fragmented, lacking a unified conceptual framework that clarifies how and when language feedback influences agents. The paper is motivated by the need to systematize this emerging area to better understand how language can be used to align and improve agents.

Method: The authors introduce the concept of Verbal Reinforcement Learning (VRL) and build a taxonomy along two dimensions: when verbal feedback influences the agent’s lifecycle and what aspect of the agent it modifies. From this, they define three main pillars—Language as Grounding Signal, Language as Deliberative Feedback, and Language as Learning Signal. Within each pillar, they review and categorize representative approaches, highlighting the mechanisms by which language affects agent behavior.

Result: The paper produces a structured taxonomy of VRL, mapping existing work into three pillars and identifying subcategories within each. It clarifies the distinct roles language can play—as a way to specify tasks and rewards, as on-the-fly guidance for reasoning, and as a training signal that updates parameters. This organization reveals commonalities and differences among disparate methods, and surfaces where current techniques are strong or limited.

Conclusion: Verbal Reinforcement Learning is a unifying paradigm for using natural language as feedback to shape language agents. By organizing prior work into three pillars based on when and how language exerts influence, the paper shows that verbal feedback is transforming how agents are specified, guided, and trained. The framework also highlights open challenges and new opportunities for building more capable and better-aligned agents through richer, more systematic use of natural language feedback.

Abstract: Natural language is emerging as a primary feedback channel for improving language agents, capable of conveying intent, preferences, and causal structure in forms interpretable by both humans and modern language models. We call this paradigm Verbal Reinforcement Learning (VRL) and offer the first unified account of it. We organize the field around a single axis, \textit{when} verbal feedback takes effect in an agent's lifecycle and \textit{what} it modifies, yielding three pillars: (1) \textbf{Language as Grounding Signal}, where language defines the task itself by specifying goals, states, and reward structures; (2) \textbf{Language as Deliberative Feedback}, where natural language guides reasoning at test time without the need to update model parameters; (3) \textbf{Language as Learning Signal}, where language-based feedback shapes model parameters through training. Within each pillar, we synthesize representative work, distinguish key subcategories of approaches, and outline the distinct role language plays in shaping agent behavior. Together, this taxonomy shows how verbal reinforcement is reshaping agent development, while also defining the challenges and opportunities for building more capable and aligned agents.

</details>


### [126] [CordisBench: Can Language Models Reason About Component Lifecycles in Dynamic Agent Harnesses?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01600)
*Damien Sileo,Dimitri Kachler*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They build CordisBench, a benchmark to test how well language models reason about the lifecycle of dynamically reconfigurable software systems, showing that performance degrades as dependency complexity grows and that heavy reasoning can help but is costly and avoidable with a formal reference semantics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dynamic agent harnesses let LLMs modify the very software environment that governs their execution (e.g., plugins, components, dependencies). This creates complex lifecycle and dependency reasoning challenges: a small local plugin change can cascade through dependency graphs and cleanup procedures. Existing benchmarks do not systematically test this structured, execution-grounded reasoning about component dependencies, teardown orders, and reconfiguration outcomes. The authors are motivated to provide a rigorous, controlled benchmark to evaluate and compare models on this specific kind of execution- and lifecycle-oriented reasoning, including under constraints on reasoning effort and interaction budget.

Method: They design CordisBench, a benchmark of about 1,200 questions built on top of Cordis, a runtime that manages software components, their dependencies, and cleanup behavior. In this controlled formal setting, programs are executed against Cordis, and questions probe several reasoning tasks: (1) identifying which components are affected by a change, (2) predicting the system state after a specified teardown order, (3) determining which properties hold for all versus some teardown orders, and (4) selecting reconfigurations that will in fact succeed when executed. They run three efficiency-oriented LLMs with constrained reasoning effort, allowing only 2–32 relevant interactions per task, and use deterministic, task-specific scoring. They also derive and employ an independent finite reference semantics that mirrors the Cordis execution for all observations and action outcomes relevant to scoring, thereby providing a ground truth independent of the runtime implementation.

Result: The evaluated models generally perform well on small, less interactive systems but become substantially less reliable as the number of relevant interactions grows, particularly when they must predict final system state or reason about different teardown orders. Increasing inference effort (e.g., allowing more interactions and more reasoning tokens) improves accuracy for some models, indicating that extra compute can partially compensate for the reasoning difficulty. However, this improvement comes with significant computational costs: on the subset of instances involving 16 interactions, the GPT-5.6 Luna model consumes nearly 3,000 reasoning tokens per question at medium effort. The independent finite reference semantics matches Cordis’s execution behavior exactly for all 528 executable questions used in evaluation, confirming the correctness and sufficiency of the formal semantics as ground truth.

Conclusion: CordisBench exposes a specific and practically important weakness in current efficiency-oriented language models: their difficulty in reliably handling complex lifecycle reasoning in dynamically reconfigurable software systems, especially as dependency interactions multiply and teardown orders vary. Although giving models more inference budget can yield sizable performance gains, the associated token cost can be high and, in the controlled setting of CordisBench, unnecessary. The existence of an independent finite reference semantics that aligns perfectly with Cordis across all tested executions suggests that such reasoning tasks can be grounded in precise, low-cost formal semantics, highlighting a path toward more efficient and reliable evaluation—and potentially toward systems that offload complex lifecycle reasoning to formal engines rather than expensive LLM inference.

Abstract: Dynamic agent harnesses let language models change the software that shapes their own execution. This flexibility brings a new reasoning burden: a local plugin change can propagate through dependencies and cleanup. We introduce CordisBench, a 1,200-question benchmark of this lifecycle reasoning. It combines a controlled formal setting with programs executed against Cordis, a runtime that manages component dependencies and cleanup, and asks models to identify affected components, predict state after a specified teardown order, determine which conditions hold under all or some orders, and choose reconfigurations that succeed when executed. Across these tasks, we evaluate three efficiency-oriented models at low reasoning effort with 2, 4, 8, 16, 24, or 32 relevant interactions, using deterministic task-specific scoring. Models usually handle small systems well but grow less reliable as more interactions become relevant, especially when predicting final state and when reasoning across teardown orders. Additional inference effort recovers marked gains for some models. The cost is nontrivial: on our 16-interaction subset, GPT-5.6 Luna uses nearly 3,000 reasoning tokens per question at medium effort. For these controlled instances, that cost is avoidable: an independent finite reference semantics agrees with Cordis execution on every observation and action outcome used for scoring across all 528 executable questions.

</details>


### [127] [Beyond Scores: Understanding LLM-as-a-Judge Mechanisms in Summarization Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01604)
*Himil Vasava,Ming Jiang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper mechanistically analyzes how LLM-based evaluators assign quality scores to generated text, revealing a two-stage evaluation pipeline and how fine-tuning modifies, rather than creates, this mechanism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based evaluators are heavily used to score and train natural language generation systems, but we lack a mechanistic understanding of how these evaluators internally compute their ratings. This opacity raises concerns about reliability, robustness to perturbations, and how fine-tuning shapes their behavior. The paper aims to fill this gap by providing a detailed, causal, layer-wise analysis of the evaluation process.

Method: The authors design an eight-attack perturbation taxonomy targeting Readability and Adequacy aspects of summaries, then generate paired clean and corrupted summaries with controlled error intensity and explicit token-level modification maps. They apply a four-part experimental suite—causal tracing, logit-lens vocabulary projection, and attention-head knockout—to two dedicated LLM evaluators, Themis (Llama-3-8B-based) and Prometheus (Mistral-7B-based). They also compare these to a base Llama-3-8B model as a control, focusing on how information about errors is routed through layers, attention heads, and MLPs, and when the final scalar rating “crystallizes” in the residual stream.

Result: Both evaluator models exhibit a structured two-stage evaluation pipeline. In lower layers (below layer 15), attention heads perform localized comparison between clean and corrupted content and route error information to the final position in the sequence. In higher layers, MLPs aggregate this routed signal and write the final rating, with a sharp crystallization of the decision at late layers (layer 26 for Themis, 25 for Prometheus). The base Llama-3-8B model shows similar routing and crystallization patterns but lacks the clear stage separation: its below-layer-15 MLPs still influence the final position. Fine-tuning for evaluation appears to suppress these lower-layer MLP contributions and shifts the crystallization earlier by about two layers, indicating targeted refinement of existing mechanisms rather than a wholly new pipeline.

Conclusion: LLM evaluators implement a coherent two-stage mechanism for NLG quality assessment: early-layer attention identifies and routes local errors, while late-layer MLPs integrate this information into a final score, with the decision sharply materializing in specific late layers. Fine-tuning primarily reshapes and sharpens pre-existing architectural tendencies—suppressing certain MLP contributions and advancing the crystallization depth—rather than creating novel circuitry. This mechanistic insight clarifies how evaluation models operate and how fine-tuning sculpts them, informing future design, diagnosis, and alignment of LLM-based evaluation systems.

Abstract: LLM-based evaluators of natural language generation (NLG) quality are widely deployed as scoring tools and as automated training signals, yet the internal procedure by which they assign a rating remains poorly understood. We investigate this procedure mechanistically through an eight-attack perturbation taxonomy across the Readability and Adequacy dimensions of NLG quality, a generation pipeline that produces paired clean and corrupt summaries with controlled error intensity and explicit token-level modification maps, and a four-experiment battery of causal tracing, logit-lens vocabulary projection, and attention-head knockout applied to Themis (Llama-3-8B) and Prometheus (Mistral-7B). Both evaluators implement a structured, coherent evaluation pipeline operating in two stages: below layer 15, attention performs local error comparison and routes the result to the final input position; above it, the MLP cascade integrates the signal and writes the rating, with the decision crystallizing in the residual stream at a sharp late layer (L = 26 on Themis, L = 25 on Prometheus). Furthermore, a base-model control at the same scale (Llama-3-8B) reproduces the routing architecture and crystallization but not the stage separation, isolating the two mechanisms that fine-tuning specifically installs, suppression of below-L15 MLP contribution at the last position and a two-layer advance of the crystallization depth, indicating that fine-tuning sculpts an existing substrate rather than building the pipeline from scratch. We release the source code and data at https://github.com/himil-v/judge-mech

</details>

### [128] [HyperWorld: Hypergraph-Structured State Serialization Improves Learned Textual World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00002)
*Yun-Jian Zhang,Chen-Wei Liang,Tian-Yi Zhang,Jian Ding,Yi-Lun Wu,Ao-Bo Li,Wei-Cong Su,Saifullah,Hong-Yu An,Mu-Jiang-Shan Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HyperWorld studies how different ways of serializing symbolic world states affect the learning and planning performance of textual world models, finding that higher-order, entity-centered hyperedge representations give the best robustness and data efficiency, especially for smaller models and distribution shifts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While world models for language agents must learn symbolic action effects from textual state descriptions, the impact of how these states are serialized (their structural representation) on learning, generalization, and planning remains unclear and underexplored. The paper aims to isolate and systematically compare serialization schemes to identify representations that serve as effective inductive biases, particularly in low-capacity or distribution-shifted settings.

Method: The authors introduce HyperWorld, a controlled benchmark that keeps the underlying ground-truth environment fixed while varying only the textual serialization of states. They compare four representations: raw textual observations, independent sentence-style symbolic facts, pairwise triples, and entity-centered hyperedge units that group multiple related facts around entities or relations. Using a unified training setup where models take a state and action and either predict symbolic effects or detect infeasibility, they train models of various scales and data budgets, then evaluate them on in-distribution and out-of-distribution test worlds, measuring effect prediction accuracy, feasibility detection, fact-level F1, and downstream greedy planning success.

Result: For model sizes around 0.5B–1.5B parameters and under distribution shift, the hyperedge serialization consistently outperforms other representations, yielding better fact-level F1, more reliable feasibility detection, and superior planning success. Larger models narrow the performance gap such that pairwise triples can match or slightly surpass hyperedges on in-distribution exact match metrics, but hyperedges maintain an advantage in out-of-distribution F1 and in balancing feasibility and effect prediction trade-offs. Overall, hyperedges provide the most robust and data-efficient performance for small-to-medium world models.

Conclusion: Organizing symbolic world state into higher-order, entity-centered hyperedges offers a strong inductive bias that improves the learning and robustness of textual world models, especially when model capacity is limited or when test environments differ from training. While larger models can compensate for weaker serializations, hyperedge-based representations provide the best overall trade-off between accuracy, feasibility detection, generalization, and downstream planning success in the studied settings.

Abstract: World models enable language-model agents to predict environment dynamics and plan before acting. In text environments, the model must learn symbolic action effects from serialized state descriptions, but the role of serialization structure remains underexplored. We present HyperWorld, a controlled study of state serialization for learned textual world models. We compare raw observations with three symbolic serializations of the same ground-truth state: independent sentences, pairwise triples, and entity-centered hyperedge units that group multiple related facts around entities and relations. All variants use the same training objective: given a state and an action, predict symbolic effects or judge the action infeasible. Across model scales, data budgets, and in-distribution and out-of-distribution test worlds, hyperedge serialization gives the clearest gains for 0.5B--1.5B models and under distribution shift. Larger models reduce the gap, and pairwise triples can match or slightly exceed hyperedges on in-distribution exact match, but hyperedges achieve the strongest out-of-distribution fact F1 and the best small-to-medium scale trade-off between feasibility detection and effect prediction. In downstream greedy planning, the hyperedge world model also attains the highest success rate among the tested representations. These results show that higher-order state organization is a simple but effective inductive bias for learned symbolic world models, especially when model capacity is limited or test environments differ from training.

</details>


### [129] [I-CARE: Analysis of interference-related phenomena in a controllable, diverse and representative unlearning setting for text-to-image models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00003)
*Leonardo Santiago Benitez Pereira,Marcos Escudero Viñolo,Luis Herranz Arribas*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes I-CARE, a standardized methodology to rigorously define, measure, and report interference—unintended forgetting of related concepts—in generative machine unlearning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current work on generative machine unlearning focuses mainly on how well models forget targeted concepts, while the side effect of damaging semantically related but supposedly retained concepts (interference) is poorly understood and evaluated in an ad-hoc, inconsistent way. This gap makes it hard to compare algorithms, draw scientific conclusions, or design unlearning methods that are safe and reliable in practice.

Method: The authors introduce I-CARE, a conceptual and experimental framework that (1) formally defines different unlearning tasks and settings for generative models, (2) specifies metrics to quantify both successful forgetting and unintended interference on related concepts, and (3) provides standardized templates for reporting results so that studies are comparable and reproducible. They implement this as an open-source software toolkit plus a web-based graphical interface, and run a feasibility study using existing state-of-the-art unlearning algorithms and common datasets.

Result: Using I-CARE with several leading unlearning algorithms and standard datasets, the authors show that their framework can reveal and analyze detailed patterns of interference across multiple unlearning settings. The experiments confirm that interference is non-trivial and that I-CARE’s metrics and reporting templates allow systematic comparison and interpretation of these effects.

Conclusion: I-CARE successfully elevates interference to a primary object of study in generative machine unlearning. By providing stable task definitions, metrics, and reporting standards—implemented in an accessible open-source toolkit and web UI—it enables rigorous, reproducible, and model-agnostic analysis of how unlearning methods affect both targeted and related concepts, supporting longer-term scientific progress beyond any single benchmark or algorithm.

Abstract: Machine unlearning studies the removal of knowledge from an AI model, making the system forget a concept it previously learned. Despite rapid progress in generative machine unlearning, the unintended degradation of semantically related concepts that should have been retained (henceforth, interference) remains poorly characterized and inconsistently evaluated. This paper introduces I-CARE, a methodology that formalizes interference as a first-class object of study in generative unlearning. Rather than proposing a new benchmark or unlearning algorithm, I-CARE provides formal definitions for tasks, metrics, and templates for reporting results, enabling the systematic and reproducible study of interference across unlearning settings. While our methodology is designed to remain valid as models and unlearning algorithms evolve, decoupling long-term scientific insight from transient empirical results, we present a feasibility demonstration with state-of-the-art algorithms and frequently used datasets. The results demonstrate that I-CARE enables meaningful analysis of interference patterns across multiple unlearning settings, establishing the practical applicability of the framework. The software implementation of the methodology is provided in an open-source framework, together with a web-based graphical interface that enables exploration of the outcomes of this study without requiring direct interaction with the codebase or specialized data analysis tools.

</details>


### [130] [Discrete-Time MDP Modeling for Multi-Item Capacitated Lot Sizing with Stochastic Demand Timing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00004)
*Léa Bayati,Mohamed Dahmoune,Melek Rodoplu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper tackles a multi-item capacitated lot-sizing problem with deterministic demand quantities but uncertain arrival times, modeling it as a DTMDP and solving it approximately with a genetic algorithm that delivers near-optimal solutions with substantial speedups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical lot-sizing models typically assume deterministic demand times; however, in many real settings, when demand arrives is uncertain within a known time window. This stochastic timing greatly complicates capacity allocation, backlog, and inventory decisions, and its true computational impact is not well understood. The paper aims to quantify this impact and to develop a practical solution method that remains effective when exact dynamic programming becomes intractable.

Method: The authors formulate the problem as a discrete-time Markov decision process at the demand level, explicitly defining states, actions, transition kernels, and one-period costs to capture capacity competition and allocation-dependent inventory. They then construct deterministic counterparts by replacing arrival distributions with the most likely arrival periods to isolate the effect of timing uncertainty on complexity. To handle the computational explosion in the stochastic model, they design a genetic algorithm that searches over feasible state-feedback policies; each policy is evaluated exactly using the DTMDP transition model. For instances too large for exact DP on their hardware, they fit an empirical regression on Bellman-solution times to extrapolate the exact time and thus estimate GA speedups.

Result: The comparison with deterministic counterparts shows that stochastic timing dramatically enlarges the DTMDP state and transition spaces, leading to higher solution times and memory usage. Across 330 benchmark instances, the GA achieves an average optimality gap of about 3.44% whenever exact stochastic solutions are computable. On a subset of 90 difficult instances, the GA stays below a 5% optimality gap while delivering an average optimization speedup factor of about 6.89 with a 95% confidence interval of ±1.41. For unsolved large instances, the Bellman-time regression allows extrapolation of likely exact-solution times and corresponding GA speedups.

Conclusion: Modeling demand-arrival times stochastically in capacitated lot-sizing substantially increases computational complexity compared with deterministic-timing approximations. Nevertheless, a carefully designed GA operating over state-feedback policies and evaluated via the exact DTMDP transitions can maintain small optimality gaps (mostly under 5%) while offering significant speedups over exact DP methods. The empirical Bellman-time regression provides a pragmatic way to quantify benefits even where exact solutions are computationally infeasible, making the approach suitable for large-scale, realistic planning problems with uncertain demand timing.

Abstract: This paper studies a finite-horizon multi-item capacitated lot-sizing problem in which demand quantities are deterministic, while demand-arrival periods are stochastic. Each demand occurs once within a known time window and must be satisfied no later than its deadline. The proposed model makes production and allocation decisions at the demand level, allowing it to represent capacity competition, demand-specific backlog, and allocation-dependent inventory dynamics. The stochastic problem is formulated as a discrete-time Markov decision process (DTMDP), including the state space, feasible actions, transition kernel, and one-period cost function. To isolate the computational effect of stochastic timing, each stochastic instance is first compared with a deterministic counterpart in which each arrival distribution is replaced by its most likely arrival period. This comparison shows that stochastic timing substantially increases the number of states, the number of transitions, solution time, and memory pressure. A genetic algorithm (GA) is then proposed for the stochastic-timing problem. The GA searches over feasible state-feedback policies and evaluates each policy exactly under the DTMDP transition model. Computational experiments on 330 benchmark instances show that the GA remains close to the exact stochastic solution whenever the latter is available, with an average optimality gap of about $3.44\%$. On the difficult benchmark instances, comprising 90 test cases, the GA remains below the $5\%$ optimality-gap threshold and achieves an average optimization speedup of $6.89 \pm 1.41$ at the $95\%$ confidence level. For instances that cannot be solved exactly on the available hardware, an empirical Bellman-time regression is used to estimate the missing exact resolution time and extrapolate the expected GA speedup.

</details>


### [131] [Incremental Risk Assessment of Progressive Elder Financial Scams via Instruction-Tuned Small Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00005)
*Parviz Ghafariasl,Weimin Fu,Xiaolong Guo,Shing I. Chang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a cumulative, turn-by-turn scam risk assessment framework for multi-turn conversations and shows that fine-tuned small language models can effectively and efficiently detect and track scam risk escalation over time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Older adults are increasingly targeted by financial scams conducted via multi-turn text and voice conversations, where risk emerges gradually, making early and continuous detection challenging, especially under resource constraints (e.g., on-device or mobile settings). Existing approaches often focus on single messages or require large models, limiting practical deployment for real-time protection.

Method: The authors design a cumulative turn-based risk assessment framework that incrementally aggregates conversation turns and re-estimates risk after each turn. They construct a multi-turn dialogue dataset spanning investment, charity, and tech support scams, where each dialogue (2–8 turns) is annotated at every cumulative stage with: (1) qualitative risk level, (2) continuous risk score, (3) explanatory rationale, and (4) safety recommendation. Within a unified training setup, they fine-tune four small language models (Phi-4, LLaMA-3.2, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3) for this incremental risk estimation task and evaluate their performance on capturing turn-aware fraud patterns.

Result: Fine-tuned small language models successfully learn fraud-related linguistic cues and cross-turn escalation patterns, providing accurate, turn-aware risk estimations while remaining compact enough for deployment in mobile and resource-constrained contexts. Among the tested models, Phi-4 and LLaMA-3.2 exhibit the best trade-off between parameter size and performance, achieving relatively stronger risk estimation compared to their scales.

Conclusion: A structured cumulative modeling approach enables dynamic, incremental scam risk assessment across evolving multi-turn conversations and is practical for deployment with small language models. Compact models like Phi-4 and LLaMA-3.2 are particularly promising for privacy-aware, on-device fraud protection, suggesting that effective scam monitoring does not require large, server-side models if the task and data are properly structured.

Abstract: Financial scams targeting older adults increasingly occur through text and voice channels such as email, SMS, and phone calls, unfolding over multiple conversational turns that begin with impersonation or casual contact, escalate through trust building and urgency, and culminate in requests for sensitive information or financial transfers. Because risk signals emerge incrementally across turns, effective detection requires models that continuously update risk estimates under resource-constrained deployment settings. We propose a cumulative turn-based risk assessment framework that incrementally aggregates conversational turns and re-estimates risk at each step, enabling dynamic scam monitoring across progressively evolving conversations. A multi-turn dialogue dataset is constructed to cover investment, charity, and tech support scam scenarios, with each dialogue containing two to eight turns and annotated at every cumulative stage with a qualitative risk level, a continuous risk score, an explanatory rationale, and a safety recommendation. Four small language models (Phi-4, LLaMA-3.2, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3) are fine-tuned and evaluated under a unified training framework. Fine-tuned small models capture fraud-related linguistic cues and cross-turn escalation patterns while maintaining compact architectures suitable for mobile and resource-constrained deployment settings. Among the evaluated models, Phi-4 and LLaMA-3.2 achieve stronger turn-aware risk estimation performance relative to their parameter scale. These results suggest that structured cumulative modeling can support incremental scam risk assessment in deployment-oriented settings while highlighting the potential of compact language models for privacy-aware and on-device fraud protection.

</details>


### [132] [Long-Horizon State Tracking in LLMs: Executing MD5 through a Deep Sequence of Dependent Tool Calls](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00012)
*Dheeraj Mohandas Pai,Lu Xian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates whether LLMs can reliably maintain and transform exact internal state over many dependent steps by having them compute an MD5 hash via long tool-call sequences, isolating state-tracking from other factors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon, tool-using LLM evaluations are rare and noisy because cascading errors mix together multiple difficulties: state tracking, instruction following, and shortcutting or hallucinating answers. It is not well understood whether LLMs can accurately carry exact intermediate computational state across many steps. The authors want a clean, controlled benchmark that isolates the pure bookkeeping aspect of long-horizon reasoning without confounds.

Method: They design a benchmark where the LLM must compute an MD5 hash step by step, implementing MD5 directly from RFC 1321. The process requires 196 dependent tool calls across 64 rounds, with the model responsible for faithfully carrying four 32-bit words (a, b, c, d) in its own context. They align each intermediate call to the ground-truth MD5 trace and check the final digest bitwise. They also explore a stronger setting where each primitive tool is itself an LLM, forming a driver-worker setup without any exact-arithmetic oracle. They vary prompting and whether the model’s intermediate reasoning is preserved, and use voting over multiple worker runs to mitigate arithmetic errors.

Result: A mixture-of-experts model, gpt-oss-120b (≈5.5B active parameters per token), at temperature 0 with a short fixed prompt is able to correctly maintain the full MD5 state across all 196 calls and returns the correct final digest in a majority of runs. In the driver-worker configuration, success depends on preserving the model's prior reasoning context each turn and using voting over a 'thinking-enabled' worker to filter out modular arithmetic mistakes. They can attribute residual failures to specific sources such as arithmetic slips or serving issues rather than state-tracking itself.

Conclusion: The study shows that at least some LLMs can reliably carry exact internal state across long sequences of dependent operations when properly prompted, and that many observed failures in long-horizon tasks stem more from arithmetic and serving errors than from state bookkeeping per se. The benchmark provides a clean way to disentangle state-carrying ability from other confounds, and highlights the importance of retaining intermediate reasoning and using ensemble/voting strategies for robust long-run tool use.

Abstract: Long-horizon tasks remain uncommon in large language model (LLM) evaluation, and for a reason: when each step depends on the last, per-step accuracy that looks excellent in isolation decays catastrophically, as errors cascade and the end-to-end failure probability grows sharply with length. Existing agentic benchmarks report end-to-end success but confound this state-tracking difficulty with instruction interpretation, give no control group that isolates it, and are vulnerable to shortcuts such as a hallucinated final answer, so they cannot say why a long run fails. Whether an LLM can carry exact intermediate state across many tool calls at all is itself not well established. We test this cleanly by having the model compute a cryptographic hash, MD5, step by step: a sequence of $196$ dependent tool calls over $64$ rounds while it carries four $32$-bit words $(a,b,c,d)$ in its own context from one call to the next. Interpretation is trivial and, because we implement MD5 from scratch (RFC~1321), we align every call to the ground-truth trace and check the digest to the bit, so any failure is pure bookkeeping. gpt-oss-120b, a mixture-of-experts model with only $\sim$5.5B active parameters per token, at temperature $0$ with a short fixed prompt, carries the full state across all $196$ calls and returns the correct digest on a majority of completed runs. In the strongest setting we replace every primitive tool with a second LLM, so a driver and a worker compute the whole hash from scratch with no exact-arithmetic oracle in the loop. Two ingredients decide success and neither changes the weights: keeping the model's own reasoning in its context each turn, and voting over a thinking-enabled worker to remove its modular-arithmetic slips. We localize the residual failures by origin, separating state-carrying from arithmetic and from serving.

</details>


### [133] [OpenAgentFlow: Enabling System-Wide Safety Boundaries for Heterogeneous AI Agent Fleets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00015)
*Dongsheng Chen,Xiangyu Zhao,Xin Yao,Xuetao Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces OpenAgentFlow, an architecture to enforce safety for heterogeneous LLM-powered agents by governing their actions at the point they are about to modify shared system state.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM-based AI agents become multi-agent, tool-using, and tightly integrated with user or enterprise environments, safety risks arise not only from single prompts or tools but from end-to-end action sequences across GUI, APIs, and internal planners. Existing safeguards are fragmented, focused on local checks, and make it hard to see or control how actions from different components interact, evolve policies, or conduct audits. There is a need for a unified, system-level mechanism that governs all agent actions before they change shared state.

Method: The authors propose OpenAgentFlow, which separates the system into a control plane and an action plane. It converts all pending actions—GUI actions, API calls, tool calls, and LLM-generated invocations—into a standardized AgentEvent stream. Each AgentEvent is routed through a central, pre-execution Policy Enforcement Point in the control plane, which uses shared session state, provenance, audit logs, and updatable policies to decide whether to allow, modify, or block actions. Policies can be updated without changing the underlying agents, prompts, or tools. The framework is instantiated on Android to evaluate its behavior in realistic mobile environments.

Result: On a 300-case action-event benchmark, OpenAgentFlow achieves 94.0% decision accuracy and blocks 95.3% of attacks. In a 30-case dynamic-policy evaluation, after installing new rules, it behaves as expected in 27 cases, demonstrating support for policy evolution. On a 100-case Android emulator suite, 98 cases are fully traced and yield 90.8% raw accuracy and a 92.9% trace-adjusted pass rate across GUI, API, and LLM-planned scenarios, indicating robust performance in heterogeneous settings.

Conclusion: OpenAgentFlow effectively establishes a shared, system-level enforcement boundary at the action-commit stage for heterogeneous AI agent ecosystems. By normalizing diverse actions into a governable event stream and centralizing policy enforcement and auditing, it improves safety, supports dynamic policy updates, and works across multiple interaction modalities without requiring changes to individual agents or models.

Abstract: AI agents powered by large language models are evolving from isolated assistants into heterogeneous systems in which multiple agents, planners, controllers, and execution backends operate over the same user or enterprise environment. In such settings, safety becomes a system-level action-governance problem: deciding whether concrete agent-generated actions should be committed before they modify shared state. Existing safeguards cover prompts, tool calls, GUI actions, and agent-local behavior, but often leave enforcement fragmented, obscure risks that emerge across multi-step action flows, and provide limited support for auditability and policy evolution.
  We present OpenAgentFlow, a control-plane/action-plane architecture that enforces safety at the action-commit boundary. It normalizes pending GUI actions, API calls, tool calls, and LLM-generated invocations into a unified AgentEvent stream, routes each event through a shared pre-execution Policy Enforcement Point, and maintains provenance, session state, audit records, and updatable policies in the control plane. This creates a shared governable action stream and allows new rules to take effect without modifying agents, prompts, models, or execution paths.
  We instantiate OpenAgentFlow on Android. On a 300-case action-event benchmark, it achieves 94.0% accuracy and a 95.3% attack block rate. On a 30-case dynamic-policy suite, it matches expected behavior in 27 cases after new rules are installed. Across 98 traced cases from a 100-case Android emulator suite, it achieves 90.8% raw accuracy and a 92.9% trace-adjusted pass rate across GUI, API, and LLM-planned cases. These results show that OpenAgentFlow provides a practical shared enforcement boundary for heterogeneous AI agent fleets.

</details>


### [134] [SCAFFOLD: A Large-Scale Structured Dataset of Computer Science Research Figures with Diagram QA and Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Traces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00018)
*Ranjit Raut,Aarav Subedi,Sagun Rai,Sudan Jha*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce SCAFFOLD, a large dataset of computer science diagrams paired with questions, answers, and reasoning traces to train vision-language models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Computer science papers use complex diagrams that encode rich information, but there is no public dataset that systematically pairs such diagrams with textual supervision (captions, context, QA, reasoning) needed to train models to understand them.

Method: They automatically build a dataset from arXiv CS papers using layout detection and PDF parsing to extract figure images, captions, and surrounding context, then use an AI-assisted procedure to generate diagram-related questions, answers, and chain-of-thought reasoning for each figure, producing multiple dataset scales (157K, 37K, 12K pairs).

Result: They construct three dataset variants: SCAFFOLD-157K (3,058 papers, 29,887 figures, 157,387 (image, text) pairs), SCAFFOLD-37K (36,797 pairs), and SCAFFOLD-12K (12,000 pairs), and run baseline experiments using SCAFFOLD-12K on the Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct model.

Conclusion: SCAFFOLD provides a new large-scale structured resource for training and evaluating vision-language models on computer science diagrams, and initial experiments demonstrate its usability as a benchmark and training corpus.

Abstract: Computer science papers rely heavily on diagrams: architecture drawings, system flowcharts, and pipeline schematics that often carry more information than the text around them. There is currently no public dataset that pairs this specific kind of figure with captions, context, questions, answers, and step-by-step reasoning, which is exactly what is needed to train a vision-language model to understand them. We present \textbf{SCAFFOLD}\footnote{https://github.com/theranjitraut/scaffold}, a large-scale structured dataset of computer science research figures with diagram QA and Chain-of-Thought reasoning traces. This dataset consists of (image, caption, context, question-answer, chain-of-thought) tuples from arXiv computer science papers prepared using layout detection and PDF parsing, with an AI-assisted question-generation step. The resulting large-sized SCAFFOLD-157K dataset spans 3,058 papers with 29,887 figures (157,387 pairs), a medium-sized SCAFFOLD-37K dataset (36,797 pairs), and a small-sized SCAFFOLD-12K dataset (12,000 pairs). We used SCAFFOLD-12K for baseline experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct.

</details>


### [135] [UI-Venus-2 Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00028)
*Venus Team,Zhuohan Cai,Haoxing Chen,Jiaxuan Chen,Weizhi Chen,Changlong Gao,Zhangxuan Gu,Yuan Guo,Yusong Hu,Jianrong Jiang,Jianguo Li,Runze Li,Jinzhen Lin,Zhenyu Ma,Changhua Meng,Han Peng,Xinyu Qiu,Shuheng Shen,Zhongyi Shui,Weiqiang Wang,Ming Wen,Zhuoer Xu,Hang Yan,Kaiwen Yang,Ruilin Yao,Nanjun Yu,Zhengwen Zeng,Lianrui Zhang,Yunzhu Zhang,Zhe Zhao,Beitong Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: UI-Venus-2 is a general-purpose multimodal GUI agent for mobile, web, and desktop that improves environment coverage, task generation, and reward verification to enable reliable real-world automation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal GUI agents work well on benchmarks but struggle in real-world deployment because they operate in limited environments, rely on brittle or shallow task construction, and lack trustworthy reward verification for training and evaluation. There is a need for a unified, scalable, and verifiable agent framework that can robustly handle diverse platforms and tasks while being safe enough for consequential actions.

Method: The authors build UI-Venus-2, a unified closed-loop reasoning–action framework that can operate on mobile, web, and desktop GUIs. They scale in three dimensions: (1) Environments: they extend support to over 170 multilingual mobile apps and to native desktop OSes. (2) Tasks: they develop a deep-research pipeline to generate function-grounded instructions that are better aligned with app capabilities. (3) Verification: they introduce trace-level and sample-level evaluators that use visual keypoints and multi-model voting to provide reliable RL training signals. They also embed safety-aware mechanisms to constrain or control high-impact actions.

Result: UI-Venus-2 functions as a capable and efficient foundation GUI agent that can operate across multiple platforms and languages, with improved task coverage and more dependable automatic verification, making it suitable for reinforcement learning-based training and evaluation. Safety mechanisms are successfully integrated to control consequential actions, and the system is released as open source.

Conclusion: UI-Venus-2 advances GUI agents toward practical real-world deployment by offering a unified, scalable, and verifiable foundation model for cross-platform GUI automation. By jointly scaling environments, tasks, and verification, and adding safety-aware controls, it enables more generalizable, reliable, and self-reflective agents that can serve as a basis for future research and applications.

Abstract: Multimodal GUI agents have emerged as a promising paradigm for digital task automation, yet transitioning from benchmark-oriented models to dependable real-world applications remains challenging due to limited environment coverage, brittle task construction, and unreliable reward verification. In this work, we present UI-Venus-2, a general-purpose foundation GUI agent designed to operate across mobile, web, and desktop environments through a unified closed-loop reasoning-action framework. To bridge the gap toward practical deployment, we jointly scale three critical dimensions: (1) Environments, expanding coverage to more than 170 multilingual mobile apps and native desktop operating systems; (2) Tasks, employing a deep-research pipeline for function-grounded instruction generation; and (3) Verification, adopting trace-level and sample-level evaluators with visual keypoints and multi-model voting to ensure reliable RL signals for training. Furthermore, we integrate safety-aware mechanisms to ensure controlled execution of consequential actions. By offering a capable, efficient, and open-source foundation, UI-Venus-2 advances the field toward more generalizable, verifiable, and self-reflective agents for real-world applications.

</details>


### [136] [EULER: Exploring Underused Links with Evidence-Checked Return for Multi-Agent Mathematical Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00032)
*Ren Zhenzhuo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EULER is a multi-agent system that searches for proofs by building and validating cross-domain “bridges” between mathematical communities, achieving several new proofs, refutations, and partial results on fresh combinatorics conjectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mathematical problems often reside in specific communities that use different objects, invariants, and techniques. Transferring a problem between these communities (e.g., from combinatorics to another domain) can be powerful but is rarely done because it is conceptually and technically expensive. The authors aim to automate this transfer process so that cross-domain methods can be systematically exploited to solve conjectures that are difficult within a single domain.

Method: They design EULER, a multi-agent system whose core search unit is a “bridge” that maps a conjecture from a source domain to another domain and then back. For a fixed conjecture, EULER launches multiple search routes: direct (within the same domain), adjacent-domain, and distant-domain. A bridge is allowed to continue consuming computational budget only if (1) it introduces at least one operation not executable in the source representation (executable operation gain), and (2) any evidence found in the target domain can be converted back into a statement about the original conjecture via a formally checked implication (valid return). To avoid wasting search, six ordered “stress tests” are applied to proposed bridges to reject invalid or low-quality ones before deeper search. They then run EULER on a large benchmark of recent, uncontaminated conjectures derived from top-tier combinatorics literature and measure full proofs, refutations, and partial progress. They also perform ablation studies to measure the contribution of bridge stress tests and interaction between bridge material and target-native operations, and they analyze whether domain distance predicts success.

Result: On 120 recent conjectures from papers by authors who had recently published in the Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A, EULER obtained 10 full proofs, 3 refutations, and 45 scoped partial results. Freezing the conjectures and screening for contamination ensured the evaluation was on genuinely open or recent problems. In ablation, the bridge-specific stress tests significantly reduced incorrect conclusions from 9 to 3, showing they are crucial for reliability. Furthermore, when bridge material was combined with target-native operations, the system solved on average 4.2 more tasks than either the bridge material or the target-native operations alone, demonstrating a positive interaction between cross-domain translation and native reasoning tools. Contrary to a naive expectation, the distance between domains (e.g., how “far” the target domain is from the original) did not reliably predict success. Instead, the key predictors were whether the bridge granted new executable operations and whether the results could be validly translated back to the source conjecture.

Conclusion: EULER demonstrates that organizing automated reasoning around cross-domain bridges can produce nontrivial mathematical results, including complete proofs and refutations, on recent research-level conjectures. The work shows that properly validated bridges, equipped with stress tests and checked implications, can safely and effectively expand the operational toolkit available to an automated theorem prover. The success of EULER depends less on naive notions of domain distance and more on whether bridges yield genuine operation gains and trustworthy returns. This suggests that future automated mathematics systems should explicitly structure search around high-value, verifiable cross-domain transfers rather than remaining within a single representation or relying solely on loosely guided heuristic transfers.

Abstract: Mathematical communities work with different objects, invariants, and tools, so transferring a problem across them is expensive and often skipped. We present EULER, a multi-agent system that takes such a transfer--a bridge--as its unit of search. Around a fixed conjecture, EULER runs direct, adjacent-domain, and distant-domain routes in competition; a bridge keeps its budget only if it supplies an operation the source representation cannot execute and its target-side evidence returns to the original statement along a checked implication. Six ordered stress tests reject invalid bridges before expensive search begins.
  We evaluate EULER on 120 recent conjectures. The conjectures were frozen before search and screened for contamination, and are drawn from public papers by authors who had recently published in the Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A, a leading journal in combinatorics. EULER produced 10 proofs and 3 refutations, plus 45 scoped partial results. Two mechanisms held up under ablation: bridge-specific stress tests cut incorrect conclusions from 9 to 3, and bridge material combined with a target-native operation yielded a positive interaction of +4.2 resolved tasks that neither factor produced alone. Domain distance did not reliably predict success; executable operation gain and valid return did.

</details>


### [137] [When Prediction Error Is Not Enough: Evaluating Nuisance-Function Prediction for Causal Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00071)
*Cong Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how well prediction error of nuisance-function models reflects performance of causal effect estimators in a partially linear model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In causal inference, practitioners often select or tune nuisance-function estimators (for propensity scores and outcome regressions) using prediction error. However, it is unclear how well low prediction error translates into good causal effect estimation—especially across different performance metrics such as bias, RMSE, and confidence interval coverage. The authors aim to clarify this relationship.

Method: Using Monte Carlo simulations under a partially linear model, the authors compare four approaches for estimating nuisance functions: OLS, GAMs, XGBoost, and Double Machine Learning with XGBoost (DML-XGBoost). They assess each method by (1) nuisance-function prediction error, (2) bias and RMSE of the causal effect estimator, (3) 95% confidence interval coverage, and (4) a proposed joint-error metric: the absolute cross-product of estimation errors from exposure and outcome nuisance functions.

Result: XGBoost achieves the lowest RMSE among non-oracle methods, indicating strong point estimation performance, while DML-XGBoost generally yields better 95% confidence interval coverage, suggesting superior uncertainty quantification. Prediction error of nuisance models does not reliably correspond to causal bias across methods or scenarios, and the method with the best RMSE does not necessarily provide the best interval coverage. The joint-error measure shows only a weak relationship with causal bias and proves unhelpful as a standalone indicator of causal performance.

Conclusion: Prediction error remains a useful diagnostic for nuisance-function estimation quality but should not be interpreted as a direct proxy for the quality of the resulting causal effect estimates. Different causal performance metrics (bias, RMSE, coverage) can favor different methods, so practitioners should evaluate causal estimators using metrics directly tied to the causal parameter rather than relying solely on prediction error or joint-error measures.

Abstract: Prediction error is widely used to evaluate nuisance-function estimators in causal inference, but its relationship with causal estimator performance may differ across performance measures. We studied this question in a partially linear model using Monte Carlo simulations. We compared ordinary least squares (OLS), generalized additive models (GAMs), XGBoost, and Double Machine Learning with XGBoost (DML-XGBoost), evaluating nuisance-function prediction error, bias, RMSE, and 95\% confidence interval coverage. We also examined a simple joint-error measure based on the absolute cross-product of estimation errors from the exposure and outcome nuisance functions. Across the simulated settings, XGBoost had the lowest RMSE among the non-oracle methods, while DML-XGBoost generally provided better confidence interval coverage. Prediction error did not consistently track causal bias across methods and settings, and the method with the best point-estimation performance did not necessarily have the best confidence interval coverage. The joint-error measure was only weakly associated with causal bias and did not provide a useful standalone measure of causal performance. These results suggest that prediction error is useful for assessing nuisance-function estimation, but it should not be treated as a direct measure of the quality of the resulting causal estimator.

</details>


### [138] [MiNER: Fine-Tuned Biomedical Natural Language Processing for Malaria Disease Entity Recognition in Clinical Texts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00073)
*V. S. Anoop,Devika N*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They fine-tune the BioBERT biomedical language model on a malaria-specific, human-annotated corpus to improve automatic extraction of biomedical entities and relations from malaria literature, achieving better performance than traditional methods and releasing the dataset for the community.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Malaria research generates a large and growing volume of scientific articles, making it difficult and time-consuming for researchers to manually extract key biomedical information (e.g., entities, relations) needed to understand mechanisms, epidemiology, and therapies. Existing generic NLP tools are not optimized for malaria-specific biomedical language, limiting the efficiency and accuracy of literature mining. The paper aims to address this gap by creating a specialized, high-performing information extraction system for malaria literature.

Method: 1) Collect a large corpus of scientific articles specifically about malaria. 2) Preprocess the texts (cleaning, tokenization, etc.). 3) Manually annotate the corpus with clinically relevant entities and relations (biomedical named entities of interest for malaria). 4) Use BioBERT, a pre-trained biomedical language model, as the base encoder to obtain context-aware text representations. 5) Fine-tune BioBERT on the malaria corpus using supervised learning with the domain-specific annotations for named entity and relation extraction. 6) Compare the fine-tuned model’s performance against alternative text encoders and conventional machine learning algorithms using standard metrics (precision, recall, accuracy). 7) Release the annotated dataset publicly.

Result: The fine-tuned BioBERT model trained on the malaria-specific annotated corpus significantly outperforms other encoding strategies and machine learning baselines in extracting biomedical named entities and relations from malaria literature, with higher precision, recall, and accuracy. Additionally, the authors provide a new, publicly available human-labeled dataset tailored to malaria information extraction tasks.

Conclusion: Domain-specific fine-tuning of a strong biomedical language model (BioBERT) on a carefully annotated malaria literature corpus markedly improves automatic biomedical information extraction compared with traditional methods. This validates the effectiveness of leveraging pre-trained language models and task-specific annotations for disease-focused literature mining, and the released dataset is intended to support further research and development of advanced malaria information extraction tools in health informatics.

Abstract: Malaria remains a significant global health burden, necessitating continuous research efforts to understand its complex molecular mechanisms, epidemiology, and potential therapeutic interventions. Extracting essential biomedical information from the vast and constantly growing malaria literature is a challenging task that demands innovative approaches. Recently, pre-trained language models have revolutionized natural language processing tasks, demonstrating remarkable capabilities in various domains. This paper proposes a fine-tuned pre-trained biomedical language model for biomedical information extraction from scientific literature on malaria disease. The proposed methodology selects and preprocesses a large corpus of scientific articles on malaria, and then annotates them with entities of clinical significance. It then leverages BioBERT, a state-of-the-art pre-trained language model, to encode the textual data into context-aware representations. We fine-tune the model using domain-specific annotations and supervised learning to enhance its ability to extract relevant biomedical named entities. Extensive experiments and comparisons with different encoding and machine learning algorithms show that the proposed approach significantly outperforms them in precision, recall, and accuracy. We also publish our human-labeled dataset for entity and relation extraction to enable other health informatics researchers to train advanced models for malaria information extraction.

</details>


### [139] [AI Morbidity and Mortality: A Framework for Clinical AI Failure Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00076)
*Paulius Mui,Dean F. Sittig,Steve Labkoff,Sanjay Basu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces AI Morbidity and Mortality (AI M&M), a structured, blame-free framework to analyze and learn from individual clinical AI failures in real-world workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As clinical AI tools are increasingly deployed in real care settings, existing safety mechanisms—like aggregate model monitoring and traditional patient safety reporting—cannot adequately reconstruct or explain how specific AI-related errors and near-misses arise from complex interactions between AI systems, clinicians, workflows, and institutional controls. There is a need for a systematic, case-based way to investigate, classify, and learn from individual AI-in-workflow failures.

Method: The authors design and describe AI Morbidity and Mortality (AI M&M), a structured process for case-based review of clinical AI failures. The framework includes standardized case intake, preservation of evidence, detailed investigator-level reconstruction of events, attribution of where and how the AI tool was in the loop, and tracking of corrective actions over time. Events are classified along four linked dimensions—Trigger, Mechanism, Clinical Pathway, and Corrective Action—to disentangle what exposed a vulnerability, how risk was produced, the consequence for care, and the remediation chosen. The framework is demonstrated on five illustrative outpatient medication and clinical decision-support cases, and inter-rater agreement is assessed between two clinician reviewers who independently applied all four axes.

Result: Application of the AI M&M framework to five outpatient AI-related cases showed that two independent clinician reviewers could consistently use the four-axis classification, reaching agreement on all 20 axis-level classifications. This suggests that the taxonomy and process are understandable and reproducible. The case demonstrations show how the framework can surface distinct types of triggers, mechanisms of risk, clinical impacts, and corresponding corrective actions for AI-in-workflow failures.

Conclusion: AI M&M provides a practical, structured, and blame-free approach to analyzing individual clinical AI failures, complementing existing mechanisms like model monitoring, patient safety reporting, and regulatory oversight. By breaking down events into Trigger, Mechanism, Clinical Pathway, and Corrective Action, it supports institutional learning and targeted remediation from AI-related incidents. Further prospective evaluation in diverse institutions, AI systems, and clinical contexts is required to validate and refine the framework and to understand its impact on safety and AI governance.

Abstract: Clinical artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in real-world care, yet existing safety mechanisms are poorly suited to reconstructing and learning from individual AI-related errors and near-misses. Aggregate model monitoring can identify performance changes, and traditional patient safety reporting can capture adverse events, but neither is designed to explain how risk emerges across the interaction among AI systems, clinicians, workflows, and institutional controls. We propose AI Morbidity and Mortality (AI M&M), a structured, blameless framework for case-based review of clinical AI failures. The framework combines standardized case intake, evidence preservation and investigator-level reconstruction, tool-in-loop attribution, and corrective-action tracking. Each event is classified across four linked dimensions: Trigger - Mechanism - Clinical Pathway - Corrective Action, separating the condition that exposed a vulnerability from the process that produced risk, its consequence for care, and the remediation assigned. We demonstrate the framework using five illustrative outpatient medication and clinical decision-support cases; two clinician reviewers independently applied all four classification axes and reached agreement across all 20 axis-level classifications. AI M&M is intended to complement, rather than replace, model monitoring, patient safety reporting, and regulatory oversight by converting individual AI-in-workflow failures into actionable institutional learning. Prospective evaluation across institutions, AI systems, and clinical settings is needed.

</details>


### [140] [Different representation learning objectives recover distinct latent structures from the same psychometric data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00100)
*Cong Cao,Tassos C. Kyriakides,Pambos Vrasidas*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper compares different representation learning objectives on preschool psychometric questionnaires to see if they capture the same latent structure, finding a trade-off between teacher-child matching and preservation of behavioral phenotypes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Psychometric questionnaires produce detailed item-level data, but it is unclear whether various modern representation learning methods (e.g., contrastive, multitask) recover the same underlying behavioral/latent structure or emphasize different aspects such as person-to-person correspondence versus behavioral organization.

Method: Using item-level responses from 757 teacher-child pairs in a preschool trial (Cyprus ProW), the authors: (1) derived behavioral structure via PCA and clustering on SDQ, ASBI, and CBRS items to define four behavioral phenotypes; (2) trained representation models with different objectives (PCA-based, contrastive for teacher-child retrieval, and a multitask objective combining contrastive alignment and behavioral prediction); and (3) compared these representations in terms of teacher-child retrieval accuracy (Top-1, Top-10) and how well they preserved the previously defined behavioral phenotype structure.

Result: Contrastive learning dramatically improved teacher-child retrieval (Top-1 from 0.13% to 7.27%, Top-10 from 1.98% to 56.14%) over PCA-based representations but weakened the preservation of the four behavioral phenotypes. Adding a multitask objective that jointly optimized alignment and behavioral prediction improved the maintenance of behavioral organization compared to pure contrastive learning, but at the cost of reduced retrieval performance compared to the pure contrastive objective.

Conclusion: Different representation learning objectives recover different latent structures from the same psychometric data: objectives that maximize teacher-child correspondence (contrastive) do not best preserve behavioral phenotypes, and multitask approaches partially balance the two at a performance cost. Thus, linked psychometric data contain multiple latent organizations, and the structure revealed depends strongly on the learning objective chosen.

Abstract: Psychometric questionnaires contain rich item-level information, yet it remains unclear whether different representation learning objectives recover the same latent organization. We investigated this question using 757 matched teacher-child pairs from the baseline assessment of the Cyprus ProW preschool trial.
