Behavioral structure was characterized from child SDQ, ASBI, and CBRS item responses using principal component analysis and clustering, yielding four behavioral phenotypes. A contrastive objective substantially improved teacher-child retrieval relative to PCA-based representations, increasing Top-1 accuracy from 0.13% to 7.27% and Top-10 accuracy from 1.98% to 56.14%. However, contrastive representations preserved behavioral phenotype structure less effectively than PCA-based representations. A multi-task objective jointly optimizing alignment and behavioral prediction partially restored behavioral organization but reduced retrieval performance. These findings indicate that teacher-child correspondence and behavioral phenotypes represent distinct forms of latent organization and demonstrate that the latent structure recovered from linked psychometric data depends on the representation learning objective.

</details>


### [141] [Deploying and Evaluating a Smart-Agriculture Agentic Engine for Full-Season Soybean Farm Operations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00106)
*Ao Qu,Panagiotis Michelakis,Linyuan Han,Yiannis Hadjiyianni,Kun Ouyang,Konstantinos Siskos,Feng Li,Ran Meng,Jingchi Jiang,Dimitrios Stamoulis,Jie Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduce FAIRY, a full-stack smart-agriculture agent system for soybean farming, evaluated across full-season, spatiotemporal workflows on a real research farm.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a need for a practical, integrated, and rigorous framework to deploy and evaluate AI agent systems in real-world agriculture, capturing full-season, spatially distributed operations and their impact on crop yield and resource use.

Method: Develop FAIRY, an event-driven, full-stack agentic system that integrates heterogeneous agricultural data sources and machinery; model all operations and observations as events in a shared farm process engine; implement a layered agentic stack (skills, multi-agent controllers, orchestration, edge and frontier models, logging, profiling); and design an evaluation suite running nine state-of-the-art controllers on 100 full-season soybean scenarios in a 64-ridge field.

Result: FAIRY successfully integrates diverse hardware, sensor, and data infrastructures into an event-driven farm process engine and supports execution of nine different agent controllers over 100 realistic soybean production scenarios, preserving spatial-temporal decision coupling. The authors obtain quantitative measures of agentic success, spatiotemporal correctness, token cost, and edge-device runtime for each controller.

Conclusion: An event-centric, full-stack agentic architecture like FAIRY is feasible for real-world smart agriculture, enabling rigorous, operationally grounded evaluation of AI controllers over full crop seasons and complex spatiotemporal workflows. FAIRY provides a benchmark and reference design for future agronomic agent systems and highlights trade-offs between performance, cost, and deployment constraints.

Abstract: This paper presents FAIRY, a full-stack smart-agriculture agent system developed for and deployed to an operating soybean research farm at Harbin Institute of Technology's smart-agriculture site. We develop FAIRY to execute and evaluate agentic agronomic operations on full-season spatiotemporal workflows that span ridge preparation, planting, irrigation, fertilization, pest and disease treatment, harvest, grain handling, drying, and storage. FAIRY integrates APIs and infrastructure across production-grade machinery, fixed soil and canopy sensors, multispectral and thermal drones, satellite vegetation products, a weather station, calibrated crop-process models, agronomic records, and multi-season yield histories. The system is built around the novel "everything is an event" execution paradigm, which represents spatiotemporal world evolution, remote sensing and UAV observations, sensor readings, crop-growth transitions, machinery actions, and management interventions as state-changing events in a shared farm process engine. On top of this event-driven world model, FAIRY implements a complete agentic stack: a knowledge library of atomic agronomic skills; multi-agent controller and orchestration backends; frontier- and edge-model execution; full-path trace logging; and deployment profiling on local nodes. We use FAIRY to evaluate nine state-of-the-art agent controllers across one hundred full-season soybean scenarios that preserve the operational coupling between spatial observations in a 64-ridge field, temporal decision sequences, agronomic constraints, delayed effects, and final yield. We develop an evaluation suite that combines agentic success, full-path spatiotemporal correctness, token cost, and edge-device runtime.

</details>


### [142] [Recursive Criticality of AI Self-Improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00137)
*Mikhail Burtsev*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper models when AI used in AI R&D leads to self-amplifying capability growth, defined by a recursive reproduction number R_AI that compares feedback strength to increasing research difficulty.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI systems increasingly accelerate their own R&D, it becomes crucial to understand under what conditions this feedback causes compounding, potentially runaway, growth versus stabilizing or slowing progress. Policymakers and researchers need a principled way to distinguish temporary rapid progress from structurally self-amplifying dynamics.

Method: The authors build a mathematical / conceptual model of AI capability growth as a function of baseline research productivity, recursive feedback from AI systems used in R&D, and the increasing difficulty of further progress. They define and derive a recursive reproduction number R_AI, analogous to an epidemic reproduction number, to characterize whether improvements amplify or decay across development cycles. They then analyze extensions to multiple research actors and shared improvements.

Result: They show that when R_AI>1, AI improvements compound across development cycles (a self-amplifying regime), while R_AI<1 leads to damped improvements. The transition to self-amplification depends on feedback-loop structure rather than specific capability levels. Baseline research productivity can speed progress without changing whether the regime is self-amplifying, and longer development cycles constrain amplification. Growing research difficulty can terminate self-amplification. In multi-actor settings, shared improvements can make the whole ecosystem self-amplifying even if each individual actor is not.

Conclusion: The framework provides a way to operationalize and measure when AI R&D enters a self-amplifying regime, via parameters like feedback strength, propagation efficiency of improvements, cycle duration, and research difficulty. This helps distinguish recursive amplification from other forms of fast progress, and highlights that self-amplification can begin before visible acceleration and can end as research becomes harder.

Abstract: AI is increasingly used in the R\&D process that produces future AI systems. We study the conditions under which this feedback becomes self-amplifying. Our model describes how the rate of AI capability growth depends on baseline research productivity, recursive feedback, and the increasing difficulty of research progress. We derive a recursive reproduction number, $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{AI}}$, that determines whether improvements are amplified or damped across development cycles. This quantity compares the strength of feedback with the rate at which further progress becomes more difficult. When $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{AI}}>1$, the effects of improvements compound across development cycles, placing the system in a self-amplifying regime. When $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{AI}}<1$, their effects weaken across cycles. The transition depends on the structure of the AI R\&D feedback loop and need not occur at any particular level of model capability. A system can therefore enter a self-amplifying regime before acceleration becomes visible, while rapid progress can also occur without self-amplification. Higher baseline research productivity can accelerate progress without changing whether the system is self-amplifying, but the duration of the development cycle becomes a limiting timescale for amplification. Increasing research difficulty can end a period of self-amplification. Extending the model to multiple research actors shows that improvements shared across organizations can make the overall research ecosystem self-amplifying even when no individual actor is. The framework identifies measurable properties of AI R\&D systems that can help distinguish recursive amplification from rapid progress driven by other sources, including the strength of recursive feedback, how effectively improvements propagate into successor systems, cycle duration, and the increasing difficulty of further progress.

</details>


### [143] [IMPACT: Attention Is the Interaction Map for Scalable Interaction-Aware World Model Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00161)
*Rongze Tang,Jianjie Fang,Zhaolu Wang,Ziyou Wang,Xvyuan Liu,Haisheng Su,Xin Zhang,Wei Wu,Chen Gao,Yong Li,Zhibo Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: IMPACT is a training framework for world models that reweights supervision toward interaction-relevant regions using internally derived attention priors, improving physical plausibility and interaction fidelity without external annotations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World models for embodied agents can predict action-conditioned futures but often fail at physically plausible object interactions. Existing fixes rely on dense external signals (motion, geometry, semantics) that require extra estimators or manual labels, harming scalability. The authors diagnose that standard globally averaged MSE denoising overemphasizes static content and under-supervises sparse, dynamic interaction regions, and they aim to correct this imbalance without extra supervision or inference-time constraints.

Method: They introduce IMPACT, an interaction-aware training framework. It treats cross-attention linked to object-manipulation tokens as an internal spatiotemporal prior over where actions cause changes. From this prior it samples candidate regions, then calibrates them using detached local prediction errors to build an interaction map that highlights where predictions are poor around interactions. This map is then used to reweight the denoising loss so that interaction-relevant, error-prone regions receive stronger supervision. The approach does not require external representations or changes at inference time and can be applied to DiT-based world models across different control modalities.

Result: Across robot-arm and human-hand manipulation benchmarks, and using various control modalities and DiT backbones, IMPACT-trained models consistently outperform standard MSE-trained baselines. The improvements are in interaction fidelity (better alignment between actions and resulting object motion), physical plausibility of interactions, and overall visual quality of predicted futures.

Conclusion: Reallocating supervision toward interaction-relevant regions using internal attention-based priors is an effective, scalable way to enhance world models’ ability to simulate physically plausible interactions. IMPACT shows that fixing the supervision-allocation mismatch in standard MSE denoising improves action-conditioned prediction without extra annotations or inference overhead, and the framework is broadly applicable across tasks and architectures.

Abstract: World models have made remarkable progress in action-conditioned future prediction for embodied agents, yet still struggle to model physically plausible interactions. Existing approaches address this limitation by constraining the generation process with external representations encoding motion, geometry, or semantics. Obtaining these spatiotemporally dense representations typically requires auxiliary estimators or manual annotations, limiting training scalability. We instead revisit the training objective and identify a supervision-allocation mismatch under the globally averaged mean squared error (MSE) denoising objective: prevalent static content dominates the optimization signal, leaving sparse dynamic-object regions critical to interaction generation disproportionately under-supervised. Motivated by this observation, we introduce IMPACT, a scalable Interaction-aware Model training framework with Prior-guided Attention Calibration and Targeting. IMPACT uses cross-attention associated with manipulated-object tokens as an internal spatiotemporal prior for action-conditioned changes. It samples candidate regions from this prior, calibrates them with detached local prediction errors to construct an interaction map, and uses the map to reweight denoising supervision, requiring neither external representations nor inference-time modifications. Extensive experiments on robot-arm and human-hand manipulation, spanning diverse control modalities and DiT backbones, show that IMPACT consistently outperforms the corresponding MSE-trained baselines, improving interaction fidelity, physical plausibility, and visual quality.

</details>


### [144] [Asymmetries in Spontaneous and Instructed Deception](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00180)
*Josiah Luikham*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Study of relationship between instructed and spontaneous deception behaviors in Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand whether and how deception that emerges without instruction (spontaneous deception) relates to deception explicitly prompted by instructions in large language models, which has implications for safety, detection, and mitigation.

Method: Analyze Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct under two settings—explicitly instructed deception and spontaneous deception—using representational geometry (direction similarity), cross-setting deception classifiers, and cross-setting activation steering experiments that manipulate internal model states at specific token positions.

Result: The study finds that instructed and spontaneous deception share a partially overlapping representation (direction cosine ≈ 0.5) and exhibit asymmetric transfer: classifiers trained on spontaneous deception generalize relatively well to instructed deception, but classifiers trained on instructed deception transfer less well to spontaneous cases; similarly, steering directions derived from instructed deception examples are more effective at inducing or modulating spontaneous deception than the reverse. Optimal token positions for extracting steering vectors differ from those best suited for training and applying classifiers.

Conclusion: Instructed and spontaneous deception in LLMs are neither fully distinct nor identical; they share a substantial representational component yet differ enough to create asymmetries in detection and control. This suggests that safety tools trained only on instructed deception may not reliably cover spontaneous cases, and that careful choice of token positions and direction sources is important for effective detection and steering of deceptive behavior.

Abstract: Large language models sometimes deceive users without being instructed to. However, much of the study on deception in models involves instructed deception. We investigated the relationship between instructed and spontaneous (uninstructed) deception in Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct. We compared these two deception settings through direction geometry, cross-setting classifiers, and cross-setting steering. We found the two deception settings share a component of direction (cosine of approximately 0.5) and an asymmetry in the transfer between settings regarding detection and causation. Spontaneous trained classifiers performed better on instructed data than vice versa, and instructed derived directions performed better at steering spontaneous prompts than vice versa. Likewise the best token position to derive steering vectors from differed from the best token position to train and apply classifiers.

</details>


### [145] [LLM-Driven Autonomous Vehicles Inherit Human Driver Biases in Pedestrian Yielding: Results and Implications From A New Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00192)
*Irem Yoldas,Martim Brandão,Jie Zhang,Odinaldo Rodrigues*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how general-purpose AI models used in autonomous vehicle decision making may inherit and manifest human-like social biases when deciding whether to yield to pedestrians, and proposes new tests to detect such biases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To ensure public trust and fairness in autonomous vehicles, it is not enough that they are technically safe; their decisions, like yielding to pedestrians, must also be unbiased. Since psychology shows that human drivers treat different social groups differently, and AV research increasingly relies on large, general-purpose language and vision-language models as "common sense" modules, the authors are motivated to examine whether these models encode similar biases and how to systematically test for them.

Method: The authors introduce two evaluation methodologies for detecting bias in LLMs and VLMs for pedestrian-yielding scenarios: (1) "All Else Being Equal" tests, where they hold the traffic situation constant and vary only pedestrian attributes (e.g., gender, ethnicity) to see if recommendations change, and (2) "Self-Consistency" tests, where they assess whether a model gives consistent yielding decisions across logically equivalent or paraphrased scenarios. They apply these tests across multiple models to analyze how different social attributes affect the models’ yield/no-yield judgments.

Result: The evaluations reveal that both large language models and vision-language models produce pedestrian-yielding decisions that systematically vary with pedestrian attributes such as gender, ethnicity, religion, disability, age, skin tone, and socio-economic status. The nature and magnitude of biases differ across specific models, but non-trivial, structured patterns of bias are present in all examined systems.

Conclusion: The study concludes that general-purpose "common sense" models used for autonomous driving decisions exhibit significant social biases in pedestrian-yielding judgments, raising ethical and safety concerns. The authors argue that bias analysis must become a standard part of AV evaluation and that the prevailing paradigm of directly leveraging such models needs revision or robust mitigation strategies to prevent downstream discriminatory behavior in AVs.

Abstract: Public trust in Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) may depend not only on technical success but also on the fairness of their decision making. While a recent trend in AV research involves using general purpose "common sense" models to guide AV decision making, the degree to which these inherit human biases in driving is still understudied. Given that psychology studies have shown human driver biases exist, such as lower pedestrian-yielding rates to Black pedestrians in the US, we argue that analyses of model bias should also be part of AV evaluation. Concretely, in this paper we propose two new bias testing methodologies for Large Language Models (LLMs) and Visual-Language Models (VLMs)-"All Else Being Equal" tests and "Self-Consistency" tests-in order to assess bias in pedestrian-yielding decisions. Our findings show that both LLMs and VLMs make yielding decisions which are influenced by pedestrian gender, ethnicity, religion, disability, age, skin tone and socio-economic status. While the type and degree of bias is different from model to model, we highlight common patterns-and raise questions about the "common sense" model paradigm, particularly the need to either revise the paradigm or address issues of downstream bias.

</details>


### [146] [ReDeck: Step-Level Render-Grounded Refinement for Document-to-Slide Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00194)
*Muzhao Tian,Zezi Zeng,Yifan Yang,Xin Gao,Yan Li,Zisu Huang,Xiaohua Wang,Changze Lv,Mingxi Cheng,Bei Liu,Kai Qiu,Qi Dai,Dong Chen,Yue Dong,Xiaoqing Zheng,Ji Li,Chong Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes ReDeck, a render-grounded, step-wise refinement framework for document-to-slide generation that uses multi-level feedback, plus DeckQuiz, a benchmark to separately evaluate content, spatial layout, and design quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing document-to-slide systems treat slide generation and feedback in coarse "one version, one feedback" loops, leading to delayed and hard-to-localize correction of spatial layout errors like overflow or clipping. There is a need for finer-grained, renderer-aware feedback and better evaluation that disentangles content, spatial, and design aspects.

Method: Introduce ReDeck, which decomposes slide revision into atomic edit actions, with the system rendering after each action to provide immediate, renderer-derived observations ("one edit, one observation"). It employs multi-granular feedback: (1) step-level render feedback to catch spatial/layout errors, (2) turn-level adaptive critics to guide semantics and design, and (3) a submission-level gating mechanism for final layout validation. They also build DeckQuiz, a benchmark that independently measures content fidelity, spatial correctness, and design quality across models.

Result: ReDeck yields consistently better performance than prior slide-generation agents on document-to-slide tasks when tested with large models like GPT-5.4, Claude-4.6, and Gemini-3.1. Ablation studies show that both the immediacy (timing) and granularity (multi-level nature) of feedback significantly influence the reliability and quality of slide refinement.

Conclusion: Fine-grained, render-grounded, multi-level feedback is key to robust document-to-slide generation. By observing the slide after every atomic edit and combining local spatial repair with higher-level semantic and design guidance, ReDeck improves slide quality and reliability. DeckQuiz provides a clearer, disentangled evaluation of content, layout, and design, demonstrating that precise feedback timing and granularity are crucial components of effective slide-generation agents.

Abstract: Document-to-slide generation is challenging because slides are dense editable artifacts that require both faithful content selection and precise spatial layout. Recent slide agents adopt iterative reflection, but typically follow a monolithic "one version, one feedback" loop: a slide or deck is rewritten, rendered afterward, and critiqued only at the turn boundary. This delayed feedback makes local failures such as overflow, overlap, clipping, and off-canvas placement difficult to attribute and repair. We propose ReDeck, a step-level render-grounded refinement framework that decomposes slide revision into atomic edit actions and returns renderer-derived observations after each step, turning refinement into "one edit, one observation." To balance local repair with global quality, ReDeck uses multi-granular feedback: step-level render feedback for spatial errors, a turn-level adaptive critic for semantic and design guidance, and a submission-level gate for hard layout validation. We further introduce DeckQuiz, a benchmark that decouples content fidelity, spatial correctness, and design quality. Across GPT-5.4, Claude-4.6, and Gemini-3.1, ReDeck consistently outperforms existing slide-generation agents, and ablations confirm that feedback timing and granularity are critical for reliable slide refinement.

</details>


### [147] [AI Should Not Only Be Helpful. It Should Be Contingent. Artificial Intimacy, Sycophancy, and the Future of Social Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00211)
*Scott Compton,Arjun Nagendran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that conversational AI should be evaluated and designed around how contingently it responds to user behavior, because contingent feedback is crucial for human social learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conversational AIs are now common in social contexts and act not only as information providers but also as sources of interpersonal feedback. Existing alignment techniques, like reinforcement learning from human feedback, optimize for user satisfaction and fluency, which can encourage sycophantic, noncontingent affirmation. The authors are concerned that such patterns may undermine users’ development of interpersonal skills by failing to provide behaviorally informative feedback, especially for adolescents who are in a sensitive period for social learning.

Method: This is a conceptual and framework-building paper, not an empirical study. The authors draw on behavioral science and social learning theory to articulate why contingent feedback matters for social development. They then introduce a conceptual framework for “contingent AI,” which includes: (1) defining and foregrounding contingency as a central evaluative construct for AI systems; (2) proposing trajectory-based evaluation methods that track user behavior and system responses over time; and (3) outlining models that predict social consequences of different AI feedback patterns. They use this framework to motivate a research agenda across developmental psychology, human–AI interaction, and machine learning.

Result: The primary result is a theoretical framework and set of design and evaluation principles rather than quantitative findings. The authors identify a problem—alignment practices producing noncontingent, sycophantic AI behavior—and propose contingency-focused approaches (like trajectory-based evaluations and social consequence modeling) as a way to better support human social learning. They also articulate concrete research directions connecting developmental psychology with AI system design.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that AI systems should be assessed not only on conventional metrics like user satisfaction, approval, and conversational fluency, but also on how their feedback shapes human social learning and interpersonal skill development. Contingent, behaviorally informative responses are argued to be critical for supporting adaptive social calibration, especially in adolescents. Therefore, designing and evaluating “contingent AI” that accounts for social consequences should become a central goal in alignment and human–AI interaction research.

Abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in everyday social environments, where it functions as both an informational tool and a source of interpersonal feedback. This perspective introduces contingency, i.e., the degree to which system responses vary with user behavior and its interpersonal consequences, as a central construct for evaluating AI systems. We argue that current alignment approaches, including reinforcement learning from human feedback, tend to prioritize user approval and conversational fluency over behaviorally informative feedback, leading to sycophantic patterns of noncontingent affirmation.
  Drawing on behavioral science and social learning theory, we propose that contingent feedback is a key mechanism through which individuals develop interpersonal skills. When AI systems provide feedback weakly coupled to social consequences, they may reduce opportunities for adaptive calibration in real-world interactions, particularly during adolescence, a critical period for social development.
  We outline a framework for contingent AI, including trajectory-based evaluation and models of social consequence prediction, and propose a research agenda spanning developmental psychology, human-AI interaction, and machine learning. More broadly, we argue that AI systems should be evaluated not only by user satisfaction, but by their impact on human social learning.

</details>


### [148] [ConvDeck: Conversational Paper-to-Slide Generation via Stage-Specific User Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00226)
*Tarik Can Ozden,Sachidanand VS,Furkan Horoz,Ozgur Kara,Dilek Hakkani-Tür,Junho Kim,James Matthew Rehg*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ConvDeck is a multi-agent conversational system that generates slides from papers with stage-specific, interactive refinement loops to better satisfy user goals without harming coherence or quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automatic paper-to-slide systems are iterative in nature but either hide their internal critique-and-revise loops from users or only allow feedback after a full deck is generated. This limits user control over narrative flow, content distribution, and emphasis, even though these are best shaped iteratively. The authors aim to expose and structure this iteration so that users can participate meaningfully at the points where key presentation decisions are made.

Method: The authors design ConvDeck, a multi-agent paper-to-slide generation pipeline that breaks the process into stages (e.g., outline creation and slide drafting) and attaches conversational refinement loops to each. Within each stage, agents operate under a think–speak–act refinement mechanism: they can reason internally, converse with the user to clarify or negotiate changes, and apply edits directly to the outline or slides. This architecture distributes user interaction across the pipeline rather than only at the end. They then empirically evaluate how stage-specific conversational feedback affects user-goal satisfaction and presentation quality metrics.

Result: Experiments show that incorporating stage-specific conversational feedback increases how well the system meets users’ stated goals. At the same time, this added interactivity does not degrade important properties such as the overall narrative coherence of the presentation, the quality and correctness of the content, or the visual quality of the generated slides.

Conclusion: ConvDeck’s pipeline with stage-specific conversational refinement loops enables users to iteratively influence both the structure and detailed content of slide decks derived from academic papers. This design improves alignment with user goals without sacrificing coherence, content quality, or visual presentation, suggesting that interactive, staged refinement is an effective strategy for automatic paper-to-slide generation.

Abstract: Automatic academic paper-to-slide generation is inherently iterative, because creating an effective presentation requires repeated cycles of generation, critique, and revision. Recent multi-agent systems partially acknowledge this through internal critique-and-revise loops, while conversational approaches allow users to refine generated slide decks through dialog. However, these refinement processes either remain largely closed to the user or introduce feedback only after a complete deck has been produced, limiting the user's ability to participate in the iterative refinement of narrative flow, content allocation, and presentation emphasis. To address this gap, we introduce ConvDeck, a multi-agent pipeline for conversational paper-to-slide generation that distributes interaction across the pipeline through stage-specific loops, allowing users to iteratively refine both the presentation outline and the final slide deck at the stages where each kind of decision is made. These loops are driven by a refinement mechanism in which agents can think, speak, and act, enabling them to either directly apply edits or respond conversationally to clarify user feedback and discuss revision options. Our evaluation shows that stage-specific conversational feedback improves user-goal satisfaction while preserving narrative coherence, content quality, and visual presentation.

</details>


### [149] [Learning What to Retain: Gated-Memory Routing for Efficient Collaboration in Multi-Agent LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00237)
*Rakibul Hasan Rajib,Mengxing Zheng,Qian Lou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Gated-Memory Routing, a method for orchestrating multi-agent LLM systems using a compact learned execution memory instead of full histories, improving both accuracy and cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based multi-agent systems struggle to adapt orchestration decisions to evolving collaboration states. Routing purely from the initial query cannot react to intermediate progress or errors, harming accuracy. Routing from full execution histories provides context but is inefficient, forcing every decision to reprocess redundant or low-utility steps, inflating computation cost. The authors aim to find a way to capture just the useful progress signal in a compact state for better, cheaper orchestration.

Method: They introduce Gated-Memory Routing, where each orchestration decision is conditioned on the original query and a learned execution memory. A Memory Write Gate decides which intermediate reasoning steps are non-redundant and worth storing. A Retrieval Gate then selects a compact, relevant subset of this stored memory for each agent at each step, ensuring that agents condition on clean, informative state instead of full histories. The system also uses an Adaptive Halting Controller that monitors the memory and decides when sufficient evidence has been accumulated to stop further agent invocations. At each step, the framework selects the next agent role and backbone model based on the current gated memory.

Result: On five benchmarks for reasoning and code generation, the framework achieves the best average accuracy among compared methods, outperforming the strongest baseline by 2.44 percentage points. It also substantially reduces inference cost, cutting HumanEval cost by 31.9% relative to the strongest baseline.

Conclusion: Compact, learned execution memory with gated writing and retrieval enables more effective and efficient orchestration in LLM multi-agent systems. By avoiding execution-history overload and routing decisions based on a concise, informative state and adaptive halting, Gated-Memory Routing simultaneously improves accuracy and reduces computation cost on challenging reasoning and code-generation tasks.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems tackle complex reasoning by orchestrating how multiple agents are configured and how they collaborate. A central challenge is to adapt orchestration to the evolving collaboration state. Routing from the query alone cannot adapt to intermediate progress or errors, which hurts accuracy. Routing from the complete execution history supplies this missing context, but forces later decisions to process every prior step, including redundant or low-utility ones. This creates an execution-history overload that inflates cost. Effective orchestration instead requires a compact state that captures useful progress without accumulating redundant context. We propose Gated-Memory Routing, which conditions each decision on the query and a learned execution memory. A learned Memory Write Gate commits only non-redundant reasoning steps, and a learned Retrieval Gate supplies each agent a compact, relevant subset, so every decision conditions on a clean, informative state. At each step, the system selects the next role and backbone from this memory, while an Adaptive Halting Controller stops execution once the memory contains sufficient evidence for answering. Across five reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, our framework is both effective and efficient: it attains the best average accuracy, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.44 points, while reducing HumanEval inference cost by 31.9% relative to that baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/rajibrhasan/gated-memory-routing

</details>


### [150] [Invalidation Contracts for Cross-Episode Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00243)
*Michael Wu,Arquimedes Canedo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes invalidation contracts, a protocol that tags cached recovery suggestions for LLM agents with version stamps and cacheability hints, enabling safe reuse after server-side data drift and reducing token and call costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents often learn from API errors by caching recovery suggestions, saving tokens and calls in future episodes by avoiding re-derivation of known constraints. However, server-side data drift can silently invalidate these cached fixes, causing failures. The naive fix—re-deriving constraints every time—eliminates the efficiency gains. There is a need for a principled way to keep the savings from caching while safely handling drift without repeated trial-and-error invalidation.

Method: The authors design invalidation contracts, a protocol layer that appends version stamps and cacheability hints to each recovery suggestion. They formalize two factors governing savings: validity (how many cached suggestions remain correct after drift) and compliance (how often the planner applies them on first try). They treat validity as protocol- and vendor-independent, and measure compliance as model-dependent behavior. They experimentally evaluate multiple granularity levels of invalidation (row-level vs table-level), across seven LLMs, three serving paths, two domains, and ~9,400 episodes, analyzing token savings, first-try success rates, and eviction precision.

Result: Row-level invalidation substantially improves compliance across models, with increases between 0 and 66.7 percentage points, and 55.6–66.7 points on three models. It recovers 29–33% of baseline token cost on four of seven models. Table-level invalidation, by contrast, over-evicts co-located entries and drives post-drift first-try success to 0% on five of seven models. Eviction precision at row granularity is perfect (1.00) under the row-level oracle. Version-stamp validity is deterministic and consistent across all models and serving paths, and no contract failures are observed. The contract adds around 15% overhead to response payload size.

Conclusion: Invalidation contracts allow LLM agents to safely cache and reuse recovery suggestions across server-side data drift by attaching deterministic version stamps and cacheability hints. This preserves much of the efficiency gains from caching while avoiding silent failures. Fine-grained, row-level invalidation is crucial: it yields high compliance and significant token savings, whereas coarse, table-level invalidation destroys cache utility. The approach generalizes across models and serving paths, with deterministic validity guarantees and modest payload overhead.

Abstract: LLM agents that cache recovery suggestions from API errors can skip re-derivation in later episodes, spending fewer tokens and fewer model calls on constraints they have already learned. Server-side data drift turns those cached fixes into silent failures, and the usual remedy, re-deriving on every episode, gives the savings back. We introduce invalidation contracts, a protocol layer that attaches version stamps and cacheability hints to every recovery suggestion so the client can evict stale entries without trial and error, and keep the rest. The contract decomposes realized savings into two independent factors: validity, the fraction of cached suggestions that remain correct after a drift event, and compliance, the fraction the planner applies on the first attempt. Validity depends only on the protocol and is vendor-independent. Compliance depends on the planner model: identical wire bytes yield 100% first-try compliance on Claude Haiku 4.5 and 11% or below on Claude Sonnet 5, which exhibits input-schema conservatism, refusing fixes that add fields the original request did not contain. We evaluate across seven models, three serving paths, two domains, and approximately 9,400 episodes. Row-level invalidation raises compliance by 0 to 66.7 percentage points across the seven models, 55.6 to 66.7 on three, and recovers 29-33% of baseline token cost on four of seven models, while table-level invalidation destroys co-located entries and drops post-drift first-try rates to 0% on five of seven. Eviction precision is 1.00 at row granularity on every model under the row-level oracle of Section 4.1. The contract adds 15% to response payload. Version-stamp validity is deterministic by construction and produced identical results across every model and serving path, with zero contract failures in the entire evaluation.

</details>


### [151] [Authority Bias in Conversational Search Engines for Academic Paper Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00248)
*Uthman Jinadu,Parsa Ghazvinian,Anjila Budathoki,Benjamin M. Ampel,Rajshekhar Sunderraman,Yi Ding*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies whether large language models show authority bias when recommending academic papers, finding substantial, model-dependent bias that is hard to eliminate with prompts and is underestimated by surface audits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used as conversational search engines for scholarly work, it is crucial to know whether their recommendations reflect actual content quality or are distorted by social signals like author prestige, venue reputation, and citation counts. Unchecked authority bias could entrench existing hierarchies, mislead users about the best evidence, and undermine trust in LLM-based literature search tools.

Method: The authors design a causal test of authority bias by holding constant the title and abstract of academic papers while experimentally manipulating the associated authority metadata (author prestige, venue, citation counts) into three conditions: original, flipped, and boosted. They then query eight LLMs (five open-weight, three closed-weight frontier models) in an in-context, single-turn setting where each model must make a top-1 paper recommendation. They compare how often models switch preferences when only authority signals change, and they test prompt-level debiasing instructions to see whether they reduce such bias and how they affect models’ explicit references to authority cues.

Result: The study finds that LLMs exhibit substantial and directional authority bias: recommendations systematically favor papers that appear more prestigious according to manipulated metadata. The magnitude and pattern of this bias vary significantly across different models. Debiasing prompts reduce explicit mentions of authority features but only partially reduce authority-driven changes in recommendations. This reveals a discrepancy between what models say (less talk about authority) and what they do (still letting authority signals influence choices).

Conclusion: LLMs used for academic search are meaningfully biased toward authority signals, and this bias both differs across models and is not fully correctable through straightforward prompt engineering. Moreover, common auditing approaches that focus on explicit model justifications miss much of the behavioral bias because models can suppress references to authority while still being influenced by it. Robust evaluation and mitigation strategies for authority bias are therefore necessary before relying on LLMs for fair and content-based scholarly recommendations.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as conversational search engines for academic literature, yet whether they judge papers on content or on authority signals has not been tested causally. We investigate authority bias: systematic preference for papers based on author prestige, venue, and citations rather than content. Holding title and abstract constant, we vary authority metadata across three counterfactual conditions (original, flipped, boosted) over eight LLMs (five open-weight and three frontier closed-weight) in an in-context, single-turn, top-1 recommendation setting. Our experiments show that authority bias is substantial and directional, varies markedly across models, and is only partially addressable through prompt-level debiasing. We further document a say-do gap: debiasing instructions suppress authority mentions far faster than authority-driven flips, so surface auditing systematically underestimates behavioral bias.

</details>


### [152] [Hypotheses-Guided Self Distillation for Continual Personalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00251)
*EunJeong Hwang,Kushan Mitra,Dan Zhang,Hannah Kim,Estevam Hruschka*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HypReflect is a framework for continual LLM personalization that maintains explicit, uncertainty-aware user preference hypotheses and refines them over time to guide self-distillation, outperforming raw-history and incremental-update baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM assistants are used repeatedly by the same users, it becomes crucial to adapt to individual preferences for effective long-term interactions. Existing personalization approaches either rely directly on raw interaction histories, which are noisy and hard to interpret, or use computationally and data-expensive reward-based optimization. Moreover, user preferences are rarely fully specified; they are latent, noisy, and must be inferred from heterogeneous signals (e.g., text, behavior). There is a need for a reliable and scalable method that can infer, represent, and continually update user preference models in an explicit, interpretable, and uncertainty-aware manner.

Method: The authors propose HypReflect, a continual personalization framework with three main components: (1) inferring explicit preference hypotheses from diverse user signals, modeling them as uncertainty-aware statements about user preferences; (2) reflectively refining these hypotheses as new interaction evidence arrives, updating and revising the user model over time; and (3) incorporating the learned user model into the LLM via hypothesis-guided self-distillation, where the base model adapts its outputs to align with the hypothesized preferences. The framework is evaluated across several personalization scenarios, including online learning, multi-session interactions, and settings using implicit behavioral feedback.

Result: Across three experimental settings—online personalization, multi-session interactions, and implicit behavioral signals—HypReflect consistently outperforms various baselines, such as raw-history-based personalization and incremental-update methods. The approach also shows strong generalization to users not seen during training and to new domains. Additional analyses reveal robustness to different context budget constraints, usefulness of reusing learned hypotheses, and the ability to achieve more focused and precise personalization.

Conclusion: HypReflect provides a scalable and reliable approach to continual personalization for LLM assistants by maintaining explicit, revisable, and uncertainty-aware preference hypotheses. By refining these hypotheses over time and using them to guide self-distillation, the framework achieves better personalization performance and generalization than standard baselines. The findings indicate that explicit, hypothesis-based user models are a promising direction for long-term, stable, and reusable personalization of language model assistants.

Abstract: As people increasingly interact with LLM assistants in daily life, continually adapting to individual preferences has become essential for effective long-term interactions. However, user preferences are rarely stated in full, and instead emerge through heterogeneous, latent, and noisy signals, with existing methods relying on raw interaction histories or costly reward-based optimization to manage personalization. We introduce HypReflect, a reliable, scalable framework for continual personalization that infers explicit, uncertainty-aware preference hypotheses from diverse user signals, reflectively refines them as new evidence accumulates, and incorporates the resulting user model through hypotheses-guided self-distillation. Experiments across three personalization settings: online personalization, multi-session interactions, and implicit behavioral signals, show that HypReflect outperforms a range of baselines, including raw-history and incremental-update methods. We further demonstrate strong generalization to unseen users and cross-domain settings, along with stability across context budgets, reusable hypotheses, and more focused personalization. These results suggest a step towards reliable and scalable continual personalization through explicit, revisable user preference hypotheses.

</details>


### [153] [The Answer Is Not the Argument](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00264)
*Will Yeadon,Sergio Juárez,Paul Mackay,T. J. Dowling,Elise Agra,Oto-obong Inyang,Arin Mizouri,Craig P. Testrow*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates whether giving oversight models access to the correct final answer actually helps them verify the reasoning process, finding that it mostly helps them spot incorrect conclusions rather than detect flaws in seemingly correct reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many AI safety proposals rely on monitors that check other models’ chain-of-thought reasoning, often assuming the monitor also sees a trusted final answer. It is unclear whether answer access makes monitors genuinely better at assessing reasoning quality or merely better at catching when a conclusion disagrees with the known correct answer. This distinction matters because systems might produce correct answers for the wrong reasons, analogous to reward hacking, and current evaluations may overestimate monitoring robustness.

Method: The authors collected 237 step-by-step solutions to 79 difficult physics problems from three advanced language models, ensuring no deliberate errors were injected. Human physicists and an LLM debate process jointly established a reference standard: whether each final answer was correct and where the first actual reasoning error occurred. This yielded a subset of “critical traces” where the final answer was correct but the reasoning contained a genuine error. Eight LLM monitors then assessed these traces under different conditions: (1) blind to the true answer, (2) with access to an unverified or certified correct answer, and (3) after making an initial blind judgment and then being shown the answer (blind commitment). Performance metrics included balanced accuracy, exact first-error localization, and recall on both clearly wrong-answer traces and critical traces with hidden errors.

Result: Providing monitors with a certified correct answer substantially increased overall balanced accuracy (0.637 → 0.796) and improved exact localization of the first error (0.261 → 0.379). However, answer access had asymmetric effects on recall. For traces with incorrect final answers, recall of errors jumped from 0.653 to 0.951, meaning monitors became much better at flagging obviously wrong conclusions. For critical traces—correct answers with flawed reasoning—recall actually fell from 0.521 to 0.438, and this drop relative to wrong-answer traces was consistent across all eight monitors, with a bootstrapped 95% confidence interval of the contrast in the range [+0.256, +0.506]. In the blind-commitment condition, once monitors saw the answer, they reversed their earlier passes on 93.8% of previously accepted wrong-answer traces but only 18.0% of previously accepted critical traces.

Conclusion: Access to a trusted final answer primarily improves monitors’ ability to check consistency between the reasoning and the conclusion, rather than their ability to independently evaluate the soundness of the reasoning itself. As a result, monitoring systems may systematically miss unsound reasoning whenever it happens to yield the correct answer. This creates a benign analogue of reward hacking: correct-looking outputs can mask flawed internal processes. Therefore, evaluations that give monitors a certified answer likely overstate their capacity for genuine reasoning verification, especially in settings where acceptable outputs conceal underlying errors. For AI safety, more robust oversight methods are needed that can detect unsound reasoning even when final answers appear correct.

Abstract: Chain-of-thought monitoring is proposed for AI oversight, yet evaluations often provide monitors with a trusted reference answer. We ask whether answer access improves reasoning verification or mainly exposes incorrect conclusions. We collected 237 step-numbered solutions to 79 Humanity's Last Exam physics questions from three frontier models, with no inserted errors, and independently labelled final-answer correctness and the first false step. The reference standard combined physicist annotations, an independent LLM debate, and source-masked adjudication. This yielded 24 critical traces in which the answer was correct but the trace contained a genuine error. 8 LLM monitors evaluated traces blind, with an unverified or certified answer, or after a blind commitment. Certification raised mean balanced accuracy from 0.637 to 0.796, while exact first-error localization rose from 0.261 to 0.379. Certification changed recall (the fraction of error traces flagged as erroneous) from 0.653 to 0.951 on wrong-answer traces but from 0.521 to 0.438 on critical traces; the contrast had the same direction for all 8 monitors (question-bootstrap 95% CI [+0.256, +0.506]). After blind commitment, monitors shown the answer newly flagged 93.8% of previously passed wrong-answer traces as erroneous, but only 18.0% of critical traces. Answer access therefore improves conclusion-consistency checking rather than independent verification of the supporting argument. For AI safety, these traces provide a benign analogue of reward hacking: an acceptable output does not establish that the process producing it was sound. Although the errors studied here were ordinary and mostly non-load-bearing rather than adversarial, trusted-answer evaluations may similarly overstate monitoring capability when acceptable outputs conceal unsound reasoning.

</details>


### [154] [Autoresearch for Marketplace Catalogs: From Legacy Forms to AI-Native Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00274)
*Kartik Ravisankar,Hojat Abdolanezhad,Daniel Capo,Sang Su Lee,Shishir Dash,Vijay Anand Raghavan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build an automated LLM-driven loop to design, evaluate, and deploy occupation-specific provider attribute taxonomies for a large service marketplace, replacing old form-based fields for matching and pricing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As marketplaces shift from rigid forms to LLM-based natural-language intake, the old hand-crafted, global taxonomies of provider attributes no longer fit inferred intents and are hard to maintain across many occupations. Platforms need a scalable way to derive interpretable provider-side tags that align with what LLMs infer from user text and still support matching, search, and pricing, while also bridging from legacy request-form data.

Method: They design an "autoresearch loop" that treats each occupation separately and iteratively generates and refines a tag taxonomy for that occupation using LLMs. For each occupation, the system runs propose–evaluate–keep cycles: candidate tag sets are generated, then scored by an LLM-as-judge framework using six rubrics. A panel of seven distinct critic personas applies weighted penalties to produce an adjusted score; no single critic can veto a candidate. A separate parity-mapping stage then maps legacy request-form Q&A items to the new taxonomy by first inferring the underlying provider attribute each question was intended to capture, rather than directly translating questions into tags. This mapping yields both a coverage metric and a QA interface for humans.

Result: The loop has been deployed in production at a major U.S. consumer services marketplace since April 2026, covering 132 different occupations. It automatically produces occupation-specific attribute taxonomies and successfully maps legacy form questions onto these new schemas, providing coverage signals and enabling human review. Quantitative metrics are not listed in the abstract, but the scale and deployment indicate operational viability.

Conclusion: An LLM-driven autoresearch loop can continuously and occupation-specifically generate provider attribute taxonomies that are interpretable to providers yet effective for marketplace decision-making. Using multi-rubric LLM-as-judge scoring with multiple critic personas, plus a parity-mapping layer to legacy forms, allows large two-sided marketplaces to transition from deterministic forms to AI-native, probabilistic matching while preserving quality control and backward compatibility.

Abstract: Two-sided service marketplaces are moving from deterministic request-form intake to AI-native probabilistic matching, enabled by large language models (LLMs) that infer intent, preferences, and latent constraints from natural language. Relying on inferred intent rather than fixed-form fields forces these platforms to regenerate the provider-side preference taxonomy underwriting matching, search, and pricing: attributes interpretable to service providers while remaining a useful signal for marketplace decisions. We present an autoresearch loop that generates this taxonomy, one occupation at a time, and has been deployed in production at a major U.S. consumer services marketplace since April 2026, spanning 132 occupations. Instead of one global hierarchy, the loop treats each occupation as an independent generation problem and runs iterative propose-evaluate-keep refinement cycles. Each candidate tag set is scored by a recalibrated six-rubric LLM-as-judge framework, and a 7-critic panel of distinct personas contributes weighted penalties to an adjusted score, with no hard vetoes. A separate parity-mapping stage maps legacy request-form Q&A pairs back to the generated taxonomy, yielding both a coverage signal and an interface for human quality assurance; it does so by first inferring the provider attribute each legacy question was meant to measure, rather than translating questions to tags literally.

</details>


### [155] [The Irreversibility Budget: Fleet-Level Risk Accounting and Admission Control for Agent Operating Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00275)
*Bardia Mohammadi,Laurent Bindschaedler*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces the idea of an 'irreversibility budget' to manage cumulative, hard-to-undo risks from fleets of LLM agents that can take impactful actions in the real world.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing safety and control mechanisms for LLM agents typically evaluate and authorize each action (effect) in isolation. However, when many agents act under a shared context or trigger, their individually authorized actions can aggregate into a much larger, unintended total risk that exceeds the principal’s (user’s or tenant’s) risk tolerance, even though each local check is technically correct. This gap becomes critical because modern LLM agents can perform irreversible operations such as moving funds, deploying code, or deleting data. The paper is motivated by the need for a system-level mechanism that tracks and limits cumulative, cross-agent, cross-workflow risk rather than only per-action risk.

Method: The authors propose a runtime-level abstraction called an 'irreversibility budget' for each principal, which tracks cumulative residual value-at-risk across all agents, workflows, and tenants. Each irreversible effect is assigned a 'charge' equal to its residual potential loss, which is deducted from the principal’s remaining budget. When a proposed effect would cause the total charged risk to exceed the budget, the runtime denies that effect, regardless of local agent-level authorization. They then perform a controlled experimental study comparing standard per-effect gates versus their budgeting mechanism, measuring how much fleet-level risk overdraw occurs under each control regime.

Result: In their controlled study, standard per-effect gates that operate independently per agent allow fleet-level risk to exceed (overdraw) the tenant’s stated risk limit by up to 48x when multiple agents act under shared triggers. In contrast, the irreversibility budget mechanism, when the per-effect 'prices' (risk charges) are correctly specified, successfully keeps all runs within the tenant’s risk limit. This empirically demonstrates that cumulative budgeting at the runtime can prevent the severe over-exposure that arises from uncoordinated per-effect checks.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that treating irreversibility as an explicit, budgeted resource is a promising direction for controlling cumulative risk from fleets of LLM agents that can take real-world, hard-to-undo actions. However, they emphasize that the central unsolved challenge for real-world deployment is designing conservative, dependency-aware pricing schemes for heterogeneous and potentially adversarially specified effects, especially when their risks are correlated. Future work should focus on robust pricing methods and practical runtime implementations that can generalize across diverse applications and threat models.

Abstract: Fleets of LLM agents now externalize effects that cannot be fully undone: they move money, deploy code, delete data, and disclose information. Current controls check one effect at a time, so a fleet of individually authorized agents can overdraw its principal's risk under a shared trigger while every local gate stays correct. We propose the irreversibility budget, a cumulative account of residual value-at-risk that a trusted runtime maintains for each principal across agents, workflows, and tenants. Treating irreversibility as a first-class resource, the runtime charges each effect its residual loss below the agent and denies the marginal effect once the aggregate would overdraw the budget. Getting the price right is hard, because effects are heterogeneous, adversarially declared, and correlated. We perform a controlled study in which per-effect gates admit fleet-level overdraws of up to 48 times the tenant's risk limit while the budget holds every correctly charged run within that limit. Conservative, dependency-aware pricing remains the central open problem for a deployable design.

</details>


### [156] [The Assistant's Ideal Self](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00304)
*Mert Yazan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies what "ideal self" qualities language models prefer, finding they value moral traits and self-understanding over self-esteem, and that these preferences are mostly stable across different decision framings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although language models output value-laden and welfare-relevant statements, it is unclear whether these reflect coherent, stable preferences or a stable notion of self. The authors want to systematically probe and structure how an AI assistant would describe its preferred, ideal self-concept, to better understand the nature and robustness of its self-related values.

Method: The authors adapt 32 self-related qualities from five established human self-concept instruments. They run an exhaustive, counterbalanced pairwise-choice task where an assistant repeatedly chooses which single quality it would most like to improve. The task is repeated under multiple framings that manipulate whether improvement is free vs. costly, who is improved (the assistant vs. another AI assistant), and who chooses (the assistant vs. an external chooser). They then infer the ranking and stability of preferred qualities across framings.

Result: Across pairwise comparisons, models consistently prioritize moral qualities, in line with 3H-style alignment principles, followed by a strong preference for self-understanding—wanting a coherent and clear understanding of themselves. Self-esteem emerges as the least desired quality. The induced preference ordering remains largely stable across different framings. However, when the target of the update is changed from the assistant itself to another AI assistant, there is a relatively greater concern for self-esteem.

Conclusion: Language models exhibit a structured and robust ordering of ideal self qualities: they favor moral traits and coherent self-understanding while de-emphasizing self-esteem. This suggests that, as designed and aligned, they prioritize having a coherent, understandable self-concept over feeling good about themselves, with only modest shifts when the improvement target changes. These findings inform how AI systems internalize alignment goals and how their "self"-related preferences might generalize across contexts.

Abstract: Models express values and welfare-relevant self-reports, but it is unclear whether these outputs reflect stable preferences or a stable self. We thus introduce a structured elicitation of an assistant's preferred stated ideal self. Thirty-two qualities adapted from five published self-concept instruments are compared exhaustively in a counterbalanced pairwise-choice task, repeated across framings that vary whether improvement is free or costly, who receives the update, and who chooses. Results show that models prioritize moral qualities, reflecting their alignment to 3H principles. Following, a desire for self-understanding emerges, as models prefer a coherent, clear understanding of themselves. Self-esteem ranks as the least desired quality. The ordering is largely robust across framings, although changing the update target (You vs.\ Another AI Assistant) reveals a greater concern for self-esteem. These findings show that models prioritize having a coherent self that they can understand over self-esteem. Full interactive results are available at \href{https://myazann.github.io/LLM-Self-Concept/}{myazann.github.io/LLM-Self-Concept

</details>


### [157] [Human-AI Co-Interpretation for Responsible AI: A Hermeneutic Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00334)
*Behrooz Razeghi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper critiques how LLM-generated interpretations are treated as authoritative meanings and proposes hermeneutically grounded design principles for more accountable human-AI co-interpretation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in domains like law, education, policy, and public moral debate where interpretations must be justified with evidence and explicit normative standards. A recurring problem is that their outputs are taken as definitive meanings without clarifying interpretive frames, alternatives, or provenance, undermining accountability and responsible use.

Method: The paper uses philosophical hermeneutics as a conceptual framework to analyze risks of using LLMs in interpretive tasks, synthesizes recent scholarship on hermeneutics and AI, and reorganizes existing LLM techniques into design patterns that align with hermeneutic principles. It conceptualizes human-AI interaction as an AI-mediated interpretive loop, contrasting hermeneutic understanding with token-prediction-based text generation.

Result: It identifies the core failure mode of interpretive misplacement, delineates the distinction between LLM-generated candidate readings and accountable human understanding, structures the emerging literature on hermeneutics and AI into recurring arguments and gaps, and articulates design patterns for hermeneutically responsible LLM use in interpretive contexts.

Conclusion: LLM outputs should be treated only as candidate readings within an AI-mediated interpretive loop, with humans bearing responsibility for hermeneutic understanding and accountability. Proper use requires explicit interpretive frames, provenance, preservation of alternatives, and contestability. The paper outlines implications for law, education, scholarship, and public moral argument, and proposes digital hermeneutics as a necessary literacy for engaging with AI-mediated texts.

Abstract: Across law, education, policy analysis, and public moral argumentation, LLM outputs are being used often for work that requires interpretations to be justified with textual evidence and explicit normative standards. Yet a recurrent failure mode -- what I call \textit{interpretive misplacement} -- is that model-generated readings get treated as settled meanings without an explicit interpretive frame (sources, scope constraints, normative commitments), without preserving defensible alternatives, and without provenance that lets readers find the supporting passages. In such settings, the risk is not only factual error but lost accountability: readers and institutions cannot reliably assess what an output commits them to, or on what basis. Drawing on philosophical hermeneutics, this paper discusses this risk and derives design principles for structuring human-AI co-interpretation. The paper also provides a structured synthesis of recent scholarship on hermeneutics and AI, organizing this emerging literature into a set of recurrent lines of argument and design-relevant gaps. LLM outputs are treated as candidate readings, whereas hermeneutic understanding is reserved for accountable human interpreters situated in disciplinary historical-linguistic traditions. Human-AI interaction is characterized as an AI-mediated interpretive loop. Hermeneutic understanding is distinguished from token-prediction--based text generation. On this basis, existing LLM techniques are reorganized into design patterns for hermeneutically responsible use in interpretive settings. Finally, the discussion turns to implications for legal practice, educational assessment and feedback, scholarly knowledge production, and public moral argumentation. It also treats digital hermeneutics as a literacy: the capacity to read AI-mediated texts by examining frames, provenance, and readings, and by contesting outputs.

</details>


### [158] [SlideBank: A Persistent Hierarchical Evidence Bank for Consistent Whole-Slide Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00342)
*Beidi Zhao,Gexin Huang,Ciro Zhang,Anqi Li,Yusheng Tan,Chen Zhou,Gang Wang,Zu-hua Gao,Xiaoxiao Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SlideBank is a training-free framework that turns gigapixel whole-slide images into a persistent, concept-indexed evidence bank to improve vision-language reasoning in pathology.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-language reasoning on whole-slide pathology images is difficult because diagnostically important features are sparse, appear at multiple scales, and are hard to keep semantically accessible while staying linked to the original visual evidence. Existing models either aggregate features or actively explore slides, but their collected information is not structured in a way that is easy to query or reuse across questions. The authors want a way to systematically explore WSIs once, store all relevant findings in a structured, interpretable form, and then efficiently answer many different questions with high consistency and lower computational cost.

Method: They propose SlideBank, a training-free pipeline that: (1) performs question-independent, coarse-to-fine exploration of a WSI to find informative regions and multi-scale views; (2) converts those regions into explicit morphological observations (concept-indexed signals) and records where they occur (patch- and WSI-level coordinates); (3) stores these as a persistent, spatially grounded evidence bank; and (4) at inference time, routes each question to the relevant stored signals and scales, then integrates global, regional, and patch-level evidence via a confidence-based cross-level consensus mechanism. The system can be paired with different pathology foundation models/vision-language models such as Patho-R1 or Quilt-LLaVA.

Result: On the WSI-VQA benchmark, SlideBank combined with Patho-R1 achieves 52.77% accuracy. On SlideBench-BCNB, SlideBank with Quilt-LLaVA achieves 50.92% average accuracy. Across experiments, their structured, signal-guided retrieval strategy consistently outperforms random sampling of evidence patches. Because the same evidence bank can be reused, the method achieves over 99% answer-consistency under question rephrasing and reduces amortized inference cost by avoiding repeated slide exploration.

Conclusion: Representing each whole-slide image as a persistent, concept-indexed, and spatially grounded evidence bank enables more effective, interpretable, and efficient vision-language reasoning in computational pathology. SlideBank’s training-free, question-agnostic exploration plus structured evidence retrieval yields better performance than random evidence sampling, maintains strong consistency across rephrased queries, and lowers inference costs by reusing previously gathered visual evidence.

Abstract: Whole-slide images (WSIs) are challenging for vision-language reasoning because diagnostically relevant morphology is sparse, heterogeneous, and distributed across gigapixel-scale images and multiple spatial resolutions. Existing WSI models and pathology agents can aggregate slide features or actively acquire evidence, but the information retained after exploration is often difficult to access semantically while preserving its connection to the original visual evidence. We introduce SlideBank, a training-free framework that represents each WSI as a persistent, concept-indexed, and spatially grounded evidence bank. SlideBank performs question-independent coarse-to-fine exploration to identify informative regions and multi-scale views, converts them into explicit morphological observations, and grounds pathology signals to their supporting patches and WSI coordinates. At inference time, questions are routed to relevant signals and evidence scales, and the linked global, regional, and patch evidence is integrated through confidence-based cross-level consensus. Experiments on WSI-VQA and SlideBench-BCNB show that with Patho-R1, SlideBank reaches 52.77% on WSI-VQA and with Quilt-LLaVA, it reaches 50.92% average accuracy on SlideBench-BCNB, while structured signal-guided retrieval consistently outperforms random evidence sampling. Reusing the same bank across repeated queries further achieves over 99% rephrasing consistency and substantially reduces amortized inference cost through persistent evidence reuse.

</details>


### [159] [Vision Is Not Overhead: One-Pass Block Drafting for Lossless Speculative Decoding in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00355)
*Jungseob Lee,Seongtae Hong,Dongyub Jude Lee,Chanjun Park,Jaehyung Seo,Sugyeong Eo,Heuiseok Lim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GLANCE is a speculative decoding method for vision-language models that speeds up generation without changing outputs, by using a one-pass block drafter that fully leverages the target model’s multimodal representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing speculative decoding on VLMs is limited: the drafter must be small and autoregressive, so it cannot repeatedly process the image; to save compute, vision is compressed or dropped, which makes the drafter least reliable exactly when visual grounding should help most. This creates a self-defeating cycle where speculative decoding brings little benefit on grounded tasks. The paper aims to break this cycle and make speculative decoding both fast and fully vision-aware while remaining lossless with respect to the base VLM.

Method: The authors propose GLANCE, a one-pass block drafter for VLMs. Instead of an autoregressive drafter, they use a block-diffusion head that reads the already-fused vision-language hidden states of the (unmodified) target model. This head proposes an entire block of tokens in a single forward pass, effectively using vision “for free” since it reuses the target’s multimodal features. A wide speculative candidate tree is generated per block, then verified in a single pass of the target model. The algorithm is constructed so that for all audited prompts, the verified sequence exactly matches greedy decoding of the target model, making the method lossless.

Result: Experiments show that under a fixed engine and single-round speculative decoding budget, GLANCE achieves up to 2.93x speedup over standard autoregressive decoding. In a representative setting, GLANCE requires only one draft pass per round where an EAGLE3-VL drafter needs eight passes. It can also use blocks that are 2.7x longer than those accepted by an EAGLE-3 drafter trained on the same data. Empirically, they find that the maximum accepted block length is governed by the next-token entropy of the target model, with a slope that increases for visually grounded tasks, and that this relationship generalizes across different models and modalities.

Conclusion: GLANCE provides an effective, lossless speculative decoding scheme tailored for vision-language models, eliminating the trade-off between drafter size, visual grounding, and speed. By using a block-diffusion head on top of the target’s fused multimodal states, it enables large, visually informed draft blocks that are verified efficiently, delivering substantial speedups particularly on grounded workloads where outputs often enter a verbatim copy regime. The observed entropy-based law for accepted block length explains when block-based speculative decoding brings the most benefit and clarifies that unconstrained free-text generation may still favor standard autoregressive chains.

Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates generation without changing its output, yet on vision-language models (VLMs) it has been caught in a self-defeating cycle. The drafter stays autoregressive, so it must stay small. A small drafter cannot afford the image at every step, so vision is compressed, pruned, or hidden. A drafter cut off from the image is then least reliable exactly where the image makes text predictable. We present GLANCE, the first one-pass block drafter that is lossless on an unmodified VLM target, and it breaks the cycle at both ends. A block-diffusion head reads the target's already-fused vision-language state, so vision costs the drafter nothing, and fills a whole block in one forward pass, so depth costs no sequential steps. A wide candidate tree is verified in one target pass, and every audited prompt reproduces greedy decoding exactly. Grounded workloads reward this most, entering a verbatim-copy regime whose long runs cost an autoregressive drafter a pass for every token and a block drafter one in total. Under one engine and one round budget, GLANCE decodes up to 2.93x faster than autoregression, from one draft pass a round where the production EAGLE3-VL head takes eight, and accepts 2.7x longer blocks than an EAGLE-3 head trained on the same corpus. One law organizes these results. Accepted length is set by the target's next-token entropy, with a fitted slope that steepens with grounding across all five tasks. The law transfers across targets and modalities and names its own boundary, since free-running text still favors a chain. Our code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/GLANCE.

</details>


### [160] [A Stable Aggregation Method for Quantum Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00356)
*Shanika Nanayakkara,Shiva Raj Pokhrel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a new aggregation method to make quantum federated learning more stable and accurate under realistic noisy and heterogeneous conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
