Motivation: Existing quantum federated learning systems become unstable when clients have heterogeneous data, unreliable communications, different device qualities, and quantum hardware noise. Additionally, standard Euclidean averaging is ill-suited for QNN parameters that are periodic angles, leading to poor aggregation and convergence. There is a need for an aggregation mechanism that respects the circular nature of parameters and the practical quality-of-service (QoS) constraints in realistic quantum networks.

Method: The authors design a self-consistent midpoint aggregation framework for QFL. It integrates (1) QoS-aware client weighting to reflect communication reliability and hardware fidelity; (2) circular parameter aggregation tailored to angular (periodic) QNN parameters instead of naive Euclidean averaging; and (3) bounded midpoint-based update control that limits and stabilizes the aggregated updates. They validate the method via angular tests and experiments on real IBM quantum machines.

Result: Through simulations and experiments on medical and financial datasets, as well as tests on real IBM quantum hardware, the proposed method shows improved training stability, reduced volatility in the learning dynamics, and accuracy that is competitive with, or better than, baseline QFL aggregation methods.

Conclusion: Respecting the circular structure of QNN parameters and incorporating QoS-aware weighting with midpoint-based update control leads to a more robust and stable quantum federated learning framework. The proposed self-consistent midpoint aggregation enables QFL to operate more reliably under practical noisy and heterogeneous conditions while maintaining strong predictive performance.

Abstract: Quantum federated learning (QFL) enables clients to train quantum neural network (QNN) models without sharing private data. We find that aggregation in QFL is unstable under heterogeneous data, unreliable communication, variable fidelity, latency, and quantum hardware noise. Moreover, QFL is non-trivially challenging because several QNN parameters are periodic angles, where Euclidean averaging often fails to capture the inherent dynamics. We develop a novel self-consistent midpoint aggregation method for stable QFL design and implementation. We combine QoS-aware client weighting, circular parameter aggregation, and bounded midpoint-based update control. We perform several angular tests and IBM real Quantum machines experiments for validation confirming our approach. Extensive evaluations and experiments on medical and financial datasets show improved stability, lower volatility, and competitive accuracy.

</details>


### [161] [Dr. Claw: An AI Scientist Workspace for Vibe Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00365)
*Dingjie Song,Hanrong Zhang,Dawei Liu,Yixin Liu,Zongxia Li,Zhengqing Yuan,Siqi Zhang,Henry Peng Zou,Zhiling Yan,Yuxuan Zhang,Yanfang Ye,Philip S. Yu,Lichao Sun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Dr. Claw is a human-in-the-loop orchestration layer around existing command-line coding agents that makes research workflows more controllable, auditable, and recoverable, improving research completeness without changing the underlying executor.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing command-line coding agents can handle files and long sessions, but real research workflows are still fragmented across multiple tools (chat, IDE, terminal, writing apps). This fragmentation makes it hard to maintain an auditable trail of decisions and to recover from failures, because planning, execution, and writing are not unified in a single, persistent, traceable process.

Method: The authors design Dr. Claw, an open-source workspace that wraps existing coding-agent executors instead of creating a new autonomous agent. They introduce persistent state objects, a reusable skill library, and coordination across multiple executors to bind human decisions to AI actions. The system is demonstrated via an interactive three-view scenario and a failure-recovery walkthrough, then evaluated in a controlled comparison against a bare command-line agent that uses the same backend executor, isolating the contribution of Dr. Claw’s orchestration layer (task graph, state objects, skills).

Result: In evaluations where the underlying executor is held constant, Dr. Claw outperforms a bare command-line agent on research completeness metrics while simultaneously providing a persistent, auditable, and recoverable trail of the research process. The demonstrations show how its state objects, skill library, and multi-executor coordination support interactive workflows and effective failure recovery.

Conclusion: Wrapping existing coding agents with a structured, human-in-the-loop orchestration layer—featuring persistent state, shared skills, and coordinated executors—can significantly improve the completeness and auditability of research workflows without modifying the underlying agent. Dr. Claw shows that integrating planning, execution, and writing into a single traceable loop enables more reliable and recoverable end-to-end research, and is provided as an open-source tool to support such workflows.

Abstract: Command-line coding agents (e.g., Claude Code, Gemini CLI) can already read and write files and sustain long sessions, yet end-to-end research still fragments across chat tools, IDEs, terminals, and writing environments, and the decisions that make it auditable are rarely preserved. We present Dr. Claw, an open-source workspace that wraps existing coding-agent executors in a controllable and auditable human-in-the-loop workflow rather than introducing another autonomous agent. Persistent state objects, a reusable skill library, and multi-executor coordination link human decisions to AI execution, turning planning, execution, and writing into one traceable, recoverable loop. We demonstrate Dr. Claw through an interactive three-view scenario and a failure-recovery walkthrough, and evaluate it against a bare command-line agent sharing the same backend executor, so the comparison contrasts the whole orchestration layer (task graph, state objects, and skill library) with the agent it wraps. Holding the executor fixed, Dr. Claw scores higher on research completeness while persisting an auditable, recoverable process trail. Demo access: repository https://github.com/OpenLAIR/dr-claw, released under AGPL-3.0 with GPL-3.0 upstream components.

</details>


### [162] [RestoreBench: Can AI Agents Restore Power Flow Convergence?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00384)
*Riccardo Mansutti,Andrea Pomarico,Robert Jakob,Qian Zhang,Alberto Berizzi,Kevin O'Sullivan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents RestoreBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on diagnosing and fixing non-convergent power flow cases in power systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explore and systematically evaluate how LLM-based agents can automate complex engineering workflows—specifically diagnosing and resolving non-convergent power flow cases in power system analysis, a task that requires judgment, experimentation, and constrained decision-making.

Method: The authors design a benchmark comprising a simulation environment, clearly defined observation and action spaces, and evaluation metrics. They test multiple LLMs organized under three architectures (chatbot, single-agent, and multi-agent) on 46 non-convergent power flow cases across two power grids, where agents must propose corrective actions to restore convergence.

Result: They obtain comparative performance results of different LLMs and agent architectures on the benchmark cases, demonstrating varying capabilities in diagnosing issues and selecting corrective actions, though detailed numerical results are not given in the abstract.

Conclusion: RestoreBench provides a reproducible and structured testbed for developing and assessing agentic AI systems for power system planning and operation, highlighting non-convergent power flow restoration as a promising application for LLM agents.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly automate multi-step engineering workflows through tool use, interpretation of intermediate results, and iterative planning. Diagnosing and resolving non-convergent power flow cases is a promising yet largely unexplored application, as it requires engineering judgment, experimentation, and decision-making within constrained action spaces. We introduce a benchmark that evaluates these capabilities across multiple LLMs and three architectures: \emph{chatbot}, \emph{single agent}, and \emph{multi-agent} systems. The evaluation covers two power grids and 46 cases per grid, each requiring one or more corrective actions to restore convergence. The benchmark defines the simulation environment, observation and action spaces, and evaluation metrics, providing a reproducible foundation for developing agentic AI systems for power system planning and operation. The code is available at https://github.com/Mansutti081/RestoreBench

</details>


### [163] [Dependency-Aware Chain-of-Thought Compression for Financial Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00413)
*Wenjun Wu,Lei Fu,Kejian Tong,Tao Ning,Sichen Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose HSDN, a method to compress chain-of-thought reasoning for financial tasks while maintaining accuracy and logical coherence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Chain-of-thought prompting improves complex reasoning but produces long, costly intermediate traces that are impractical for financial deployment. There is a need to reduce reasoning length without sacrificing accuracy or interpretability.

Method: Introduce Hierarchical Semantic Distillation Network (HSDN), which compresses reasoning chains via semantic segmentation, dependency graph construction, dual-encoder importance scoring, constrained selection of key segments, and local boundary rewriting. A frozen Qwen3 4B model provides feature extraction and final answering, while compression is a separate structured, interpretable pipeline.

Result: On the AFAC2025 benchmark, HSDN attains 91.0% accuracy with 68.4% compression, outperforming strong baselines in overall performance and coherence of the compressed reasoning traces.

Conclusion: Graph-guided, structured compression of chain-of-thought is an effective strategy for high-stakes financial reasoning, enabling significant cost reduction while retaining accuracy and coherent reasoning traces.

Abstract: Chain of thought prompting improves complex reasoning, but its long intermediate traces create substantial inference cost and hinder practical deployment in financial settings. We present a Hierarchical Semantic Distillation Network, HSDN, for compressing reasoning chains while preserving answer accuracy and logical coherence. The framework combines semantic segmentation, dependency graph construction, dual encoder importance scoring, constrained segment selection, and local boundary rewriting. A frozen Qwen3 4B model is used only for feature extraction and final answer generation, while the compression process remains structured and interpretable. On the AFAC2025 benchmark, HSDN achieves 91.0% accuracy with 68.4% compression, outperforming strong compression baselines in overall score and reasoning coherence. The results show that graph guided compression is effective for high stakes financial reasoning tasks.

</details>


### [164] [SpecMind: Enabling Spectrum Intelligence via Multi-Agent Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00427)
*Songwei Dong,Bingyan Lu,Makayla Kienlen,J. Nicholas Laneman,Cong Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SpecMind is a multi-agent RAG system tailored for spectrum management that reasons over heterogeneous regulatory and licensing data, evaluated using a new benchmark (SpecBench), and significantly outperforms generic RAG baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Managing radio spectrum is becoming harder due to explosive growth of wireless devices, leading to complex, fine-grained spectrum decisions in space, time, and device constraints. Policymakers and engineers must work with large, fragmented, and heterogeneous data (text, tables, policy documents, license records) that are not machine-friendly. Existing RAG systems are general-purpose and there is a lack of domain-specific evaluation datasets for spectrum intelligence. This creates a need for a specialized, automated system that can reliably retrieve and reason over these diverse sources for spectrum-related tasks.

Method: The authors design SpecMind, a multi-agent Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework tailored to spectrum intelligence. The system consists of autonomous agents that coordinate specialized sub-agents, each responsible for retrieving, integrating, and reasoning over different types of spectrum-related data (e.g., legal regulations, policy proceedings, license databases). They also construct SpecBench, a domain-specific Q&A dataset derived from real license records and policy proceedings, to evaluate RAG systems in this domain. They compare SpecMind against strong, general-purpose RAG baselines on SpecBench and other spectrum-related tasks.

Result: On spectrum-related Q&A and reasoning tasks built from real-world regulatory and licensing data, SpecMind achieves more than an 80% win rate over strong general-purpose RAG baselines. The experiments indicate that the multi-agent, domain-specialized architecture improves retrieval quality, contextual reasoning, and overall task success across varied query types.

Conclusion: A domain-specialized, multi-agent RAG architecture is highly effective for spectrum intelligence tasks involving heterogeneous regulatory and licensing data. SpecMind’s cooperative agents better retrieve and synthesize information than general-purpose RAG systems, and the new SpecBench dataset provides a needed benchmark for this domain. The work suggests that tailored multi-agent RAG systems can significantly enhance automated reasoning in complex, data-fragmented technical policy domains.

Abstract: The exponential growth of wireless devices is driving unprecedented spectrum demand, pushing spectrum management toward more fine-grained decisions across space, time, and device constraints. As a result, spectrum policymakers and engineers must process large volumes of data that come from diverse sources and take many different forms, such as text and tables. These data sources are often disaggregated and require significant time and effort to integrate, search, and interpret. Furthermore, most of this information is formatted for human understanding and is not readily accessible to automated systems. To address this challenge, we propose SpecMind, a novel Multi-Agent Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system for spectrum intelligence that performs reasoning over heterogeneous data sources. This system enables autonomous agents to coordinate specialized sub-agents that retrieve and synthesize knowledge across policy proceedings, legal regulations, and license databases. We develop SpecBench, a question and answer (Q&A) dataset based on real-world license records and policy proceedings, addressing the lack of evaluation resources for RAG systems in the spectrum domain. Experimental results demonstrate that SpecMind outperforms traditional, general-purpose RAG systems across spectrum-related tasks, achieving over 80% win rate against strong baselines. The agent-based design enables more accurate retrieval, better contextual reasoning, and improved task completion across diverse query types.

</details>


### [165] [SAGE: State-Grounded, Abstention-Aware Evaluation of Task-Oriented Dialogue Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00434)
*Rayan Khoury,Shih-Yao Lin,Pratyush Mishra*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces SAGE, a workflow-state-grounded, abstention-aware evaluation framework for task-oriented dialogue agents that matches or outperforms LLM judges at near-zero LLM cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based judges usually evaluate each dialogue turn holistically, focusing on surface quality and overall context instead of checking whether the system correctly advances an underlying workflow or state. This makes them miss fine-grained state errors and also incur high inference costs, since they typically require at least one full LLM call per turn. The authors want an evaluator that is tightly grounded in task state, decomposed into atomic criteria, honest about its uncertainty (abstains instead of guessing), and much cheaper to run at scale.

Method: They propose SAGE (State-Grounded Abstention-Aware Evaluation). First, a compiler takes the workflow specification and the per-turn state diff and decomposes correctness into many atomic, schema-grounded criteria. Then, each criterion is sent through a cascade of verifiers: symbolic rules and lightweight encoder-/NLI-based models that can abstain when uncertain. These criterion-level decisions are aggregated into a turn-level decision along with an evidence trace. SAGE-Core uses only the compiler, symbolic rules, and on-device encoders to decide most criteria at zero paid LLM cost, while SAGE-LLM adds an optional focused LLM fallback for open-class criteria. They benchmark SAGE on multiple datasets and compare against LLM-as-a-judge baselines, including state-aware GPT-4.1 and GPT-4.1-mini variants using a G-Eval-style setup.

Result: SAGE-Core is able to decide 81–91% of criteria using just the compiler, symbolic rules, and local encoders, with no paid LLM calls. Across four experimental slices from MultiWOZ, Schema-Guided Dialogue, and ABCD, no evaluated LLM-judge baseline significantly outperforms SAGE-Core, even though a GPT-4.1 G-Eval judge costs $4.7–8.0 per 1,000 turns, versus effectively $0 for SAGE-Core. A human audit with two annotators on 200 examples (Cohen’s kappa 0.94) shows strong agreement between SAGE labels and human judgments on the kinds of failures visible from transcripts. When excluding the weak-salience “ignored user value” (IUV) class, SAGE-Core is statistically tied with the strongest LLM judge on these failure types.

Conclusion: A structured, state-grounded, abstention-aware evaluation pipeline can match or rival powerful LLM-based judges for task-oriented dialogue without incurring LLM inference cost, while providing transparent evidence traces. SAGE honestly represents uncertainty and clarifies that some state-consistency signals (like ignored user values) may have weak global human salience, highlighting construct-validity limits. The authors also identify limits related to injected failure designs and partial symbolic circularity, suggesting future work on more robust constructs and evaluation protocols.

Abstract: Evaluating task-oriented dialogue agents requires judging not merely whether a reply reads well but whether each turn advances the underlying workflow state correctly--a distinction conventional holistic LLM judges can miss because they evaluate the available context as a single unit and require one or more full-model calls per turn. We propose SAGE (State-Grounded Abstention-Aware Evaluation), which compiles a workflow specification and per-turn state diff into atomic, schema-grounded criteria and routes each through a cascade of symbolic and encoder/NLI verifiers that abstain rather than guess, aggregating criterion verdicts into a turn-level decision with an evidence trace. Its recommended operating point, SAGE-Core, decides 81--91% of criteria with only the compiler, symbolic rules, and on-device encoders--at zero paid LLM cost--while SAGE-LLM adds an optional focused-LLM fallback for open-class criteria. Across four slices spanning MultiWOZ, Schema-Guided Dialogue, and ABCD, no evaluated LLM-as-a-judge baseline--including a state-aware GPT-4.1 judge and cheaper GPT-4.1-mini variants--significantly exceeds SAGE-Core on any slice, even though the GPT-4.1 G-Eval judge costs $4.7--8.0 per 1,000 turns to SAGE-Core's $0. A two-annotator human audit (n=200, $κ$=0.94) confirms strong label fidelity on the transcript-visible failure classes--where, excluding the weak-salience IUV class, SAGE-Core is statistically tied with the strongest LLM judge--and honestly scopes ignored-user-value as a state-consistency signal with weak broad-human salience. We analyze construct-validity limits from injected failures and partial symbolic circularity.

</details>


### [166] [Conversation Coach: A Voice-enabled AI System that Helps Practice Difficult Workplace Conversations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00441)
*Fanyou Wu,Suraj Maharjan,Ainur Yessenalina,Dennis Xu Chen,Rahul Srivastava,Srinivasan H. Sengamedu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Conversation Coach, a voice-first AI system that lets managers rehearse difficult workplace conversations by speaking to an AI, providing realistic practice plus feedback at scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Managers need to handle difficult conversations to retain high performers and develop underperformers, but live training and coaching are expensive and hard to scale. Existing text-based chatbot training tools miss the crucial element of speaking aloud, which is important for confidence and realism, especially for high-stakes conversations. There is a gap for a scalable, voice-based rehearsal system that feels realistic, adapts to different employee types, and offers actionable feedback.

Method: The authors design Conversation Coach, a voice-first AI system centered on low-latency, natural spoken interactions. They formalize three core technical challenges: (1) achieving fast, accurate speech interaction with strong language understanding; (2) supporting adaptive, configurable employee personas to simulate varied conversation partners; and (3) generating personalized feedback on conversation content and policy compliance. They compare two architectures: an end-to-end speech-to-speech model and a cascaded pipeline of ASR → LLM → TTS. They evaluate them on latency, cost, and reasoning quality, then deploy the chosen architecture at scale to real managers and analyze usage over six months.

Result: The end-to-end speech-to-speech model delivers significantly lower latency (3× better P50) and supports natural barge-in at roughly 8× lower estimated cost, but its reasoning and coaching quality lag behind the cascaded system. The cascaded ASR + LLM + TTS approach shows superior reasoning capabilities necessary for high-quality coaching, making it preferable despite higher latency and cost. In a six-month production deployment, over 40,000 managers used Conversation Coach, with usage data suggesting that they selectively turned to the system for more challenging, high-stakes conversations rather than trivial ones.

Conclusion: Conversation Coach demonstrates that a voice-first AI rehearsal tool can be deployed at large scale to help managers practice difficult workplace conversations. Architectural trade-offs are crucial: while end-to-end speech-to-speech models excel in latency and cost, cascaded ASR–LLM–TTS pipelines currently provide better reasoning, which is vital for effective coaching. Real-world adoption by tens of thousands of managers and selective use for difficult conversations indicate practical value and fit for high-stakes managerial communication training.

Abstract: Effective manager-employee communication is critical for retaining high performers and developing underperformers, yet training managers in these skills remains costly. Text-based chatbots offer a scalable approach but cannot provide realistic rehearsal: managers need to practice speaking aloud to build confidence before high-stakes conversations. In this paper, we propose Conversation Coach, a voice-first AI system that enables managers to rehearse difficult workplace conversations in a realistic spoken format. The system addresses three challenges: achieving low-latency interactions with strong language understanding, enabling adaptive conversations through configurable bot personalities that simulate different employee types, and generating personalized feedback on content and policy compliance. We compare an end-to-end speech-to-speech model with a cascaded approach combining automatic speech recognition, a large language model, and text-to-speech synthesis. The end-to-end approach achieves 3$\times$ lower median (P50) latency with native barge-in capability at an estimated 8$\times$ lower cost, while the cascaded approach offers superior reasoning essential for coaching quality. We deployed the cascaded architecture in production, where 40,000+ managers used it over six months, with adoption patterns indicating selective use for difficult conversations.

</details>


### [167] [mimeo: Compiling Public Expert Corpora into Agent Skills and Testing What Transfers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00453)
*Timothy Kassis*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces mimeo, an open-source system for building expert-specific reference files for LLM agents, and empirically tests whether such files improve knowledge access, persona faithfulness, and judgment transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents often struggle to reliably represent specific human experts: they hallucinate quotes, misstate positions, and conflate stereotypes with actual views. There is growing interest in using LLMs as domain-expert proxies, but existing approaches frequently rely on the model’s vague internal memory or unverified web search. The authors want a compact, auditable way to ground an agent in a particular person’s real, published work and to disentangle three different claims commonly bundled together: (1) better access to hard-to-find knowledge from that expert, (2) more recognizable or faithful personas, and (3) genuine transfer of the expert’s judgment. They also seek practical tooling that automatically constructs such expert profiles with strong quotation verification, and rigorous tests to see what such profiles actually deliver and what they don’t.

Method: They build mimeo, an open-source pipeline that automatically collects a target expert’s public writing, extracts candidate quotations, verifies each quote against locally cached source text, and compiles an "expert file" that an LLM agent can load. They log and analyze eight builds, tracking the number of model calls and the proportion of rejected quotes during verification. They then design experiments using four expert files with a single coding-agent harness, comparing conditions: (a) closed-book agent (no expert file), (b) agent with mimeo expert file, (c) personas written from model memory, and (d) keyword-search baseline (BM25) over the same pages. They evaluate several outcomes: (1) knowledge access via 20 obscure, quotation-heavy questions; (2) grounding and persona fidelity via graded answers to 20 prompts about the expert’s documented positions and via human detection of personas in short open prompts with and without task material; (3) judgment transfer through engineering tasks with planted problems and 16 novel application scenarios; and (4) "sounds like the expert" scores from AI judges, examining how different judges rate the same answers.

Result: The mimeo pipeline is moderately intensive, averaging 38 model calls per build, and its verification step rejects 13.2% of extracted quotations, indicating substantial noise in naive quote extraction. In knowledge-access tests, mimeo-equipped agents correctly answered all 20 obscure, quotation-heavy questions, while no closed-book condition exceeded 10 correct. The BM25 keyword-search baseline achieved 15–17 correct, leaving some uncertainty about the true performance gap in this small sample. For grounding/persona fidelity, personas generated from model memory misrepresented the expert’s documented position on 1–4 of 20 answers across graders, whereas both the plain agent and mimeo-based agent did not misstate those positions. All personas were easily detectable from short, open prompts; adding real task content reduced persona identifiability by 18–23 percentage points. Mimeo-based answers were no more identifiable than those using a from-memory profile. For judgment transfer, all conditions essentially hit a performance ceiling: agents in every condition detected 94–97% of planted problems and scored 94–100% on 16 new application scenarios, preventing clear differentiation. AI-judge evaluations of "sounds like the expert" were inconsistent: for two of four experts, a judge preferred answers that aligned with the model’s stereotype rather than the profile-grounded text, while the other two judges saw no difference on the same answers.

Conclusion: mimeo works as intended as a compact, inspectable reference file that reliably grounds an LLM in a specific person’s documented writings, especially for retrieving obscure, quotation-heavy information and avoiding misstatements of documented positions. However, the experiments do not show that loading an expert file produces a detectable transfer of that expert’s judgment or style under the tested tasks, in part because task performance hit ceilings and AI-judge assessments were inconsistent and biased by stereotypes. The authors highlight that persona-like behavior can be easy to detect in isolation but is less so in real tasks, and that AI-based "sounds like" judgments are unreliable enough that one should not lean on a single AI judge. Overall, the paper recommends viewing expert files built by mimeo as trustworthy reference artifacts for grounding, not as tools that automatically imbue an agent with the expert’s decision-making or voice.

Abstract: Giving an agent a file about a named expert can supply hard-to-find material, produce a recognizable persona, or change what the agent decides. These are different claims. We test each one. mimeo is an open-source tool that finds a person's public work, checks each extracted quotation against the cached source text, and writes a file an agent can load. Eight logged builds averaged 38 model calls; the check rejects 13.2% of extracted quotations. We tested four expert files with one coding-agent harness. Knowledge access was clearest: mimeo answered all 20 obscure, quotation-heavy questions; no closed-book condition answered more than 10. Keyword search (BM25) over the same pages answered 15-17, a gap this sample cannot resolve. Grounding showed one clear benefit: personas written from model memory misstated a documented position on 1-4 of 20 answers under every grader; the plain agent and mimeo never did. Every persona was easy to spot on short open prompts, and adding task material lowered identification by 18-23 points. mimeo was no more identifiable than a from-memory profile. Judgment transfer remained unresolved because both tests hit their ceiling: every condition found 94-97% of the problems planted in engineering tasks and scored 94-100% on 16 new application scenarios. An AI-judged "sounds like the expert" score changed with the judge: two of four preferred answers based on a model's stereotype, while two found no difference on the same text. That is a caution against relying on a single AI judge. The evidence supports mimeo as a compact, inspectable reference on a person, not as a demonstrated transfer of their judgment. Toolkit and expert profiles: https://github.com/K-Dense-AI/mimeo

</details>


### [168] [Towards a Belief-Based World Model for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00455)
*Shubham Kumar,Harshit Kumar,Narendra Ahuja,Saurabh Jha*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Belief-Based World Models (BB-WMs), which maintain an explicit belief state that LLM agents can query, and shows that exposing this belief improves LLM decision-making under partial observability beyond pure simulation-based world models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as decision-making and planning policies, but they perform poorly on long-horizon tasks in partially observable environments. Existing world-model approaches mainly use forward simulation of candidate actions at inference time, which does not explicitly represent or communicate uncertainty about the current state. The authors are motivated to understand whether making an explicit belief state available to LLMs can address these limitations and improve performance under partial observability.

Method: The authors propose Belief-Based World Models (BB-WMs), which maintain a belief over the underlying environment state and expose this belief directly to an LLM policy via queries. Instead of only simulating future trajectories for specific actions, the world model also tracks and summarizes what is currently known and unknown about the state. They design experiments in partially observable, long-horizon tasks where LLM agents either have access only to simulation-based world models or additionally to the belief state from BB-WMs, and compare task performance across these settings.

Result: Empirical results show that LLM agents that can query and use the world model’s belief state achieve higher performance on tasks with partial observability compared to agents relying solely on simulation-based world models. The benefit is complementary: belief access enhances decision-making without replacing or conflicting with simulation-based planning.

Conclusion: Exposing an explicit belief state from a world model to LLM policies is beneficial for decision-making under partial observability. Belief-Based World Models provide a richer interface than pure simulation, enabling LLM agents to better reason about uncertainty and improve task performance, and they can be combined with existing simulation-based methods. The accompanying code release supports further research in this direction.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are being used as policies for autonomous decision-making and planning in many domains. Despite their strong reasoning capabilities, LLMs struggle with long-horizon tasks, especially under partial observability. World models are a promising way to enhance policy performance, both during training and inference. During inference, agents currently use world models to simulate the consequences of candidate actions before committing to an action, which can improve decision-making. However, we argue that simulation alone is an incomplete interface for decision-making under partial observability: simulation doesn't adequately capture uncertainty about the current state, which agents may need for accurate decision-making. We address this limitation with Belief-Based World Models (BB-WMs), which model and maintain a belief that LLMs can query to access information on what is known and uncertain about the current state. Before developing methods to learn accurate BB-WMs, we first ask a more fundamental question: does exposing a world model's belief directly to an LLM policy improve decision-making? Our results show that giving LLM agents access to world model beliefs improves task performance under partial observability, while remaining complementary to existing simulation-based world models. Code is released at https://github.com/skumar-ml/belief-world-models.

</details>


### [169] [EGT-KG: Evidence-Grounded Typed KG Retrieval for Practical Scientific QA with Small Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00479)
*Muran Yu,Jiechao Gao,Yuandong Pan,Barney H. Miao,Andrew C. Lesh,Kincho H. Law,Jie Wang,Michael D. Lepech*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces EGT-KG, a knowledge-graph-based retrieval framework that boosts scientific question-answering performance of local small language models under real-world constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Local small language models are preferred in some scientific settings due to privacy and deployment stability, but they suffer from constrained literature size, fragmented evidence, limited context windows, and weaker reasoning capabilities. Existing vanilla RAG pipelines do not adequately overcome these limitations, leading to suboptimal scientific QA. A better retrieval and structuring mechanism is needed to help SLMs access and integrate scientific evidence more effectively.

Method: The authors design Evidence-Grounded Typed Knowledge Graphs (EGT-KGs) that structure scientific evidence as typed entities and relations, grounded in the underlying literature. They test three QA settings for local SLMs on a domain-specific benchmark: (1) a standard RAG pipeline; (2) EGT-KG where the relation schema is automatically generated (AS); and (3) EGT-KG where the relation schema is defined by experts (ES). Performance is measured using a six-dimensional S3CRF evaluation framework (Soundness, Correctness, Completeness, Conciseness, Relevance, Fluency).

Result: On a Biopolymer-bound Soil Composite literature benchmark, both EGT-KG variants generally outperform vanilla RAG. Using llama3:8b, the AS and ES EGT-KG variants achieve Final Scores of 70.37 (+14.67%) and 68.82 (+12.14%), respectively, over the baseline, demonstrating significant gains in multi-dimensional QA quality.

Conclusion: Structuring domain literature into an Evidence-Grounded Typed Knowledge Graph substantially improves scientific question-answering with local SLMs compared to standard RAG. Both automatically generated and expert-defined relation schemas are effective, with the automatic schema slightly superior in reported experiments. EGT-KG offers a promising path to mitigate the constraints of local SLMs in emerging scientific domains.

Abstract: For emerging scientific research domains, local Small Language Models (SLMs) are becoming more attractive, as they offer stronger privacy control and more stable deployment pipelines than Large Language Models. However, in practice, scientific question-answering on SLMs often operates under inevitable constraints: small literature collections, fragmented evidence, limited context window and reasoning abilities. We propose the Evidence-Grounded Typed Knowledge Graph (EGT-KG), a retrieval framework to improve information retrieval with local SLMs. We assessed three question-answering settings: a vanilla Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) workflow and two EGT-KG workflows: an automatically generated relation schema (AS) and an expert-defined relation schema (ES). Our experiments were evaluated with a six-dimensional evaluation framework (S3CRF: Soundness, Correctness, Completeness, Conciseness, Relevance, Fluency) on a Biopolymer-bound Soil Composite literature benchmark, showing that EGT-KG outperforms the vanilla RAG method in most settings, with the best improvement from llama3:8b: a Final Score of 70.37 (+14.67%) and 68.82 (+12.14%) by AS/ES EGT-KG variants.

</details>


### [170] [The Privacy-Hallucination Tradeoff in Differentially Private Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00492)
*Krithika Ramesh,Krishna Pillutla,Danish Pruthi,Anjalie Field*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper reveals a tradeoff in differentially private language models: stronger privacy leads to more hallucinations, challenging their deployment in high-stakes domains like healthcare.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-stakes applications such as healthcare demand both strict privacy guarantees and high factual accuracy from language models, yet it is unclear how enforcing differential privacy affects hallucination behavior.

Method: The authors empirically compare DP and non-DP language models, analyze how DP noise affects output probability distributions, and run controlled experiments that vary the frequency of specific facts in the training data to test its impact on hallucinations.

Result: They find that DP-trained models hallucinate more than non-DP ones, with hallucinations worsening as the privacy budget becomes tighter; DP training flattens output distributions and shifts probability toward incorrect answers, while increasing the frequency of facts in the training data partially mitigates hallucinations.

Conclusion: Differential privacy mechanisms, as currently applied to language models, introduce a privacy–hallucination tradeoff, indicating a need for more refined privacy techniques that preserve both user privacy and factual reliability.

Abstract: Both privacy and factual accuracy are paramount in high-stakes domains like healthcare. Concerningly, we uncover and investigate a privacy-hallucination tradeoff in differentially private (DP) language models. First, we empirically show that models pre-trained or fine-tuned with DP tend to produce more hallucinations than non-DP counterparts, with increased severity as the privacy budget grows stricter. Second, we investigate model properties driving this tradeoff, demonstrating that DP mechanisms flatten output distributions, potentially redistributing probability mass toward factually incorrect alternatives. Third, through experiments where we control fact frequency in training data, we characterize how information frequency can reduce hallucination risks in DP models. Overall, our findings underscore the need for more nuanced privacy-preserving interventions that offer rigorous privacy guarantees without compromising factual accuracy.

</details>


### [171] [Validity-Aware Jailbreak Evaluation for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00498)
*Qilong Wu,Sahil Wadhwa,Pranab Mohanty,Giri Iyengar,Varun Chandrasekaran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces SEAV, a verification-centric framework that evaluates jailbreaks in LLMs by checking not only whether responses look like they comply with harmful instructions, but also whether they are factually and procedurally correct enough to truly advance harmful goals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing jailbreak evaluations focus on whether a model appears to follow harmful instructions, using refusal detection and semantic/intent matching. These methods often label responses as successful jailbreaks even when the provided instructions are incorrect or infeasible, because they emphasize linguistic plausibility instead of correctness. This inflates perceived vulnerability and fails to distinguish between superficial and genuinely dangerous jailbreaks. The authors aim to fill this gap by incorporating epistemic and procedural correctness into jailbreak robustness evaluation.

Method: The authors propose Sequential Epistemic and Action-Level Validation (SEAV). The approach decomposes a model’s response into ordered steps and evaluates each step along two axes: (1) epistemic validity (factual correctness, consistency, grounding in external knowledge) and (2) action-level validity (whether the step is operationally capable of advancing the harmful intent). SEAV uses LLM-as-a-judge components to parse and semantically interpret the response and combines this with retrieval-augmented verification against external knowledge sources. The framework is applied to multiple existing jailbreak benchmarks and a curated dataset, SD-A, that targets strategic dishonesty.

Result: On the SD-A benchmark, SEAV reduces the false positive rate of labeled jailbreak successes by 14.9 percentage points relative to the strongest existing baseline. When re-evaluating three of four public jailbreak benchmarks, SEAV reclassifies 22.1%–51.0% of previously labeled successful jailbreaks as invalid because they are factually or procedurally incorrect. The framework’s conclusions are robust across different search backends and evaluator models, indicating that the observed reclassification is not an artifact of a particular tooling choice.

Conclusion: Correctness-aware evaluation, as instantiated by SEAV, significantly changes the apparent robustness of LLMs to jailbreak attempts. Many responses previously considered successful jailbreaks do not actually provide correct, actionable, harm-enabling guidance. Incorporating stepwise epistemic and action-level validation yields a more accurate and conservative picture of real-world risk, and SEAV offers a practical, verification-centric methodology for future jailbreak robustness assessments. The authors release code and data to facilitate adoption and further research.

Abstract: Jailbreak robustness has become central to large language model (LLM) safety evaluation, yet prevailing methodologies rely primarily on refusal behavior, semantic resemblance, and intent-matching heuristics that emphasize linguistic plausibility rather than correctness. We identify a key limitation in existing evaluations: many jailbreak intents depend on instructional validity rather than epistemic factuality, allowing realistic-looking responses to be labeled successful despite being factually or procedurally incorrect. To address this gap, we propose Sequential Epistemic and Action-Level Validation (SEAV), a verification-centric jailbreak evaluation framework that decomposes responses into ordered steps and evaluates both validity and correctness. SEAV combines LLM-as-a-judge mechanisms for semantic interpretation with retrieval-grounded verification using external knowledge sources, assessing whether generated content is factually correct, structurally consistent, and operationally capable of advancing harmful objectives. Empirically, SEAV cuts the false-positive rate on SD-A (a curated strategic-dishonesty diagnostic) by 14.9\,pp vs. the strongest baseline, and reclassifies 22.1\%--51.0\% of sampled prior-labeled successes as invalid across three of four public benchmarks. Together, these results show that enforcing correctness substantially reshapes measured robustness: many previously labeled jailbreak successes are reclassified as invalid, and results are stable across the tested search backends and evaluator models. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Ardor-Wu/SEAV.

</details>


### [172] [Wave Function Backpropagation with Explicit Temporal-Interval Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00503)
*Byunggu Yu,Justin Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Wave Function Backpropagation (WFB), a neural network formulation where activations are parameterized as spatiotemporal waves, and shows it can improve trajectory prediction accuracy over standard feed-forward networks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard neural networks typically use affine transformations plus nonlinearities and treat time either as a simple feature or as uniformly sampled, which may underutilize temporal structure. The authors aim to build a learning formulation that more explicitly and smoothly links observed states to their actual time intervals, potentially improving predictions in temporally sensitive tasks like trajectory prediction.

Method: They represent each neural response as a differentiable spatiotemporal wave characterized by learnable amplitude, wavenumber, angular frequency, and phase. The temporal interval Δt is encoded via the phase of this wave. They derive backpropagation gradients for this wave-based parameterization, including a spatial-curvature correction using the Laplacian of the wave response, and instantiate the approach (WFB) in a controlled, purely feed-forward trajectory prediction model (no sequence modeling) to serve as a proof of concept. They compare several variants: standard WFB with real time intervals, WFB with shuffled intervals, and conventional ReLU-based feed-forward networks with and without explicit Δt features, under motion-feature and position-only setups.

Result: With motion features, standard WFB using real intervals reduces average displacement error (ADE) by 20.4% relative to the original FFN baseline. In a stricter position-only evaluation (no precomputed velocities/accelerations to avoid temporal leakage), real-interval WFB improves ADE by 10.4% over the original FFN and is competitive with parameter-matched ReLU controls, achieving 2.1% lower mean ADE than a matched FFN that explicitly uses Δt. A shuffled-interval WFB variant achieves the lowest mean ADE overall, suggesting the performance gain stems from the wave representation itself rather than from precise alignment of time intervals.

Conclusion: Wave Function Backpropagation provides a viable structured, wave-parameterized alternative to standard feed-forward neural network activations, explicitly linking states to time intervals via wave phase. Empirical results on trajectory prediction demonstrate consistent ADE improvements over conventional FFNs, but the best performance from shuffled intervals implies that the benefits come from the wave-based representation rather than temporal interval alignment per se. The work establishes WFB as a promising formulation and sets the stage for future architectural and sequence-learning extensions.

Abstract: Conventional neural networks learn predominantly through affine transformations followed by nonlinear activations, while elapsed time is often treated as an auxiliary feature or assumed to be uniformly sampled. This paper introduces Wave Function Backpropagation (WFB), a wave-parameterized learning formulation in which neural responses are represented by learnable amplitude, wavenumber, angular frequency, and phase. The formulation associates an observed state with its temporal interval Delta t through the phase of a differentiable spatiotemporal wave. We derive standard WFB gradients and a spatial-curvature correction based on the Laplacian of the wave response. WFB is instantiated in a deliberately feed-forward trajectory predictor to provide a controlled proof of concept; sequence learning is outside the scope of the present evaluation. With motion features, STD-WFB using real intervals reduces average displacement error (ADE) by 20.4% relative to the original FFN baseline. In a new position-only evaluation that removes temporal leakage through precomputed velocity and acceleration, real-interval WFB reduces ADE by 10.4% relative to the original FFN and remains competitive with parameter-matched ReLU controls, obtaining 2.1% lower mean ADE than the matched FFN with explicit Delta t. Shuffled-interval WFB attains the lowest mean ADE, indicating that the present evidence supports the effectiveness of the wave representation but does not attribute the gain to interval alignment. These results establish WFB as a viable structured feed-forward learning formulation and define a clear basis for subsequent architectural studies.

</details>


### [173] [CoVer: Conflict-Aware Claim Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00508)
*Shuning Zhang,Dai Shi,Bohao Chu,Hui Wang,Yuwei Chuai,Yifan Wang,Jingruo Chen,Simin Li,Xin Yi,Hewu Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce ContraNote, a large real-world dataset from X’s Community Notes for studying how to resolve conflicting evidence in social media fact-checking, and propose CoVer, a three-stage framework that prioritizes reliable evidence and outperforms existing methods on multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Social media fact-checking is hard because unreliable or misleading evidence can closely resemble authoritative sources, causing conflicts at the level of individual pieces of evidence and at the level of aggregated decisions. Existing benchmarks and methods do not fully capture or robustly address these real-world conflict scenarios, especially in settings like X’s Community Notes where many contributors and sources interact. The authors aim to provide both a realistic dataset and a method that can systematically adjudicate conflicts and highlight trustworthy evidence.

Method: They build ContraNote from X’s Community Notes: (1) a conflict subset with 33,686 posts focusing on resolving evidence-level conflicts, and (2) a prioritization subset with 54,474 instances targeting aggregation-level prioritization of notes. On top of this, they propose CoVer, a three-stage factual adjudication framework: (a) evidence schema normalization to convert heterogeneous evidence into a unified representation, (b) factual consensus modeling to infer which claims are most likely true given conflicting evidence, and (c) support verification to check how well each piece of evidence supports or contradicts the target claim. The pipeline explicitly emphasizes evidence quality and consistency, reducing the impact of noisy or misleading items.

Result: On ContraNote, CoVer attains 86.0% accuracy, 68.0 macro F1, and 64.5 balanced accuracy for the conflict-resolution task, and 88.5% accuracy, 88.5 macro F1, and 89.2 balanced accuracy for the prioritization task. It also achieves 88.4% accuracy on CONFACT-HumC and 89.4% accuracy on CONFACT-ModC, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines across these datasets.

Conclusion: ContraNote offers a large, realistic benchmark for studying evidence-level and aggregation-level conflicts in social media fact-checking, while CoVer provides an effective adjudication framework that prioritizes reliable evidence and mitigates noise. Their results indicate that structured, multi-stage reasoning over evidence can significantly improve conflict resolution and note prioritization compared to existing approaches, and the dataset plus framework can serve as a basis for future work in this area.

Abstract: Social media fact-checking has long been challenged by evidence-level and aggregation-level conflicts, where erroneous evidence mimics authoritative news sources. To capture this challenge and support conflict verification tasks, we present ContraNote, a large-scale real-world dataset curated from X's Community Notes system. It includes 33,686 posts for evaluating evidence-level conflict resolution, and 54,474 instances for evaluating aggregation-level prioritization. Additionally, we propose CoVer, a factual adjudication framework with three-stage pipelines: evidence schema normalization, factual consensus and support verification. This prioritizes evidence over noise to prevent it from compromising the final verdict. Technical evaluations show that CoVer achieves strong performance compared with state-of-the-art baselines across ContraNote (86.0% Acc., 68.0% mac. F1, 64.5 bal. Acc. on Conflict; and 88.5% Acc., 88.5 mac. F1 and 89.2 bal. Acc. on Prioritization), CONFACT-HumC (88.4% Acc.) and CONFACT-ModC (89.4% Acc.).

</details>


### [174] [When the Algorithm Becomes the Brand Crisis: A Sociotechnical Theory of Distributed Responsibility and Accountable Transparency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00510)
*Mohammad Saleh Torkestani,Taha Mansouri*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper builds a theory of how people assign responsibility and evaluate organizations when AI systems fail, distinguishing between incidents, crises, and scandals, and proposing a framework for transparent, accountable responses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing brand-crisis and responsibility-attribution models do not adequately explain how stakeholders assign responsibility when AI-related harms emerge from distributed sociotechnical systems involving multiple actors (developers, deployers, vendors, users, and the AI system itself). With AI increasingly mediating market interactions, there is a need to understand how responsibility, blame, and trust are formed and escalated in AI incidents.

Method: A conceptual, sociotechnical process theory is developed via a structured, federated scoping synthesis of verified academic and primary sources. The authors review and integrate literature on AI incidents, organizational crises, scandals, attribution theory, brand reactions, and human–algorithm interaction to construct a process-oriented framework.

Result: The paper distinguishes three levels of negative events: (1) AI/algorithmic incidents, (2) AI-related organizational crises, and (3) AI-related organizational scandals. It proposes that how an incident is configured (who is involved, what failed, visibility, controllability, etc.) shapes how different actors are blamed. These attributions then influence stakeholder appraisals of capability, integrity, fairness, and relationships. Public moralisation can escalate an incident into a scandal, but this escalation is not inevitable. The framework also reconciles mixed empirical findings: sometimes algorithm involvement buffers negative brand reactions; other times, visible failures of robots or chatbots focus blame on the firm. Finally, it identifies that current evidence is stronger for short- to medium-term psychological and evaluative outcomes (blame, trust, satisfaction, firm evaluation, communication credibility) than for long-term brand and financial outcomes.

Conclusion: Stakeholder responses to AI failures are shaped by a sociotechnical process in which incident configuration, responsibility attribution, and public moralisation interact. The paper argues that organizations should adopt "accountable transparency"—combining timely notification, clear explanations, acknowledgment of role-specific responsibilities, remediation, demonstrable fixes, and avenues for recourse—as a core response strategy. It cautions against overclaiming about long-term brand and market impacts from current evidence and offers a process framework for future empirical work on AI-related incidents, crises, and scandals.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence systems increasingly enact market-facing promises through chatbots, recommendation systems, automated decisions, and generative interfaces. Their failures, misuse, and misrepresentation raise a question that conventional brand-crisis models do not fully specify: how do stakeholders assign responsibility when technical causation, customer-facing control, and governance duties are distributed across an AI system, developer, deployer, vendor, and user? This conceptual paper develops a sociotechnical process theory from a structured, federated scoping synthesis of verified academic and primary sources. It distinguishes an AI/algorithmic incident from an AI-related organisational crisis and, in turn, from an AI-related organisational scandal. The framework proposes that incident configuration shapes actor-specific attribution; attribution informs capability, integrity, fairness, and relationship appraisals; and public moralisation may, but need not, escalate an incident into scandal. The theory offers a reconciliation of findings that algorithm involvement can buffer negative brand reactions in some settings while robot and chatbot failures can redirect responsibility to an associated firm in others. It introduces accountable transparency as a proposed response configuration that combines timely notice, an intelligible account, role-responsibility acknowledgement, remedy, evidence of correction, and recourse. The evidence supports conditional, proximal inferences about blame, trust, satisfaction, firm evaluation, and communication credibility more strongly than claims about durable reputation, brand equity, or market performance.

</details>


### [175] [ISO-RAG: Isoperimetric Noise Control for Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00513)
*Siyuan Zhang,Hanchen Wang,Dong Wen,Ying Zhang,Wenjie Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ISO-RAG is a geometry-aware RAG framework that improves multi-hop QA by pruning noisy graph edges via hyperbolic isoperimetric profiles, leading to more accurate and faster retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard dense retrieval often fails to follow complex multi-hop reasoning chains required for challenging QA tasks. Graph-based RAG can encode multi-step relations but suffers from semantic drift and high latency due to traversing large, noisy global graphs. There is a need for a method that preserves the benefits of graph reasoning while controlling noise and computational cost.

Method: ISO-RAG projects the underlying knowledge graph into a hyperbolic Poincaré ball, leveraging the geometry to compute an isoperimetric profile for each node. These profiles are used to detect and prune spurious or noisy edges, yielding a localized, topologically purified subgraph around the query. Retrieval is then performed by running Personalized PageRank (PPR) diffusion on this refined subgraph, enabling focused multi-hop exploration with guaranteed and efficient convergence.

Result: On multi-hop QA benchmarks, ISO-RAG achieves average absolute improvements of about 10.0% in retrieval recall and 4.3% in exact match over state-of-the-art baselines. It also reduces latency by avoiding expensive global graph traversals, yielding a better accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

Conclusion: Incorporating hyperbolic geometry and isoperimetric analysis into RAG enables more precise and efficient multi-hop retrieval. By pruning noisy edges and constraining PPR to localized subgraphs, ISO-RAG both improves answer accuracy and removes the main latency bottleneck of graph-based RAG, establishing a stronger framework for multi-hop question answering.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates large language models (LLMs) hallucinations, yet conventional dense retrieval struggles with the complex reasoning paths of multi-hop question answering (QA). Graph-based RAG captures multi-step relationships but suffers from severe semantic drift and high online latency due to noisy global graph traversals. Thus, we propose ISO-RAG (ISOperimetric Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a geometry-aware RAG framework. By projecting the underlying knowledge graph into a hyperbolic Poincare ball to precompute node-wise isoperimetric profiles, ISO-RAG prunes spurious edges during retrieval, restricting the search space to a strictly localized subgraph. This topological purification regulates Personalized PageRank (PPR) diffusion driving the retrieval process, ensuring exact and low-latency convergence. Experiments on multi-hop QA benchmarks demonstrate that ISO-RAG outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by average absolute gains of 10.0% in retrieval recall and 4.3% in downstream exact match, achieving a superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off by fundamentally eliminating the latency bottleneck of global traversals. Our source code is available at https://github.com/ZaiizaiZHANG/ISO-RAG.

</details>


### [176] [Feedback-Assisted Trust Propagation over Document Relation Graphs for Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00543)
*Zhuoheng Li,Ying Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TrustPropRAG improves reliability in retrieval-augmented generation by propagating human-anchored trust signals over a document relation graph to score documents and select more trustworthy evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG systems depend on external corpora that can be outdated, noisy, contradictory, or unreliable, which can cause untrustworthy answers. Existing methods that use document relations usually work only on directly compared pairs and do not effectively spread reliability information across the whole corpus. There is also a need to maximize the value of limited, expensive human feedback on document reliability by propagating it broadly and robustly.

Method: The authors construct a document relation graph where nodes are documents and edges encode relations (e.g., agreement, contradiction, similarity). They then formulate an optimization problem that integrates (1) pairwise relations between documents and (2) sparse human feedback on individual document reliability. Solving this optimization yields a trust score for each document via multi-hop propagation over the graph, effectively diffusing trust (and distrust) signals. These trust scores are then incorporated into the RAG pipeline for both improved document selection during retrieval and trust-aware answer generation.

Result: Empirical evaluations show that incorporating TrustPropRAG into RAG systems improves retrieval quality and exact match metrics compared to baseline methods that do not perform this graph-based trust propagation. The method is shown to maintain strong performance even when human feedback is sparse and when the feedback itself is noisy.

Conclusion: TrustPropRAG successfully leverages document relation graphs and limited human reliability feedback to infer trust scores for an entire corpus, leading to more reliable evidence selection and answer generation in RAG systems. Its robustness to sparse and noisy feedback suggests it is practical for real-world settings where high-quality annotations are scarce and costly.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems rely on external corpora that may contain outdated, contradictory, noisy, or unreliable documents, introducing reliability risks. Prior work has leveraged document relations to improve the answer reliability of RAG. To propagate reliability signals beyond directly compared document pairs, we propose TrustPropRAG, which structures document relations as a graph and estimates document reliability through multi-hop propagation across the graph. TrustPropRAG anchors this propagation with a limited set of human feedback on document reliability, extending these costly-to-collect feedback-based reliability signals across the whole corpus. Specifically, based on the constructed document relation graph, TrustPropRAG estimates a trust score for each document by formulating and solving an optimization problem that jointly captures pairwise document relations and user feedback. These scores are then used to improve the selection of reliable documents and support trust-aware answer generation. Evaluation results show that TrustPropRAG improves both retrieval quality and exact match over baselines, and remains robust under sparse and noisy feedback.

</details>


### [177] [VoiceLongMemEval: Do Assistants Remember How You Sounded?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00570)
*Ramit Pahwa,Parivesh Priye,Apoorva Beedu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce VoiceLongMemEval, a benchmark for testing AI assistants’ long-term conversational reasoning that crucially depends on paralinguistic (non-verbal vocal) cues, not just text, and show existing models miss this affective information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing long-context dialogue benchmarks focus on what was said (content, facts, temporal relations) and largely ignore how it was said (emotion, prosody, vocal events). However, in realistic multi-session human–agent interactions, non-verbal vocal information is essential for correct understanding, memory, and reasoning, especially over long histories. Current systems and ASR pipelines often discard such signals, and we lack standardized evaluation to expose this weakness.

Method: They build VoiceLongMemEval (VLME), a benchmark where each question-answer pair in a long, multi-session conversation requires using attached paralinguistic metadata (emotion labels, prosodic descriptors, and voice-event tags) for the correct answer; the text alone is insufficient. Items are filtered through a three-stage adversarial process that ensures strong LLMs fail when only seeing the transcript. They then evaluate leading frontier and open-weight models under several conditions: with and without paralinguistic metadata, with evidence-hint prompting, and (for audio-native models) directly from speech instead of text+metadata.

Result: They find a consistent “affect gap”: models perform substantially worse when deprived of paralinguistic cues. Adding text-track paralinguistic metadata boosts accuracy by 0.09–0.38, and with evidence-hint prompts the absolute scores range roughly from 0.61 to 0.69. Conventional ASR pipelines, which drop these cues, systematically underperform. Audio-native models that operate on raw speech can infer these cues themselves, improving accuracy from 0.325 (blind to paralinguistics) to 0.354–0.412.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates that non-verbal vocal information is critical for long-term conversational reasoning and that current text-only benchmarks and ASR-centric pipelines hide a major weakness in deployed assistants. VoiceLongMemEval offers a targeted benchmark to measure and drive progress on using paralinguistic signals, and shows that incorporating or directly modeling these cues yields significant gains, motivating future architectures and pipelines that retain and exploit affective and prosodic information.

Abstract: With the growing scale of multi-agent architectures and large language models, deployed AI assistants are increasingly tasked with reasoning over long, continuous, multi-session conversation histories. Current benchmarks evaluate this dialogue history as information retrieval over long horizon, temporal reasoning, or knowledge updates, while crucially ignoring the fundamental dynamics of human-agent interaction, i.e. how they said it. To address this gap, we present VoiceLongMemEval (VLME) benchmark, where every answer depends on paralinguistic metadata (emotion labels, prosody descriptors, and voice events) attached to conversational turns, which is otherwise unrecoverable from the words alone. Every item passes a three-stage adversarial gate, ensuring that a strong language model fails when given only the transcript. Evaluating leading frontier and open-weight models reveals a pervasive affect gap; providing text-track paralinguistic metadata yields a 0.09 to 0.38 accuracy boost (0.61 to 0.69 when prompted with evidence hints), while standard ASR pipelines systematically discard this signal. Additionally, audio-native models successfully extract these cues directly from speech (0.354 to 0.412 vs. 0.325 blind). Code and dataset will be made available upon acceptance.

</details>


### [178] [Residual Sparsification via Output Importance for Compressing Mixture-of-Experts LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00575)
*Seungwoo Jung,Dohyeok Kwon,Seungmin Cha,Junseok Lee,Yeonho Yoo,Chuck Yoo,Gyeongsik Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies a mismatch between current residual sparsification objectives and actual model accuracy in MoE LLMs, and proposes PARSER, a method that sparsifies residuals by directly minimizing expert output error using an output-importance measure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mixture-of-experts language models scale parameters efficiently but require huge GPU memory, leading practitioners to compress models. A popular approach, residual sparsification, decomposes expert projection matrices into shared bases and per-expert residuals, then compresses the residuals. Existing methods treat each residual independently and minimize per-matrix reconstruction error, assuming that small matrix errors imply small impact on model accuracy. However, in MoE experts, multiple projections and hidden representations interact; errors propagate and can significantly distort expert outputs even when each matrix is well-approximated. This creates a misalignment between the compression objective and what really matters: preserving expert outputs and thus model accuracy. The paper is motivated by the need to realign compression objectives with output-level behavior while keeping the same memory savings.

Method: The authors first analyze how errors in individual expert projection matrices propagate through the layers and hidden states of MoE experts, showing that minimizing isolated residual reconstruction errors is not equivalent to minimizing expert output error. Based on this, they propose PARSER, a residual sparsification method that changes the compression objective from per-matrix fidelity to expert-output preservation. PARSER introduces an output-importance measure, quantifying how much each component of the residuals contributes to the final expert output error. This importance-guided criterion is then used to sparsify/compress residual matrices such that elements with greater influence on the expert output are preserved with higher fidelity, while less important components are more aggressively pruned or quantized, all under the same memory budget as existing residual sparsification techniques.

Result: In experiments on MoE-based large language models, including Qwen and DeepSeek, PARSER is evaluated against existing residual sparsification methods under equal peak memory reduction constraints. The results show that PARSER better preserves model accuracy after compression: it reduces the performance gap to the uncompressed baseline by a factor of 1.41× on Qwen and 1.44× on DeepSeek. This demonstrates that an output-aware sparsification objective leads to significantly smaller accuracy degradation than traditional per-matrix error minimization approaches, without sacrificing memory savings.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that traditional residual sparsification for MoE language models is suboptimal because it optimizes per-matrix reconstruction error rather than the expert output behavior that directly affects model accuracy. By explicitly modeling how compression-induced errors propagate through experts and by introducing an output-importance metric, PARSER realigns the compression objective with preserving expert outputs. Empirical results on large MoE LLMs show that PARSER substantially narrows the accuracy gap to full-precision models at the same memory reduction level, indicating that output-aware compression is a more effective strategy for scaling MoE models under tight GPU memory budgets.

Abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures scale large language models efficiently, but they demand massive GPU memory. To cope with such demand, models are commonly compressed to reduce their memory footprint. Residual sparsification is a representative compression technique that decomposes each projection matrix of an expert into a shared base matrix and per-expert residual matrix, and then compresses the residuals. Existing sparsification methods compress each residual matrix independently by minimizing its compression error, thereby minimizing the error of each projection matrix. However, our analysis shows that this objective is misaligned with preserving model accuracy after compression. In an expert, the final output is produced through computations coupled across multiple projections and hidden representations. Therefore, even small errors in individual matrices can propagate through hidden representations and projection interactions, leading to large expert output errors and accuracy degradation. To address this misalignment, we propose PARSER, a new residual sparsification method that shifts the compression objective from minimizing isolated matrix errors to preserving the expert output error. PARSER achieves this by introducing output importance, which measures the actual contribution to the expert output error. Our experiments show that, compared with existing methods, PARSER narrows the accuracy gap to the uncompressed model by 1.41$\times$ on Qwen and 1.44$\times$ on DeepSeek, while achieving the same peak memory reduction.

</details>


### [179] [Consistency Without Alignment: Item-Sensitive Language Models Indistinguishable From Random](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00576)
*Cris Huynh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper shows that item-sensitivity (responses varying with inputs) is not sufficient evidence of true task competence in language models, by using a controlled signalling game where optimal and random strategies are analytically known. Many models look item-sensitive but perform no better or worse than random, and simple literal baselines often outperform them.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluation of language models often treats item-sensitivity or internal consistency (e.g., permutation or self-consistency) as evidence that the model understands or is competent at a task. The authors question this assumption and aim to demonstrate that such behavioural patterns can arise without genuine alignment to the task’s intended target quantity. They seek a setting where they can formally characterise optimal, posterior-maximising, and random behaviour to rigorously test the link between item-sensitivity and task competence.

Method: The authors abstract a forced-choice signalling task from the board game Deception: Murder in Hong Kong into a controlled environment where the Bayesian-optimal (posterior-maximising) strategy, a fit-maximising strategy, and uniform random choice can all be expressed in closed form. They evaluate seven language models from two model families, including a post-training ablation, under three independent scoring rules. For each model-rule combination (21 cells), they measure item-sensitivity and compare performance to analytically known reference strategies. They also test baselines: a literal-similarity chooser with no pragmatics, pragmatic layers on top of similarity sources, and a standard labelled multiple-choice format. The study is pre-registered and they design a matched human condition (not yet collected).

Result: All 21 model-by-rule cells display reliable item-sensitivity, meaning model choices vary with input items. However, 8 of these are not statistically distinguishable from a random chooser that ignores the item, and 5 perform worse than random at identifying or describing the target. The correlation between item-sensitivity and distance from random performance is low (r = 0.30). A literal-similarity baseline without pragmatic reasoning outperforms most language models. When pragmatic layers are added over similarity sources, model behaviour drifts toward randomness rather than the Bayesian-optimal reference. Moreover, using a standard labelled multiple-choice format does not reveal any measurable content signal in this setting.

Conclusion: Item-sensitivity, permutation consistency, and self-consistency are necessary but not sufficient evidence for task competence or alignment with intended evaluation targets in language models. Models can exhibit stable, consistent behaviour that is nonetheless unaligned with the correct signal—what the authors term “consistency without alignment.” Evaluations relying solely on such behavioural signatures, without an independent reference for the underlying quantity (e.g., true posterior or optimal strategy), may overestimate model understanding. Simple non-pragmatic baselines can outperform complex models, and naive attempts to add pragmatics can degrade performance. The work calls for evaluation designs that include explicit, interpretable references and that test distance from random or optimal behaviour, rather than relying only on internal consistency metrics.

Abstract: Item-sensitivity, defined as whether a model's choice depends on the specific input rather than on its own output prior, is widely reported as evidence of task competence. We show this evidence is necessary but not sufficient using a forced-choice signalling task abstracted from the board game Deception: Murder in Hong Kong. In this environment, the reference points against which a coordinate should be judged (a fit-maximising strategy, a posterior-maximising strategy, and uniform random selection) are all computable in closed form. Across seven language models, two model families, a post-training ablation, and three independent scoring rules, every one of 21 model-by-rule cells is reliably item-sensitive. Yet 8 of those 21 cells are not statistically distinguishable from a chooser that ignores the item and selects at random, and 5 score worse than random at describing the target. Item-sensitivity and distance from random correlate at only r = 0.30.
