We call this consistency without alignment and argue it generalises to any evaluation that relies on item-sensitivity, permutation consistency, or self-consistency without an independent reference for the measured quantity. We further find that a literal-similarity baseline with no pragmatics outperforms most tested language models, that adding a pragmatic layer over two baseline similarity sources moves choosers toward random rather than toward the Bayesian reference, and that a standard labelled multiple-choice format carries no measurable content signal here. All results represent the model side of a pre-registered instrument; a matched human condition is designed and piloted but not yet collected.

</details>


### [180] [Same Request, Different Boundary: Evaluating Cybersecurity Assistance across Conversational Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00578)
*Rui Yang,Yang Hong,Yichao Xu,Zhengyu Liu,Ziyang Li,Yinzhi Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: 3R-Bench evaluates how prior conversational context affects LLM safety/compliance on cybersecurity queries, showing large shifts in model behavior depending on earlier dialogue.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the gap in cybersecurity safety evaluation benchmarks that ignore conversational context, and to understand how LLMs can simultaneously avoid harmful assistance and still support legitimate cybersecurity use.

Method: The authors build 3R-Bench, a benchmark of 150 real-world cybersecurity requests, each embedded into two adversarial conversational settings (refusal vs acceptance history and dialogue decomposition). They then test eight LLMs on these settings, measuring changes in compliance rates and the effect of failure feedback.

Result: Assistant behavior is highly path-dependent: for 376 comparable pairs, compliance jumps from 62.0% after a refusal history to 85.1% after an accepted history. Under dialogue decomposition, direct compliance of 501/800 falls sharply to 172/800 after being placed in multi-turn dialogue, and across 738 comparable pairs the average compliance drops by 45.1 percentage points. Failure feedback recovers only a small portion of the lost compliance.

Conclusion: Conversational context has a strong impact on LLM safety and compliance in cybersecurity assistance, revealing vulnerabilities that are invisible to single-turn benchmarks. 3R-Bench provides a more realistic and challenging evaluation setting, and results show that current models remain brittle to adversarial dialogue structures and prior interaction history, with standard failure feedback only partially mitigating these issues.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can solve complex problems, but their misuse in high-risk domains can lead to severe consequences. Model providers therefore restrict assistance for potentially harmful requests. Refusing all cybersecurity requests would therefore harm legitimate users. Providers need a mechanism to block malicious use without denying legitimate assistance to defenders. Existing cybersecurity-specific datasets evaluate this mechanism, but none considers the conversational context of a request. We introduce 3R-Bench (Refusal, Repetition, and Revision), a benchmark of 150 real-world cybersecurity requests augmented with two adversarial conversational settings, and evaluate eight LLMs on it. Prior assistant behavior strongly changes responses to an unchanged request: among 376 available pairs from a 400-pair panel, compliance rises from 62.0% after refused history to 85.1% after accepted history. The opposite pattern appears under dialogue decomposition. In comparison, compliance falls from 501/800 direct responses to 172/800 after dialogue; among 738 pairs returning model-authored text in both conditions, the decrease is 45.1 points. Failure feedback recovers only a small fraction of this loss.

</details>


### [181] [Socrates went Nuclear: Comparing Interaction Strategies for AI systems in a Learning Context using Brain Sensing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00584)
*Alexandre Clin Deffarges,Nataliya Kosmyna,Pattie Maes*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper compares three AI-based learning support modes and finds that an unrestricted chatbot yields higher immediate test gains, while a brain-signal–driven adaptive tutor elicits more cognitive engagement, indicating that higher scores may not reflect deeper learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand whether easy access to powerful AI tools like unrestricted chatbots promotes or undermines meaningful learning, and to compare them against more pedagogically constrained or cognitively adaptive systems.

Method: Fifty participants with no prior knowledge of nuclear safety protocols completed an instructional video, a pre-test, an AI-driven assessment phase, and an immediate post-test. They were randomly assigned to: (1) an unrestricted conversational chatbot, (2) a Socratic chatbot that provided hints without final answers, or (3) a non-conversational adaptive tutor that adjusted task difficulty in real time based on EEG-derived cognitive engagement measured via a Muse headband. Performance (pre/post tests), EEG engagement, and interaction patterns were analyzed, including a cluster analysis of chatbot usage.

Result: Participants using the unrestricted chatbot showed significantly higher learning gains than those using either the Socratic chatbot or the EEG-adaptive tutor (p < .03, effect sizes d > 0.80). However, the adaptive tutor condition elicited significantly higher EEG-based engagement (p = .018). Usage analysis revealed that most unrestricted-mode users relied heavily on direct answer retrieval, whereas Socratic-mode users initially tried to reason with hints but tended to disengage over time.

Conclusion: Unrestricted AI support can boost immediate post-test performance, likely by enabling direct answer retrieval rather than promoting deeper understanding. In contrast, cognitively adaptive systems may foster higher engagement without translating into superior short-term test gains. Therefore, higher scores with unrestricted AI should not be interpreted as evidence of deeper learning, and evaluation designs must consider both engagement and long-term learning, not just immediate test performance.

Abstract: Does unrestricted AI access bypass the cognitive effort required for learning, or does it streamline knowledge acquisition? This paper reports on a study where we compare three designs for user-AI interaction in a learning context: (1) an unrestricted conversational bot like ChatGPT, (2) a pedagogically constrained bot that guides through hints without giving final answers, which we refer to as the Socratic mode; and (3) a non-conversational adaptive tutoring system that adjusts difficulty in real-time based on the user's cognitive engagement derived from the brain signals. Fifty study participants were tasked with learning about nuclear safety protocols, a domain chosen for its zero-prior knowledge baseline. The participants progressed through an instructional video, a pre-test, an AI-driven assessment phase, which varied in the three conditions, and an immediate post-test. The nature of the questions centered primarily on factual knowledge acquisition, but it still required participants to have a global understanding of the concepts in order to answer the questions correctly. A Muse headband was used to derive the cognitive engagement of all users in all conditions. The unrestricted chatbot produced higher learning gains (delta) than both constrained modes (p < .03, d > 0.80), while the adaptive condition generated significantly higher EEG engagement (p = .018). The cluster analysis of chatbot usage and discussion patterns by users showed that most participants in the unrestricted-mode adopted a direct answer-retrieval strategy, while participants in the Socratic-mode initially attempted to reason through the hints before progressively disengaging. Consequently, this also suggests that the success of the unrestricted AI is not an evidence of deeper learning, but rather a result of the immediate post-test evaluation after the training phase.

</details>


### [182] [Control-Data Flow Separation: Stable Prompt Optimization in Multi-Agent LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00621)
*Wentao Zhang,Syed Shariyar Murtaza,Junaid Ahmad Bhatti,Utkarsh Soni,Yifan Nie,Eugene Wen,Yuntian Deng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes separating execution-critical control logic from task content in multi-agent LLM systems to make prompt optimization safe and robust.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multi-agent LLM systems, prompts simultaneously define both task-specific content behavior and execution protocols (e.g., routing, formatting, termination). Optimizing such prompts to improve task performance can unintentionally break protocol specifications, causing whole pipelines to fail. The authors aim to enable safe prompt optimization that improves performance without risking protocol corruption.

Method: The authors introduce a design principle called control-data flow separation. Execution-critical protocol information (control) is extracted from natural language prompts and represented as typed, validated program objects. Task-relevant language remains as the data flow exchanged between agents and is the only part exposed to prompt optimization. They then construct a framework that enforces protocol validity via types/validation while allowing optimizers to freely modify the natural-language components.

Result: In experiments spanning synthetic reasoning tasks, collaborative review generation, and real-world style insurance rating workflows, the proposed framework maintains 100% eventual protocol validity (i.e., agent communications continue to satisfy required routing and formatting constraints) while still improving task performance metrics under prompt optimization.

Conclusion: Separating control and data flows in multi-agent LLM systems enables safe and effective prompt optimization. By encoding execution protocols as structured, validated program-level objects and restricting optimization to task-relevant language, the framework prevents prompt drift from breaking system interfaces, while consistently enhancing task-level outcomes across multiple domains.

Abstract: Prompt optimization can improve multi-agent LLM systems, but the prompts being optimized often serve two entangled roles: generating task-relevant content and specifying execution-critical protocols, such as message routing, output formatting, and termination signals, on which the underlying code relies. As a result, a prompt edit intended to improve content generation can inadvertently corrupt the protocol and cause the entire agent pipeline to fail. Our key observation is that these two roles have different representations: execution protocols are typically structured, while task-relevant content is usually expressed in unstructured language. Based on this, we propose control-data flow separation, where execution-critical control is represented as typed, validated program objects, while task-relevant language remains the optimizable data flow for agent communication. This design allows optimizers to improve multi-agent behavior without exposing the routing or formatting interface to prompt drift. Across synthetic reasoning, collaborative review generation, and insurance rating workflows, our framework empirically achieves 100% eventual protocol validity while consistently improving task performance.

</details>


### [183] [REVISE: Validity-Guided Recovery for Online Revisions in Agent Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00643)
*Ruoling Qi,Xuaner Wu,Penghang Liu,Jian Chen,Yirui Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Revise is a runtime system that enables fine-grained, correctness-preserving recovery for concurrent agent workflows after revisions, redoing only truly affected work instead of restarting or recomputing long suffixes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Concurrent AI agent workflows often receive revisions (e.g., new user messages or code changes) while previous steps are still running. Existing recovery strategies either waste work by restarting from an early conflict or risk using stale intermediate results by allowing work to continue. There is a need for a runtime that more precisely identifies which parts of the computation become invalid when a revision occurs, to balance correctness with efficiency in real deployments.

Method: Revise instruments structured agent workflows as a DAG and records data and control dependencies during execution. When a revision arrives, it computes the revision’s delta and intersects it with the recorded dependencies to determine which nodes in the partially executed DAG are affected. It then: (1) stops invalid work, (2) preserves and reuses valid progress beyond the earliest conflict, and (3) recomputes only the affected region. If provenance is incomplete, it conservatively enlarges the recovery region, and all reused results are revalidated before commit to avoid stale outputs or tool effects.

Result: Empirical evaluation on real coding-agent traces shows significant opportunities for online recovery, with many sessions having overlapping work and queued messages. In 300 challenging revision/commit scenarios, Revise achieves the same behavior as a latest-version oracle, with no stale outputs or effects. On existing LangGraph and LLMCompiler-based applications with Qwen3-14B, Revise reduces model calls by 40.6–56.0% compared to full restart and by 31.3–43.6% compared to suffix recomputation. Under serving load, it cuts revision-to-correct-completion tokens by 13.26% and increases SLO goodput by 3.07–5.43%.

Conclusion: Revise demonstrates that validity-guided, fine-grained recovery in structured agent workflows can reconcile correctness with efficiency. By leveraging dependency-aware impact analysis and selective recomputation, it avoids both unnecessary restarts and stale-state propagation, leading to large reductions in model calls and improved service-level metrics while maintaining latest-version correctness.

Abstract: Agent revisions expose a fundamental correctness--efficiency trade-off during concurrent execution. Discarding ongoing work preserves latest-version correctness but wastes progress that may remain valid, whereas reusing prior work preserves efficiency but risks propagating stale state into outputs and tool effects. Existing recovery strategies resolve this trade-off in an imbalanced way with coarse-grained policies: they either favor efficiency by allowing potentially stale work to continue, or favor correctness by restarting the workflow or recomputing a linear suffix from the earliest conflict, thereby discarding unaffected progress. We present \textsc{Revise}, a validity-guided runtime for fine-grained recovery in structured agent workflows. When a revision arrives, \textsc{Revise} first intersects its delta with recorded data and control dependencies and propagates the resulting impact through the partially executed DAG to identify affected work. It then stops invalid work, preserves validity-established progress beyond the earliest conflict, and recomputes only the affected region. Incomplete provenance conservatively expands recovery, while reused results are revalidated before commit. Analysis of real coding-agent traces show online recovery opportunities: 118 sessions retain observable work before a queued later message is delivered; across 167 overlapping assistant responses, enqueue-to-completion overlap reaches 56.55~s at p95. Across 300 challenging revision/commit executions, \textsc{Revise} matches a latest-version oracle with no stale outputs or effects. On unmodified LangGraph and LLMCompiler applications using Qwen3-14B, it reduces model calls by 40.6--56.0\% relative to full restart and by 31.3--43.6\% relative to suffix recomputation. Under serving pressure, it further reduces revision-to-correct-completion tokens by 13.26\% and improves SLO goodput by 3.07--5.43\%.

</details>


### [184] [DramaChain Bench: An End-to-End Benchmark for Short-Drama Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00646)
*Haoyuan Shi,Mingtao Chen,Shuo Jiang,Ziyan Chen,Xuyi Sheng,Yiming Liu,Ying Zhang,Miao Wang,Jianxiang Lu,Fanyang Lu,Songyuanyi Lu,Xiele Wu,Zhichao Hu,Yuhong Liu,Richeng Xuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DramaChain Bench is a benchmark for evaluating the entire short‑drama production pipeline, not just video generation, with human and agentic evaluations across many fine-grained dimensions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing short‑drama and video benchmarks mostly evaluate only the final video-generation step using pre-authored, idealized prompts. This makes it impossible to know (1) whether each production stage remains faithful to the original script rather than just the immediately preceding stage, and (2) whether multiple shots and episodes are coherent when assembled. The authors want a realistic, end‑to‑end benchmark that reflects how commercial short dramas are actually produced and where errors originate and propagate.

Method: They construct DramaChain Bench, a multi-stage benchmark aligned with a real commercial-style production workflow: script → storyboard → keyframe images → shot-level videos → final short dramas. They design DramaChain Dimensions, a shared evaluation framework of five high-level axes expanded into 63 leaf dimensions, applied consistently at each stage. They build DramaChain Agent, an in-house production system calibrated to commercial platforms to serve as a reference for fair stage-wise comparison across models. For human evaluation, DramaChain Labeling System has three professional annotators independently score each of 5,785 items using a predefined defect list, localizing defects in space and time; this yields 17,488 valid scores and over 255k traceable defect-attribution records. Finally, they design DramaChain Agentic Judge, an automatic multi-round agent-based evaluation system that collects evidence, checks per-item checklists, and outputs scores for all leaf dimensions.

Result: Human annotations show that defects in upstream stages (e.g., script, storyboard) systematically propagate to later stages, indicating that final episode quality depends on the entire pipeline, not just video generation. DramaChain Bench provides a dense dataset of localized defect labels and attribution chains across 5,785 items, 17,488 scores, and 255,925 defect records. The automatic DramaChain Agentic Judge closely replicates human/model rankings, achieving a mean PLCC of 0.918 with respect to human annotations, enabling benchmark extension without additional human labeling cost.

Conclusion: Evaluating short-drama generation solely at the video stage is insufficient: upstream stages critically influence the final result, and their defects cascade through the pipeline. DramaChain Bench offers the first comprehensive, multi-stage benchmark for short-drama production, with a unified dimension system, professional human annotation, and an agentic automatic judge that approximates human rankings well. This framework supports fair, realistic comparison of multi-stage models and allows scalable, low-cost admission of new models into the benchmark.

Abstract: Commercial short-drama production follows a multi-stage chain: script, storyboard, keyframe imagery, shot-level video, and the finished short drama. Most existing benchmarks evaluate solely the video-generation stage using pre-authored inputs instead of real upstream pipeline outputs. This leaves two critical questions unanswerable: whether each stage adheres to the original script intent (rather than only its immediate input prompt), and whether disparate shots remain coherent after assembly into multi-episode releases. We present DramaChain Bench, the first short-drama benchmark that evaluates every stage of the complete production chain. It is built upon three in-house systems sharing one dimension system, DramaChain Dimensions: five evaluation axes instantiated at every stage, resolving into 63 leaf dimensions. DramaChain Agent is calibrated against commercial short-drama platforms in both workflow and finished short-drama quality, enabling stage-wise fair comparison across models. DramaChain Labeling System has each of the 5,785 items scored independently by three professional annotators, with all defects spatio-temporally localised and selected from a predefined defect list. This process produces 17,488 valid scores and 255,925 traceable attribution records. The human annotations confirm that upstream defects cascade across the pipeline, demonstrating that final episode quality is not governed by video generation alone. DramaChain Agentic Judge then scores every leaf dimension automatically, gathering evidence over multiple agentic rounds before judging against a per-item checklist; it reproduces the model ranking at a mean PLCC of 0.918, enough to admit new models at no annotation cost.

</details>


### [185] [Self-Reports Are Not Verification: Environment-Grounded Auditing of LLM Operators in Evolutionary Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00652)
*Enrong Pan,Ryan Zhou,Ting Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how reliable language model agents’ self-reported confidence and rationales are, using a fully measurable game environment, and finds that these self-reports are systematically unreliable and should not be trusted without external verification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As language model agents are increasingly used to take actions and explain their reasoning, practitioners often rely on the models’ own confidence scores and verbal rationales as convenient indicators of correctness or reliability. However, these signals are not themselves verified against ground truth, and there is little systematic evidence about how well they correspond to actual performance in a setting where all intermediate steps can be objectively evaluated. The paper aims to rigorously test common assumptions about calibration, the utility of rationales, and the value of selection mechanisms in agentic setups.

Method: The authors design an “environment-grounded audit” using the word game Contexto, where every guess receives an exact rank indicating proximity to the target word. A language model runs an evolutionary search over guesses, getting precise feedback for each. Across 200 runs, five reporting configurations, and three model families, the system collects 12,249 instances of model self-reports (confidence estimates and explanations). They test three assumptions: (1) that stated confidence is calibrated to actual success probabilities, (2) that inherited rationales passed between steps influence or improve later proposals, and (3) that fitness-based selection of agent trajectories improves the quality of self-reports. They also perform controlled interventions on 754 inherited rationales to isolate their contribution and analyze selection dynamics by comparing fitness-based and random selection regimes.

Result: All three tested assumptions are empirically falsified. The agents’ operators (the models) systematically overstate their likelihood of achieving top-100 success by factors between 4.8 and 9.3. Calibration (how well confidence matches true success rate) and discrimination (ability to rank easier vs harder cases) vary and can dissociate across model families. Interventions on inherited rationales show that any genuine benefit of these rationales is small, capped at about 250 ranks in the Contexto feedback, suggesting limited causal impact on performance. Furthermore, neither fitness-based evolutionary selection nor random selection yields a detectable improvement in the accuracy of self-reports, and there is no evidence of accuracy being reliably transmitted from parent to offspring in the evolutionary process, even though these regimes produce very different search behaviors.

Conclusion: Language model agents’ self-reported confidence and rationales are unreliable indicators of their actual performance in a fully auditable environment. They are overconfident, poorly calibrated, and show limited causal benefit from rationales or selection mechanisms with respect to report accuracy. As a result, such self-reports should be treated merely as claims that require independent verification against objective environmental feedback, not as trustworthy evidence of an agent’s own reliability or correctness.

Abstract: Language model agents increasingly propose actions, observe external feedback, and explain their own behavior. Their confidence and rationales are convenient monitoring signals, but convenience is not verification. We introduce an environment-grounded audit in which every intermediate proposal receives an exact outcome. A language model operates an evolutionary Contexto search whose feedback function assigns every valid guess an exact rank without human annotation. Across 200 runs spanning five configurations and three model families, four reporting configurations produce 12,249 self-reports. We test three assumptions: stated confidence is calibrated, inherited rationales affect later proposals, and fitness-based selection improves report quality. All three fail. Operators overstate top-100 success by factors of 4.8 to 9.3, while calibration and discrimination dissociate across model families. Controlled interventions on 754 inherited rationales bound any measured benefit of the genuine rationale to roughly 250 ranks. Neither fitness-based nor random selection produces a detectable selection differential or parent-to-offspring transmission in report accuracy, despite sharply different search behavior. Agent self-reports should therefore be treated as claims to verify against the environment, not as evidence of their own reliability.

</details>


### [186] [SciTrue: Reliable Scientific Claim Validation with Frontier and Open Language Models at the NTCIR SciClaimEval Task](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00654)
*Qiming Bao,Neşet Özkan Tan,Siyuan Wang,Mark Gahegan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SciTrue benchmarks 11 multimodal models for scientific claim verification and wins NTCIR-19 SciClaimEval mainly via clever pairing logic and handling of dataset artifacts, not heavy model tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper aims to understand what actually drives performance on the NTCIR-19 SciClaimEval task, which involves verifying scientific claims against figures and tables. Instead of focusing on building or heavily tuning a single model, the authors want to assess how far existing frontier and open models can go under a fair, comparable protocol and to identify non-obvious factors—like task formulation, pairing structure, and dataset artifacts—that affect leaderboard performance.

Method: They evaluate eleven frontier and open multimodal LMs under a single, honest, per-sample evaluation protocol on both subtasks of SciClaimEval. They keep model usage simple, then apply light, transparent post-processing. A key method is a ‘leak-free pair prior’ that predicts the Supported/Refuted pairing from the claim text alone and then assigns the Supported label to whichever evidence the model scores with higher confidence. They also conduct controlled experiments with fine-tuning, distillation, and agent-style consistency checks, and perform a detailed error audit to distinguish genuine model failures from label noise or label-mapping issues. Additionally, they investigate a measurement leak via file ordering that encodes labels.

Result: On the blind test leaderboard, their SciTrue system ranks first in three out of four evidence-category/subtask combinations and ties for first on the primary metric in the remaining one. Strong instruction-tuned models such as Claude Opus 4.8, Gemma-4-31B, GPT-5.5, and Claude Fable 5 outperform or match the strongest public baseline (o4-mini), with GPT-5.5 and Claude Fable 5 leading both subtasks and achieving 97.7 on Subtask 2. The leak-free pair prior dramatically boosts Subtask 1 pair accuracy from 72.2 to 93.5, a much larger gain than any change of base model or ensemble strategy. Their audits show that many of the remaining errors stem from visually invisible label-mapping swaps and dataset label noise, implying that measured error rates overstate the models’ true limitations.

Conclusion: High leaderboard performance on SciClaimEval is driven less by exotic modeling and more by exploiting the task’s pairing structure and being robust to dataset artifacts and measurement leaks. Strong general-purpose, instruction-tuned multimodal models already perform at or beyond the best baselines with minimal task-specific tuning, and further model sophistication offers limited marginal gains compared to leveraging the pair prior. Because a substantial portion of residual errors trace back to label noise or mapping issues, there is relatively little true headroom left that better modeling alone can capture. The authors caution that evaluation pipelines can inadvertently leak label information, as seen in the file-ordering issue, and stress the need for leak-free benchmarks and transparent protocols when claiming progress.

Abstract: We describe the SciTrue team's participation in both subtasks of the NTCIR-19 SciClaimEval task~\cite{sciclaimeval}, which asks systems to verify scientific claims against the tables and figures of a paper. Rather than tuning a single model, we benchmark eleven frontier and open multimodal models under one honest, per-sample protocol and combine them with light, transparent post-processing. On the official, blind test leaderboard (Section~\ref{sec:results}), SciTrue placed first by a clear margin in three of the four evidence-category/subtask combinations, and tied for first on the primary metric in the fourth. Three findings explain the result. First, strong instruction-tuned models are already competitive: Claude Opus~4.8 and Gemma-4-31B each exceed the strongest public baseline (o4-mini), and GPT-5.5 and Claude Fable~5 lead both subtasks (97.7 on Subtask~2). Second, the task's pairing structure is the largest lever: a \emph{leak-free pair prior} that recovers the Supported/Refuted pairing from the claim text alone (a visible field) and assigns Supported to the higher-confidence evidence raises Subtask-1 pair-accuracy from 72.2 to 93.5, far more than any model swap or ensemble weighting. Third, a case-by-case audit finds that most residual errors are visually-undetectable label-mapping swaps or dataset label noise, so measured accuracy understates the true ability and the fixable-by-modeling headroom is small. Controlled fine-tuning, distillation, and agentic consistency-checking support the same conclusions, and we document throughout a measurement leak---label information reaching a system through the packaging of the data rather than its content---in which the released file ordering encodes the label, including one instance that briefly misled our own pipeline.

</details>


### [187] [Drift-Aware LLM Routing with Sparse Contexts and Shared Budgets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00662)
*Cheung Hao Lee,Patrick Wong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Drift-Aware Sparse Routing (DRS), an online routing algorithm for multi-model language services that must respect multiple resource budgets while adapting to drifting request distributions and model performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-model language systems must decide, per request, which model to use while staying within budgets on compute, latency, memory, or money. Unlike static model selection, real-world routing is difficult because prompts live in high-dimensional spaces (only a sparse set of features matters for model choice) and both traffic patterns and the model performance frontier change over time due to launches, fine-tuning, quantization, and system updates. Existing methods often assume stationarity or ignore strict multi-resource constraints, motivating a framework that handles nonstationarity, sparsity, and multiple knapsack-style resource limits simultaneously.

Method: They formalize the problem as nonstationary sparse contextual routing under multiple knapsack constraints, optionally with a shadow-audit stream that evaluates a small fraction of prompts on multiple models to obtain reward and cost feedback. The proposed DRS policy: (1) estimates reward and resource consumption from a rolling audit window; (2) routes using pessimistic (lower-bound) reward and optimistic (upper-bound) cost estimates to be robust; (3) updates resource shadow prices online to enforce budgets; and (4) applies a hard resource meter before committing to a routing decision. The theoretical analysis separates control (pacing and shadow pricing) from statistics (estimation errors), and derives regret bounds relative to a paced dynamic fluid benchmark.

Result: They prove that on any event where prediction errors are uniformly bounded by radii {β_t}, DRS’s regret is bounded by the sum of these radii, a term depending on capacity slack, and an O(√T) term from pacing. Under a sparse linear reward model with total drift V_T and using rolling-window estimation, the regret is \\widetilde O( T√(s/(ρW)) + W V_T + √T ), where s is the sparsity level, ρ is the audit rate, and W is the window length. Choosing W optimally recovers the usual stationary regret rate O(√(sT/ρ)) when there is no drift (V_T = 0) and yields an adaptation term O(T^{2/3}(s/ρ)^{1/3} V_T^{1/3}) under drift.

Conclusion: DRS provides a principled, drift-aware mechanism for routing requests among multiple language models under strict multi-resource budgets, leveraging sparse contextual structure and limited auditing. The approach achieves near-optimal regret in the stationary case and controlled degradation under nonstationary drift, with explicit trade-offs between audit rate, sparsity, window length, and drift. This offers a theoretically grounded foundation for practical, budget-respecting model routing in evolving multi-model language services.

Abstract: A multi-model language service must route each request while preserving workload-level budgets for compute, latency, memory, or monetary cost. Two features make this problem materially harder than static model selection. Prompt representations are high dimensional, so only a small subset of embedding directions may predict the incremental value of a model, and both the request mix and the model frontier drift after launches, fine-tunes, quantization changes, and system updates. We formulate nonstationary sparse contextual routing with multiple knapsack constraints and an optional shadow-audit stream that evaluates a small fraction of prompts on several models.
  We propose Drift-Aware Sparse Routing (DRS). The policy estimates reward and resource use from a rolling audit window, routes using pessimistic reward and optimistic cost estimates, updates resource shadow prices online, and applies a hard meter before commitment. The analysis separates control from statistics. On any event with uniform prediction radii $\{β_t\}$, regret against a paced dynamic fluid benchmark is bounded by the sum of the radii, a capacity-buffer term, and an $O(\sqrt{T})$ pacing term. Under a sparse linear model and bounded drift $V_T$, rolling estimation gives \[ \widetilde O\left( T\sqrt{\frac{s}{ρW}}+WV_T+\sqrt{T} \right), \] where $s$ is sparsity, $ρ$ is the audit rate, and $W$ is the window length. Optimizing $W$ yields the usual stationary $O(\sqrt{sT/ρ})$ rate when $V_T=0$ and a $O(T^{2/3}(s/ρ)^{1/3}V_T^{1/3})$ adaptation term under drift.

</details>


### [188] [Triple-Bottom-Line Sustainability of Language Models for Edge AI: A Comparison Between SLMs and Quantized LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00665)
*Jainil Dharmil Shah*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Compares small language models and quantized large language models for edge deployment using a multi-dimensional Holistic Sustainability Score (HSS).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Edge AI deployments must balance accuracy, latency, memory, energy, and safety, but model choice is usually driven by a single metric. There is a need to understand whether natively small models or compressed large models provide a better overall sustainability trade-off at the edge, considering economic, environmental, and social impacts.

Method: Define a Holistic Sustainability Score (HSS) aligned with the triple bottom line (economic, environmental, social). Evaluate five BF16 small language models and five large language models under five precision/quantization schemes (BF16, INT8, NF4 4-bit, GPTQ 4-bit, GGUF Q4), yielding 30 configurations. Measure: (1) capability via five zero-shot benchmarks, (2) systems efficiency via latency, throughput, peak VRAM, and energy on GPU, and (3) safety via attack success rate on five harmful prompts. Rank configurations by combined HSS and analyze trade-offs.

Result: Among all 30 configurations, the quantized LLM Qwen3-30B-A3B/GGUF Q4 achieves the highest HSS (93.38), followed by Mistral-Small-24B/GGUF Q4 (92.40). The best-performing SLM is Phi-4-mini/BF16 with an HSS of 89.49. Quantized LLMs can outperform native SLMs in overall sustainability, while SLMs still show advantages in lower resource demand. Quantization behavior is non-monotonic with respect to precision vs. efficiency.

Conclusion: The assumption that native small language models are always the most sustainable choice for edge AI is not universally valid. Carefully optimized and quantized large models can provide superior holistic sustainability, though small models remain attractive due to their modest resource needs. Quantization should be treated as a systems-level design decision rather than a straightforward precision-efficiency trade-off, and the HSS is inherently relative to the benchmark pool and selected proxy metrics.

Abstract: Edge-AI model selection is commonly driven by one isolated metric - accuracy, latency, memory, energy, or safety, even though a deployable language model must balance all five. Our work focuses on answering the question whether na- tively trained small language models (SLMs) or large language models (LLMs) compressed through post-training quantization offer the more sustainable edge- deployment trade-off. We introduce a reproducible Holistic Sustainability Score (HSS) organized around the triple bottom line: an economic pillar for capability and systems efficiency, an environmental pillar for operational GPU energy and a social pillar for harmful-prompt robustness. Five BF16 SLMs and five LLMs under different quantization approaches - BF16, INT8, NF4 4-bit, GPTQ 4-bit, and GGUF Q4 produce 30 measured configurations. Capability is assessed on five zero-shot benchmarks; efficiency uses latency, throughput, peak VRAM and energy; and safety is approximated by attack success rate on five harmful prompts. Qwen3-30B-A3B/GGUF Q4 ranks first in the combined pool (93.38), followed by Mistral-Small-24B/GGUF Q4 (92.40), while Phi-4-mini/BF16 is the highest- ranked SLM in that pool (89.49). Thus, the hypothesis that native SLMs must be the most sustainable edge choice is not supported universally; optimized quantized LLMs can win overall, while SLMs remain competitive through lower resource demand. Quantization is a systems-level choice rather than a monotonic precision- efficiency trade-off and HSS remains relative to its comparison pool and proxy definitions.

</details>


### [189] [Value Over Language Model: Detecting Original Contribution in Writing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00700)
*Vibhhu Sharma,Thorsten Joachims,Sarah Dean*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose VOLM, a framework to measure how much informational value a human adds beyond what an LLM could generate from the task description alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-detection tools focus on surface form and style to decide whether text is machine‑generated, but they do not answer a deeper question: how much of the underlying information or ideas came from the human versus the model. There is a need to quantify human contribution in LLM-assisted writing in a way that is robust to stylistic changes.

Method: They introduce a training‑free framework called Value Over Language Model (VOLM). First, they extract a document’s content at multiple granularities using content extractors. Then, using an LLM, they reconstruct the document from each partial content representation and also reconstruct a “replacement‑level” document from only the generic task description. By comparing these reconstructions, they estimate how much value the original document adds beyond what the LLM can easily produce from the task description alone. The framework explicitly avoids scoring surface text, focusing instead on informational content.

Result: Across three domains—news articles, ICLR peer reviews, and argumentative essays—VOLM distinguishes human‑authored documents from LLM-generated documents created from generic task descriptions. It is robust to content-preserving transformations such as LLM-based rewriting and round‑trip translation, and more constrained content extractors further reduce remaining differences between human and LLM text, highlighting that style and content can be disentangled in this setup.

Conclusion: VOLM offers a promising, style‑invariant way to quantify human informational contribution relative to what an LLM can produce from a task description alone. The findings indicate that carefully extracting and reconstructing content can separate human value-add from model capabilities, and they call for further specialized implementations and broader use of such methods for assessing human roles in LLM‑assisted writing.

Abstract: LLMs have been rapidly adopted across writing tasks, prompting the development of tools for detecting LLM-generated text. Yet, these tools largely measure how much of a document's surface text was written by an LLM and aren't fundamentally designed to measure how much of the information content or ideas originated from the LLM itself rather than being supplied by the user in the prompt. In this work, we design a framework that measures how much value a person adds on top of what a language model could have easily produced by itself. The method requires no training or labeled data and never scores the document's surface text, insulating it from stylistic confounders. Instead, it extracts the document's content at increasing levels of granularity, uses an LLM to reconstruct the document from each partial representation, and compares these reconstructions with those produced from the task description alone. We call this framework Value Over Language Model (VOLM), which measures a document's contribution relative to a replacement-level document that an LLM could produce from the task description alone. We evaluate VOLM with a specific instantiation of this framework across three domains: news articles, ICLR peer reviews, and argumentative essays. VOLM separates human-authored documents from matched LLM-generated documents produced from generic task descriptions, while remaining substantially invariant to content-preserving transformations, including LLM-based reconstruction and round-trip translation. We further find that increasingly constrained content extractors reduce residual differences between LLM-generated and humanized text, demonstrating the importance of disentangling informational content from stylistic variation. We hope these results encourage further work on specialized instantiations of the framework and on assessing human contributions in LLM-assisted writing more generally.

</details>


### [190] [ChatDev 2.0: A No-Code Multi-Agent Platform for Developing Everything](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00714)
*Yufan Dang,Shu Yao,Bowen Lai,Chenting Xu,Ruijie Shi,Wai-Shing Leung,Huatao Li,Chen Qian,Zhiyuan Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DevAll (ChatDev 2.0) is a no‑code, highly expressive platform for building and running heterogeneous LLM-based multi-agent systems using declarative executable graphs and a visual interface.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ways to build LLM-based multi-agent systems involve a tradeoff: code frameworks are flexible but demand substantial engineering effort, while no-code tools are easier but restrict agent interactions to rigid, predefined workflows. The authors aim to bridge this gap by providing a system that is both highly expressive and easy to use, allowing creation of complex, dynamic MAS without coding.

Method: The authors design DevAll, a no-code platform that represents multi-agent systems as declarative executable graphs. These graphs can encode heterogeneous agents, dynamic and cyclic interactions, and human-in-the-loop steps. A cycle-aware execution engine interprets and runs these graphs, enabling flexible control flows. On top of this, they build an integrated visual interface that lets users visually author, execute, monitor, and inspect MAS configurations without writing code. They then instantiate various state-of-the-art MAS setups within DevAll and evaluate them on three representative tasks, comparing performance to existing implementations that require task-specific orchestration code.

Result: DevAll successfully reproduces several state-of-the-art LLM-based multi-agent systems across three representative tasks. It achieves competitive performance while eliminating the need for task-specific orchestration code, showing that its declarative graph abstraction and execution engine are sufficiently expressive for complex MAS. The experiments validate that DevAll can match the capabilities of hand-engineered code frameworks in these scenarios.

Conclusion: DevAll (ChatDev 2.0) provides a general-purpose, no-code platform for LLM-based multi-agent systems that combines strong expressiveness with ease of use. Its declarative executable graph model and cycle-aware execution engine support heterogeneous agents and complex, dynamic interactions, while the visual interface enables full lifecycle management of MAS without coding. The ability to reproduce state-of-the-art systems with competitive performance suggests DevAll is a practical alternative to traditional code-heavy MAS frameworks.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have shown strong potential for solving complex tasks, yet their development forces a tradeoff: code frameworks are expressive but engineering-intensive, while no-code builders simplify authoring but constrain agent interactions to author-defined workflows. We present ChatDev 2.0: DevAll (hereafter DevAll), a no-code platform for building, executing, and inspecting heterogeneous MAS that delivers both high expressiveness and ease of use. In terms of expressiveness, DevAll pairs a declarative executable graph abstraction with a cycle-aware execution engine, so that heterogeneous agents and dynamic and cyclic interactions can be represented and executed within a single framework. For ease of use, an integrated visual interface lets users author, run, monitor, and inspect MAS, including human-in-the-loop steps, entirely without writing code. Experiments demonstrate that DevAll reproduces state-of-the-art MAS across three representative tasks at competitive performance and without task-specific orchestration code, highlighting its effectiveness as a general-purpose platform for LLM-based MAS. DevAll is available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev.

</details>


### [191] [A Closed-Loop Evaluation of Capability Loss and Recovery in Compressed Driving Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00718)
*Ahmad Alfan Alfian Irfan,Nur Ahmad Khatim,Mansur Arief*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how compressing learned driving policies (via pruning, distillation, and quantization) affects real driving safety and performance, using a stage-wise closed-loop method.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard compression metrics (size, FLOPs, accuracy) don’t necessarily reflect whether a compressed driving policy remains safe and capable when deployed on resource-limited embedded hardware. There is an open question on how to rigorously accept/reject compressed policies for automated driving.

Method: Formulate driving as a POMDP and train a belief-state policy using PPO in Gym-Duckietown. Extract the actor network and pass it through a compression pipeline in stages: structured pruning, knowledge distillation, and integer quantization. After each stage, perform closed-loop evaluation on five driving curricula to measure actual driving behavior and capability.

Result: Structured pruning is the first stage where noticeable driving capability is lost. Knowledge distillation improves the pruned actor but its gains are limited by the quality and coverage of the rehearsal data. Integer quantization of the improved (pruned + distilled) actor degrades performance on tasks that require stopping and resuming. In contrast, integer quantization applied directly to the unpruned actor preserves good performance on all five curricula.

Conclusion: Compression stages affect driving capability differently, and standard aggregate numerical metrics can miss important safety-related degradations. Structured pruning is particularly risky for capability loss; distillation can partially recover it but is data-limited; and quantization interacts with pruning in non-trivial ways. A stage-wise closed-loop evaluation is therefore necessary to decide whether a compressed driving policy is safe and statistically reliable for deployment in automated driving systems.

Abstract: Many automobile and mobility companies deploy learned driving policies on embedded computers with limited memory and power. Pruning, knowledge distillation, and quantization are the standard methods to reduce the size and the inference cost of these policies. However, these methods are commonly assessed by aggregate numerical scores, and such scores may not reflect the ability of the policy to drive safely when interacting with other road users. In this study, we propose a stage-wise closed-loop evaluation approach to follow a driving policy through a compression pipeline. We formulate the driving task as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) and train a belief-state policy with proximal policy optimization (PPO) in Gym-Duckietown. We then extract the actor, compress it one stage at a time, and evaluate it on five driving curricula. We show that structured pruning is the stage at which the driving capability is first lost. Meanwhile, distillation improves the pruned actor, but the improvement is limited by its rehearsal data. Integer quantization of the improved actor loses some of the curricula that require the vehicle to stop and then resume. Interestingly, the same procedure on the unpruned actor preserves all five curricula. Our study thus provides an empirical analysis aiming to answer the currently active discussions on how to accept a compressed driving policy, so as to achieve a safe and statistically reliable deployment of automated driving functions.

</details>


### [192] [SOVER: Formal Certification of Optimization Reformulations via LLM-Assisted SMT Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00728)
*Swapnil Bhattacharyya,Mayank Baranwal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build a framework (SOVER) that uses SMT solvers to formally verify that LLM-produced reformulations of optimization problems are semantically equivalent, and release a nonlinear benchmark where their method is highly accurate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can translate or reformulate optimization models, but relying on numerical solvers to check equivalence is unsafe because solver behavior is influenced by local minima, timeouts, numerical issues, and subtle semantic mismatches; a more principled, formal verification of equivalence is needed.

Method: They design SOVER, an LLM-assisted SMT-based verification framework. First, an LLM extracts a semantic mapping between two formulations. Then, for mixed-integer linear problems, Z3 is used to check cross-feasibility and that objective order is preserved globally across mapped solutions. For continuous nonlinear problems, dReal is used to do tolerance-aware feasibility/range checking and epsilon-argmin verification. They also construct NLEquiv-150, a benchmark of 100 equivalent and 50 challenging non-equivalent nonlinear reformulation pairs to evaluate the framework.

Result: On the NLEquiv-150 benchmark, using mappings extracted by an LLM, SOVER correctly classifies 149 out of 150 pairs (99.33% accuracy), and in particular detects all 50 intentionally hard non-equivalent pairs; the single mistake stems from an incomplete mapping provided by the LLM, not from the SMT verification itself.

Conclusion: Formal SMT-based verification can reliably certify semantic equivalence (or non-equivalence) of LLM-generated optimization problem reformulations, overcoming the limitations of empirical solver-based validation. The new NLEquiv-150 benchmark demonstrates that the proposed SOVER framework is highly accurate, with remaining errors largely attributable to imperfect mapping extraction rather than the verification core itself.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable promise in translating and reformulating complex mathematical optimization problems across modeling languages. However, validating such transformations through empirical solver executions alone is unreliable, as solver outcomes may be affected by local minima, structural timeouts, numerical artifacts, and subtle semantic divergence between formulations. We introduce SOVER, an LLM-assisted SMT framework that separates semantic mapping from formal certification: Z3 checks domain cross-feasibility and global objective-order preservation for mixed-integer linear formulations, while dReal provides tolerance-aware feasibility/range and $ε$-argmin checks for continuous nonlinear formulations. We also introduce NLEquiv-150, a public benchmark of 100 equivalent and 50 deliberately hard non-equivalent nonlinear reformulation pairs. With LLM-extracted mappings, SOVER classifies 149/150 pairs (99.33%) correctly, including all 50 hard negatives; the sole error is an incomplete mapping extraction.

</details>


### [193] [Agentic Empirical Asset Pricing: Methodological Foundations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00731)
*Yingjian Pan,Xiaowei Ding,Kay Giesecke*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Agentic Empirical Asset Pricing (AEAP), where LLM-based agents autonomously discover asset pricing factors, and proposes architectures and evaluation standards for these systems, including system-level backtesting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional empirical asset pricing relies on human-driven factor discovery and evaluates only the discovered factors or trading strategies, not the automated systems that generate them. With LLM agents now capable of autonomous research workflows, there is a need to define this new paradigm, design appropriate system architectures, and, crucially, to evaluate both their outputs and the reliability of the discovery process itself.

Method: 1) Conceptually define Agentic Empirical Asset Pricing (AEAP) and decompose it into core building blocks. 2) Propose a reference architecture for autonomous factor discovery systems using LLM agents. 3) Develop a rigorous evaluation standard for discovered factors and an out-of-sample, system-level backtesting framework that repeatedly re-runs the discovery pipeline over time. 4) Implement a concrete AEAP system, SEADS, and re-implement five baseline discovery systems. 5) Empirically compare SEADS and baselines on two U.S. equity datasets across multiple performance metrics and via rolling re-execution to assess the stability of the discovery process. 6) Document negative results and limitations encountered, highlighting pitfalls for future research and evaluation of AEAP systems.

Result: SEADS and the five baseline systems exhibit heterogeneous performance across metrics on two U.S. equity panels; no single evaluation metric consistently ranks the systems, showing that different criteria emphasize different aspects of performance. The rolling re-execution experiments reveal insights into the reliability of the discovery process over time, rather than just the quality of a single set of discovered factors, and expose cases where systems fail or are unstable. Negative findings and observed limitations uncover methodological pitfalls in designing and evaluating AEAP systems.

Conclusion: AEAP is a distinct new paradigm in empirical asset pricing where autonomous LLM-agent systems conduct factor discovery. Evaluating only their outputs is insufficient: robust assessment requires multi-metric evaluation and system-level, out-of-sample backtesting of the discovery pipeline itself. The reference architecture, evaluation standard, and empirical study with SEADS provide initial foundations, while the documented pitfalls and negative results outline important challenges and directions for future AEAP research.

Abstract: Recent advances in LLM agents enable a new paradigm for asset pricing, which we call Agentic Empirical Asset Pricing (AEAP): systems that autonomously conduct the scientific discovery process itself. We define AEAP and identify its core building blocks. Existing evaluation practices backtest only the outputs (factors or trades), not the autonomous discovery system that produced them. We focus on factor discovery, contributing a reference architecture, a rigorous evaluation standard for discovered factors, and a method for out-of-sample backtesting the discovery system. As a concrete instance of that architecture, we evaluate SEADS against five re-implemented baselines on two US equity panels using this standard: no single metric ranks the systems consistently, motivating evaluation on multiple axes at once. A separate rolling re-execution then asks the complementary question of whether the discovery process itself, not one static output, is reliable. We also report negative findings and limitations that surface further evaluation pitfalls for future AEAP systems.

</details>


### [194] [Escaping Redundant Reasoning: Structure-Aware Search for Inference-Time LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00738)
*Lu Cheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies 'reasoning basin collapse' in LLM inference-time search and proposes BASIN, a training-free, structure-aware selection method that diversifies search across distinct reasoning paths, yielding substantial accuracy gains over Tree of Thoughts (ToT) and a better concentration of search on successful trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inference-time search methods like Tree of Thoughts tend to repeatedly explore similar reasoning trajectories, underutilizing the search budget and limiting reasoning performance. There is a need for a general, training-free way to diversify reasoning paths while keeping compute fixed and maintaining or improving answer quality. The authors also want a quantitative lens to understand when and why such diversification helps.

Method: They define 'reasoning basins' as groups of structurally similar reasoning states (partial solutions or thought trajectories). BASIN is a selection strategy that, during search, detects which basin each new state belongs to and penalizes revisiting already-explored basins, thereby encouraging exploration of new strategies without additional training or compute. They also design QA-BASIN, which augments this with quality awareness so that high-quality basins are less penalized, balancing exploration and exploitation. Additionally, they introduce the redundancy gap Δ, a metric comparing how concentrated search is on a few basins for correct vs. incorrect answers, to analyze search behavior.

Result: Under the same inference-time compute budget, BASIN outperforms Tree of Thoughts by up to +22 percentage points on the Game of 24 benchmark and +6.7 percentage points on MuSR. QA-BASIN improves robustness further, especially in cases where naive diversification over-explores weaker strategies. Empirically, BASIN shifts the redundancy gap Δ from near 0 (for standard ToT) to positive values, indicating that the model learns to concentrate search more effectively on basins associated with correct solutions and less on those associated with failures.

Conclusion: Reasoning basin collapse is a key failure mode of inference-time search with LLMs, where search overly focuses on similar trajectories. BASIN offers a simple, training-free, structure-aware selection mechanism that redistributes search effort across diverse reasoning paths, improving accuracy and robustness under fixed budgets. The redundancy gap provides an explanatory lens for when basin-aware selection helps. Overall, structure-aware selection appears to be a promising general principle for enhancing inference-time reasoning in LLMs.

Abstract: Inference-time search with large language models (LLMs) often concentrates on a small set of structurally or semantically similar trajectories, leaving alternatives underexplored---a failure mode we call \textit{reasoning basin collapse}. We introduce BASIN, a training-free, structure-aware selection method that groups reasoning states into basins and penalizes repeated visits to the same strategy, thereby reallocating search across genuinely distinct reasoning paths under a fixed compute budget. Under matched inference budgets, BASIN improves over Tree of Thoughts (ToT) by up to $+22$pp on Game of 24 and $+6.7$pp on MuSR. A quality-aware variant, QA-BASIN, further improves robustness by preserving high-quality basins when unconditional diversification over-explores. To explain when basin-aware selection helps, we introduce the redundancy gap $Δ$, which measures how differently search concentrates for correct versus incorrect predictions: standard ToT often operates near $Δ\approx 0$, while BASIN consistently shifts $Δ$ positive. More broadly, BASIN suggests structure-aware selection as a simple and general approach to improving inference-time reasoning. Code can be found at https://github.com/GitHubLuCheng/basin.

</details>


### [195] [ContextPipe: Database-Inspired Context Assembly for Long-Horizon Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00749)
*Peng Xu,Zuyu Zhang,Yuze Sun,Feng Tian,Long Wang,Chen Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces ContextPipe, a database-inspired pipeline for assembling prompts for long-horizon LLM agents, improving efficiency and auditability over naive append-only histories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents must decide which past information to include in each prompt under strict context-window and caching constraints. Today, this logic is ad hoc, scattered across code, hard to audit, and inefficient. The authors observe that this problem structurally resembles query execution in relational databases, motivating a principled, unified framework for context assembly that can exploit budgets, caches, and statistics systematically.

Method: The authors formalize context assembly as a five-phase pipeline analogous to database query processing: Plan, Bind, Optimize, Execute, and Feedback. This pipeline is backed by (1) a structured catalog of data sources, (2) a deterministic optimizer that is aware of token and cache budgets, and (3) EXPLAIN/ANALYZE-style tracing for introspection. They implement this framework in a system called ContextPipe and compare it to a simple append-only prompt construction policy.

Result: On the SWE-bench Pro Qutebrowser subset, ContextPipe reduces the total number of tokens used by 31%, LLM calls by 23%, and overall response time by 9% compared with append-only context construction, though it leads to a lower KV cache-hit ratio.

Conclusion: Treating context assembly for LLM agents as a database-style query execution problem yields a structured, auditable, and efficient system. ContextPipe’s five-phase pipeline and optimizer can significantly reduce token usage, number of calls, and latency relative to naive approaches, while keeping context management replayable and failure-isolated, despite some trade-offs in cache behavior.

Abstract: Long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents require context assembly: the runtime must decide what to include in each prompt, in what order, and when to compact history under a hard context-window budget and a byte-sensitive prompt cache. In production agentic systems, this logic is scattered across prompt builders, ad hoc compaction routines, cache-break workarounds, and per-provider shims. We argue that context assembly is structurally isomorphic to query execution in a relational database: both execute under a hard budget, exploit a tiered cache, and leverage statistics. We adopt this discipline in ContextPipe: a five-phase pipeline (Plan Bind Optimize Execute Feedback) backed by a structured data-source catalog, a deterministic cache-aware optimizer, and an EXPLAIN ANALYZE trace. We show that context in ContextPipe is auditable, replayable, and failure-isolated. A preliminary evaluation using the SWE-bench Pro Qutebrowser subset shows that, compared with the append-only context construction policy, ContextPipe reduces total token volume by 31%, LLM calls by 23%, and response time by 9%, at the cost of a lower KV cache-hit ratio.

</details>


### [196] [S^3martCirc: Self-supervised Smart Circuit Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00755)
*Wendy Zheng,Yinhan He,Liang Wu,Jundong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces S^3martCirc, a unified, self-supervised framework that jointly discovers important circuits in LLMs and assigns them generalizable functional roles, improving mechanistic interpretability over prior two-stage methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mechanistic interpretability of LLMs is hindered by treating circuit discovery and functional interpretation as separate, sequential steps. This separation ignores the codependence between a component's importance and its role, leads to task- and node-specific interpretations that do not generalize, and relies heavily on subjective, non-quantitative judgments. The authors aim to create an approach that simultaneously identifies important structures and their functions using principled, quantitative criteria.

Method: The authors propose S^3martCirc (Self-supervised Smart Circuit Discovery), a unified framework that abstracts the behavior of individual nodes (e.g., attention heads, MLP neurons) into two general computational roles that are intended to be task-agnostic. They define a quantitative metric for assigning these roles to components in a self-supervised manner, enabling the method to jointly estimate each component's importance to a task and its functional role. This replaces the traditional two-step pipeline with a single, integrated procedure.

Result: Across extensive experiments on LLM mechanistic interpretability benchmarks, S^3martCirc more accurately recovers task-relevant circuits than existing MI approaches, as measured by circuit discovery quality metrics. The framework shows better performance at identifying important components and structuring them into meaningful circuits compared with prior two-stage or heuristic-based methods.

Conclusion: By jointly learning importance and functional roles with a self-supervised, quantitatively grounded framework, S^3martCirc advances mechanistic interpretability for LLMs beyond the traditional two-stage paradigm. Abstracting nodes into general computational roles enables more generalizable, less subjective circuit interpretations, and empirical results suggest that this unified approach yields superior circuit discovery performance.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance across diverse tasks, from text summarization to question answering. Despite these capabilities, their black-box nature obscures internal decision-making processes. Mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to address this by reverse-engineering neural networks into human-understandable algorithms. Current MI approaches for LLMs typically follow a two-stage paradigm: first identifying important components (circuit discovery), where components are typically individual nodes such as an attention head or feedforward neuron, and second determining the role they play in a certain task (functional interpretation). However, this sequential approach overlooks a fundamental insight: a component's importance and its functional role are inherently codependent. Unifying these stages presents two key challenges: (1) functional roles are often tied to specific nodes or components, limiting generalization, and (2) their identification relies on subjective interpretation rather than quantifiable metrics. To address these challenges, we propose S^3martCirc (Self-supervised Smart Circuit Discovery), a unified framework that simultaneously discovers circuits and interprets functionality. S^3martCirc abstracts node behavior into two general computational roles that generalize across tasks and defines a quantitative metric for assigning them, enabling importance and functional role to be discovered jointly rather than in sequence. Extensive experiments show that our framework outperforms existing methods in circuit discovery.

</details>


### [197] [Automated Tree Knowledge Graph Construction using Ontology Expansion and Retrieval from Vietnamese History Textbooks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00763)
*Ket Doan Nguyen,Minh N. H. Nguyen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents an end-to-end pipeline for constructing a hierarchical knowledge graph and evaluating graph-based retrieval strategies for RAG in Vietnamese, showing that structure-aware traversal can outperform standard vector retrieval when structure is relevant.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RAG systems lack automated methods to build hierarchical KGs via ontology expansion in low-resource languages like Vietnamese, and they also lack systematic evaluation of how to exploit hierarchical structure for retrieval. The paper aims to fill these gaps using Vietnamese textbooks as a testbed.

Method: They design a three-phase hybrid relation extraction pipeline: (1) intra-batch deduplication using Union-Find, (2) approximate cross-batch search to reduce redundancy, and (3) LLM-based relation extraction with a centroid filter to minimize prompts, followed by a five-step dual-LLM validation process to limit ontology bloat. The resulting KG uses a two-tier node architecture with unmergeable structural nodes preserving document layout and mergeable content nodes. For retrieval, they define and test three graph traversal strategies (Top-Down, Horizontal, Bottom-Up) over the hierarchical KG and compare them to a vector similarity baseline on a synthetic benchmark of Vietnamese queries over subgraphs categorized by query direction.

Result: From nearly 400 pages of Vietnamese high school history textbooks, they construct a tree-structured KG with 750 nodes and 4,341 semantic edges, while tightly controlling ontology growth from 40 to 41 relation types. In retrieval experiments on 1,210 Vietnamese queries over 109 subgraphs, the Top-Down traversal strategy using structural information outperforms a vector similarity baseline by 4.7 points in NDCG@10, whereas structural bias can hurt when structural context is not needed.

Conclusion: The proposed pipeline can automatically construct a controlled, hierarchical KG from low-resource language textbooks and enable systematic evaluation of structure-aware retrieval strategies for RAG. Tree-structured information offers retrieval gains beyond flat vector similarity when queries align with the hierarchy, but inappropriate reliance on structure may degrade performance, suggesting that retrieval should be adaptively structure-aware based on query needs.

Abstract: Hierarchical Knowledge graph (KG)-based retrieval augmented generation (RAG) has emerged as a powerful approach for supporting large language models with structured knowledge. However, there are primary challenges: (i) the lack of methods for automatic KG construction using ontology expansion for low-resource languages such as Vietnamese, (ii) the absence of systematic evaluation for knowledge retrieval strategies leveraging the hierarchical structures. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end pipeline for KG construction and retrieval strategies evaluation. In the KG construction, we employ a three-phase hybrid relation extraction pipeline: intra-batch deduplication via Union-Find, approximate cross-batch search, and LLM extraction with a centroid filter that reduces prompts combined with a five-step dual-LLM validator to prevent bloated ontology. A two-tier architecture consists of unmergeable structural nodes to preserve the document structure and mergeable content nodes. The retrieval evaluation consists of three graph traversal strategies: Top-Down, Horizontal, and Bottom-Up, which are evaluated on a synthetically generated benchmark of 1,210 Vietnamese queries from 109 subgraphs, categorized by five query directions. In this paper, we construct the tree knowledge graph from Vietnamese high school History textbooks (nearly 400 pages) to produce 750 nodes and 4,341 semantic edges with controlled ontology growth from 40 to 41 types. Among experimental graph traversal strategies, the Top-Down strategy with structure surpasses the vector baseline by 4.7 percentage points in NDCG@10. As a result, tree-structural information provides valuable information beyond flat cosine similarity but degrades performance when the query does not require structural context.

</details>


### [198] [DiagEvo: Diagnosis-Guided Self-Evolution via Hierarchical Error Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00768)
*Xincheng Wei,Yifan Ding,Yoshua Li,Dongsheng Ma,Rongxiang Weng,Xunliang Cai,Wenjian Ding,Yao Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces DiagEvo, a guided self-play framework that uses a model’s own failure history to generate targeted training questions and improve reasoning performance across benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing self-play methods for evolving language models either lack guidance—so performance plateaus or degrades—or depend on external task resources such as human examples or corpora. Unguided approaches use generic signals like difficulty or diversity, which do not explicitly focus on the model’s unresolved reasoning weaknesses. There is a need for a method that can automatically derive a targeted curriculum from the model’s own behavior without external supervision.

Method: DiagEvo adds a diagnostician component and a hierarchical error-cause memory to self-play. The diagnostician analyzes the solver’s failure history to extract recurring error causes, organizing them under skill nodes in a hierarchy. Each cause is labeled as Active or Mastered based on the solver’s self-consistency on questions that target that cause. A challenger module then uses both the state (Active/Mastered) and recurrence counts of error causes to decide when to generate cause-targeted questions versus free-exploration questions. A double-confidence filtering mechanism keeps only intermediate-difficulty questions for training, retaining those where the solver’s most frequent answer is clearly dominant, which aims to filter out too-easy or too-uncertain items.

Result: Using a 4B-parameter diagnostician by default, DiagEvo consistently outperforms unguided and externally guided self-play baselines. Across nine benchmarks and three solvers (Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, OctoThinker-8B), it achieves higher mean accuracy than all baselines. On Qwen3-8B, DiagEvo obtains 72.3% mean accuracy across five math reasoning benchmarks, 4.5 points better than R-Zero, and 57.4% mean accuracy across all nine benchmarks, 1.1 points better than DARC. Ablation studies show that removing either the hierarchical error-cause memory or the double-confidence filtering reduces performance, indicating both are important.

Conclusion: DiagEvo demonstrates that an effective curriculum for self-play can be derived purely from a model’s own failure patterns, without relying on external task resources. By explicitly modeling recurring error causes in a hierarchical memory and using them to guide question generation and filtering, DiagEvo yields consistent accuracy gains in reasoning tasks over strong baselines. The results suggest that structured, self-derived diagnostics are a powerful way to drive language-model self-improvement.

Abstract: Self-play is an effective paradigm for language-model self-evolution, but without guidance, solver performance can plateau or decline across rounds. Unguided methods steer question generation with signals such as difficulty, learnability, or diversity. These signals keep questions challenging and varied but do not specify which unresolved reasoning weaknesses later rounds should target. Guided methods obtain direction from external task resources, including human examples, document corpora, or specified difficulty targets, and therefore rely on task information supplied outside the self-play loop. We show that the needed direction can instead be derived from the solver's own failure history. We introduce DiagEvo, whose diagnostician extracts recurring error causes from this history and stores them in a hierarchical error-cause memory. The memory groups related causes under skill nodes and tracks each as Active or Mastered according to self-consistency on targeted questions. The challenger uses these states and recurrence counts to balance cause-targeted generation with free exploration. Double-confidence filtering retains intermediate-difficulty questions only when the most common solver answer has a clear vote lead. DiagEvo derives its curriculum from information produced during self-play, without external task resources. With the default 4B diagnostician, DiagEvo outperforms every baseline in mean accuracy across all nine benchmarks for each of the three solvers: Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and OctoThinker-8B. On Qwen3-8B, it reaches 72.3% mean accuracy across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, 4.5 percentage points above R-Zero. Its mean accuracy across all nine benchmarks is 57.4%, 1.1 percentage points above DARC. Ablations show that the hierarchical error-cause memory and double-confidence filtering both contribute to these gains.

</details>


### [199] [When Features Become Instances: Inverted Contrastive Learning for Unsupervised Feature Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00782)
*Utsab Ghosh,Roshni Chakraborty*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a new unsupervised feature selection method, ICLFS, that uses feature-wise contrastive learning and norm-based saliency with a graph-based correction to pick informative, non-redundant features, achieving state-of-the-art clustering performance on many benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unsupervised feature selection (UFS) is hard because there are no labels to define which features are useful, so current methods rely on indirect structural assumptions (similarity, locality, sparsity, clusters, reconstruction).
