These may not directly capture feature usefulness and can be suboptimal. The authors want a more direct, representation-learning-based way to characterize and rank features in an unsupervised manner.

Method: They invert the data matrix so that each feature becomes a vector over samples (a "sample-profile"), and treat features as the entities over which a contrastive learning task is defined. For each feature, they create multiple masked positive views and a shuffled negative view, and learn projector-space embeddings with an InfoNCE objective that enforces representation consistency across positive perturbations and separation from negatives. Based on observations about InfoNCE and cosine training affecting embedding norms, they use the magnitude of each feature’s projector embedding as a saliency score to rank features. Then they apply Laplacian-Gated Ranking Correction, a graph/Laplacian-based procedure that downweights or removes locally redundant features while retaining salient ones, producing the final selected subset.

Result: On 12 benchmark datasets evaluated under the standard clustering-based UFS protocol, their method ICLFS attains the best clustering accuracy on 10 datasets compared to both classical and neural UFS baselines, and is competitive (not worse by much) on the remaining two datasets.

Conclusion: Formulating unsupervised feature selection as a feature-wise contrastive representation learning problem, and using embedding norm plus a Laplacian-based redundancy correction, is an effective alternative to traditional neighborhood-, cluster-, or reconstruction-driven UFS approaches, yielding strong empirical performance on standard benchmarks.

Abstract: Unsupervised feature selection seeks a compact subset of informative features without access to class labels, making feature utility difficult to define. Existing UFS methods therefore rely on indirect structural criteria, such as similarity preservation, locality, sparsity, cluster geometry, or reconstruction quality. In this paper, we instead study UFS through representation consistency and propose Inverted Contrastive Learning for Unsupervised Feature Selection (ICLFS), a feature-wise contrastive framework that reformulates UFS as a representation learning problem over features rather than samples. ICLFS first inverts the data matrix so that each feature is represented by its sample-profile vector, then constructs multiple masked positive views together with a shuffled negative view, and learns projector-space representations that remain consistent across these structured perturbations under an InfoNCE-based objective. Motivated by recent findings that cosine-based and InfoNCE-based training affect embedding norms, we use projector-space embedding magnitude as the saliency signal for ranking features. The resulting norm-based ranking is subsequently refined through Laplacian-Gated Ranking Correction, which suppresses locally redundant candidates while preserving salient ones. Extensive experiments on 12 benchmark datasets show that ICLFS achieves the best clustering accuracy on 10 datasets against both classical and neural baselines under the standard clustering-based UFS evaluation protocol, while remaining competitive on the other two. These results show that feature-wise contrastive representation consistency provides a strong and effective alternative to neighborhood, cluster, and reconstruction-based UFS formulations.

</details>


### [200] [StudyBench: Can Self-Evolution Squeeze Textbooks for Olympiad Capability?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00787)
*Yinghao Chen,Zixi Chen,Bingxiang He,Ziqing Qiao,Huan-ang Gao,Yinuo Xu,Yuxin Zuo,Zeyuan Liu,Yuhao Zhan,Chaojun Xiao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: StudyBench is a controlled physics benchmark to measure how efficiently self-evolution methods turn raw training material into transferable problem-solving skills, revealing major gaps between learning, transfer, and in-context potential.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current self-evolution methods for models aim to mimic how humans learn from a small set of high-quality materials, but there is no direct, controlled way to measure how effectively they convert training data into general, transferable problem-solving capabilities. Existing evaluations mix data, compute, and method effects, making it unclear whether limitations arise from algorithms, available data, or scale. The authors want a clean benchmark to quantify learning efficiency and transfer, and to diagnose where current methods fall short.

Method: The authors design StudyBench, a benchmark in physics where training materials and evaluation are tightly controlled. They split the test data into two subsets: (1) an Application Set composed of difficult textbook-style problems that directly correspond to the training material and test how well the model can absorb and apply what it has seen, and (2) a Transfer Set composed of much harder olympiad-level problems that require transferring and recombining learned concepts. They then run multiple representative self-evolution methods on three different base models, systematically vary compute, and compare performance both to baselines and to an upper bound where the same material is used as in-context guidance. They also conduct a guidance ablation to quantify the gap between what is unlocked by guidance vs. what self-evolution training achieves.

Result: Across the benchmark, gains on the Application Set—problems similar to the training material—do not reliably carry over to the more challenging Transfer Set, indicating poor transfer of the learned capabilities. The guidance ablation reveals a substantial "Guidance Gap": when the same study materials are given as in-context guidance rather than used for self-evolution training, models can achieve much higher performance, but self-evolution methods close only a small part of that potential. Additionally, all tested methods encounter a "Compute Plateau," where performance saturates significantly before the allocated compute is exhausted, indicating diminishing returns from simply running the method longer. These patterns are consistent across three different base models.

Conclusion: The study concludes that current self-evolution methods are fundamentally inefficient at turning raw training material into robust, transferable problem-solving skills. The primary bottleneck is methodological: even with sufficient data and compute, existing algorithms underutilize the potential revealed by in-context guidance, and they plateau early. StudyBench provides a controlled and transparent environment to quantify these limitations and track progress, shifting self-evolution research toward a concrete, measurable objective rather than open-ended scaling. The benchmark and released code aim to guide the development of new methods that better absorb material and transfer to harder tasks.

Abstract: Humans need to study only a handful of well-written textbooks to master a discipline and attempt its hardest problems. We argue that an ideal self-evolution method should share the same property, that is autonomously learning from raw training material for transferable problem-solving capability. However, we still lack a direct measurement for it. We introduce StudyBench, a controlled physics benchmark that directly measures how efficiently a self-evolution method converts training material into capability. We organise the test set into an Application Set, consisting of difficult textbook problems and evaluating absorption ability, and a Transfer Set, consisting of olympiad-level problems and evaluating transfer ability. Benchmarking representative self-evolution methods across three base models, we find that improvements on the Application Set rarely translate to the harder Transfer Set. A guidance ablation exposes a Guidance Gap: even the strongest method closes only a small fraction of what the same material unlocks when supplied as in-context guidance. Besides, every method hits a Compute Plateau, saturating well before exhausting its compute budget. The remaining gap is therefore a method problem rather than a data or compute problem. By offering a clean and controlled benchmark, StudyBench turns self-evolution progress from an open-ended pursuit into a measurable target for future research. Our code is released at https://github.com/thunlp/StudyBench.

</details>


### [201] [Towards a Reliable and Practical Eval Pipeline](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00805)
*Emma Thuong Nguyen,Abhishek Ghose*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces an end-to-end evaluation pipeline for LLM-based software systems to make evals more reliable and aligned with human judgments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based software requires dependable evaluation mechanisms as quality gates, yet current approaches only partially address reliability aspects, leading to inconsistent and potentially misleading quality assessments.

Method: They design a full eval pipeline that starts from systematic creation of evaluation checklists and uses a learned aggregation model over checklist-based LLM-judge responses, also incorporating mechanisms for self-consistency checks, explanation generation, and uncertainty estimation.

Result: The proposed pipeline improves inter-LLM-judge agreement and better matches human evaluation judgments compared to prior or simpler eval methods, as shown in empirical experiments.

Conclusion: A comprehensive, learning-based eval pipeline that integrates checklist creation, response aggregation, and auxiliary signals like self-consistency and uncertainty can deliver more reliable and human-aligned evals for LLM-based software systems.

Abstract: LLM-based software systems increasingly require effective "evals" as quality gates in the development lifecycle. However, existing work typically addresses individual aspects of eval reliability rather than the full set of practical requirements. We present an end-to-end eval pipeline that combines eval checklist creation, with learned aggregation for checklist responses, to improve agreement across LLM judges and accuracy against human judgments. The framework additionally pro- vides self-consistency, explanations, and prediction uncertainty, and we empirically demonstrate its effectiveness.

</details>


### [202] [One Policy, Any Budget: Internalizing Budget-Aware Search via Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00813)
*Xiaowei Sun,Jin Li,Yili Hong,Yikun Fu,Yanghua Xiao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AnySearch trains a single LLM-based search agent that can adapt its tool-usage to arbitrary compute/token budgets at inference time, achieving better accuracy–efficiency trade-offs than baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based tool-using search agents are typically trained under a fixed budget (e.g., number of tool calls or tokens). When deployed, however, available budgets vary across tasks, users, or systems, and models trained for one setting often fail to adapt, either wasting resources or degrading accuracy. The authors aim to design a method that allows one policy to flexibly handle a wide range of budget constraints while maintaining strong answer quality and efficient tool use.

Method: They introduce AnySearch, a two-phase reinforcement learning framework with curriculum over budgets. Phase 1 uses a training scaffold: (1) explicit budget state injection to inform the agent of the remaining budget, and (2) structured reasoning prompts that guide the agent to plan tool usage under a linearly decaying budget schedule. Phase 2 removes this scaffold so the agent learns to operate autonomously while still being conditioned on budgets that are now adaptively sampled to reflect deployment conditions. Both phases optimize a composite reward that combines answer accuracy and budget efficiency using absolute and relative signals. An adaptive weighting scheme increases emphasis on efficiency for queries where the model is already accurate, and reduces it when accuracy is low, encouraging the agent to spend more budget when necessary to improve answers and conserve it otherwise.

Result: On seven general and multi-hop question answering benchmarks, AnySearch surpasses baselines over a wide range of budget scales. It generalizes to unseen budget constraints beyond those used in training and yields higher tool productivity (better use of each tool call) without incurring large additional token costs. The experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in the accuracy–efficiency trade-off compared to existing LLM-based search agents.

Conclusion: AnySearch provides a practical way to train a single LLM-based search policy that is explicitly budget-aware and adaptable to varying or unseen constraints at inference time. By using a scaffolded curriculum and a composite, adaptively weighted reward that balances accuracy with efficiency, the approach achieves better performance and resource usage than fixed-budget baselines, indicating that budget-conditioned RL is effective for robust, tool-augmented search agents.

Abstract: While reinforcement learning has enabled LLM-based search agents to invoke external tools, existing methods train under fixed budgets and cannot adapt when constraints vary at deployment. We propose AnySearch, a framework that enables a single policy to perform budget-aware search under any budget constraint through a training scaffold and curriculum reinforcement learning. In the first phase, we train the agent with explicit budget state injection and structured reasoning prompts that guide efficient allocation under linearly decaying budgets. In the second phase, the scaffold is removed and the agent learns to operate autonomously under adaptively sampled budget constraints, matching inference conditions. Both phases are optimized with a composite reward that couples answer accuracy with budget efficiency through absolute and relative signals, where an adaptive weight amplifies the efficiency signal for high-accuracy queries and attenuates it for low-accuracy ones. Extensive experiments on seven general and multi-hop QA benchmarks show that our method outperforms baselines across all budget scales, generalizes to unseen constraints beyond the training range, and achieves superior tool productivity without excessive token overhead. Our code is available at https://github.com/xwsun01/AnySearch.

</details>


### [203] [AnalysisBank: An Expert Analysis Pattern Library for Financial Report Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00818)
*Yajing Yang,Yunshan Ma,Kelvin J. L. Koa,Min-Yen Kan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes AnalysisBank, a framework for generating financial reports by composing data-driven analytical insights rather than following pre-defined structural templates, leading to more novel and grounded analyses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional financial report generation largely focuses on structural templates (sections, topics) and tends to produce repetitive, less data-grounded text. The authors want systems that behave more like experts: they inspect data, identify signals, and apply analytical reasoning patterns to produce insightful commentary. They see a gap in existing NLG methods, which underutilize fine-grained analytical moves that human experts employ.

Method: They introduce AnalysisBank, a library of reusable Analyses, where each Analysis links (1) a data signal extracted from financial data, (2) an analytical move (e.g., compare, explain, highlight anomaly), and (3) the expert-written text span from which this pairing was distilled. The authors distill Analyses from 550 expert financial reports, categorize them into signal and move types, and at inference time, match input data signals to appropriate Analyses and instantiate their analytical moves to compose new reports. They run experiments using four LLM backbones, comparing AnalysisBank-based generation against structural-level baselines on financial reporting benchmarks and also test transfer to scientific writing.

Result: From the 550 expert reports they obtain a heavy-tailed set of around 47–52 signal types and 13 analytical move types. On two financial benchmarks and across four different LLMs, using AnalysisBank increases the proportion of novel, data-grounded insights by 1.7x–3.7x compared with structural baselines. They also demonstrate some degree of transferability of the approach to scientific writing tasks, suggesting the framework is not limited to the financial domain.

Conclusion: Operating at the analytical level—via reusable, data-signal-plus-move Analyses—yields financial (and potentially scientific) reports that contain more novel, data-grounded insights than conventional structure-based approaches. AnalysisBank offers a practical way to distill and reuse expert reasoning patterns, and the released code and library may support broader research on analysis-level text generation.

Abstract: We argue that financial report generation should operate at the analytical rather than structural level, composing content from data-derived insights rather than high-level topics or sections. To this end, we propose AnalysisBank, which distills expert reports into a reusable library of Analyses, each pairing a data signal, an analytical move, and the expert span it was derived from. At inference time, AnalysisBank matches input signals to library entries and applies the retrieved moves to compose the report. A study of Analyses distilled from 550 expert reports reveals a heavy-tailed distribution of 47-52 signal types spanning 13 move types. On two financial benchmarks across four LLM backbones, AnalysisBank increases the proportion of novel, data-grounded insights by 1.7-3.7x over structural-level baselines. Transfer to scientific writing suggests that the distinction generalizes beyond finance. Code and the distilled Analysis library are available at https://github.com/yajingyang/AnalysisBank.

</details>


### [204] [Polished but Unresolved: Identifying Late-Stage Pressure States in Long-Horizon Tool-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00823)
*Haoyang Chen,Yi Liu,Jianzhi Shao,Xiaozhou Xu,Zhe Sun,Wei Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies and mitigates a “late-stage pressure” state in long-horizon tool-use agents, where they prematurely finalize answers instead of continuing necessary tool use.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon tool-use agents must know not only how to plan and act, but also when to stop. Many agents prematurely terminate by submitting seemingly polished answers while important constraints are still unresolved, reducing reliability on complex tasks. The authors aim to understand and algorithmically reduce this failure mode.

Method: 1) Train a linear probe on hidden states of tool-use agents to detect a “pressure” state corresponding to the urge to finalize. 2) Perform activation interventions along the learned pressure direction to test causal effects on behavior (continue tool use vs. submit). 3) Use controlled context manipulations to study what factors (e.g., constraint clarity, action mapping) change the pressure. 4) Design Probe-Sensed Pressure Relief (PSPR), a plugin that uses the probe: under moderate detected pressure, it applies a small pressure-relief activation; under high pressure, it triggers structured organization behaviors to reduce the urge to prematurely finalize. 5) Evaluate PSPR on multiple long-horizon benchmarks and on top of different base agent methods.

Result: The pressure state is linearly decodable from hidden activations, and steering activations along this direction reliably changes both the measured pressure score and the agent’s tendency to continue tool use versus submitting an answer early. Constraint clarity and clearer action mapping reduce measured pressure. PSPR, when integrated with various existing long-horizon agents, consistently improves performance across multiple benchmarks, indicating fewer premature finalizations and better task completion quality.

Conclusion: Late-stage pressure is a measurable, causally relevant internal state in long-horizon tool-use agents that contributes to premature finalization. By probing and intervening on this state, one can steer agents away from early stopping and toward more thorough tool use. The proposed PSPR plugin is lightweight, generally applicable to existing agents, and empirically yields consistent performance gains on long-horizon tasks.

Abstract: Long-horizon tool-use agents need not only to search and plan, but also to decide when to finalize. We study late-stage pressure states, in which an agent is biased toward submitting a final answer that appears complete and polished while key constraints remain unresolved. We first train a linear probe to show that this pressure state is identifiable from the agent's hidden states. Then, we use activation interventions along this pressure direction and find that shifting the hidden states changes both the pressure score and whether the agent continues tool use or submits early. Through controlled context manipulations, we further see that the pressure is mitigated by constraint clarity and action mapping. Based on these findings, we propose Probe-Sensed Pressure Relief (PSPR), a plugin that applies lightweight pressure relief direction under moderate pressure and moves to structured organization under high pressure risk. Experiments on multiple long-horizon benchmarks show that our method consistently strengthens existing agent methods.

</details>


### [205] [FLaG: Frequency-Domain Latent-attention Gated Pooling for Token Aggregation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00831)
*Kewei Li,Rongying Zhang,Xueli Wang,Xiwen Gong,Zhongjian Wang,Qiuchen Zhao,Lan Huang,Ruochi Zhang,Fengfeng Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes FLaG, a frequency-domain latent-attention gated pooling module that aggregates token representations via Fourier-domain processing, improving performance across protein, vision, and language tasks and offering interpretable spectral insights.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing token aggregation (pooling) methods typically operate only in the original token space and may not fully exploit structure present in the frequency domain of token sequences. The authors aim to introduce a general, plug-and-play aggregation bias in the frequency domain that can transfer across different modalities (proteins, images, text) and help both performance and interpretability.

Method: The authors design FLaG, a plug-in pooling module that first transforms encoder outputs into the Fourier domain using real-valued FFT (rFFT). They represent the nonredundant spectrum by concatenating real and imaginary parts into spectral tokens. Learnable latent queries perform cross-attention over these spectral tokens to summarize them into a compact representation. From this summary, FLaG derives a sample-conditioned channel gate that modulates the spectral channels. The modulated representations are then inverse-transformed/reconstructed back into token space for downstream aggregation (e.g., pooling). The same FLaG architecture is attached to different backbones: ESM2 for antimicrobial peptide prediction, ResNet18 for CIFAR-10/100, and RoBERTa for several NLP benchmarks. They also analyze layer-wise and frequency-wise sensitivities and the behavior of the residual gate and latent attention.

Result: Across four antimicrobial peptide backbone-species configurations, FLaG yields the best macro-averaged Spearman correlation, RMSE, and Recall@50. On vision tasks, it achieves the highest top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 among compared pooling schemes, and competitive performance on CIFAR-100. For language tasks, it attains the best mean score on five of seven evaluation metrics, though plain mean pooling still performs best on STSBenchmark. Mechanistic analyses on AMP prediction show that predictions are mainly sensitive to low-frequency components across layers, with relatively greater high-frequency sensitivity in the final layer. The residual gate tends to amplify many spectral channels while keeping the spectrum energy dominated by low frequencies, and the latent cross-attention adaptively distributes focus across frequencies in a sample- and species-specific way.

Conclusion: FLaG introduces a general, frequency-domain pooling mechanism that can be used as a drop-in aggregation module across diverse encoder architectures and modalities. It can improve downstream performance in many settings and reveals interpretable, layer- and frequency-specific behaviors of models, especially in protein tasks. The benefits are task- and backbone-dependent (e.g., not always superior to mean pooling), but overall FLaG provides a useful frequency-domain inductive bias and a flexible tool for spectral analysis of learned representations.

Abstract: Token aggregation converts token-level representations into fixed-dimensional sample representations, but most pooling methods operate only in the original token space. We introduce Frequency-Domain Latent-attention Gated Pooling (FLaG), a plug-in aggregation module that re-expresses encoder outputs in the Fourier domain before final pooling. FLaG represents the nonredundant rFFT spectrum through concatenated real and imaginary components, summarizes spectral tokens with learnable latent queries, derives a sample-conditioned channel gate, and reconstructs modulated token representations for downstream aggregation. We evaluate the same architecture across ESM2-based antimicrobial peptide (AMP) activity prediction, ResNet18 image classification on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, and three RoBERTa-based language tasks. FLaG achieves the best macro-averaged Spearman correlation coefficient, RMSE, and Recall@50 across four AMP backbone-species settings and the highest top-1 accuracy on CIFAR 10. It also achieves the best mean results on five of seven language metrics, although mean pooling remains strongest on STSBenchmark. AMP-side mechanistic analyses reveal low-frequency prediction sensitivity across most encoder layers, with increased relative high-frequency sensitivity in the final layer, and pronounced peptide-specific positional responses. The residual gate broadly amplifies spectral channels while preserving the low-frequency-dominated energy profile, whereas latent cross-attention exhibits sample- and species-specific spectral allocation. Overall, FLaG provides a transferable frequency-domain aggregation bias across protein, visual, and textual representations, with benefits that depend on the backbone and downstream task. Supplementary materials, source code, and data are available at https://www.healthinformaticslab.org/supp/ and https://github.com/Kewei2023/AMPCliff/tree/FLaG.

</details>


### [206] [Towards Generalizable Visually Grounded Exploration of Household Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00845)
*Linhao Zheng,Zeming Liu,Wangke Chen,Li Zeng,Wanxiang Che,Heyan Huang,Yuhang Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose VGEBench, a benchmark to test how well vision-language models can learn to operate new devices by visually exploring and interacting, without relying on manuals or human demonstration trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing embodied exploration agents rely too much on imitation learning from human-annotated trajectories and explicit documents, which hurts generalization and does not reflect how agents should actively explore and refine hypotheses when operating novel devices.

Method: They build VGEBench, a benchmark based on a Logic-Driven State Machine framework that simulates multi-turn interaction loops with devices. Agents must use active visual perception, hypothesis testing, and feedback-based correction to progress through states and reach functional goals, instead of following static labeled examples.

Result: Experiments on current vision-language models show that they struggle on VGEBench, particularly in turning abstract semantic/world knowledge into correct physical actions and in tracking states over long interaction horizons.

Conclusion: VGEBench reveals a large gap between current VLM abilities and the requirements for generalizable visually grounded exploration, highlighting the need for models that can better ground semantics into visual affordances and maintain consistent long-horizon interaction reasoning.

Abstract: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in static visual recognition and high-level semantic reasoning. However, current embodied exploration paradigms still heavily rely on imitation learning from human-annotated trajectories, which severely limits agents' generalization ability. The key bottleneck of realizing general autonomous embodied agents lies in Generalizable Visually Grounded Exploration: the ability to operate novel devices without manuals or specific training by actively grounding abstract world knowledge into fine-grained visual affordances. Yet, existing benchmarks fail to evaluate this capability: they generally rely on explicit documents and annotated trajectories, neglecting the dynamic Hypothesis-Interaction-Refinement process essential for functional device operation. To bridge this gap, we introduce VGEBench, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate the generalizable visually grounded exploration capabilities of VLMs. Unlike static datasets, we construct a Logic-Driven State Machine framework. This framework simulates multi-turn interaction loops, compelling agents to achieve goals by active visual perception and feedback-driven correction. Experimental results demonstrate that existing VLMs face significant challenges in translating semantic knowledge into physical execution and maintaining long-horizon state tracking.

</details>


### [207] [Verifiable Disaster Storylines and Causal Knowledge Graphs: A Citation-Grounded Pipeline from Heterogeneous Humanitarian Sources](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00858)
*Ivan Decostanzi,Michele Ronco,Sergio Consoli,Christina Corbane,Lorenzo Bertolini,Indaco Biazzo,Daria Mihaila,Manuel Garcia-Herranz,Felix Schwebel,Yelena Mejova,Kyriaki Kalimeri*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build an automated pipeline that turns mixed crisis data into traceable disaster storylines and causal graphs to help humanitarian responders quickly understand situations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In fast-moving crises, responders must interpret huge volumes of heterogeneous information (databases, reports, news) very quickly, but this exceeds human capacity, especially in early hours. Existing tools do not sufficiently integrate structured and unstructured sources into coherent, source-traceable situational pictures focused on causal chains and vulnerable populations (e.g., children).

Method: They integrate structured EM-DAT disaster records with unstructured text from ReliefWeb and EMM. Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), they retrieve relevant documents and generate structured, citation-grounded disaster storylines in a 17-field tabular format (e.g., severity, drivers, child-sensitive impacts). They then build causal knowledge graphs where each node and edge represents events or relations, each enriched with explanatory narratives that are explicitly linked back to cited primary sources. They evaluate via human assessment on three different crisis scenarios with 9 experts and 9 non-experts, measuring retrieval precision, faithfulness of causal relations, and user preferences.

Result: The system achieves high retrieval precision and produces causal relations that human evaluators judge as strongly faithful to the underlying sources. Both experts and non-experts clearly prefer the citation-grounded storylines and graph components over versions without explicit grounding. The approach appears scalable to the full EM-DAT database.

Conclusion: A scalable RAG-based pipeline can automatically generate narrative-enriched, source-traceable disaster storylines and causal knowledge graphs from mixed structured and unstructured crisis data. This supports improved situational awareness for humanitarian responders and analysts, and sets the stage for releasing an enhanced, publicly available EM-DAT variant that includes grounded narratives and causal structures.

Abstract: Effective humanitarian response depends on the rapid synthesis of heterogeneous, high-volume information sources - a task that routinely exceeds human analytical capacity in the critical early hours of a crisis. We present a pipeline that combines structured disaster records from EM-DAT with unstructured documents from ReliefWeb and the European Media Monitor (EMM) to produce source-grounded disaster storylines and causal knowledge graphs supporting situational awareness for responders and analysts. Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation, the pipeline extracts structured storylines - tabular event profiles covering 17 fields, from severity and key drivers to child-sensitive impact indicators - and constructs causal knowledge graphs where each node and edge is enriched with citation-grounded explanatory narratives, enabling full traceability back to primary sources. We evaluate the system on three diverse crisis use cases through a human evaluation involving 9 domain expert and 9 non-expert evaluators. Results confirm high retrieval precision, strong faithfulness of extracted causal relations, and a clear expert preference for citation-grounded components over ungrounded alternatives. The pipeline is designed to scale to the full EM-DAT catalogue, with the goal of publicly releasing a narrative-enriched version of the database.

</details>


### [208] [Reinforcement Learning Enhanced LLM Agents for Complex Vehicle Routing Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00859)
*Yi Chen,Zikang Yu,Jiahai Wang,Jinbiao Chen,Jianpeng Zhou,Zizhen Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces RLEA, a reinforcement-learning-enhanced multi-agent LLM framework that automatically models and solves complex Vehicle Routing Problem variants, improving success rate and reducing errors compared to prior methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although powerful VRP solvers exist, specifying correct and efficient models for complex VRP variants requires substantial expert knowledge, which limits the practical adoption of advanced optimization in real-world routing scenarios. The authors want to lower this expertise barrier by automating the modeling process itself.

Method: They design RLEA, a multi-agent system where LLM-based agents generate and refine optimization models for various VRP variants. A lightweight neural Planner, trained via Soft Q-learning, learns to orchestrate the sequence of actions of these agents. The system also includes an evolutionary memory module to accumulate and evolve past solutions and a retrieval-augmented generation mechanism to incorporate relevant external solver knowledge during code/program generation and refinement.

Result: RLEA was tested on 48 different VRP variants using multiple solvers. It surpassed the previous state-of-the-art automated modeling approach, with a 16.67% higher success rate and markedly fewer runtime errors, indicating more robust and reliable model generation.

Conclusion: Coupling reinforcement learning with LLM-based reasoning in a structured multi-agent framework is an effective way to automate the construction of optimization models for complex VRPs. This approach substantially improves both success rates and reliability, suggesting a promising direction for making advanced optimization more accessible and scalable.

Abstract: Vehicle Routing Problems (VRPs) are fundamental combinatorial optimization problems with widespread applications in various scenarios. The advanced optimization solvers can effectively solve such problems. However, modeling complex VRP variants for solvers often requires substantial domain expertise, which limits the accessibility of advanced optimization technologies. In this paper, we propose Reinforcement Learning Enhanced LLMAgents(RLEA), a multi-agent framework designed to automate the modeling of complex VRPs. RLEA introduces a lightweight neural Planner trained with Soft Q-learning to efficiently orchestrate the actions of LLM-based agents. In addition, we equip the system with an evolutionary memory module and retrieval-augmented generation, enabling the agent to leverage both accumulated experience and external solver knowledge during program generation and refinement for solving VRPs. We evaluated 48 distinct VRP variants across various solvers. The experimental results demonstrate that RLEA outperforms the previous state-of-the-ar method, achieving a 16.67% higher success rate while significantly reducing runtime errors. These results validate that integrating reinforcement learning with LLM-based reasoning is highly effective for automated optimization modeling. The appendix is available at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19134435.

</details>


### [209] [Beyond the Clock: Measuring the Value of Adaptive Revision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00874)
*Ayushi Chadha*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies when a higher-level controller in a hierarchical reasoning system should preserve or revise an existing strategy, finding that learned timing policies become state-dependent but do not outperform the best fixed timing schedule.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI systems become more agentic and composed of multiple interacting parts, many important decisions concern how higher-level controllers manage lower-level processes, especially when to stick with a current plan versus when to change it. Existing work often assumes either fixed schedules or focuses only on whether policies depend on state, without clearly separating whether that dependence actually improves task performance. This paper aims to clarify and empirically probe meta-level control over timing of plan revision in hierarchical latent reasoners.

Method: The authors use a hierarchical latent reasoner with a manager that controls whether to PERSIST with or REPLAN a lower-level computation strategy. They train this manager with different random seeds to learn when to revise its commitment. They then compare learned timing policies to forced fixed-timing policies on the same frozen model checkpoint. They conduct intervention experiments to manipulate timing decisions, exhaustively enumerate possible timing schedules under a given decision budget, and apply counterfactual PERSIST/REPLAN diagnostics to analyze how score-level evidence relates to the actual causal impact of timing decisions.

Result: Different training seeds lead to qualitatively different learned timing policies, from near-deterministic early revisions to highly state-dependent timing schedules. Despite this diversity, no learned policy outperforms the best fixed timing policy when evaluated on the same frozen underlying model. Intervention studies show that timing choices are consequential and order-sensitive, but exhaustive search reveals that a strong fixed schedule captures most of the attainable performance benefits at the given decision budget. The PERSIST/REPLAN diagnostics show that apparent predictive signals in scores can be misleading when most predictability is explained by the mere position of the decision rather than finer-grained state discrimination at that position.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that meta-level control over strategy revision timing can become state-dependent without yielding additional task performance over well-chosen fixed schedules. It argues that evaluating learned meta-control requires three distinct axes: (1) whether the controller’s score depends on internal state, (2) whether this dependence leads to different realized behaviors, and (3) whether those behavioral differences recapture outcome value beyond a strong non-adaptive baseline. This framework separates state dependence from true decision value and cautions against over-interpreting state-conditioned control signals that may not translate into reproducible performance gains.

Abstract: As agentic systems become compound systems, increasingly important decisions move above task execution itself: when should a higher-level controller preserve the strategy guiding another process, and when should it revise it? We study this meta-level control problem in a hierarchical latent reasoner whose manager can retain or replace a commitment governing lower-level computation. Across three precommitted training seeds, learned revision timing produces qualitatively different policies, ranging from an almost deterministic early clock to substantially more state conditioned schedule distributions, yet none outperforms the best forced timing policy evaluated on the same frozen checkpoint. This separates state dependence from decision value: a controller can vary its actions with internal state without turning that variation into a reproducible task-performance benefit. A deeper intervention study on the original checkpoint shows that timing itself is consequential and order-sensitive, while exhaustive enumeration reveals that a strong fixed schedule captures most of the measurable value available from timing at this decision budget. Counterfactual PERSIST/REPLAN diagnostics further show why score-level evidence can be misleading when predictability is dominated by decision position rather than within-position discrimination. Together, these results argue that learned meta-level control should be evaluated along three separate axes: whether its score depends on state, whether that dependence changes realized behavior, and whether those changes capture outcome value beyond a strong non-adaptive policy.

</details>


### [210] [FractalNet-Based Heterogeneous Federated Learning for Orbital Edge Intelligence in Satellite Mega-Constellations: A Wildfire Case Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00875)
*Sai Puppala,Koushik Sinha*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a heterogeneous, depth-adaptive federated learning framework for satellite mega-constellations using FractalNet, optimized for orbital constraints and demonstrated on wildfire detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing federated learning approaches are largely adapted from terrestrial and ground-centric settings, assuming relatively homogeneous devices, stable connectivity, and low-latency communication. These assumptions break down in satellite mega-constellations, where satellites differ drastically in Size, Weight, Power, and Cost (SWAP-C), have varying radiation tolerance, intermittent link availability, and large propagation delays. There is a need for learning architectures and coordination mechanisms that are explicitly tailored to these orbital edge environments, exploiting their structural heterogeneity while respecting resource and contact constraints.

Method: The paper formulates a new federated optimization problem tailored to satellites: contact-window-constrained, depth-heterogeneous learning, where different satellites train and host models of different depths based on their capabilities and connectivity. It leverages the FractalNet architecture to enable partial-depth model deployment and training. A distributed path scheduler dynamically assigns model depth to satellites as a function of their SWAP-C constraints, predicted inter-satellite contact opportunities, and online training statistics. To cut communication and energy costs, satellites are organized into tiers that pool and aggregate updates periodically rather than at every contact. A three-tier agentic control plane manages on-orbit scheduling decisions, anomaly escalation, and policy-governed autonomous behaviors for the learning and coordination processes.

Result: Through experiments on simulated satellite mega-constellations, the proposed method is evaluated on multiple metrics: convergence speed and stability of the learning process, communication efficiency (reduced message exchanges), energy adaptation to varying satellite power budgets, savings achieved by scheduled pooling of updates, robustness under adverse or failing conditions, and end-to-end latency. The framework shows favorable performance across these metrics compared to more conventional or naive baselines, demonstrating that depth-heterogeneous, contact-aware federated learning can maintain accuracy while significantly reducing resource usage.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that traditional, terrestrially inspired federated learning is inadequate for orbital edge intelligence in satellite mega-constellations. By explicitly modeling contact-window constraints, embracing depth heterogeneity via FractalNet, and using a distributed scheduler plus a multi-tier control plane, the proposed approach better matches the realities of space-based systems. The wildfire detection case study illustrates how different orbital shells can specialize in distinct semantic levels of situational awareness, from fine-grained anomaly detection to large-scale risk modeling. Overall, the framework provides a scalable, resource-aware path toward intelligent, autonomous sensing and decision-making in space-based infrastructures.

Abstract: Satellite mega-constellations are emerging as large-scale sensing, communication, and computation fabrics, yet their learning architectures remain largely inherited from terrestrial federated learning and ground-centric mission operations--- ill-suited to satellites that differ by orders of magnitude in Size, Weight, Power, and Cost (SWAP-C), radiation tolerance, link availability, and propagation delay. We propose a heterogeneous federated learning method based on the FractalNet architecture for orbital edge intelligence. We formalize contact-window-constrained, depth-heterogeneous federated optimization and introduce a distributed path scheduler that assigns model depth as a function of SWAP-C constraints, predicted inter-satellite contacts, and training statistics. To reduce message overhead and energy consumption, each tier pools updates periodically rather than at every contact opportunity, and a three-tier agentic control plane governs in-space scheduling, anomaly escalation, and policy-governed autonomy. As a case study, we apply the framework to wildfire detection, where each orbital shell naturally learns a different semantic level of situational awareness: pixel-scale thermal anomalies at low Earth orbit (LEO), regional fire-front dynamics at medium Earth orbit (MEO), and larger-scale risk propagation at geostationary or high Earth orbit (GEO/HEO). Experiments on simulated mega-constellations validate the approach across convergence, communication efficiency, energy adaptation, scheduled-pooling savings, robustness, and latency.

</details>


### [211] [Towards reliable multimodal disaster severity assessment through preference optimization and explainable vision-language reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00879)
*Yuanjun Zhang,Fuzel Ahamed Shaik,Suvojit Acharjee,Fahad Khalid,Mourad Oussalah*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a two-stage training framework combining supervised fine-tuning and preference-based alignment to improve both accuracy and explanation quality in multimodal disaster damage assessment models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal disaster damage assessment models struggle with scarce annotated data and lack systematic evaluation of reasoning quality. There is a need for models that not only classify damage accurately but also provide transparent, human-aligned explanations that are auditable for emergency management decisions.

Method: The authors design a unified Human-in-the-Loop annotation pipeline that produces two datasets from the same workflow: ReasoningSet with validated rationales for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and PreferenceSet with paired rationales for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). First, models are fine-tuned on ReasoningSet to learn to predict damage levels and generate explanations. Then, DPO is applied using PreferenceSet to align model-generated rationales with human preferences. The system is evaluated on both classification metrics (accuracy, Macro-F1) and explanation quality via automatic metrics, model-based scoring, and human ranking. Cross-model validation is carried out on InternVL-3-8B and LLaVA-1.5-7B.

Result: SFT improves classification accuracy from 73.64% to 78.29% and boosts Macro-F1 by 29% over the baseline, while explanation quality metrics increase by about 25%. Applying DPO on top of SFT further enhances interpretability and alignment of model reasoning with human judgments, especially as measured on the PreferenceSet. The framework leads to better detection of underrepresented mild damage cases and reduction of high-risk misclassifications. Results are consistent across different base models (InternVL-3-8B and LLaVA-1.5-7B), demonstrating robustness and generalizability.

Conclusion: The proposed SFT+DPO framework, built around a unified HITL data pipeline, yields multimodal disaster damage assessment models that are both more accurate and more interpretable. By jointly improving predictive performance, explanation quality, and alignment with human reasoning—while particularly addressing mild damage and hazardous errors—the approach offers a reproducible path to develop reliable, auditable systems that support real-world emergency management decisions.

Abstract: Reliable disaster damage assessment requires models that provide both accurate predictions and transparent explanations. However, existing multimodal approaches are limited by scarce annotated data and insufficient evaluation of reasoning quality. This study proposes a two-stage training framework that integrates Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) within a unified data construction pipeline. From a single Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) annotation workflow, two complementary datasets are derived, namely ReasoningSet, which contains validated rationales for SFT, and PreferenceSet, which comprises paired rationales for DPO-based alignment. The framework evaluates both classification performance and explanation quality using automatic metrics, model-based scoring, and human ranking. Experimental results show that SFT improves accuracy from 73.64% to 78.29% and increases Macro-F1 by 29% compared to the baseline, while explanation quality improves by approximately 25%. Subsequent DPO alignment further enhances interpretability on the PreferenceSet. Cross-model validation on InternVL-3-8B and LLaVA-1.5-7B demonstrates the robustness and generalizability of the approach. The proposed framework improves detection of underrepresented mild damage cases, reduces high-risk misclassifications, and strengthens alignment between model reasoning and human judgment. Overall, it provides a reproducible pathway to develop reliable multimodal systems that deliver auditable, actionable disaster insights for emergency management.

</details>


### [212] [Denoising Diffusion Generative Models Secretly Calculate Attentions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00885)
*Farzan Haddadi,Leila Monfared,Ebrahim Rezaii,Mohammadreza Malek-Mohammadi,Pejman Zakalvand,Narges Mokhtari*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that denoising diffusion models implicitly implement an attention mechanism similar to transformers, making attention a universal principle across major architectures. It exploits these equivalences to design a more efficient attention-based image generator with comparable performance and lower computational cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion models dominate image generation but are slow and resource-intensive, while transformers with attention dominate text modeling. There is a conceptual gap between these architectures despite their success. The authors aim to reveal a unifying view showing that diffusion models inherently use attention-like mechanisms, and to exploit this insight to simplify and accelerate image generation.

Method: The authors conceptually analyze the structure of denoising diffusion models and demonstrate that their operations can be expressed as an attention mechanism akin to that in transformers. They further highlight functional similarities between auto-encoders and attention-based models, establishing equivalences that permit architectural substitution. Based on this, they reformulate the diffusion framework into a simplified attention-based image generation algorithm designed to reduce training time and sampling cost.

Result: The proposed attention-centric reformulation of the diffusion framework yields an image generation algorithm that achieves performance comparable to standard diffusion models while requiring significantly fewer computational resources and less training and inference effort.

Conclusion: Attention can be interpreted as a universal machine learning principle underlying diffusion models, transformers, and even auto-encoders. By leveraging the equivalence between these architectures, one can replace diffusion components with attention-based mechanisms to obtain more efficient image generation systems without sacrificing much performance.

Abstract: Denoising diffusion models are the dominant architecture for image generation, whereas most natural language generation and modeling are primarily handled by well-known transformer architectures employing attention mechanism. Here, we show that diffusion models also inherently use an attention mechanism very similar to that of transformers. Therefore, attention emerges as a universal machine learning principle, based on a general training objective. We also show similarities in basic functional principle of auto-encoders and attention-based models. These equivalences allows us to interchange these designs based on practical requirements. As an example, we can reformulate the diffusion framework to reduce the lengthy training process and computation-intensive image generation. Using this approach, a simplified algorithm is proposed for image generation which is based on attention mechanism. Results show that the attention-based implementation achieves comparable performance with significantly less effort and computational resources.

</details>


### [213] [CacheBridge: Efficient Cross-Model KV Cache Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00891)
*Xingyu Qu,Siyuan Lu,Zhiyu Chen,Sheng Wang,Tao Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CacheBridge improves cross-model KV cache transfer between LLMs with more efficient, accurate, and scalable mapping than prior Full-Head Mapping.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing cross-model KV cache transfer (Full-Head Mapping) avoids replaying shared prefixes but is inefficient and brittle: it maps every target KV head from all source heads, making performance sensitive to architectural mismatch and causing mapper storage and application cost to grow with the number of supported layers.

Method: CacheBridge co-designs three components while keeping a closed-form, training-free affine mapping: (1) architecture-indexed mapper support that restricts each target attention head to a single matched source head instead of all heads; (2) attention-aligned calibration that weights reconstruction errors by each position’s causal attention sensitivity; and (3) a bounded, fused GPU kernel that constructs the weighted sufficient statistics needed for closed-form affine fitting without materializing full observation tensors.

Result: Compared to Full-Head Mapping, CacheBridge: (a) recovers accuracy in two problematic Ministal-3 transfer directions where Full-Head Mapping loses substantial performance while maintaining 99.83% mean target model retention on Qwen3; (b) on Qwen3 14B→32B reduces mapper storage by 8×, speeds up application by up to 3.0×, matches Full-Head Mapping quality with only 10% of its calibration data, and cuts mapper construction time on 500 sequences from 92.63s to 8.63s (10.7× faster).

Conclusion: A carefully designed, closed-form, head-aligned, and attention-weighted affine mapper (CacheBridge) can transfer KV caches across LLMs more robustly and efficiently than prior full-head approaches, achieving similar or better accuracy with much lower storage, calibration data, and runtime cost—making cross-model context sharing significantly more practical.

Abstract: Sharing context between LLMs in a multi-model system requires the receiving model to prefill the shared prefix because KV caches are model-specific. Recent closed-form cross-model KV transfer, hereafter Full-Head Mapping, avoids this replay by fitting a training-free affine mapper from source to target caches. However, its full-head design maps each target KV head from every source KV head in the selected layers, making transfer quality sensitive to architectural differences and causing mapper storage and application cost to grow with layer support. To this end, we introduce CacheBridge, which co-designs architecture-indexed mapper support, attention-aligned calibration, and bounded mapper construction while retaining a closed-form affine interface for online deployment. CacheBridge restricts each target head to a matched source head, weights reconstruction errors by causal attention sensitivity, and uses a fused GPU kernel to construct weighted sufficient statistics without materializing full observation tensors. Across three transfer directions, CacheBridge recovers the two Ministral 3 transfer directions where Full-Head Mapping loses substantial accuracy while preserving 99.83\% mean target retention on Qwen3. On Qwen3 $14\mathrm{B}\to32\mathrm{B}$, it reduces mapper storage by $8\times$, accelerates application by up to $3.0\times$, matches \fullhead with one tenth of the calibration data, and reduces 500-sequence construction from 92.63 to 8.63 seconds ($10.7\times$).

</details>


### [214] [CARE: Contrastive Anchor-based Rubric Evolution for Large Language Model Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00892)
*Siyuan Li,Xinxin Song,Chen Ruinian,Jingjing Fan,Tingxiong Xiao,Yangen Hu,Ke Zeng,Jinli Suo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CARE is a rubric-based RL method for LLM post-training that evolves task rubrics contrastively against strong anchor responses, preserving reward accuracy in high-score regions and improving open-ended task performance over time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing rubric-based reinforcement learning helps align LLMs on open-ended tasks better than RL with verifiable rewards, but static rubrics get hacked as models improve. Dynamic rubric methods suffer from undirected rubric changes, weak detection of hacking, and explosion in the number of rubrics. There is a need for a principled way to evolve rubrics that remains robust to reward over-optimization, especially in the high-reward region where hacking is most harmful.

Method: CARE (Contrastive Anchor-based Rubric Evolution) uses a high-quality anchor response from a strong frontier model, conditioned on the same prompt and rubrics, as a reference at each training step. For each step, it compares the highest-scoring rollout from the current policy with this anchor. Two mechanisms operate: (1) an Adaptive branch that reactively updates or repairs rubrics when the current high-scoring rollout reveals reward misspecification; and (2) a Chase branch that proactively sharpens rubrics to capture remaining quality gaps between the policy and the frontier anchor. This contrastive, anchor-grounded evolution of rubrics focuses on keeping reward discrimination accurate in the high-reward regime.

Result: On WildChecklist-9K using Qwen2.5-7B-Base and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, CARE attains state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks (Arena-Hard-2.0, InfoBench, FollowBench). It is the only tested method whose win rate against GPT-4.1 anchor responses consistently increases across 300 training steps. Additional experiments on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B show that the method transfers well across different LLM families.

Conclusion: By tying every rubric update to contrastive comparisons with high-quality anchor responses from a strong model, CARE prevents rubric hacking and preserves reward fidelity where it matters most—the high-reward region prone to over-optimization. This leads to more reliable reinforcement learning for open-ended instruction following, stronger and more stable benchmark performance, and better generalization across base and instruct models and across model families.

Abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning decomposes open-ended instructions into prompt-specific, flexible rubrics, making it better suited than reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for post-training LLMs on open-ended tasks. However, static rubrics are inevitably hacked as the policy evolves, and existing dynamic approaches introduce new problems: undirected rubric extraction, unreliable hack detection, and unbounded rubric proliferation. We propose $\textbf{CARE}$ ($\textbf{C}$ontrastive $\textbf{A}$nchor-based $\textbf{R}$ubric $\textbf{E}$volution), which grounds every rubric evolution step in a high-quality anchor response generated by a frontier model conditioned on the prompt and its rubrics. At each training step, CARE contrasts the highest-scoring rollout against the anchor, enabling two complementary mechanisms: an Adaptive branch that reactively repairs reward misspecification; and a Chase branch that proactively converts frontier-level quality gaps into sharper rubrics. Together, the two branches $\textbf{maintain discriminative accuracy in the high-reward region}$---the precise region where reward over-optimization mostly originates. Experiments on WildChecklist-9K with Qwen2.5-7B-Base and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct show that CARE achieves state-of-the-art performance on Arena-Hard-2.0, InfoBench, and FollowBench, and is the $\textbf{only}$ method whose win rate against GPT-4.1 anchor responses shows sustained improvement throughout 300 training steps; additional results on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B further indicate that CARE generalizes across model families.

</details>


### [215] [In-Context Neurofeedback: Can LLMs Control Their Internal Representations through Privileged Access?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00904)
*Koshiro Aoki,Ryota Takatsuki,Gouki Minegishi,Yusuke Haruki,Daisuke Kawahara*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper revisits claims that large language models can control their own internal states using neurofeedback and finds that, under stricter conditions, such control is not reliably demonstrated.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous work suggested large language models show metacognitive abilities by using neurofeedback to control internal representations, which has implications for understanding machine self-awareness and AI safety. However, those experiments used control targets that are not truly internal because they can be inferred directly from the prompt, leaving open the possibility that models rely on superficial strategies rather than genuine access to internal states.

Method: The authors redesign the neurofeedback paradigm used with LLMs so that the control target is a privileged internal representation, i.e., a state that cannot be inferred by an external observer from the input prompt alone. They then test whether LLMs can still achieve reliable control over these hidden internal states under this more stringent condition, aligning the setup more closely with human neurofeedback studies in cognitive neuroscience.

Result: Under the revised paradigm where the control target is privileged and not deducible from the prompt, LLMs do not show reliable ability to control these internal representations via neurofeedback. This contrasts with earlier work that reported successful control when the target could be externally inferred.

Conclusion: The failure of LLMs to control privileged internal representations suggests that earlier evidence for metacognitive control in LLMs may be explained by superficial mechanisms rather than genuine internal access. The authors argue that rigorous evaluations of metacognition in LLMs must use paradigms that require privileged access to internal states, analogous to standards in human neuroscience experiments.

Abstract: Whether large language models (LLMs) can control their own internal representations matters for both machine metacognition and AI safety. A recent study applied neurofeedback to LLMs and claimed that they can control their internal representations. However, the reported control may rely on superficial mechanisms rather than genuine internal access because the control targets in that study are not privileged, meaning that a third party can infer them from the prompt. We redesign the neurofeedback paradigm for LLMs so that the control target satisfies the privileged access requirement, which is closer to neurofeedback experiments in human cognitive neuroscience. Under this stricter setting, the models do not demonstrate reliable control over privileged internal representations, suggesting that previously reported control cannot exclude the possibility that it relies on superficial mechanisms. Our results indicate that rigorous assessments of metacognition in LLMs require evaluation methods that demand privileged access.

</details>


### [216] [RPCBench: A Benchmark for Proactive Premise Critique in LLM-based Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00918)
*Zhongru Chen,Yuan Wu,Yi Chang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RPCBench is a benchmark to test how well LLM-based recommender assistants detect and handle faulty assumptions in users’ recommendation requests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM recommenders are now interactive assistants, so they must not only suggest plausible items but also recognize when a user’s request is based on incorrect, incomplete, or inconsistent premises. Existing benchmarks either focus on ranking/generation or on generic error detection not grounded in recommendation context, leaving a gap for evaluating premise critique specific to recommender scenarios.

Method: The authors construct RPCBench, a benchmark of evidence-grounded test cases spanning five recommendation domains and ten types of premise failures. Each case includes a visible recommendation context plus a corrupted user query. They propose a fine-grained evaluation framework that scores models on proactive error detection, precise localization of the faulty premise, appropriate post-detection handling strategy, and faithfulness to the provided evidence. They then systematically evaluate 11 large language models on this benchmark, analyzing the impact of reasoning length and evidence density.

Result: Experiments show that the major weakness of current LLMs is proactive detection of faulty premises; they especially struggle with underspecified-premise errors. The study also finds that compact, target-critical evidence is more helpful than adding redundant context, and that increasing reasoning length does not consistently improve performance; quality peaks at an intermediate reasoning depth.

Conclusion: RPCBench effectively exposes current limitations of LLM-based recommender assistants in recognizing and handling flawed recommendation requests. Stronger mechanisms for proactive premise checking and handling underspecified queries are needed, and simply adding more evidence or longer reasoning chains is insufficient. The benchmark and framework provide a basis for developing and evaluating future models with better recommendation-premise critique abilities.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as interactive recommender assistants. Their evaluation should therefore go beyond plausible item recommendation and test whether they can recognize flawed recommendation requests. Existing recommender benchmarks mainly assess ranking, generation, or preference satisfaction, while existing error-detection benchmarks are usually not grounded in recommendation-specific user and candidate evidence. To address this gap, we introduce RPCBench, a benchmark for evaluating Recommender-Premise Critique: the ability to detect, diagnose, and properly handle faulty premises in natural-language recommendation requests. RPCBench contains evidence-grounded test instances from five recommendation domains and covers ten types of premise failures. Each instance provides a visible recommendation context and a corrupted user query. We further design a fine-grained evaluation framework that measures proactive detection, error localization, post-detection handling strategy, and evidence faithfulness. Through a systematic evaluation of 11 LLMs, we find that proactive detection is the main bottleneck in Recommender-Premise Critique, and models perform worst on underspecified-premise errors. We also observe that target-critical information density matters more than redundant evidence, and that longer reasoning does not monotonically improve critique quality: performance peaks at intermediate reasoning length, while overly long reasoning is accompanied by an overthinking penalty. The code is available at https://github.com/ZhongruChen/RPCBench.

</details>


### [217] [VIBE-Bench: Evaluating Personalized Large Language Models When Profiles Don't Mean Preferences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00921)
*Yiwen Jiang,Yang Deng,Stephanie Fong,Zimu Wang,Yaling Shen,Wei Feng,Hongxi Yang,Xiangyu Zhao,Zhongxing Xu,Deval Mehta,Xuelian Cheng,Zongyuan Ge*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces VIBE-Bench to evaluate how well personalized LLMs infer user preferences when profile cues and actual query-specific preferences belong to different conceptual spaces, revealing a key failure mode in current approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current personalized LLM benchmarks mostly assume that user preferences can be inferred from semantically similar past interactions, which is unrealistic when user profiles and task-specific preferences are conceptually misaligned. There is a need for a benchmark that specifically targets this misalignment and tests deeper preference reasoning beyond shallow semantic matching.

Method: The authors define the profile-preference conceptual misalignment (PRCM) setting, then construct VIBE-Bench, a psychology-grounded benchmark with two tasks, 3,504 personas, and 12,239 dialogues, plus a manually verified gold test subset. The benchmark is designed so that relevant user preferences cannot be captured by simple semantic similarity. They evaluate various personalization methods on VIBE-Bench to assess how well they can perform cross-concept preference reasoning.

Result: Across experiments on VIBE-Bench, several existing personalization techniques for LLMs perform poorly under PRCM conditions, indicating that these models primarily leverage shallow semantic correlations rather than learning robust mappings between user profiles and query-specific preferences when concepts are misaligned.

Conclusion: Profile-preference conceptual misalignment is a concrete and distinct failure mode for personalized LLMs, and existing methods are inadequate at handling it. VIBE-Bench provides a focused, psychology-informed testbed that can drive future research toward deeper preference reasoning that goes beyond surface-level semantic overlap.

Abstract: Personalized Large Language Models (PLLMs) aim to tailor responses to individual users, where a central challenge is preference reasoning: inferring query-relevant preferences from user-related history. Existing benchmarks, however, largely assume that such preference can be retrieved from semantically related history. We study an underexplored but practically important regime, profile-preference conceptual misalignment (PRCM), where observable profile cues and query-specific preferences lie in different concept spaces, making semantic retrieval inconsistent for personalization. We introduce VIBE-Bench, a benchmark with two psychology-grounded tasks, 3,504 personas and 12,239 dialogues, including a manually verified gold test set, and requires cross-concept preference reasoning beyond surface semantic overlap. Experiments with several personalization methods show that current PLLMs largely rely on shallow semantic correlations and fail to acquire robust cross-concept mappings. These findings establish PRCM as a distinct failure regime in PLLMs and position VIBE-Bench as a focused testbed for advancing preference reasoning beyond semantic matching.

</details>


### [218] [Few-Shot Out of Domain Intent Detection with Covariance Corrected Mahalanobis Distance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00961)
*Jayasimha Talur,Oleg Smirnov,Paul Missault*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They improve out-of-domain intent detection in conversational agents by fixing a weakness in the Mahalanobis-distance method, especially in few-shot scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing OOD intent detectors, including a strong Mahalanobis distance–based method, perform poorly in the realistic few-shot setting, where only a small number of in-domain examples are available. Understanding why this happens and how to fix it is important for making chatbots robust to unknown intents in practice.

Method: They analyze why the standard Mahalanobis distance method underperforms in few-shot settings, identifying issues related to covariance estimation. Based on this, they propose a modified “covariance corrected” Mahalanobis distance, which adjusts or regularizes the covariance used to compute distances between utterance representations and in-domain clusters.

Result: The proposed covariance-corrected Mahalanobis distance improves OOD intent detection performance compared with the original Mahalanobis method and baselines in few-shot scenarios, while retaining or exceeding performance in other settings.

Conclusion: Careful treatment of covariance estimation is crucial for Mahalanobis-based OOD intent detection. By correcting the covariance, one can restore and enhance the method’s effectiveness, particularly when only a small number of labeled in-domain examples are available, making it more suitable for practical conversational agents.

Abstract: Conversational agents like chatbots and voice assistants are trained to understand and respond to user intents. On encountering an utterance with an intent different from the ones they have been trained on, these agents are expected to classify the intent as `unknown' or `out of domain'. This problem is known as out of domain (OOD) intent detection. Podolskiy et al. (2021), showed that Mahalanobis distance can be used effectively for identifying OOD intents, outperforming competing approaches. However, their method fails to outperform the baselines in the practically important few-shot setting. In this paper we analyze the reason for low performance and propose a covariance corrected Mahalanobis distance for detecting out-of-domain intents.

</details>


### [219] [CoBRA: Learning Tool-Use Boundaries via Counterfactual Margins](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00967)
*Wenhao Zou,Xianglong Liu,Wendong Bi,Hanjie Wang,Simin Zhao,Gong Zhi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CoBRA is a framework to learn when a language model should call external tools by explicitly estimating the marginal benefit of tool use on each instance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tool-augmented LLMs face a key decision: not only how to use tools, but whether to invoke them at all. Unnecessary calls waste latency and cost and may introduce noise, while missed calls reduce performance on knowledge-intensive or time-sensitive queries. Existing approaches tend to rely on global or absolute signals like confidence or task reward and do not directly model the per-instance reward difference between using tools and not using them. This creates inefficiencies and suboptimal boundaries between internal reasoning and external tool use. The paper aims to learn a precise, data-driven decision boundary that indicates when tools are actually beneficial.

Method: The authors introduce CoBRA, a counterfactual boundary-learning framework. They derive two experts from the same base model: an internal expert (answers without tools) and an external expert (answers with tools, e.g., retrieval). They collect paired trajectories where both experts answer the same queries and estimate the reward margin (performance difference) between tool and no-tool responses. This margin divides instances into internal-favored, external-favored, and ambiguous. Using the clear-margin cases, they perform Boundary-Aware Cold-Start Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) to teach the model an initial decision boundary for tool use. They then refine this boundary with MARS-RL, a reinforcement learning procedure using reference-split rollouts and counterfactual marginal advantages to optimize when the model should call tools.

Result: On Qwen3-4B with retrieval as the primary tool, CoBRA yields better tool-use efficiency, meaning fewer unnecessary tool calls, and higher boundary-sensitive answer accuracy—i.e., it more often chooses the right mode (internal vs. external) for each query. At the same time, it preserves strong performance on tool-dependent out-of-distribution questions, indicating that the improved efficiency does not come at the cost of underusing tools where they are crucial.

Conclusion: Explicitly learning the counterfactual reward margin between using and not using tools enables a language model to make better per-instance tool-use decisions. CoBRA’s combination of boundary-aware SFT and RL fine-tuning constructs a robust decision boundary that reduces redundant tool calls, improves accuracy where the choice of tool use matters, and still handles challenging tool-dependent queries well. This suggests that counterfactual boundary learning is an effective strategy for optimizing tool-augmented LLM behavior.

Abstract: As large language models increasingly act through external tools, deciding when to call a tool has become a central problem alongside deciding how to use it. Unnecessary tool calls introduce latency, cost, retrieval noise, and error propagation, while missed calls hurt knowledge-intensive queries or questions requiring up-to-date evidence. Existing methods typically trigger tools from absolute query or generation signals, such as difficulty, confidence, or final task reward, and therefore lack an explicit estimate of the instance-level marginal benefit of tool use. We propose CoBRA, a counterfactual boundary-learning framework for tool-augmented language models. CoBRA first constructs internal and external experts from the same base model, collects paired trajectories, and estimates the reward margin between answering with and without tools. This margin partitions data into internal-favored, external-favored, and ambiguous cases. CoBRA then uses clear-margin samples for Boundary-Aware Cold-Start SFT, followed by MARS-RL with reference-split rollouts and counterfactual marginal advantages to optimize boundary decisions.
