Experiments with retrieval as the main tool on Qwen3-4B show that CoBRA improves tool-use efficiency and boundary-sensitive answer accuracy while maintaining strong performance on tool-dependent out-of-distribution questions.

</details>


### [220] [Figures as Programs: Recursive Generation of Editable Scientific Figures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01006)
*Yepeng Liu,Dasen Dai,Chengzhi Liu,Yiren Song,Hai Ci,Yu Zhang,Qi Zhang,Mike Zheng Shou,Xin Eric Wang,Yuheng Bu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A system called FigTree automatically converts scientific papers into editable, high-quality SVG methodology figures using a multi-agent, program-based approach with refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Creating clear scientific methodology figures is important but currently labor-intensive, often requiring multiple refinement iterations and relying on raster images that are hard to precisely edit. Existing image-generation models help but still struggle to produce satisfactory results in one shot and make fine-grained edits, especially with raster outputs.

Method: The authors formulate figure generation as recursive SVG program construction. Their system, FigTree, is a multi-agent pipeline that (1) grounds figure content in the source paper, (2) decomposes the figure into a hierarchy of local regions, (3) generates each region as a short SVG program, and (4) assembles these programs. They add a render-critic refinement loop that jointly analyzes the rendered SVG and its underlying code to locate and repair visual defects by editing specific SVG statements.

Result: Through extensive evaluations on both the visual quality and editability of generated figures, FigTree is shown to produce high-quality scientific figures and to support more effective editing workflows compared with existing raster-based image generation and editing approaches.

Conclusion: Program-based, multi-agent SVG generation with a render-critic loop enables automated creation of scientific methodology figures that are both visually strong and easily editable, outperforming raster-based methods on figure quality and editability.

Abstract: Scientific methodology figures are essential for communicating complex methods clearly, yet creating them remains labor-intensive and typically requires multiple rounds of refinement. Recent image-generation models can synthesize visually appealing raster figures, but producing a human-satisfactory result in a single generation step remains difficult. Moreover, precise edits to raster figures are challenging for both humans and models. We formulate scientific figure generation as recursive SVG program construction and propose \textsc{FigTree}, a \textit{multi-agent} system that automatically transforms a scientific paper into a structured vector figure. \textsc{FigTree} grounds figure content in the source paper, decomposes a figure into a hierarchy of local regions, generates each region as a short SVG program, and assembles the resulting fragments. A render-critic refinement loop jointly inspects the rendered figure and its underlying program, enabling visual defects to be traced to specific statements and accurately repaired. We conduct extensive evaluations of \textsc{FigTree} on figure quality and editability, showing that \textsc{FigTree} produces high-quality figures, while also enabling more effective editing than existing raster-based methods.

</details>


### [221] [Spawn Freely, Act Sparingly: Progressive Risk Vesting for Recursive LLM-Agent Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01035)
*Molly Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Progressive Risk Vesting (PRV), a formal framework for deciding when recursive LLM agent branches get real-world authority, ensuring a trajectory-level harm bound while preserving useful search behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recursive LLM agents can spawn many specialized branches, some of which may be granted tools that affect the real world (e.g., sending data or deploying code). Granting such authority is risky because some actions are irreversible and harms can accumulate over a branching search process. Existing approaches lack a principled way to allocate and control risk across adaptively generated branches while still enabling broad search. The authors aim to provide a formal, quantitative framework for budgeting and charging risk as authority is granted to branches.

Method: The authors distinguish two regimes: sandbox spawning (no real harm possible due to external controls) and capability activation (granting real authority that can cause irreversible harm). They introduce Progressive Risk Vesting (PRV), which maintains a trajectory-level risk budget in escrow and deducts from it each time a branch is granted authority. They provide theoretical analysis of adaptively generated branching trees, proving an anytime harm bound under PRV. They require that local risk certificates remain valid conditional on the full history, including how branches were selected. They compare PRV to irrevocable spawn charging, showing that with fixed gates, charges, and compute, delayed vesting is not more restrictive. They analyze a stylized branching model with an “authority reproduction number” R_A, deriving scaling laws for trajectory harm as local risk p→0, and use a finite-type occupancy model to derive risk and compute shadow prices, which yield threshold rules for nested fanout modes. They illustrate their claims with branching calculations and a split-sample experiment on synthetic tasks.

Result: Theoretically, the authors obtain an anytime upper bound on harm for recursively branching agents using PRV, even when branch outcomes are dependent and selection is adaptive. They show that delayed risk vesting can replicate any policy achievable under a simpler irrevocable charging scheme, so safety constraints need not reduce available policies. In the stylized model, they find that as local risk p→0, trajectory harm scales proportionally to p when the authority reproduction number R_A<1 (subcritical), scales as √p at the critical point R_A=1, and remains bounded away from zero for R_A>1 (supercritical). The occupancy model yields explicit shadow prices for risk and compute that support a threshold rule for granting authority under nested fanout with diminishing marginal value per unit risk. Experiments and branching simulations qualitatively validate the theoretical predictions, but are explicitly synthetic and not estimates of real deployed safety.

Conclusion: Progressive Risk Vesting offers a principled way to manage and charge risk when granting real-world authority to branches in recursive LLM agents. By holding a trajectory-level risk budget in escrow and vesting it only when capabilities are activated, the framework maintains an anytime harm bound while preserving the flexibility of broad sandboxed search. The analysis highlights the importance of keeping the authority reproduction number below criticality and using shadow prices of risk and compute to set threshold rules for when to grant recursive authority. The practical design implication is to encourage wide exploration in a sandbox and to grant high-impact authority rarely, explicitly charging against a global risk budget each time authority is vested.

Abstract: Recursive LLM agents can broaden their search by spawning specialists. Some branches later request tools that send data or deploy code. When should a branch receive authority to act? We distinguish sandbox spawning, in which external controls prevent the specified harm, from capability activation, in which a selected branch crosses an irreversible-action boundary. Progressive Risk Vesting (PRV) holds a trajectory-level risk budget in escrow and debits it as branches are activated. We prove an anytime harm bound for adaptively generated trees. Branch outcomes may be dependent, but each local certificate needs to remain valid conditional on the full pre-activation history, including the information used to select the request. When activation gates, branch charges, and compute constraints are held fixed, delayed vesting preserves every policy available under irrevocable spawn charging. Marginal risk estimates can still fail after branch selection. In a stylized branching model, trajectory harm changes as the authority reproduction number $\mathcal{R}_A$ crosses one. As local risk $p$ approaches zero, trajectory harm is proportional to $p$ below criticality, proportional to $\sqrt{p}$ at criticality, and retains a positive floor above it. A finite-type occupancy model yields risk and compute shadow prices. For nested fanout modes with decreasing marginal value per unit risk, these prices produce a threshold rule. Branching calculations and a split-sample experiment illustrate the results. These synthetic studies do not estimate safety in deployed agents. The analysis suggests a design rule: search broadly in the sandbox and grant recursive authority sparingly, with an explicit risk charge.

</details>


### [222] [Data-Driven Persona-Conditioned Agents for A/B Test Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01038)
*Ziyad Benomar,Weronika Łajewska,Leonardo Perelli,Saab Mansour*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build an LLM-based simulation framework that predicts the outcome of A/B tests using agents powered by data-driven user personas instead of synthetic ones, achieving strong directional accuracy and enabling cheap pre-screening of experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A/B testing is slow and costly because each test uses real user traffic, engineering work, and weeks of data collection. Product teams need a way to estimate which candidate changes are promising before committing to full online experiments. Existing persona-based simulations rely on synthetic or rule-based personas that are often unrealistic and not grounded in real behavior.

Method: They construct LLM-powered agents conditioned on personas derived from anonymized behavioral data such as activity patterns, engagement signals, and inferred demographics. They pose A/B test simulation as a structured question-answering task to the LLM agents. The study systematically varies: (i) the format of the questions that represent experimental conditions, (ii) the sources and domain alignment of persona data, (iii) the trade-off between depth of behavioral detail per persona and diversity across personas, and (iv) strategies for efficient subsampling of the simulated user population. They then compare simulated predictions to outcomes from 40 real A/B tests across two types of evaluation metrics.

Result: On a benchmark of 40 historical A/B tests, their best configuration of LLM agents and persona construction achieves 0.75–0.90 directional accuracy (i.e., correctly predicting which variant wins or the sign of the effect), depending on the metric type considered. This indicates that the simulation can reliably forecast the direction of impact for many experiments.

Conclusion: Data-driven personas grounded in actual behavioral signals, when combined with LLM-powered agents and structured question formulations, can reliably predict the directional outcome of many A/B tests. This makes them a promising tool for fast, low-cost pre-screening of product experiments, potentially reducing the number of full online A/B tests that need to be run.

Abstract: A/B testing is the gold standard for evaluating product changes, but each experiment requires real user traffic, engineering effort, and weeks of measurement. We propose a simulation framework that predicts A/B test outcomes using LLM-powered agents conditioned on data-driven personas grounded in real user behavioral signals. Unlike prior work that relies on synthetic or rule-based personas, our agents are constructed from anonymized behavioral data-activity patterns, engagement signals, and inferred demographics-enabling more faithful population modeling. We frame A/B test simulation as a structured question task and systematically study (i) question design formats, (ii) the impact of persona data source and domain alignment, (iii) the trade-off between per-persona behavioral depth and population diversity, and (iv) efficient population subsampling. On a benchmark of 40 A/B tests spanning two metric types, our best configuration achieves 0.75-0.90 directional accuracy depending on the test metric, demonstrating that data-driven personas are a viable path toward fast, low-cost experiment pre-screening.

</details>


### [223] [AgentFactory: Towards Automated Agentic System Design and Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01045)
*Enci Zhang,Haofeng Wang,Yuesheng Zhu,Xiaole Cui,Guibo Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgentFactory is a framework that automatically co-optimizes both LLM-based workflows (agentic system structures) and the underlying models themselves, balancing performance, cost, and efficiency, and significantly outperforming manual and prior automated designs across multiple domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Designing and tuning LLM-based agentic systems is currently manual, labor-intensive, and difficult to scale or adapt to different domains. Existing automated workflow-optimization methods ignore model capability choices, rely on a single metric, and do not adequately account for real-world constraints like cost and efficiency. There is a need for an automated way to jointly optimize model selection/fine-tuning and agent workflow design under multiple objectives.

Method: The authors propose AgentFactory, a framework that uses advanced LLMs as optimizers to search over a large joint space of (1) workflow structures for agentic systems and (2) choices of foundation models, including fine-tuned variants. It employs a three-stage optimization pipeline with iterative search and evaluation, where candidate agentic system designs are generated, assessed on multiple objectives (performance, cost, efficiency), and refined based on task-specific requirements. This closed-loop process systematically explores and converges toward more effective combinations of models and workflows.

Result: Across eight benchmarks in five domains (general reasoning, coding, mathematics, medicine, finance), AgentFactory consistently outperforms both manually designed agentic systems and existing automated optimization methods. It achieves an average performance gain of 9.1% over baselines, with larger improvements on domain-specific benchmarks, including 19.6% on MedQA and 18.7% on FinEval, while respecting operational constraints like cost and efficiency.

Conclusion: AgentFactory demonstrates that jointly optimizing both the workflow structure and foundation models of LLM-based agentic systems, under multi-objective criteria, can yield significantly more capable and efficient systems than manual design or prior automated methods. This establishes automated, LLM-driven co-optimization as a promising direction for building scalable, high-performing agentic systems tailored to diverse, real-world tasks.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities as powerful components in agentic systems, enabling sophisticated reasoning and complex task execution. However, current approaches to manually designing and optimizing agentic systems heavily rely on manual effort, limiting their adaptability and scalability. Recent work has explored the automated optimization of workflow designs. However, these approaches often overlook the crucial role of model capabilities and focus on single performance metrics, failing to address real-world deployment constraints. In this paper, we present AgentFactory, a framework that jointly optimizes both foundation models and workflow structures in agentic systems while considering multiple objectives including performance, cost, and efficiency. AgentFactory leverages advanced LLMs as optimizers to navigate the vast search space of possible configurations, employing a three-stage optimization pipeline to automatically discover effective combinations of fine-tuned models and optimized workflows. Through an iterative optimization process, our framework systematically explores and evaluates different agentic system designs, adapting to task-specific requirements while maintaining operational efficiency. We evaluate AgentFactory across eight benchmarks spanning five domains, including general reasoning, coding, mathematics, medicine, and finance. Our experiments demonstrate that AgentFactory consistently outperforms both manually designed methods and existing automated approaches, achieving an average improvement of 9.1% across all benchmarks, with particularly significant gains in domain-specific tasks (19.6% on MedQA and 18.7% on FinEval). These results establish AgentFactory as a promising approach for developing more capable and efficient agentic systems through automated optimization.

</details>


### [224] [QILP-0: Constructing Observational Declarative Twins of Quantum Circuits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01049)
*Marina de la Cruz Echeandía,César Luis Alonso,Tony Ribeiro,Alfonso Ortega de la Puente*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: QXymb/QILP-0 builds exact logical “twins” of quantum circuit behavior as finite multi-valued logic programs, separating logical explanation from numerical and hardware uncertainty.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To obtain faithful, declarative, and auditable logical representations (“twins”) of quantum circuit behavior that are independent of specific targets, backends, and discretization noise, improving interpretability and verification in quantum machine learning.

Method: Define a general framework (QXymb) for observational declarative twins of quantum circuits and instantiate its order-0 specialization (QILP-0). QILP-0 incrementally traverses a structured family of quantum observables within a declared observational scope and reference horizon, measures coverage relative to a fixed target-independent reference, geometrically organizes observable responses, and deterministically maps them back to original observables. It discretizes selected observable profiles into a finite relation, then uses the target only to audit twin-admissibility and induce a finite multi-valued propositional logic program that exactly reconstructs the discrete relation. Uncertainties from hardware, numerics, and discretization are kept as audit metadata, not in the logic itself.

Result: In Bars & Stripes experiments (16–100 qubits, using product and grid-CZ embeddings) and Low-Depth MNIST (14,708 0/1 digits before and after a trained variational circuit), every resulting finite relation is reconstructed completely and conflict-free by the induced QILP-0 theory, achieving strict accuracy of 1, regardless of whether native discrete or continuous-to-discrete paths are used.

Conclusion: QXymb, via its QILP-0 specialization, can produce exact, conflict-free declarative logical twins of quantum circuits across diverse QML tasks, with logical exactness cleanly separated from implementation and discretization uncertainties that are relegated to audit metadata. This supports interpretable, auditable, and target-independent analysis of quantum circuit behavior.

Abstract: This paper introduces QXymb, a general framework for constructing observational declarative twins of quantum circuits, and develops QILP-0, its first complete order-0 specialization. QILP-0 constructs a finite multi-valued propositional logic program from observed circuit behaviour within a declared observational scope.
  The pipeline traverses a declared family of quantum observables incrementally according to a reproducible structural grading and a declared observational reference horizon. Progress is quantified through reference-relative coverage against a fixed target-independent reference. Observable responses are organized through target-independent geometry, while retained latent structure is mapped deterministically back to original observable columns before symbolic processing, preserving observational semantics and provenance.
  Selected observable profiles are converted into a finite relation through admissible target-independent discretization. The target is used only afterwards to audit twin-admissibility and induce the declarative theory. A theory is certified as an exact observational declarative twin when it completely and correctly reconstructs the resulting finite task-conditioned discrete relation. Logical exactness is therefore separated from numerical, backend, provider, and discretization uncertainty, which is retained as audit metadata.
  Validation uses two complementary QML settings. Exhaustive Bars & Stripes experiments compare product and grid-CZ embeddings from 16 to 100 qubits and exercise the native-discrete branch. Low-Depth MNIST analyses all 14,708 digit-0/1 instances before and after a trained variational quantum transformation and exercises continuous discretization. In every reported relation, the induced QILP-0 theory achieves complete, conflict-free reconstruction with strict accuracy equal to one.

</details>


### [225] [WorldBench: Culturally Grounded Benchmark for Multilingual Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01056)
*Leonardo Ranaldi,Sherrie Shen,Jushi Kai,Alexandra Birch*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WorldBench is a multilingual, persona-grounded benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on realistic, multi-step workflows with a focus on state preservation and grounded actions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-agent benchmarks do not adequately test agents on preserving environment state, operating across multiple languages and cultures, and handling realistic everyday workflows in grounded environments. The authors want a more comprehensive, realistic, and multilingual benchmark to stress-test agent robustness in such settings.

Method: They construct WorldBench, a benchmark of 1,600 grounded, everyday tasks spanning seven languages and eight cultures, where agents act via structured actions in a sandboxed environment. Tasks are persona-grounded, designed and refined with input from language- and culture-specific human annotators. For evaluation, they extend existing metrics and introduce Constrained Task Success (CTS), which combines natural-language instructions with programmatic testbeds to assess not only task completion but also minimal modification and other constraints, using a mix of deterministic checks and LLM-as-a-judge scoring.

Result: When evaluated on WorldBench, state-of-the-art LLM agents achieve only 49.2% on the new CTS metric. Across models, there are substantial discrepancies between getting the end result correct and preserving the environment/state correctly, especially on long-horizon tasks and in multilingual settings.

Conclusion: Current LLM-powered agents are still brittle when executing long-horizon, multilingual, grounded workflows, particularly under strict state-preservation constraints. WorldBench exposes these weaknesses and provides a challenging, culturally diverse benchmark for future agent development and evaluation.

Abstract: Despite the growing use of LLM-powered agents to solve multi-step tasks in complex environments, existing benchmarks rarely test state preservation, performance across languages, and application to realistic, grounded scenarios. To address these concerns, we present WorldBench: a comprehensive, multilingual benchmark of genuine, persona-grounded everyday workflows, where agents can act in a sandbox via structured actions. WorldBench comprises 1,600 tasks across seven languages and eight cultures, filtered and refined through feedback from human annotators with language- and culture-specific expertise. For evaluation, we extend metrics from previous works and introduce Constrained Task Success (CTS), which combines natural language instructions and testbeds to score task completion, minimal modification, and other complementary metrics through deterministic and LLM-as-a-Judge evaluations. Our experiments show that frontier models reach only 49.2% CTS, with all models demonstrating large gaps between correctness and environment preservation. We thereby show that current agents remain brittle in multilingual, agentic scenarios, especially for long-horizon tasks and under state-preservation constraints

</details>


### [226] [User Representation via Cross Multi-source Behavior Pre-training for Mobile Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01057)
*Chengqi Yang,Yiran Qiao,Feng Liu,Xingyu Lou,Zijun Zhou,Xiaoyun Mo,Changwang Zhang,Jiayuan Xu,Jun Wang,Xiang Ao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a new pre-training model for user representation that uses multi-source, device-level behavior logs to improve mobile game recommendation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing user representation pre-training largely relies on single-app or app-level behaviors, ignoring that real user behavior on devices spans multiple sources (apps, system events, etc.) and multiple granularities (device-level, app-level, action-level). This limitation makes it hard to capture true user intent, especially for mobile game recommendation where user interests are embedded in complex cross-app patterns.

Method: They introduce CM-PTM, a Cross Multi-source Behavior Pre-Training Model tailored to device-level logs. The key idea is a hierarchical cascaded mask-then-predict pretext task: first predict the source of the next behavior (which app/source the next action will come from), then refine the prediction to the app-action level. This allows the model to jointly learn cross-source dependencies and fine-grained behavioral dynamics in a single pre-training framework.

Result: On large-scale real-world mobile datasets, the pre-trained CM-PTM user representations lead to significant and consistent improvements on downstream mobile game recommendation tasks compared with existing approaches.

Conclusion: Modeling user behavior at the device level with a hierarchical, cross-source pre-training objective more effectively captures users' intrinsic interests than traditional app-centric methods, bringing substantial gains to mobile game recommendation. The approach demonstrates the value of unified, multi-source, multi-granular behavior modeling for personalization tasks.

Abstract: User representation pre-training has become a fundamental paradigm for alleviating data sparsity in downstream personalization tasks. However, existing studies predominantly focus on single-app or app-level behaviors, overlooking the inherently cross-source and multi-granular nature of user activities on mobile devices. At the device level, user intent emerges from complex interactions among heterogeneous behavior sources and hierarchical action structures, posing challenges that cannot be addressed by conventional app-centric modeling. To tackle this issue, we propose CM-PTM, a novel Cross Multi-source Behavior Pre-Training Model tailored for mobile game user representation learning on device-level behavioral logs. CM-PTM employs hierarchical cascaded mask-then-predict proxy tasks that first infer the source of the next behavior and then progressively refine predictions at the app-action level. This design enables unified modeling of cross-source dependencies and fine-grained behavioral dynamics within a single pre-training paradigm. Extensive experiments on large-scale real-world mobile datasets demonstrate that CM-PTM effectively captures users' endogenous interests and consistently delivers significant performance gains on downstream mobile game recommendation tasks.

</details>


### [227] [ARISE-RL: Agentic Rubric-Grounded Iterative Self-Evolution with Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01058)
*Fanrui Zhang,Ruixue Ding,Qiang Zhang,Xi Chen,Boli Chen,Shihang Wang,Qiuchen Wang,Hongmin Zhan,Jinxin Bian,Li xingchao,Peijin Zheng,Hao cheng,Pengjun Xie,Kaipeng Zhang,Jiawei Liu,Zheng-Jun Zha*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ARISE-RL is a self-evolving RL framework where a task/rubric generator and a reasoning solver co-evolve via rubric-based feedback, enhanced with a reward-gated self-distillation method and evaluated on a new benchmark, ECR-Bench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-ended RL agents struggle because such tasks lack verifiable gold answers and scalable grading rubrics. Rewards for long-horizon, open-ended, tool-using tasks are brittle and unstable, giving weak learning signals and noisy comparisons between rollouts. This makes it hard to train strong, general-purpose reasoning and tool-use policies near their capability limits. The paper seeks a way to generate appropriate tasks, design grounded rubrics, and extract stable, fine-grained reward signals at scale, while avoiding overfitting to noisy supervision.

Method: The authors propose ARISE-RL, a closed-loop self-evolution system combining: (1) a Generator that produces tool-using tasks and their rubrics, with rubric criteria grounded directly in actual tool observations; it is rewarded when tasks are valid, of suitable intermediate difficulty, and aligned with the Solver’s evolving competence; (2) a Solver that performs multi-step reasoning and tool use, receiving fine-grained rubric-based rewards for partial and full criteria satisfaction. They also introduce Reward-Gated Self-Evolution Distillation (RG-SED), where a memory-augmented variant of the policy is distilled back into the base policy only when the added memory demonstrably improves reward, thereby controlling for distribution shift and discarding unhelpful traces. Finally, they build ECR-Bench, an expert-designed rubric benchmark for single-tool deep research and multi-tool travel planning, to systematically evaluate performance.

Result: Using ECR-Bench and other benchmarks, ARISE-RL delivers consistently strong and stable performance, outperforming existing methods across all evaluated tasks. The framework yields more robust training signals, better utilization of tools, and improved long-horizon reasoning, with less reward instability than prior RL approaches. RG-SED further contributes by selectively reinforcing only empirically beneficial behaviors, enhancing policy quality without amplifying noise.

Conclusion: Rubric-mediated co-evolution between a task/rubric Generator and a reasoning Solver provides a scalable way to train open-ended RL agents for complex tool-using tasks. Grounded rubric design and reward-gated self-distillation help overcome brittle, noisy rewards and distribution mismatch, enabling more stable and effective group-based policy optimization. ECR-Bench offers a rigorous, expert-calibrated evaluation suite, and experiments show that ARISE-RL establishes a new robust state of the art on these open-ended, long-horizon agent benchmarks.

Abstract: Training open-ended agents via reinforcement learning (RL) is hindered by the lack of verifiable gold answers and scalable rubrics. Moreover, even near the model's capability boundary, long-horizon open-ended agentic tasks often yield brittle and unstable rewards, resulting in weak or noisy rollout contrast that obscures fine-grained optimization signals for group-based policy learning. To address these challenges, we propose ARISE-RL, a novel full-cycle self-evolution framework that couples a task/rubric Generator and a reasoning Solver through rubric-mediated co-evolution. The Generator grounds tool-related rubric criteria in real tool observations and is rewarded for producing valid, intermediate-difficulty tasks aligned with the Solver's evolving capability boundary. The Solver, in turn, learns from fine-grained rubric satisfaction signals through multi-step reasoning and tool use. We further introduce Reward-Gated Self-Evolution Distillation (RG-SED), which selectively distills a memory-augmented variant of the same policy back into itself only when the memory yields empirical reward improvement, thereby reducing distribution mismatch and avoiding blind imitation of noisy guidance. Finally, to support rigorous evaluation, we present ECR-Bench, an expert-calibrated rubric benchmark suite covering single-tool deep research and multi-tool travel planning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ARISE-RL consistently achieves robust and stable overall state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated benchmarks.

</details>


### [228] [Space Generative AI with Solar Energy Harvesting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01062)
*Jierui Zhang,Jianhao Huang,Zhanwei Wang,Kaibin Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Framework for optimizing diffusion-based image generation and downlink over solar-powered satellites by jointly managing computation and communication under energy-harvesting constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Provide generative AI services, like diffusion image generation, to remote areas via satellites, which face stringent, time-varying energy limitations from solar harvesting and must meet strict latency and reliability requirements.

Method: Model the satellite’s compute–communication coupling under a shared harvested-energy budget; exploit deterministic orbital solar energy-harvesting dynamics; use a two-step optimization: (1) characterize maximum downlink throughput for a fixed generation depth under continuous EH and show a separation principle between waiting time and transmit power control; (2) formulate and solve a joint computation–communication utility-maximization problem and derive a closed-form, low-complexity policy for selecting the number of diffusion steps in a dominant constant-power regime.

Result: The derived policy adaptively selects generation depth and transmission strategy based on solar-EH state, balancing semantic image quality and downlink reliability, and achieves significantly better end-to-end performance than fixed, computation-only or communication-only baselines in realistic orbital simulations.

Conclusion: By jointly optimizing computation and communication using predictable solar energy-harvesting patterns, satellites can deliver higher-quality generative AI services within strict time windows, outperforming static strategies and effectively managing the trade-off between image quality and transmission reliability.

Abstract: Satellites are emerging as promising platforms to extend generative \emph{artificial intelligence} (AI) services to remote areas lacking terrestrial infrastructure. However, deploying space generative AI is fundamentally constrained by the limited, time-varying onboard energy supplied by solar \emph{energy harvesting} (EH). This paper presents a framework for solar-powered space generative AI in which a satellite receives a user prompt, executes a diffusion-based image-generation model, and downlinks the compressed result within a strict time window. We identify the fundamental \emph{computation--communication} (C$^2$) trade-offs governed by the shared harvested-energy budgets. Specifically, increasing the number of generation steps improves intrinsic image quality but depletes energy and time available for downlink transmission, whereas prioritizing communication guarantees reliable delivery but sacrifices semantic quality. To balance these trade-offs and maximize \emph{end-to-end} (E2E) generative performance, we exploit the predictable solar-EH dynamics induced by deterministic orbital motion and develop a joint C$^2$ resource-optimization framework using a tractable two-step approach. First, we characterize the maximum downlink throughput for a fixed generation depth under continuous solar EH. This establishes a separation principle that decouples waiting-time selection from optimal transmit-power control. Next, we formulate a joint C$^2$ utility-maximization problem and derive a closed-form, low-complexity step-selection policy in the dominant constant-power regime. Extensive experiments under realistic orbital dynamics demonstrate that the proposed policy dynamically balances generation quality and transmission reliability. This yields significant E2E performance gains over static computation- and communication-centric baselines across diverse solar-EH states.

</details>


### [229] [Latent Recurrent Thoughts: Recurrent Refinement of Proposed Latents for Reasoning with Frozen LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01117)
*Zhaoliang Chen,Jie Fu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Latent Recurrent Thoughts (LRT), a method that lets a small recurrent network iteratively refine continuous latent states that are then decoded by a frozen LLM, achieving better reasoning performance and efficiency than prior continuous-space methods and standard CoT prompting without trace supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Chain-of-thought reasoning in token space is constrained by discrete steps, error propagation, and the need for supervision from existing reasoning traces. The authors want a way to perform deep, iterative reasoning in a continuous latent space that avoids these limitations while still leveraging the strengths of large, pretrained LLMs as sequence decoders. They also aim to decouple reasoning depth from model size and reduce inference compute compared to standard CoT prompting.

Method: They freeze a pretrained LLM and add a small auxiliary system composed of: (1) a task-specific proposer that generates initial continuous latent states ("base latents"), and (2) a tiny recurrent reasoner that iteratively refines these latents via bounded residual updates over many recurrence steps. The LLM then takes the final latent state as conditioning input and decodes the answer in text. This architecture, called Latent Recurrent Thoughts (LRT), operates entirely in latent space for the reasoning process, leaving the LLM to handle only sequence modeling and decoding. Training uses only answer supervision (no reasoning traces) under a fixed training budget, comparing against other frozen-decoder continuous reasoning methods and standard CoT prompting on the same backbone.

Result: On symbolic reasoning tasks with only answer supervision (Countdown-4, Sudoku) and on several natural-language reasoning and code-generation benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, StrategyQA), LRT significantly outperforms previous frozen-decoder continuous-space reasoning approaches when controlling for decoder, prompt, data, and training budget. It also beats non-thinking-mode chain-of-thought prompting on the same backbone while using only a small fraction of the inference compute, indicating both higher accuracy and better efficiency for reasoning.

Conclusion: Reasoning in continuous latent space with a small recurrent module, while keeping a large LLM frozen as a decoder, is an effective and compute-efficient alternative to token-level chain-of-thought. The proposed Latent Recurrent Thoughts architecture demonstrates that deep, iterative reasoning can be offloaded to a compact recurrent reasoner whose outputs are decoded by an LLM, yielding superior performance to prior frozen-decoder methods and standard CoT without requiring explicit reasoning trace supervision.

Abstract: Chain-of-thought reasoning unfolds in discrete token space: each step is committed as text, errors propagate, and eliciting good traces presupposes traces to imitate. Reasoning instead in a model's continuous representation space - where intermediate states are vectors rather than words - sidesteps these constraints, but leaves open how those latent states should be computed. We approach this along two axes. First, we keep a large language model (LLM) frozen and use it for what it is already good at - modeling and decoding sequences - while a small auxiliary network supplies continuous latent thoughts as input. Second, we produce those latents by recurrence: a tiny recurrent reasoner refines them over many steps, decoupling the depth of computation from the size of the model, so that the latents are a product of iterative processing rather than a single forward pass. We instantiate this as Latent Recurrent Thoughts (LRT): a task-dedicated proposer supplies base latents, a recurrent reasoner refines them through bounded residual corrections, and the frozen LLM decodes the answer. On symbolic reasoning with answer supervision but no reasoning traces (Countdown-4, Sudoku) and on natural-language reasoning (HumanEval, MBPP, StrategyQA), LRT substantially outperforms prior frozen-decoder continuous-space reasoning methods under an identical decoder, prompt, data, and training budget, and outperforms non-thinking-mode chain-of-thought prompting on the same backbone at a small fraction of its inference compute.

</details>


### [230] [Jailbreaking Text-to-Image Models Through Cracks: Navigating Heterogeneous Safety Filters via Multi-Agent Debate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01168)
*Kaiyan Wen,Shijie Zhang,Lu Yu,Guangdong Bai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies why current text-to-image safety stacks are vulnerable to jailbreaks and proposes a new framework and attack method that can reliably bypass multiple heterogeneous filters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Text-to-image models, even when protected by layered safety systems (text filters, image classifiers, cross-modal detectors), can still be jailbreaked to produce NSFW content. Existing attacks either target one filter at a time or treat the whole pipeline as a black box with aggregate feedback, which makes it hard to understand or exploit the interaction between different safety layers. There is a need for a principled way to model these interactions and design adaptive attacks that navigate conflicting constraints across layers.

Method: 1) They define the "Detection Surface", a geometric framework that models each safety filter as inducing a decision boundary in a shared space and characterizes the joint feasible region where prompts evade all filters. This highlights the sparsity, non-convexity, and cross-layer conflicts of the effective jailbreak region. 2) Based on this view, they design CRACK, a multi-agent debate system with three roles: an Attack Agent that proposes prompt mutations, a Defense Agent that interprets and diagnoses which safety layers are blocking a given prompt, and a Judge Agent that arbitrates, gives reward signals, and refines search strategies. The system iteratively queries the T2I pipeline, gets layer-specific diagnostic signals, and uses reward-guided optimization to adapt mutation strategies while retaining the original malicious intent.

Result: Across multiple T2I models, datasets, and composite safety configurations, CRACK reaches very high jailbreak success, with Attack Success Rates up to 99.63%, while also using fewer queries than prior approaches. It preserves semantic similarity to the original harmful prompt, indicating that it is not simply degrading or changing the prompt meaning to evade filters.

Conclusion: Layered T2I safety defenses create a complex, sparse, and non-convex safe/unsafe landscape, which can be systematically modeled via the proposed Detection Surface. Leveraging this understanding, the CRACK multi-agent debate framework can efficiently and adaptively search this landscape to find prompts that bypass all layers while retaining harmful semantics, greatly outperforming existing jailbreak methods. This exposes a serious weakness in current multi-layer safety designs and suggests that defenses must account for cross-layer interactions rather than optimizing each filter in isolation.

Abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that elicit Not-Safe-For-Work (NSFW) content, despite increasingly being guarded by heterogeneous, multi-layer safety stacks combining text filters, image classifiers, and cross-modal detectors. Existing jailbreak studies either optimize against individual filters or query the complete pipeline with aggregate feedback, making it difficult to identify the active constraint and adapt to conflicts across safety layers.In this paper, we introduce the \emph{Detection Surface}, a unified geometric framework that characterizes the decision boundaries induced by heterogeneous T2I safety filters and their joint effect on the jailbreak search space. This formulation reveals that successful evasion is governed by a sparse and non-convex region shaped by cross-layer conflicts, where mutations that bypass one filter may increase exposure to another. Motivated by this analysis, we propose \emph{CRACK}, a multi-agent debate framework for adaptive jailbreak search that decomposes jailbreak search into exploration, diagnosis, and arbitration. CRACK coordinates an Attack Agent, a Defense Agent, and a Judge Agent to iteratively generate prompt mutations, obtain layer-specific diagnostic feedback, and optimize mutation strategies through reward-guided refinement. Through repeated rounds of debate, CRACK adapts its search direction to the evolving cross-layer constraints while preserving the original harmful intent. Extensive experiments across multiple T2I models, datasets, and safety configurations show that CRACK achieves Attack Success Rates (ASR) of up to 99.63\% under composite defenses, while requiring fewer queries than existing methods and maintaining semantic fidelity.

</details>


### [231] [FinLifeBench: Exhaustive Life-Event History and Financial-State Reconstruction from Longitudinal Banking Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01198)
*Hangyeul Lee,Juyoung Oh,Jaeyong Ko,Sunmin Kim,Jaeik Park,Hyunkyu Kim,Jungmin Son,Pilsung Kang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Paper introduces FinLifeBench, a benchmark for testing how well language models maintain and reconstruct long-term banking customer records across many sessions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In real banking, assistants must track evolving customer life events and financial states over long periods, not just answer isolated questions. Existing benchmarks focus on short episodes, narrow recall tasks, or QA, and do not evaluate exhaustive, temporally consistent tracking of all relevant life events and financial states. The authors want to measure whether LLMs can maintain complete, time-aware longitudinal records as customer lives change.

Method: The authors build FinLifeBench, a benchmark of 6,000 eight-turn Korean banking dialogues derived from 20 independent synthetic customer trajectories. Over these cumulative multi-session dialogues, they define two tasks: (1) reconstruct every life-event instance and identify the session where it was first established (event-anchor reconstruction), and (2) reconstruct a full 34-dimension financial state at a sequence of checkpoints (state-path reconstruction). The data provide deterministic gold labels for 24 event types and 34 financial-state paths, with consensus-based quality checks. They evaluate eleven large language models in a full-context setting and measure recall for event anchors and a GCA@15 metric for financial-state reconstruction, while analyzing error types and correlations between task performances.

Result: Across eleven LLMs, recall for correctly retrieving events with their first-establishing session declines as the dialogue history grows: from 0.591 at 15 sessions to 0.445 at 300 sessions, mainly due to omitted events rather than misplacing anchors. For financial-state reconstruction, models often mis-handle temporal validity, incorrectly treating outdated or superseded information as current; the best model achieves a GCA@15 of 0.470. Performance on life-event reconstruction and financial-state reconstruction is only weakly correlated, indicating they stress different capabilities.

Conclusion: FinLifeBench reveals that current LLMs struggle to maintain complete and temporally consistent longitudinal records in banking-style interactions, even when they can localize supporting evidence. Models tend to miss events and mis-handle the temporal updating of financial states as the history lengthens. The benchmark highlights the need for improved methods and representations for long-term, time-aware memory and state tracking in task-oriented dialogue systems, particularly in financial domains.

Abstract: Repeated banking interactions require assistants to maintain complete, current, and traceable customer records as life changes emerge incidentally in routine requests. Existing benchmarks emphasize question answering, bounded episodes, or targeted recall rather than exhaustive longitudinal reconstruction. We introduce FinLifeBench, which evaluates two tasks over the same cumulative dialogue: reconstructing every life-event instance with its first-establishing session and reconstructing a complete 34-path financial state at consecutive checkpoints. The benchmark contains 6,000 eight-turn Korean banking sessions from 20 independent synthetic trajectories, with deterministic, exhaustive gold for 24 event types and 34 state paths and consensus quality assurance. Across eleven LLMs under a full-context condition, event-anchor recall falls from 0.591 at 15 sessions to 0.445 at 300. Errors are driven primarily by omitted events rather than poor anchor localization, while financial-state reconstruction frequently treats superseded or potentially outdated information as current; the best GCA@15 reaches 0.470. Performance on the two reconstruction tasks is only weakly associated. These results show that models can localize evidence for recovered events while still failing to maintain complete and temporally valid longitudinal records.

</details>


### [232] [H2Table: Hierarchical Hypergraph-Enhanced Large Language Models for Complex Table Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01216)
*Jia Ling,Yangfan Wang,Chen Tang,Haoming Tan,Yang Yang,Yi Guan,Jingchi Jiang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces H2Table, a framework that models complex tables with hierarchical headers as nested hypergraphs and uses a hypergraph encoder plus learnable queries to improve table question answering, significantly outperforming prior methods on the HiTab dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based table reasoning methods usually flatten tables into sequences, which discards the inherent 2D and hierarchical structure, especially in tables with deeply nested headers. This leads to poor performance on complex table question answering. The authors aim to create a representation and processing method that directly captures the rich structural and semantic relationships within complex tables so models can reason more effectively over them.

Method: The authors propose H2Table, which represents tables as hierarchical nested hypergraphs where hyperedges correspond to headers and nodes to cells, capturing multi-level header-cell relationships. They design a specialized hypergraph encoder that performs message passing between hyperedges and nodes to model semantic entailment and structural dependencies in the table. To connect this structure-aware encoder with an LLM, they introduce a small set of learnable query vectors that extract compact structural embeddings from the hypergraph encoder and feed them into the LLM as a lightweight interface for downstream table question answering.

Result: On complex table QA benchmarks, particularly the HiTab dataset with hierarchical nested headers, H2Table substantially improves performance. For highly complex tables with nesting depth four, it achieves an average performance gain of 22.88% over state-of-the-art baselines. This demonstrates its advantage specifically on structurally rich and challenging tables compared with sequence-based or less structure-aware methods.

Conclusion: Modeling tables as hierarchical nested hypergraphs and using a dedicated hypergraph encoder with learnable query vectors provides a powerful way to preserve and exploit the structural and semantic relationships in complex tables. This leads to significantly better table question answering, especially on datasets with deep header nesting, suggesting that future table reasoning systems should explicitly encode table structure rather than rely solely on linearized representations.

Abstract: Tables are ubiquitous across diverse domains, yet reasoning over them remains a significant challenge for modern large language models (LLMs). Current approaches typically linearize tables into sequences, inherently overlooking their intrinsic two-dimensional and hierarchical structure. To address this, we propose H2Table (Hierarchical Hypergraph-Enhanced Table Reasoning), a novel framework that represents complex tables as hierarchical nested hypergraphs. To process this representation, we design a tailored hypergraph encoder to facilitate message passing between hyperedges (headers) and nodes (cells), thereby perceiving the semantic entailment relationships between them within complex tables. Furthermore, we introduce a set of learnable query vectors acting as a lightweight bridge to extract representative structural embeddings from the encoder into the LLM. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach effectively handles complex table question answering tasks with hierarchical nested headers. Notably, on the HiTab dataset, H2Table achieves an average improvement of 22.88% over state-of-the-art baselines on highly complex tables with a nesting depth of four. Our code is available at: https://github.com/lila120/h2table.

</details>


### [233] [Prompt-Robust Language Models: Which Training Strategies Work?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01217)
*Frederic Sadrieh,Michal Štefánik*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how robust large language models are to different prompt formulations and evaluates methods meant to reduce this sensitivity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models perform well but their outputs can vary widely depending on small changes in prompt wording. This instability is problematic for reliability and deployment, motivating a systematic comparison of methods that claim to make models more robust to prompt variations.

Method: The authors reproduce and evaluate several robustness strategies under controlled conditions. They compare robustness-focused fine-tuning methods (such as CoIN for contrastive alignment and PPCL for consistency regularization) against simpler data construction approaches, including training with one template per batch versus mixing multiple prompt formulations. They also run diagnostics on gradient behavior across templates to understand why methods behave as they do.

Result: Robustness-oriented fine-tuning methods outperform standard fine-tuning and plain in-context learning in reducing prompt sensitivity, but a large performance gap (40–57%) between the best and worst prompts remains. CoIN and PPCL often do not outperform a very simple baseline: training with a single prompt template per batch. Gradient-based diagnostics reveal that templates often induce conflicting gradient directions on a large fraction (57–64%) of parameters, so batches that mix templates can cause the optimizer to juggle competing updates rather than find a shared robust representation.

Conclusion: Current robustness fine-tuning strategies only partially mitigate prompt sensitivity and do not generalize robustness beyond the specific auxiliary objectives they optimize. Simple data construction choices, such as avoiding mixed-template batches, can match or beat more complex robustness methods. Because different prompt templates drive conflicting parameter updates, naively mixing prompt formulations during training can hinder learning a prompt-agnostic solution.

Abstract: Despite their strong performance, large language models remain highly sensitive to prompt formulation. Prior work addresses this through refined data construction or through dedicated robustness objectives. We reproduce and compare these strategies under controlled conditions, and measure how effective they are in addressing models' prompt sensitivity. We find the current robustness fine-tuning methods improve over standard fine-tuning and in-context learning, but the best-to-worst prompt gap remains as high as 40-57% of performance. Moreover, the recent robustness-enhancing methods we test - CoIN for contrastive alignment and PPCL for consistency regularization - often fail to outperform the simplest data construction strategy: training on one template per batch. Our diagnostics explain these results. The auxiliary objectives move the quantity they penalize, but do not generalize beyond it. Additionally, data construction strategies differ due to the conflicting signs of per-template gradients on 57-64% of parameters. Thus, batches that mix formulations force the optimizer to reconcile competing updates instead of finding a shared, prompt-agnostic one.

</details>


### [234] [Measuring the Behavioral Fidelity of Long-Horizon Human Activity Simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01257)
*Yi Fei Cheng,Fan Yang,Iremsu Bas,Koichiro Niinuma,Narishige Abe,David Lindlbauer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes and tests a framework for evaluating how faithfully LLM-based human simulators reproduce real long-term behaviors, showing that different conditioning methods trade off different aspects of behavioral fidelity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents are increasingly used to simulate human behavior for tasks like policy analysis, evaluation, and training, but most prior work tests them only on short, survey-like or dialog tasks. It is unknown whether they can realistically simulate long-horizon, real-world activity patterns, which are critical for many applications. There is a need for systematic ways to measure and compare the behavioral fidelity of such simulations over extended periods and at multiple levels of granularity.

Method: The authors introduce an evaluation framework for long-horizon activity simulations that analyzes behavior across multiple temporal granularities and levels (e.g., actions, sequences, routines, individuals vs. aggregates). As a concrete case study, they collect a 43-hour, multi-camera dataset capturing real, in-the-wild office behavior. They then simulate corresponding office activity using LLM-based human simulators under different trace-derived conditioning mechanisms: (1) persona descriptors, (2) few-shot behavioral exemplars, and (3) statistical priors encoding transition probabilities and time-of-day patterns. They compare the simulated behaviors against real traces using various metrics of behavioral fidelity, such as activity distributions and sequence structures.

Result: The study finds that no single conditioning method yields uniformly high behavioral fidelity across all metrics. Statistical transition and time-of-day priors produce simulated behavior whose activity and sequence distributions most closely match the real-world data. However, this same approach tends to over-fragment behavioral routines and reduces within-person variability, indicating that high aggregate similarity can hide important deficiencies at finer-grained and individual levels.

Conclusion: Behavioral fidelity of LLM-based human simulators is multifaceted and cannot be captured by single, aggregate metrics. Statistical priors can improve alignment with real activity distributions but may distort routine structure and individual variation. Therefore, evaluating LLM-based human simulators requires a holistic framework that spans multiple metrics, temporal scales, and analytic levels. The authors’ framework and case study highlight both the promise and current limitations of using LLMs to simulate long-horizon real-world human behavior, and point toward the need for richer models and evaluation protocols.

Abstract: As LLM-based human simulators are increasingly used for policy, evaluation, and training, they must faithfully reproduce real behavioral patterns. While prior work has examined behavioral fidelity in survey responses and dialogue, longer-horizon real-world activity remains largely unexplored. We introduce a framework for evaluating behavioral fidelity in long-horizon activity simulations across temporal granularities and levels of analysis. As a case study, we collect a 43-hour multi-camera dataset of in-the-wild office activity and compare trace-derived conditioning mechanisms: persona descriptors, few-shot exemplars, and statistical transition and time-of-day priors. We find that behavioral fidelity is not uniform across metrics: statistical priors bring activity and sequence distributions closest to real behavior, yet over-fragment routines and suppress within-person variability. These findings motivate a more holistic evaluation that spans multiple metrics, temporal granularities, and levels of analysis.

</details>


### [235] [Dual Process Motion Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01260)
*Jiayi Yan,Francesco Fabiano,Alessandro Abate*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a dual-process neuro-symbolic motion planning framework for robots that integrates fast learned components with slower symbolic solvers to improve efficiency, accuracy, and generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical control and planning for robots provide strong guarantees but are computationally expensive and inflexible, while learning-based methods are adaptive and efficient but often lack robustness and guarantees. There is a need for a planning approach that combines the strengths of both to handle complex nonlinear motion planning problems in a scalable way.

Method: They adopt a neuro-symbolic, dual-process architecture inspired by the Thinking Fast and Slow framework. The system has a fast "System-1" composed of experience-driven learned modules and a slower, precise "System-2" built from state-of-the-art symbolic solvers for nonlinear motion planning. A metacognitive controller decides online when to use or switch between the intuitive (learned) and deliberative (symbolic) components, orchestrating their interaction during planning.

Result: Across a variety of nonlinear benchmark environments, the proposed architecture achieves consistent improvements in planning efficiency (speed), solution accuracy (quality of plans), and generalization (performance on new tasks) compared with baselines. The framework also shows evidence of solution reuse across tasks.

Conclusion: A tightly integrated combination of learning-based components with structured symbolic reasoning, mediated by a metacognitive controller, provides a scalable and adaptive approach to nonlinear motion planning. This neuro-symbolic dual-process design can yield more capable, efficient, and generalizable robotic systems than purely classical or purely learning-based methods alone.

Abstract: Robotic systems are deeply embedded in both industry and everyday life, where they are expected to act with speed, precision, and reliability. Classical control and planning methods have long delivered strong guarantees, but often at the cost of computational efficiency and adaptability. More recently, learning-based approaches have shown promise in overcoming these limitations, enabling agents to leverage experience to accelerate decision-making and address previously intractable problems. In this work, we bridge these two approaches through a neuro-symbolic perspective on nonlinear motion planning. Inspired by the Thinking Fast and Slow paradigm, we introduce a dual-process architecture that combines the strengths of robust reasoning and learning. Our framework integrates state-of-the-art symbolic solvers as a ``System-2'' component with experience-driven ``System-1'' modules. A metacognitive controller dynamically orchestrates their interaction, selecting when to rely on fast intuition versus slower, more precise reasoning. By evaluating the framework across diverse nonlinear benchmark environments, we demonstrate that this architecture yields consistent gains in planning efficiency, accuracy, and generalization, while promoting reuse across tasks. The results suggest that tightly coupling learning with structured reasoning offers a scalable path toward more capable and adaptive robotic systems.

</details>


### [236] [Making Prospective Memory SLM-Shaped: Typed Intention Stores for Small-Model Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01272)
*Jinqing Zhao,Chengcan Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Prospective Intention Store (PIS), a training-free agent scaffold that greatly improves large and small language models’ performance on prospective memory tasks, achieving new state-of-the-art results on PM-Bench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prospective memory—executing future intentions when the right cue appears while other tasks are ongoing—is a critical agent skill. Existing benchmarks like PM-Bench show that even frontier LLMs perform poorly (best Set-F1 ~65%), and current methods treat it as open-ended reasoning, typically requiring fine-tuning or complex training. The authors believe that this capability is more about structured state tracking with constrained action space than general reasoning, and that small models should be able to do it if the loop is properly scaffolded. They aim to design a lightweight, training-free framework that externalizes lifecycle logic so models of various sizes can reliably handle prospective memory.

Method: The authors propose the Prospective Intention Store (PIS), an external, code-based module that manages the full lifecycle of deferred intentions (creation, storage, monitoring, triggering, and retirement). The LLM is only responsible for scoped language tasks, such as interpreting cues, mapping them to stored intentions, and generating actions, while the PIS handles schema-constrained state tracking and typed action spaces. The framework is agentic but training-free: it does not require additional selector fine-tuning or trajectory distillation. They integrate PIS with different models (e.g., DeepSeek-Chat and Gemma-E2B) and evaluate performance on the PM-Bench benchmark, comparing against baselines with no store and with retrospective memory-based methods with varying numbers of stored memories.

Result: On PM-Bench, DeepSeek-Chat equipped with PIS attains 82.9% Set-F1, surpassing the previous best published scaffold (65.1% Set-F1). For the smaller Gemma-E2B model, performance without a store is only 4.2% Set-F1 and improves only to a maximum of 6.6% even when enhanced with up to seven retrospective memories; with PIS, Gemma-E2B reaches 66.2% Set-F1. In further comparisons where retrospective memory methods peak at 54.4% Set-F1, PIS achieves 70.1% Set-F1. Overall, PIS substantially boosts both large and small models on prospective memory tasks.

Conclusion: The study concludes that prospective memory in agentic LLM setups is better viewed as schema-constrained state tracking than as generic open-ended reasoning. By offloading lifecycle and state management to the Prospective Intention Store and keeping the model’s role focused on localized language processing within a typed action space, even relatively small models can reliably execute deferred intentions. PIS is training-free, improves upon prior scaffolds, and establishes new state-of-the-art results on PM-Bench, demonstrating that appropriate external structure can unlock strong agent capabilities without additional model training.

Abstract: Prospective memory means carrying out a deferred intention at the right future cue while other work continues. Benchmarks now isolate it as an agent skill, yet frontier LLMs still struggle: the best published PM-Bench scaffold reaches only 65.1% Set-F1. We argue that this loop is schema-constrained state tracking rather than open-ended reasoning, and that small models can execute it when the action space is typed. We propose the Prospective Intention Store (PIS) that puts lifecycle logic in code and scoped language work on the model. The scaffold is agentic and training-free: no selector fine-tuning and no trajectory distillation. On PM-Bench, DeepSeek-Chat with PIS reaches 82.9% Set-F1. On Gemma-E2B, Set-F1 is only 4.2% without a store and at most 6.6% under seven retrospective memories, while PIS reaches 66.2%. PIS further reaches 70.1% Set-F1, where retrospective memory methods stay at most 54.4%. PIS sets a new state of the art on this benchmark and enables small models to surpass the published large-model scaffold.

</details>


### [237] [Analog-DB: An Agent-First Analog Integrated Circuit Database, From Blocks to Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01286)
*Danial Noori Zadeh,Mohamed B. Elamien*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce analog-db, an open, versioned database and DSL to share, parameterize, and reuse analog IC designs in a process-neutral way, enabling AI agents to resimulate and re-size circuits across foundry kits, with validation across a regulator corpus and a case study on op-amp cores.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Analog IC designs are hard to share and reuse because of foundry NDAs, hidden testbenches, and tight coupling to specific processes, which also limits AI-assisted design. A neutral, fully specified, and shareable representation is needed so designs can be re-simulated, retargeted, and composed across different process kits.

Method: They build analog-db, a versioned database backed by a domain-specific language that encodes each design as process-neutral topology, reusable testbenches, and a machine-readable datasheet in a unified schema. They introduce a parameterization scheme that exposes sub-blocks and device sizes as named parameters with matching constraints, enabling composability and retargeting. A schema-based contract and searchable catalog allow AI design agents to discover and use these circuits. They validate it on a corpus of regulator circuits and a supervised case study with a coding agent sizing op-amp cores on an open 130nm kit.

Result: On a corpus of regulator designs bound to three open process kits, all 23 circuit-kit bindings meet their own recorded spec bands (under typical, schematic-only conditions), and 10 of 23 satisfy a common class band. Most imported sizings initially failed but were successfully closed using a gm/ID sizing loop driven by annotated sub-block roles, typically in 1–3 iterations. In a supervised case study, a coding agent using the released artifacts resized op-amp cores, uncovering four manual-entry errors and a missing CMFB loop that a sizing-only baseline missed. The final database contains 68 circuits across 16 classes, all verifiable at schematic level and tracked on a power/performance scoreboard.

Conclusion: Analog-db and its DSL make analog IC designs shareable, re-simulatable, and composable across processes, providing a structured interface for AI agents and human designers. Their experiments show that many existing designs can be automatically re-sized to meet specs on open kits and that AI agents can leverage the database to detect design issues and perform nontrivial sizing tasks. The released corpus and infrastructure aim to serve as a foundation for reproducible analog design research and AI-driven analog automation.

Abstract: Sharing analog integrated circuit designs remains difficult: foundry non-disclosure agreements restrict the process details a design depends on, and the testbenches behind published results are rarely released. We present analog-db, an open-source, versioned database built on a shareable design representation. A domain-specific language captures each design as a process-neutral topology, reusable testbenches, and a machine-readable datasheet under one schema, so a design is shared in full and re-simulates on the process kits it is bound to. A parameterization scheme exposes functional sub-blocks and device sizes as named parameters that carry their matching constraints, making circuits composable and retargetable; a schema-governed contract and queryable catalog let AI design agents discover and reuse them directly. Across the regulator corpus, all 23 circuit-kit bindings on three open kits meet their own recorded specification bands (typical corner, matched devices, no layout) and 10 of 23 meet a common class band. Seventeen of the 23 imported sizings failed their testbenches and closed under a gm/ID sizing loop driven by the annotated sub-block roles, typically within one to three iterations. In a supervised case study, a coding agent working from the released artifacts sized the op-amp cores of a chopper instrumentation amplifier on an open 130nm kit, locating four hand-entry defects and a missing common-mode feedback loop that the sizing-only baseline did not repair. The database holds 68 circuits across sixteen classes, verifiable at schematic level under a tiered harness and tracked on a power/performance scoreboard, released at https://github.com/MacAnalog/spicexplorer-release.

</details>


### [238] [A Composable Evaluation System for Reproducible Omni-Modal Foundation Model Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01315)
*Hodong Lee,Sanghee Park,Dohoon Ryu,Jungwhan Kim,Junyeob Kim,Soyoon Kim,Geewook Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OmniEvaluator is a unified evaluation framework that connects multiple inference engines and evaluation libraries across text, image, video, and audio, enabling reproducible, comparable benchmarking of omni-modal foundation models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Omni-modal models must be evaluated across many benchmarks and modalities, but existing toolkits are siloed: each has its own inference engine, prompts, metrics, and environment, making it hard to maintain, reproduce, and compare results across modalities and models. The authors needed a way to coordinate and standardize evaluation without re-implementing all benchmarks.

Method: Instead of recreating benchmarks, the system wraps and connects existing inference engines and curated evaluation libraries behind a single interface. It integrates four inference backends and four evaluation frameworks to expose 1000+ benchmarks. Each evaluation run is logged as an artifact with complete configuration for reproducibility and visualization in a shared dashboard. It supports a federated mode that shares GPU inference servers across concurrent evaluations. Additionally, it includes a lightweight verifier model that runs on CPU to stabilize scoring across different engines and prompt templates, matching the reliability and cost-efficiency of commercial LLM-based judges without ongoing API fees.

Result: The framework delivers a unified way to launch, track, and compare multimodal benchmark runs from different engines and toolchains. It scales across many benchmarks and concurrent jobs via federated GPU sharing, and its built-in verifier produces stable, configuration-robust scores that align with more expensive commercial LLM judges. All components, including system, demo video, and dashboard, are released publicly via GitHub.

Conclusion: OmniEvaluator simplifies and standardizes evaluation for omni-modal foundation models by unifying heterogeneous toolchains, enabling reproducible benchmarking at scale, and providing reliable, low-cost automatic judging. This reduces engineering overhead, improves cross-model comparability, and offers a practical, open resource for the community to evaluate multimodal systems.

Abstract: Building an omni-modal foundation model means evaluating it across text, image, video, and audio. Excellent evaluation toolkits exist for each modality, but their inference engines, prompt conventions, and metric implementations are mutually incompatible, so practitioners end up maintaining separate environments for every toolchain and still struggle to compare results across them. OmniEvaluator grew out of this need in our own model development: rather than reimplementing benchmarks, it connects existing inference engines and curated evaluation libraries at a higher level, exposing four inference backends, four evaluation frameworks, and over a thousand benchmarks through a single interface. Every run is recorded as an artifact capturing the full configuration for exact reproduction, and results flow into a shared dashboard for cross-model comparison. A federated mode shares GPU inference servers across concurrent evaluations, and a built-in verifier, small enough to run on CPU, keeps its score stable across engines and prompts where rule-based scoring fluctuates under configuration mismatch, matching cost-efficient commercial LLM judges without their recurring API cost. The system, demo video, and dashboard are publicly available. (https://github.com/naver-ai/omni-evaluator)

</details>


### [239] [Automated Event Log Generation from Unstructured Text Using Finetuned LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01320)
*Maximilian Seeth,Gabriel Marques Tavares,Daniel Schuster*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies using fine-tuned large language models to automatically convert unstructured organizational text (e.g., tickets, manuals) into structured event logs for process mining, showing fine-tuning beats zero/few-shot prompting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Process mining needs structured event logs, but many organizations mainly have unstructured text such as incident tickets and manuals. Manually constructing logs from this text is expensive and requires experts, leaving valuable process knowledge unused. The authors want to see if LLMs can automatically translate text into structured event logs at scale to unlock this hidden data.

Method: They build a scalable framework that uses LLMs as automated data translators from unstructured text to structured event logs. They create a dedicated text-to-log dataset and fine-tune large language models on it. They then compare the fine-tuned models against zero-shot and few-shot prompting baselines for event extraction quality and log fidelity.

Result: Fine-tuned LLMs can produce high-fidelity event logs from various unstructured textual resources. Quantitative evaluation shows that the fine-tuned models significantly outperform zero-shot and few-shot prompting approaches, indicating much higher reliability and accuracy in the generated event data.

Conclusion: Fine-tuning LLMs on a targeted text-to-log dataset is necessary to obtain reliable process event logs from unstructured text. The proposed framework forms an effective and scalable pipeline that converts previously unused organizational text into structured event data, broadening the applicability and impact of process mining on real-world organizational workflows.

Abstract: Process mining (PM) provides a powerful framework for discovering and optimizing operational processes from event data. However, the efficacy of PM techniques is strictly predicated on the availability of structured event logs. Thus far, event logs have often been laboriously created by domain and process mining experts. This costly effort causes large portions of organizational knowledge, including incident tickets, manuals, and textual reports, to remain underutilized. We address this bottleneck by investigating the efficacy of Large Language Models (LLMs) as automated data translators. We propose a scalable framework that leverages LLMs as data translators to bridge the gap between unstructured textual resources and structured event data. We finetune LLMs on a newly created text-to-log dataset, demonstrating that the resulting models can extract high-fidelity event logs from unstructured resources.
