Our results show that this finetuning approach outperforms few-shot or zero-shot prompting by a large amount, highlighting finetuning as a necessary pre-condition for generating reliable event data. We conclude that our method provides a promising pipeline for making previously unused data available to process mining ecosystems, effectively expanding the possibilities of using PM to further investigate organizational workflows.

</details>


### [240] [LEAP: Likelihood Elicitation and Aggregation for LLM-based Probabilistic Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01337)
*Yufei Chen,Yiran Zhao,Xiaogang Xu,Qipeng Xie,Jiafei Wu,Zhe Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose LEAP, a new way for LLM agents to turn evidence into probabilistic forecasts by eliciting likelihoods per evidence item and aggregating them via an explicit probabilistic model, improving accuracy and calibration over standard monolithic prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based forecasting agents often perform a monolithic prediction step where the model reads all gathered evidence at once and outputs a forecast. This approach hides how each piece of evidence contributes, makes it hard to reason about or reproduce the influence of individual items, and tends to over-collapse uncertainty between competing outcomes. There is a need for a more structured, interpretable, and well-calibrated way to turn evidence into probabilistic forecasts while still fitting into common agent loops and tool-using settings.

Method: They introduce LEAP (Likelihood Elicitation and Aggregation for Probabilistic forecasting). Instead of feeding the entire evidence set jointly into the LLM for a final answer, LEAP processes each evidence item separately. For each item, the LLM is asked to elicit likelihood parameters that quantify how that piece of evidence supports or undermines each possible outcome. These per-item likelihoods are then combined with an explicit prior via a deterministic probabilistic model, yielding a posterior distribution over outcomes. The procedure is designed to handle continuous outcomes, single-choice categorical questions, and multiple-choice settings, and it ensures that each evidence item’s contribution is explicit and reproducible. They evaluate LEAP within their own agent loop and across several existing command-line agent frameworks on a benchmark spanning forecasting, information-seeking, and web browsing tasks.

Result: Across a variety of models and agent setups, and holding the collected evidence fixed, LEAP yields better forecasting performance than standard monolithic prediction. It improves key prediction and calibration metrics (e.g., more accurate probabilities, better alignment between predicted and empirical frequencies) and maintains these advantages even when controlling for factors like access to priors, compute/inference budget, and the aggregation mechanism. The results show that structured per-evidence likelihood elicitation and explicit aggregation are beneficial over having the LLM directly output final forecasts from the entire evidence set.

Conclusion: Reorganizing the prediction stage of LLM-based forecasting agents around explicit likelihood elicitation and probabilistic aggregation leads to more accurate, calibrated, and interpretable forecasts than monolithic prediction. LEAP demonstrates that separating evidence interpretation (per item) from the mathematical aggregation step improves reliability while still working across diverse task types and agent frameworks. This suggests that future forecasting systems should treat evidence combination as a transparent probabilistic modeling problem rather than an opaque end-to-end LLM task.

Abstract: LLM-based forecasting systems have improved on real-world tasks such as financial markets and sports outcomes, largely through stronger search and tool use. Many systems still ask an LLM to read all collected evidence together and produce the final forecast. We call this design Monolithic Prediction. It can obscure how individual evidence items affect the result and collapse uncertainty across competing outcomes. We propose LEAP (Likelihood Elicitation and Aggregation for Probabilistic forecasting), which reorganizes how collected evidence is used in the prediction stage. LEAP examines each evidence item separately and elicits likelihood parameters that describe its implications for the target. An explicit prior and a deterministic probabilistic model then combine these likelihoods into a posterior distribution. This procedure supports continuous, single-choice, and multi-choice forecasts while preserving reproducible evidence contributions. We build a benchmark covering forecasting, information-seeking, and browsing tasks, and evaluate LEAP on our own agent loop and several agent CLI frameworks. Given the same evidence, LEAP improves most prediction and calibration metrics across models and remains stronger under controlled comparisons of prior access, inference budget, and aggregation.

</details>


### [241] [Cheap Verifiers, Large Blind Spots: Measuring the Reliability Cost of Cost-Saving Cascades](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01345)
*Dushyant Rajput*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper studies self-improving inference cascades for LLMs and shows that using a strong verifier and iterative fine-tuning of a cheaper student can be unreliable and even harmful, due to verifier blind spots and misleading internal metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inference cascades are used to reduce the cost of using large language models by having a cheap student model answer most queries and escalating uncertain or hard cases to an expensive frontier verifier. A tempting idea is to make this process self-improving by fine-tuning the student on verifier-rejected answers to continually reduce escalation and cost. However, it is unclear how reliable, stable, and safe this self-improvement loop is in practice, and whether internal cascade metrics can be trusted to reflect true performance.

Method: The authors implement self-improving cascades with real LLMs of varying sizes as students and verifiers. They measure verifier blind spots (fraction of wrong student answers that the verifier incorrectly accepts) across model scales and capabilities. They run multiple rounds of the self-improvement loop, where the student is fine-tuned on verifier rejections, and track both true error rates and cascade-reported metrics. They also develop a theoretical model based on a two-population conservation law (ε∞ ≲ q0 β0) explaining why internal metrics can improve while true quality does not, and validate this mechanism in synthetic experiments.

Result: (1) Verifier blind spots are large and adversarially structured: they increase with student capability (β from 0.12 to 0.55 as student scales from 0.5B to 32B) and decrease with verifier capability, making them worst in the cheap-student, cheap-verifier regime. (2) Using a frontier verifier greatly reduces blind spots (β≈0.05) but leads to frequent escalations (46% on hard-MATH) close to the student’s true error rate (39%), eroding cost savings. (3) Naively fine-tuning the student on verifier-rejected examples fails to improve small students and instead degrades and ultimately collapses them, for every teacher configuration tested, so the self-improvement loop is self-defeating at this scale. (4) Throughout degradation, cascade-internal metrics derived from the verifier stay apparently excellent (around 3% error), while the true delivered error can rise to 32%, revealing that the system is effectively blind to its own failure.

Conclusion: Self-improving inference cascades that rely on a verifier to both correct and evaluate a cheaper student are fundamentally unreliable under the studied conditions. Verifier blind spots and the two-population conservation law imply that all metrics computed through the verifier can improve while actual end-to-end performance deteriorates. Strong verifiers can reduce blind spots but at the cost of frequent and expensive escalations, undermining the economic motivation for cascades. Therefore, the reliability and safety of such self-improving systems cannot be inferred from their own internal, verifier-based metrics; external measurement or alternative designs are required.

Abstract: Inference cascades cut cost by answering most queries with a cheap model and escalating a hard tail to a frontier model that acts as verifier. A natural extension closes the loop: fine-tune the cheap student on the verifier's rejections so the escalation rate, and cost, fall each round. We measure this loop on real LLMs and report four findings. First, the verifier's blind spot, the fraction of the student's wrong answers it accepts, is large and moves adversarially: it grows with student capability ($β$ from 0.12 to 0.55 as the student scales 0.5B to 32B) and shrinks with verifier capability, so it is worst in the cheap-student, cheap-verifier regime cascades exist to create. Second, buying it away returns the saving: a frontier verifier drives $β$ to about 0.05 but then escalates on 46% of hard-MATH queries against a 39% true error rate, paying the frontier price on nearly half of all traffic. Third, naive corrective fine-tuning on the verifier-rejected tail does not improve the small student but degrades and ultimately collapses it, across every teacher we tried (cross-family and same-family), so at this scale the self-improving loop is self-defeating. Fourth, through all of this the cascade's own dashboard, every metric computed through the verifier, reads a flat 3% error while true delivered error swings up to 32%: the system is blind to its own degradation by construction. We then give the theory that explains the blindness, a two-population conservation law, $ε_\infty \lesssim q_0 β_0$, under which every in-loop metric improves while true quality does not, and a synthetic study that validates the mechanism. The practical conclusion: the reliability of a self-improving cascade cannot be read from any metric computed through its own verifier.

</details>


### [242] [SymFold: Synergizing Evolutionary and Structural Priors for Accurate Protein Inverse Folding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01353)
*Handong Wang,Jiaxin Qi,Baisheng Lai,Jianqiang Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a new inverse protein folding model that jointly uses sequence and structure language models in a symmetric, iterative architecture, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing inverse folding methods use a pipeline: a structure encoder proposes a sequence which is then refined by protein language models. This serial setup limits performance because the PLM can only make local edits to an imperfect initial sequence, and recent multimodal PLMs that include structure have not worked well directly for inverse folding. There is a need for a design that fully exploits both sequence-evolution knowledge from PLMs and structural knowledge from multimodal models in a more integrated way.

Method: They design a symmetric dual-path architecture in which a protein language model (trained on sequences) and a multimodal protein language model (trained on sequence plus structure) interact to iteratively guide sequence generation from a fixed 3D structure. The architecture is symmetric in that both paths contribute comparably rather than one being just a post-processing stage. The model repeatedly exchanges information between the sequence-knowledge path and the structural-knowledge path to refine sequence predictions during generation, rather than only after an upstream prediction is complete.

Result: On standard protein inverse folding benchmarks, their dual-path model achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming previous pipeline-based approaches and models based solely on MPLMs or PLMs. Ablation experiments, where parts of the symmetric architecture are removed or modified, show clear performance drops, supporting the importance of the full design.

Conclusion: Integrating sequence and structural knowledge symmetrically and iteratively is more effective for protein inverse folding than traditional serial pipelines. The results suggest that tightly coupling PLMs and multimodal PLMs during the entire generation process is a promising direction for designing next-generation protein design models.

Abstract: Protein inverse folding aims to recover amino acid sequences for a given 3D protein structure, underpinning broad applications such as enzyme engineering and drug discovery.Current methods often follow a serial pipeline, in which a structure encoder predicts a coarse sequence, which is then refined by protein language models (PLMs). However, because PLMs only perform post-hoc sequence edits, the refinement is bounded by the quality of upstream predictions.Thanks to recent multimodal protein language models (MPLMs), we could directly encode structure to generate sequences with pretrained structural knowledge, but we observe that they are not effective for inverse folding. Therefore, we introduce a symmetric dual-path architecture that both leverages PLMs for pretrained sequence evolution knowledge and MPLMs for pretrained structural knowledge to iteratively guide protein sequence generation.Through extensive experiments across standard protein inverse folding benchmarks, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing prior approaches, and ablation studies validate the rationale of our symmetric design, revealing a promising direction for the community.

</details>


### [243] [EDGE: Error Dependency Graph-Guided Multi-Error Attribution in Multi-Agent LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01360)
*Jun Hou,Priya Pitre,Yi Fang,Xuan Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EDGE is a framework that models and exploits dependencies between multiple simultaneous errors made by LLM agents to better attribute, explain, and repair failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents often fail with cascades of related errors rather than a single mistake. Existing attribution methods typically look for one responsible agent, step, or root cause and ignore how errors depend on and trigger each other. This limits diagnostic power, explanation quality, and the ability to systematically repair complex failures. The paper aims to explicitly capture and use error dependencies for more accurate multi-error attribution and better understanding of agent failures.

Method: The authors propose EDGE, a multi-error attribution framework centered around an Error Dependency Graph (EDG). First, they construct an error dependency graph from observed error events in an LLM agent’s trajectory, representing hypothesized dependencies between errors. Then, they validate a causal subset of this graph via counterfactual rollouts: intervening on certain errors or steps and observing whether downstream errors disappear or change. This yields an intervention-validated inference subgraph. On top of this graph, they build a two-stage LLM-as-judge detector: (1) detect and categorize errors, and (2) attribute responsibility using the structure of the dependency graph. They evaluate EDGE on multi-error attribution benchmarks (TRAIL and MAST) and also adapt Who&When-style prompting, assessing how the graph helps across different prompting strategies and models.

Result: On TRAIL and MAST benchmarks, EDGE improves category-level multi-error attribution performance across most tested models and configurations, outperforming baselines that do not explicitly model error dependencies. The counterfactual validation step produces more reliable causal subgraphs than using raw dependency hypotheses alone. Incorporating the graph structure into Who&When-style prompts also leads to better attribution outcomes compared to prompting without explicit dependency modeling. Overall, experiments show consistent gains in multi-error attribution quality when dependency structure is used.

Conclusion: Modeling error dependencies via an Error Dependency Graph and validating these dependencies through counterfactual rollouts yields more reliable, fine-grained multi-error attribution for LLM agents. The EDGE framework demonstrates that moving beyond single root-cause analysis to structured multi-error reasoning improves diagnostic accuracy and explanation quality. Dependency structure emerges as a valuable prior for understanding and repairing complex agent failures, and can be integrated with various prompting strategies and models to enhance error analysis in practice.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agent failures often contain multiple related errors rather than a single mistake. Existing attribution methods usually identify a responsible agent, step, or root cause, but do not explicitly model dependency between errors. We introduce EDGE, an Error Dependency Graph-guided multi-Error attribution framework. EDGE constructs an error dependency graph from observed error events and validates a reliable causal subset through counterfactual rollout. The inference graph guides a two-stage LLM-as-judge detector for error attribution, and the intervention-validated subgraph provides a more reliable basis for explanation and repair analysis. Experiments on TRAIL and MAST show that EDGE improves category-level multi-error attribution across most evaluated models and settings. Experiments with adapted Who&When-style prompts show that the graph helps across prompting strategies. These results suggest that dependency structure is a useful diagnostic prior for agent failures beyond isolated root-cause prediction.

</details>


### [244] [Neuro-Symbolic Geometric Abstraction (NeuSOGA): From Observations to Symbolic Mathematical Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01408)
*Qingde Li,Qingqi Hong,Jie Tian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces NeuSOGA, a neuro-symbolic framework that converts geometric observations into explicit symbolic mathematical representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern AI excels at perception via large-scale statistical learning but typically stores knowledge in opaque latent parameters that are hard to interpret, edit, or reason with symbolically. The paper is motivated by the need for an explainable, mathematically explicit pathway from raw observations (like point clouds or images) to symbolic representations, inspired by neuro-symbolic AI and human abstraction processes.

Method: NeuSOGA progressively transforms raw observations into three levels of abstraction: (1) topological abstractions via topology-guided structural discovery using Euclidean Distance Transforms; (2) geometric abstractions using an adaptive multi-scale process informed by foundation-model perception (Segment Anything) for segmentation; and (3) symbolic mathematical representations via symbolic synthesis using Implicit Area Splines, yielding an analytical implicit model.

Result: On datasets such as ModelNet40 point clouds, arbitrary-view projections, and segmented optical observations, NeuSOGA is shown to convert varied input observations into compact symbolic representations that preserve key geometric and topological properties across different sensing modalities and viewpoints.

Conclusion: NeuSOGA delivers an interpretable, explainable, and mathematically explicit route from observations to symbols. It produces analytical implicit models with arbitrary-order smoothness, additive composition, and closed-form evaluation, offering advantages over opaque neural latent encodings and establishing a general pathway from observation to symbolic mathematical representation.

Abstract: A fundamental challenge in artificial intelligence is the transformation of observations into explicit symbolic representations suitable for abstraction, interpretation, and reasoning. While modern AI systems achieve remarkable perceptual capabilities through large-scale statistical learning, the resulting knowledge is typically encoded within latent parameters that are difficult to inspect or manipulate analytically. Inspired by Neuro-Symbolic AI and theories of human abstraction, this paper investigates the formation of symbolic mathematical representations from geometric observations.
  We propose NeuSOGA (Neuro-Symbolic Geometric Abstraction), a framework that progressively transforms observations into topological abstractions, geometric abstractions, and ultimately symbolic mathematical representations. The architecture combines topology-guided structural discovery using Euclidean Distance Transforms, foundation-model perception using Segment Anything, adaptive multi-scale geometric abstraction, and symbolic synthesis through Implicit Area Splines.
  The resulting representation is an analytical implicit model supporting arbitrary-order smoothness, additive composition, and closed-form evaluation. Unlike neural latent encodings, the generated representation remains interpretable, editable, and mathematically explicit. Experiments on ModelNet40 point clouds, arbitrary-view projections, and segmented optical observations demonstrate that NeuSOGA transforms diverse observations into compact symbolic representations while preserving essential geometric and topological structure across sensing modalities and viewing directions.
  NeuSOGA provides an interpretable and explainable pathway from observation to symbol and establishes

</details>


### [245] [EdiTikZ: Scientific Figure Editing from Revision Trajectories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01409)
*Christian Greisinger,Zhixue Zhao,Steffen Eger*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build a large-scale dataset and benchmark of real scientific figure edits in TikZ, then train compact VLM-based editors that rival or beat much larger proprietary models on scientific figure editing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific figure generation with VLMs is good, but real publication-ready figures require many iterative edits. Existing editing work is limited, often uses synthetic edits or expensive proprietary systems, so there is a need for scalable, realistic supervision and strong open models for scientific figure editing.

Method: Mine naturally occurring scientific figure revision trajectories from arXiv, GitHub, and TeX SE to build DaEdiTikZ, a dataset of 391K TikZ edit pairs, and infer 781K directed edit instructions using a VLM conditioned on rendered figures and code. Construct DaEdiTikZ-Bench, a human-refined benchmark. Train two Qwen3.5-based EdiTikZ models (4B, 9B) via joint reconstruction+editing training and then RL with rewards for render fidelity and correct application of edits. Evaluate vs. baselines and proprietary models.

Result: DaEdiTikZ contains hundreds of thousands of realistic figure edits and associated instructions. The 9B EdiTikZ model outperforms all tested automatic baselines; in human evaluation (9 annotators, 4,320 ratings) it surpasses GPT-5.6-Sol and matches Gemini-3.1-Pro. Under strong distribution shifts and long sequences it remains competitive with GPT-5.6-Sol near the 2K token regime.

Conclusion: Naturally occurring scientific revision data can be mined at scale to supervise high-quality figure editing models. Compact open models trained on DaEdiTikZ with tailored RL can reach or match the performance of much larger proprietary systems, and the released datasets and models provide a foundation for further research on scientific figure editing.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong performance in generating scientific figures from text or images. However, producing publication-ready figures requires iterative refinement, making scientific figure editing an important yet largely unexplored task. Existing approaches rely on costly proprietary agentic systems, focus primarily on evaluation, or construct training supervision from synthetically generated edits. Instead, we leverage naturally occurring scientific revision and development trajectories as a scalable source of supervision. To this end, we introduce DaEdiTikZ, the first large-scale dataset of revision-derived scientific figure edits, constructed by mining 391K plausible TikZ edit pairs from arXiv, GitHub, and TeX SE and inferring 781K directed edit instructions with a VLM conditioned on rendered figures and TikZ code. We further introduce DaEdiTikZ-Bench, a human-refined benchmark with 790 instances, and train two compact Qwen3.5-based EdiTikZ models (4B and 9B) by jointly learning reconstruction and editing, followed by reinforcement learning (RL) with complementary rewards for rendered fidelity and edit application. Automatic evaluation places our 9B model above all tested baselines, while human evaluation with 9 annotators and 4,320 ratings places it above GPT-5.6-Sol and on par with Gemini-3.1-Pro. Under severe out-of-distribution shifts, it remains competitive with GPT-5.6-Sol near its 2K training sequence-length regime. Models and datasets will be released.

</details>


### [246] [Parsing the Stream: A Live Trace Model for Long-Horizon Agents and Their Observers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01466)
*Egor Pakhomov,Erik Nijkamp*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a structured, incremental way to log and summarize long agent traces so they remain usable for both human monitors and the agent itself, achieving big token and cost savings while maintaining or improving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon agents generate traces that are too large for humans to monitor effectively and too big for the agent to re-ingest within its context window. There is a need for a principled way to compress, structure, and reuse these traces so that both humans and agents can query or build on past behavior accurately and efficiently, without losing determinism or auditability.

Method: The authors introduce a "live trace model": an append-only event ledger that is incrementally folded into a typed run state. From this state, they compile specialized, per-consumer views: one for a human (or LLM) observer and one for the agent itself. They evaluate these compiled views against deterministic ground truth. On the observer side, they compare an LLM reading the compiled view versus a budget-capped single-pass read of the raw trace. On the agent side, they run 120-step sequential-dependency tasks, comparing mechanisms that maintain a running statistic in per-step state (folded trace) to full-context prompting and to a prompt-level scratchpad. They also perform a two-arm decomposition to separate the effects of deterministic aggregation vs compactness and derive requirements for effective trace folding based on failure analyses, including constructing an order-sensitive task family where folding stops helping.

Result: For the observer, using a compiled view enables an LLM monitor to answer questions with about 14–15x fewer input tokens and 5–7x lower cost than reading the raw trace directly under a single-call, budget-capped setup, while improving accuracy from 0.48 to 0.85–0.87. Because questions were co-designed with the view schema, the token and cost savings are reported as conditional on schema coverage. For the agent, on 120-link sequential dependency tasks, methods that maintain the running task statistic in per-step state achieve perfect success (30/30) under a clean protocol, compared to 8/30 for full-context prompting, with a prompt-level scratchpad matching the folded trace’s accuracy but at lower cost. A two-arm analysis attributes the fold’s accuracy to its deterministic aggregate representation and its cost advantage to its compactness. They also identify an order-sensitive task family where folding no longer provides an advantage, and from empirical failures articulate eleven candidate design requirements for trace-folding systems.

Conclusion: An incremental, typed folding of an append-only event ledger into per-consumer views is an effective way to handle long-horizon agent traces. It can substantially reduce token usage and cost for monitoring while improving or preserving accuracy, and it can enable agents to reliably solve long sequential tasks when naive full-context prompting fails. However, cheaper alternatives like in-prompt scratchpads can sometimes match performance, leaving the main unique advantages of folding as deterministic auditability and serving both humans and agents from the same structured state. The authors formalize practical requirements and limitations for when trace folding is useful, and they release code, benchmarks, a synthetic corpus, and traces to support further work.

Abstract: A long-horizon agent's trace outgrows both of its consumers: the human observer monitoring the run, and the agent itself, whose bounded context the trace must be folded back into. We present a live trace model, an append-only event ledger folded incrementally into typed run state and compiled into per-consumer views, and evaluate it for both consumers against deterministic ground truth. For the observer side, evaluated with an LLM reader as proxy, the compiled view answers monitoring questions using approximately 14x and 15x fewer input tokens (by reader) and at 5-7x lower cost than a budget-capped single-call reading of the raw trace, with higher accuracy (0.85-0.87 versus 0.48). Because the questions were co-designed with the view schema, we treat the token and cost reduction, conditional on schema coverage, as the transferable result. For the agent, on 120-link sequential-dependency tasks, mechanisms that maintain the task's running statistic in per-step state succeed where full-context prompting fails (30/30 versus 8/30 under a clean protocol, n=30, labeled descriptive owing to benchmark-system co-development); a prompt-level scratchpad matches the fold's accuracy at lower cost, and a two-arm decomposition attributes the fold's accuracy to its deterministic aggregate and its cost advantage to its compactness. The fold's remaining value over cheaper alternatives is deterministic auditability and serving the observer from the same state. We derive eleven candidate requirements for trace folding from observed failures and delimit them with an order-sensitive task family on which the fold ceases to help. Code, benchmarks, a regenerable synthetic corpus, and all workbench traces are released.

</details>


### [247] [Harness-of-Harness: Multi-Day Autonomous Software Development with Continual Improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01481)
*Haoyang Yan,Min-le Su,Hangfan Zhang,Zhanhao Li,Chen Zhang,Shao Zhang,Yang Chen,Lei Bai,Shuyue Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Harness-of-Harness (HoH), a meta-framework that wraps existing LLM coding-agent harnesses in iterative plan-code-test loops to autonomously build and continually improve full software systems, yielding large performance gains over baseline harnesses and enabling long-horizon projects like a playable FPS game.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM coding agents and harnesses can generate code from high-level requirements, but they struggle with sustained, iterative software development: maintaining improvement across iterations, managing scope, separating testing and evaluation, reusing prior work, and handling long-horizon, multi-component systems. There is a need for a principled framework that lets existing harnesses coordinate planning, implementation, and testing over many iterations so that software can be autonomously refined and extended without human intervention.

Method: HoH is a meta-framework that wraps around existing coding-agent harnesses and organizes them into iterative planning–coding–testing loops. It: (1) balances bug repair with capability and feature growth across iterations; (2) decomposes development into small, verifiable increments; (3) separates implementation-time testing from independent evaluation to avoid overfitting; (4) constrains outputs via verifiable specs instead of prescribing internal workflows; (5) progressively unlocks deliverables, tools, and skills for different roles; (6) promotes reuse of existing artifacts instead of recreating them; and (7) maintains versioned project histories. The framework is evaluated on several benchmarks (GameCraft-Bench, FrontierSWE, ProgramBench) using three harness–model combinations, and in a long-running real-world style deployment building an FPS game over >70 iterations.

Result: Across GameCraft-Bench, FrontierSWE, and ProgramBench, the HoH framework consistently improves the performance of three different coding-agent harness/model pairs (Codex+GPT-5.5, OpenCode+DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Pi+MiniMax-M3), yielding on average a 52.25% relative improvement and up to 82.86% improvement after three iterations compared with the standalone harnesses. In a multi-day, >70-iteration deployment, HoH autonomously develops a full first-person shooter game with coherent story, complete core mechanics, polished visuals, integrated audio, and a human-playable experience, demonstrating its ability to handle complex, long-horizon software projects.

Conclusion: HoH demonstrates that treating coding-agent harnesses as components in an iterative, meta-level orchestration framework can substantially enhance autonomous software development. By structuring work into verifiable increments, carefully managing testing and evaluation, encouraging reuse, and tracking project history, HoH reliably improves upon existing harnesses across benchmarks and enables the autonomous creation of complex, production-like software systems such as a full FPS game. This suggests that meta-harness design and long-horizon orchestration are key levers for advancing LLM-based autonomous software engineering.

Abstract: This paper studies autonomous software development, in which LLM-based coding agents transform high-level requirements into complete, functional, and usable software systems without human intervention. We introduce Harness-of-Harness (HoH), a framework that enables coding agents to continually improve software during autonomous development. HoH operates on existing coding-agent harnesses, and organizes their executions into iterative planning-coding-testing loops. To sustain improvement across loops, HoH balances repair with capability growth, scopes development into small and verifiable increments, separates implementation-time testing from independent evaluation, and constrains verifiable outputs rather than prescribing agent workflows. It progressively exposes deliverables, role-specific tools, and skills, encourages reuse rather than recreation, and maintains versioned project histories. On GameCraft-Bench, FrontierSWE, and ProgramBench, three harness-model pairs (Codex with GPT-5.5, OpenCode with DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and Pi with MiniMax-M3), HoH consistently outperforms the corresponding standalone harnesses, achieving an average relative gain of 52.25 percent and a maximum gain of 82.86 percent after three iterations. In a multi-day deployment with more than 70 iterations, HoH autonomously develops a first-person-shooter game, featuring a coherent storyline, fully implemented core mechanics, human-playable experience, polished visuals and integrated audio. Github: https://github.com/Flesymeb/HarnessOfHarness Project Page: https://flesymeb.github.io/HarnessOfHarness/

</details>


### [248] [When Guardrails Look Effective: Construct Validity Failures in LLM Agent Commerce Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01519)
*Peiying Zhu,Sidi Chang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper audits whether simulated market experiments using language-model agents genuinely measure economic behavior like welfare or just produce numbers that look economic. It finds that earlier reported large welfare gains from marketplace guardrails are not robust once experimental confounds are removed and that apparent benefits are largely unidentified without stronger validity checks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As language models are used as agents in interactive economic simulations, researchers and practitioners are beginning to draw policy conclusions (e.g., the value of guardrails) from these experiments. However, it is unclear whether such simulations have construct validity: do they truly capture economic concepts like incentives, welfare, and strategic behavior, or are they artifacts of experimental setup, prompts, and randomness? The authors aim to diagnose and structure this risk.

Method: The authors build and audit a multi-turn buyer–seller testbed for configurable hotel transactions, where both sides are language-model agents. They replicate an initial setup that reported large welfare gains from two marketplace guardrails across different model sizes (Qwen2.5 1.5B–14B). They then systematically vary and hold constant key elements such as offer schemas and buyer choice procedures, run multiple generations per profile-condition, and examine how welfare estimates change. They also perform a seller-incentive check by varying profit pressure in prompts and design scripted positive control scenarios where the seller’s optimization objective is explicitly specified (profit-maximizing vs. forced inefficiency). Finally, they formalize a "construct-validity contract" that defines conditions like incentive validity, protocol isolation, stochastic stability, and welfare accounting, and use it to label results as INVALID or INCONCLUSIVE when these conditions fail.

Result: When they control for differences in offer schemas and buyer choice procedures, originally large welfare gains from guardrails shrink dramatically and sometimes reverse sign. Multi-generation runs show that single-run effects at 14B (+~229) drop to much smaller and statistically uncertain effects (+37.6 with a wide bootstrap interval crossing zero), with generation-level randomness explaining about half of the remaining variation. The seller-incentive manipulation behaves anomalously: stronger profit prompts do not monotonically increase profit and can underperform the default prompt. The positive-control experiments show that a truly profit-maximizing seller already achieves first-best welfare, so guardrails mainly reallocate or even reduce welfare, only increasing it when the seller is hard-coded to be inefficient. Applying their construct-validity contract, the authors judge the original guardrail welfare claims INVALID under protocol isolation and the new controlled estimates INCONCLUSIVE under incentive validity and stochastic stability.

Conclusion: Apparent welfare improvements and other economic-looking outcomes in LLM-based market simulations can be artifacts of protocol design, prompt choices, and stochastic variation rather than genuine economic behavior. Before drawing substantive policy conclusions (e.g., about the benefits of guardrails), simulations must satisfy a construct-validity contract, including incentive validity, protocol isolation, stochastic stability, and sound welfare accounting. In the studied case, these conditions are not met, so the earlier strong claims about guardrails’ welfare gains are unsupported; the work offers a methodological framework to prevent similar misinterpretations in future LLM-agent policy evaluations.

Abstract: Interactive simulations increasingly evaluate policies in markets populated by language-model agents. Their outputs can look economic---prices, profits, consumer surplus, and welfare---without instantiating the behavior named in the claim. We audit this risk in a multi-turn buyer--seller testbed for configurable hotel transactions. An initial implementation reported welfare gains from two marketplace guardrails of +87.4, +35.0, and +28.8 across a Qwen2.5 1.5B--14B ladder. It also gave guarded and unguarded agents different offer schemas and choice procedures. Holding the schema and buyer chooser fixed changes the paired contrasts to +7.2, -13.9, and +23.8. The four largest 14B single-generation effects averaged +229; after three generations per profile-condition, they averaged +37.6 (95% bootstrap interval [-34.2, 109.3]), while generation residuals account for 49.9% of variation in this post-hoc probe. A seller-incentive check is non-monotone: increasing profit pressure produces less profit than the default seller prompt. Scripted positive controls show why this matters. A profit-maximizing seller already attains first-best welfare, so guardrails mostly redistribute and reduce welfare; they create welfare only when the seller is explicitly programmed to force inefficient bundles. We contribute a construct-validity contract separating incentive validity, protocol isolation, stochastic stability, and welfare accounting, and returning INVALID or INCONCLUSIVE before substantive policy claims. In our case, the original estimate is INVALID under protocol isolation, while the controlled study remains INCONCLUSIVE under incentive validity and stochastic stability. The case does not show that guardrails are ineffective; it shows their apparent value is unidentified until the simulated agents and protocol pass these checks.

</details>


### [249] [EvoSCM: Scientific Belief Revision Through Causal Model Evolution and Experimentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01526)
*Qing Zhao,Haowei Li,Weijian Deng,Pengxu Wei,Liang Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EvoSCM is a framework that gives LLM-based scientific agents explicit, evolving structural causal models to improve hypothesis formation, experimentation, and prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM agents express scientific hypotheses only in free-form text, so their beliefs are implicit, hard to formalize, test, compare, or revise systematically. The authors want agents that behave more like scientists: maintaining explicit causal world-models that can be falsified, updated, and used to design informative experiments.

Method: They propose EvoSCM, which maintains a population of explicit structural causal model (SCM) hypotheses. In each closed-loop round, the agent: (1) performs abduction to infer latent mechanisms from past evidence; (2) designs discriminative interventions (experiments) that best distinguish between competing SCMs; (3) makes explicit, falsifiable predictions; (4) runs experiments and compares observations to predictions; (5) inductively distills prediction–observation discrepancies into correction rules to revise the causal structures and mechanisms of each SCM; and (6) deductively validates the revised SCM population against accumulated evidence and structural consistency before the next round.

Result: On the DiscoverPhysics benchmark, where agents must uncover hidden dynamics of unfamiliar physical worlds via experimentation, EvoSCM outperforms baseline agents. It produces more accurate causal explanations and predictions and extracts more information per experimental interaction, indicating more efficient scientific discovery.

Conclusion: Equipping LLM agents with explicit, evolving structural causal models, as done in EvoSCM, leads to better scientific reasoning and discovery than relying on implicit, text-only hypotheses. The closed abduction–intervention–revision–validation loop enables agents to systematically refine causal beliefs in response to new evidence.

Abstract: Scientific agents must learn not only how to reason, but also what to believe. However, existing LLM agents typically express scientific hypotheses in free-form text, leaving their beliefs implicit and difficult to test or revise. We introduce EvoSCM, which equips scientific agents with explicit structural causal models that evolve as new experimental evidence is collected. EvoSCM maintains a population of competing SCM hypotheses, each encoding a candidate causal explanation of the environment, and evolves them through a closed discovery loop. In each round, the agent abduces latent mechanisms from accumulated evidence, designs discriminative interventions, and commits to falsifiable predictions that it tests through experimentation. Discrepancies between prediction and observation are inductively distilled into correction rules that revise the causal structures and mechanisms of each hypothesis, and the agent then deductively validates the revised population against accumulated evidence and structural consistency to guide the next round. We evaluate EvoSCM on DiscoverPhysics, a benchmark requiring agents to uncover the hidden dynamics of noncanonical physical worlds through experimentation. EvoSCM consistently improves scientific discovery over baselines, yielding more accurate explanations and predictions while making more effective use of experimental interactions.

</details>


### [250] [Can LLMs Discover Scientific Laws in Real and Parallel Worlds?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01552)
*Yiming Huang,Ziche Liu,Zhuohang Wu,Yiqian Wang,Junxia Cui,Xinkai Zou,Linjun Mao,Nan Huang,Naicheng Yu,Kaijie Zhu,Yue Ma,Kun Zhou,Letian Peng,Jingbo Shang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce SCILAWS-BENCH, a benchmark to test whether LLMs can truly discover scientific laws from real data instead of synthetic or memorized examples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of LLMs for scientific equation discovery are limited because they often rely on synthetic problems or previously published equations that models may already have seen, making it unclear if models are genuinely discovering new laws or just recalling known ones.

Method: They construct a benchmark from 381 real scientific papers, resulting in 118 problems that cover 291 candidate laws and about 8 million real data points in six disciplines. For each problem, they define two settings: (1) SCILAWS-REAL, where models propose laws from fixed real observations and are evaluated on predictive fit and scientific validity according to the source literature; and (2) SCILAWS-PARALLEL, where models actively query a simulated world (residual-calibrated) to recover a hidden law synthesized from the published forms, allowing active discovery evaluation.

Result: Using this benchmark, they observe that good predictive fit does not always imply scientific validity, that LLM memorization affects whether models simply reproduce known formulas or generate novel ones, and that in a best-of-N evaluation, selecting the truly valid law among many candidates is a major bottleneck.

Conclusion: SCILAWS-BENCH offers a paper-grounded, realistic benchmark for evaluating LLMs' ability to discover scientific laws, and their empirical findings highlight key challenges such as separating memorization from discovery, aligning predictive performance with scientific correctness, and overcoming selection bottlenecks in AI-driven scientific discovery.

Abstract: Scientific equation discovery has long been central to scientific progress, proceeding through iterative cycles of hypothesis generation, observational testing, and refinement under scientific constraints. As LLM capabilities advance and their role in AI for Science expands, it remains an open problem whether they can genuinely discover scientific laws and how this ability should be evaluated. Existing evaluations, however, often either simplify discovery through synthetic settings or reuse published targets that may already be familiar to LLMs. We therefore introduce SCILAWS-BENCH, a benchmark for scientific law discovery built from published research and real scientific data. It comprises 118 problems drawn from 381 scientific papers, covering 291 candidate laws and roughly 8M real data points across six scientific disciplines. Each problem is instantiated in two complementary settings: (1) SCILAWS-REAL asks models to propose laws from fixed real observations and evaluates held-out predictive fit and scientific validity derived from the source literature, and (2) SCILAWS-PARALLEL asks models to actively query residual-calibrated worlds and recover synthesized hidden laws derived from published forms. This two-setting task design preserves each problem's scientific context while separately evaluating fixed-record law discovery and active recovery of a newly synthesized hidden law. We find that predictive fit can diverge from scientific validity, memorization shapes whether models reproduce or move beyond published formulas, and our best-of-N study reveals a selection bottleneck. Our work provides a paper-grounded benchmark and new empirical perspectives for evaluating AI for scientific discovery. Project page: https://yiyihum.github.io/SciLaws-Bench

</details>


### [251] [Selective Agent Guidance via Entropy: Learning Autonomous Policies from Imperfect VLM Teachers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01567)
*Matteo Merler,Giovanni Bonetta,Davide Zago,Rossella Cancelliere,Bernardo Magnini*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SAGE is a framework that selectively queries an expensive, imperfect Vision-Language Model during training when the RL agent is uncertain, then distills its (advantage-weighted) guidance into a cheap autonomous policy that no longer needs the VLM at test time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Directly using Vision-Language Models as interactive decision-making policies is computationally expensive, requires querying them at every step, cannot leverage environment interaction to improve, and tends to repeat their systematic errors. There is a need for a way to exploit VLM priors while training a cheaper, more robust policy that can act autonomously and potentially surpass the teacher.

Method: Introduce SAGE (Selective Agent Guidance via Entropy), which:
1) Trains a lightweight RL agent while having access to an online VLM teacher.
2) Uses the learner’s uncertainty (e.g., policy entropy) to decide when to query the VLM, reducing the number of expensive calls.
3) Executes the VLM-suggested action on those selected steps during training.
4) Distills the teacher’s suggestions into the student policy, but weights imitation by environment-derived advantages to down-weight unreliable teacher actions instead of treating all advice equally.
5) Produces a final policy that no longer requires VLM queries at evaluation time.

Result: On sparse-reward visual reasoning and navigation tasks, SAGE-trained policies operate without any VLM calls at evaluation and outperform unguided RL baselines in several environments. In some cases the learned policy even surpasses its VLM teacher. The approach substantially reduces VLM usage by querying only on a subset of training steps and completely eliminating VLM dependence during deployment. The study also reveals that selective guidance is particularly beneficial when VLM hints help discover high-reward trajectories, but less helpful when standard exploration already works or when teacher actions are not informative.

Conclusion: VLMs are most valuable as temporary, imperfect sources of guidance during training rather than as fixed deployed policies. By selectively querying them when the learner is uncertain and filtering their advice through advantage-weighted distillation, SAGE can internalize useful priors into an efficient RL policy that acts independently at test time, often outperforming both unguided RL and the original VLM teacher while using far fewer VLM calls.

Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) provide useful priors for interactive decision-making, but using them directly as policies is expensive and brittle: they must be queried at every step, do not improve from environment interaction, and can repeat systematic errors. We study how to learn a cheap autonomous policy from an online, expensive, and imperfect but informative VLM teacher. We propose SAGE (Selective Agent Guidance via Entropy), a framework that queries a VLM only when the learner is uncertain, executes the suggested action during training, and distills guidance into a lightweight Reinforcement Learning (RL) policy. Because VLM advice is not always reliable, SAGE can weight teacher-action distillation using environment-derived advantages rather than treating all suggestions as equally useful. Across sparse-reward visual reasoning and navigation tasks, SAGE learns policies that act without VLM guidance at evaluation time and improves over unguided RL in several environments, including settings where the learned policy exceeds its VLM teacher. The results show that selective guidance is most beneficial when the VLM can help the agent discover high-reward trajectories, and less useful when unguided exploration already succeeds or teacher actions do not lead to informative experience. SAGE also reduces VLM usage by prompting the teacher only on a fraction of training steps and requiring no VLM calls at deployment. Overall, our results suggest that VLMs don't need to be used as fixed policies to be useful; they can instead act as temporary, imperfect sources of guidance whose value is tested and internalized through interaction.

</details>
